knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function f:T\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} is a normal integrand if and only if (i) f(t,\cdot) is lower semicontinuous for every t\in T, and (ii) for every x\in\mathbb{R}^n there exists \varepsilon>0 such that, for every \delta\in(0,\varepsilon), the function t\mapsto\inf\{f(t,x'):x'\in\mathbb{B}(x,\delta)\} is measurable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of normality through measurable infima over standard families of subsets of the state space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:T\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} satisfy that f(t,\cdot) is lower semicontinuous for every t\in T, and define p_D(t):=\inf_{x\in D}f(t,x). knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is a normal integrand}\iff\forall D\in\mathcal D,\ p_D\text{ is measurable, for any listed testing collection }\mathcal D.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normality of the Pointwise-Argmin Indicator Integrand
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-integrand stability for the extended-valued indicator of pointwise minimizers over a fixed compact decision set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B\subset\mathbb{R}^p\) be compact and let \(g\) be a normal integrand on \(\Omega\times B\). Define
\[
g_0(x,a)=\begin{cases}
0,&g(x,a)=\min_{b\in B}g(x,b),\\
+\infty,&g(x,a)>\min_{b\in B}g(x,b).
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(g_0\) is a normal integrand on \(\Omega\times B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a normal integrand on a compact decision set, the extended-valued indicator of its pointwise minimizers is also a normal integrand.
assumptions_latex: g\text{ is a normal integrand on }\Omega\times B
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_0\text{ is a normal integrand on }\Omega\times B

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Measurability of subderivatives and subgradient mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized derivatives of a proper normal integrand evaluated along a measurable domain selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:T\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be a proper normal integrand and let \(x:T\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be measurable with \(x(t)\in D_f(t)\) for every \(t\in T\). Then \((t,w)\mapsto\widehat d f(t,x(t))(w)\) and \((t,w)\mapsto d f(t,x(t))(w)\) are normal integrands. The mappings \(t\mapsto\widehat\partial f(t,x(t))\), \(t\mapsto\partial f(t,x(t))\), and \(t\mapsto\partial^\infty f(t,x(t))\) are closed-valued and measurable, and \(t\mapsto\operatorname{gph}\partial f(t,\cdot)\) and \(t\mapsto\operatorname{gph}\partial^\infty f(t,\cdot)\) are measurable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper normal integrand and any measurable selection from its effective domains, the regular and limiting subderivatives are normal integrands. The regular, limiting, and horizon subgradient mappings are closed-valued and measurable, as are the graphs of the limiting and horizon subgradient mappings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat d f(\cdot,x(\cdot))(\cdot),\ d f(\cdot,x(\cdot))(\cdot)\text{ are normal integrands, and the stated subgradient and graph mappings are measurable with the subgradient mappings closed-valued}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lusin-type continuity characterizations of normal integrands
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of normality, near-continuity, near-lower-semicontinuity, and an almost-everywhere Borel representative over a Euclidean parameter space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let T\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d), let \mathcal A=\mathcal L(T), let \mu be d-dimensional Lebesgue measure restricted to \mathcal A, and let f:T\times\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R} have f(t,\cdot) lower semicontinuous for every t. Then f is a normal integrand if and only if any one of the following holds: (a) for every \varepsilon>0 there is a closed T_\varepsilon\subset T with \mu(T\setminus T_\varepsilon)<\varepsilon such that t\mapsto f(t,\cdot) is epi-continuous relative to T_\varepsilon; (b) for every \varepsilon>0 there is such a closed T_\varepsilon on which f is lower semicontinuous relative to T_\varepsilon\times\mathbb R^n; (c) there is a \mathcal B(T\times\mathbb R^n)-measurable g with g(t,\cdot) lower semicontinuous and f(t,\cdot)=g(t,\cdot) for every t in some T'\in\mathcal A satisfying \mu(T\setminus T')=0. If \mu(T)<\infty, the sets T_\varepsilon in (a) and (b) may be chosen compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Borel subset of Euclidean parameter space with completed Lebesgue measure, a fiberwise lsc function is normal exactly when it is epi-continuous, or jointly lsc, outside sets of arbitrarily small measure; equivalently, it agrees almost everywhere with a jointly Borel-measurable fiberwise lsc function. Under finite measure, the large closed sets may be chosen compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is normal}\iff\text{(a)}\iff\text{(b)}\iff\text{(c)},\quad \mu(T)<\infty\Rightarrow T_\varepsilon\text{ may be compact}.

children.title: Epigraphical Measurability
children.top_down_role: Normal-integrand structure represented through measurable epigraph mappings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Joint Measurability Does Not Imply Closed Epigraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the converse without lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(h(\omega,x)=\mathbf 1_{\{0\}}(x)\) on \(X=\mathbb R\) is jointly Borel measurable, but its state fiber is not lower semicontinuous at \(0\). Its epigraph is therefore not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint scalar measurability alone does not imply lower-semicontinuous fibers or closed epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{joint measurability}\centernot\Rightarrow\text{closed epigraphs}.
knowledge_statements.title: Joint Measurability Does Not Imply Closed Epigraphs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar measurability implied by measurable closed epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X\) is Polish and \(h:\Omega\times X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) has lower-semicontinuous fibers and a measurable epigraph mapping, then \(h\) is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normal integrand on a Polish state space is jointly measurable as an extended-real function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h:(\Omega\times X,\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(X))\to\overline{\mathbb R}\text{ is measurable}.
knowledge_statements.title: Joint Measurability of Normal Integrands

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Countable measurable representation of nonempty closed epigraph fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under Polish and nonempty closed-epigraph hypotheses, epigraphical measurability is equivalent to measurable maps \((x_n,r_n):\Omega\to X\times\mathbb R\) satisfying \(\operatorname{epi}h_\omega=\overline{\{(x_n(\omega),r_n(\omega)):n\ge1\}}\) for every \(\omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A measurable closed epigraph mapping admits a countable measurable dense family of epigraph points.
assumptions_latex: Every epigraph is nonempty and closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}h\text{ is measurable}\iff\operatorname{epi}h\text{ admits a Castaing representation}.
knowledge_statements.title: Castaing Representation of Measurable Epigraphs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent scalar tests for a nonempty closed epigraph mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be Polish and suppose every \(h_\omega\) is lower semicontinuous with nonempty epigraph. Then \(\omega\mapsto\operatorname{epi}h_\omega\) is Effros measurable if and only if \(\omega\mapsto d((x,r),\operatorname{epi}h_\omega)\) is measurable for every \((x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R\). It suffices to test a countable dense subset of \(X\times\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed epigraph measurability is equivalent to measurable distances to epigraphs, with countably many tests sufficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}h\text{ is measurable}\iff d(z,\operatorname{epi}h_\omega)\text{ is measurable in }\omega\ \forall z.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance Tests for Epigraphical Measurability

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\) is epigraphically measurable when \(\omega\mapsto\operatorname{epi}h_\omega\) is a closed-valued measurable multifunction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph-multifunction formulation of normal-integrand measurability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h:\Omega\times X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), write \(h_\omega(x):=h(\omega,x)\) and \[\operatorname{epi}h_\omega:=\{(x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R:h_\omega(x)\le r\}.\] The integrand is epigraphically measurable when the multifunction \(\omega\mapsto\operatorname{epi}h_\omega\) is Effros measurable. If every \(h_\omega\) is lower semicontinuous, these epigraphs are closed; the combination of closed epigraphs and epigraphical measurability is the normal-integrand condition in this setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrand is epigraphically measurable when its parameterized epigraph mapping is measurable; lower semicontinuous fibers make those epigraphs closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraphical Measurability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The epigraph-multifunction formulation fits the leaf and is appropriately classified as a definition. The precise convention connecting Effros-measurable epigraphs, lower semicontinuous fibers, and normal integrands requires a cited definition or theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes normality through measurable closed sublevel multifunctions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:T\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is a normal integrand if and only if, for every \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), the multifunction \(t\mapsto\operatorname{lev}_{\leq\alpha}f(t,\cdot)=\{x\mid f(t,x)\leq\alpha\}\) is closed-valued and measurable. Moreover, if \(\alpha:T\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is measurable, then \(t\mapsto\{x\mid f(t,x)\leq\alpha(t)\}\) is closed-valued and measurable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normality is equivalent to closed-valued measurability of every constant-threshold sublevel mapping; measurable variable thresholds also produce closed-valued measurable sublevel mappings.
assumptions_latex: \alpha:T\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\text{ is measurable for the variable-threshold conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is normal}\iff \bigl[t\mapsto\operatorname{lev}_{\leq\alpha}f(t,\cdot)\text{ is closed-valued and measurable for all }\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb{R}}\bigr].

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the sectional-to-joint measurability implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard implication from measurable parameter sections and continuous state sections to product measurability uses separable metrizability, or a comparable countability hypothesis, for the state space. The sectional assumptions alone do not provide that conclusion for arbitrary topological state spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The usual Carathéodory joint-measurability theorem depends on a countability hypothesis on the state space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{sectional measurability and continuity do not imply joint measurability in arbitrary topological spaces}.
knowledge_statements.title: Separability Boundary for Joint Measurability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion of finite-valued Carathéodory data in the normal-integrand class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a separable metric state space, a real-valued Carathéodory integrand is jointly measurable and has continuous, hence lower-semicontinuous, fibers. Its epigraph mapping is therefore closed-valued measurable, so it is a finite-valued normal integrand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued Carathéodory integrand on a separable metric state space is a normal integrand.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h\text{ is a finite-valued normal integrand}.
knowledge_statements.title: Carathéodory Integrands Are Normal

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Countable formulas for extrema of continuous state sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(D\subset X\) is countable and dense and \(h\) is Carathéodory, then \(\sup_{x\in X}h(\omega,x)=\sup_{x\in D}h(\omega,x)\) and \(\inf_{x\in X}h(\omega,x)=\inf_{x\in D}h(\omega,x)\). Consequently both extended-real extrema are measurable in \(\omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fiber extrema of a Carathéodory integrand can be computed on one countable dense state set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_Xh(\omega,\cdot)=\sup_Dh(\omega,\cdot),\quad\inf_Xh(\omega,\cdot)=\inf_Dh(\omega,\cdot).
knowledge_statements.title: Countable Dense-State Extremum Formulas

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation of a Carathéodory integrand along a measurable state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be separable metric, let \(h:\Omega\times X\to\mathbb R\) be Carathéodory, and let \(x:\Omega\to X\) be measurable. Then \(\omega\mapsto h(\omega,x(\omega))\) is measurable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluating a Carathéodory integrand along a measurable state gives a measurable scalar function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \omega\mapsto h(\omega,x(\omega))\text{ is measurable}.
knowledge_statements.title: Measurable Composition Theorem

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(h(\cdot,x)\) is measurable and each \(h(\omega,\cdot)\) is continuous; consequently \(h\) is jointly measurable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued Carathéodory condition on a separable metric state space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(h:\Omega\times X\to\mathbb R\) is a Carathéodory integrand when \(\omega\mapsto h(\omega,x)\) is \(\mathcal A\)-measurable for every \(x\in X\), and \(x\mapsto h(\omega,x)\) is continuous for every \(\omega\in\Omega\). If \(X\) is separable metric, these two sectional conditions imply that \(h\) is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(X)\). Its continuous fibers are lower semicontinuous, placing it within the finite-valued normal-integrand regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Carathéodory integrand is measurable in the parameter and continuous in the state; separability yields joint measurability.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Growth Characterization and Continuity of Nemytskii Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when a Carathéodory superposition operator maps \(L^p(E)\) into \(L^q(E)\), including automatic continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be bounded and measurable, let \(\varphi:E\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) satisfy the Carathéodory condition, and let \(1\le q\le p<\infty\). The Nemytskii operator \(\Phi(y)=\varphi(\cdot,y(\cdot))\) maps \(L^p(E)\) into \(L^q(E)\) if and only if there exist \(\alpha\in L^q(E)\) and \(\beta\in L^\infty(E)\) such that \(|\varphi(x,t)|\le \alpha(x)+\beta(x)|t|^{p/q}\) for almost every \(x\in E\) and every \(t\in\mathbb R\). If this mapping property holds, then \(\Phi:L^p(E)\to L^q(E)\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a bounded measurable set, a Carathéodory superposition operator maps Lp into Lq exactly when its generator satisfies an Lq-plus-L-infinity growth bound of order p/q. Such an operator is automatically continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi(L^p(E))\subset L^q(E)\iff \exists\alpha\in L^q(E),\ \beta\in L^\infty(E): |\varphi(x,t)|\le\alpha(x)+\beta(x)|t|^{p/q}\text{ a.e. in }x\text{ and for all }t;\text{ moreover, }\Phi\text{ is continuous}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fréchet Derivative of a Nemytskii Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiability from \(L^p(E)\) to \(L^q(E)\) under a mapping condition for the pointwise derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the preceding Carathéodory setting, let \(\Phi(y)=\varphi(\cdot,y(\cdot))\), let \(1\le q<p<\infty\), and set \(r=pq/(p-q)\). Suppose that \(\varphi_y(x,t)\) exists for almost every \(x\) and that the Nemytskii operator generated by \(\varphi_y\) maps \(L^p(E)\) into \(L^r(E)\). Then \(\Phi:L^p(E)\to L^q(E)\) is Fréchet differentiable, and for every \(y,h\in L^p(E)\), \((\Phi'(y)h)(x)=\varphi_y(x,y(x))h(x)\) for almost every \(x\in E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the pointwise derivative of the generator induces a map from Lp into Lr, where 1/r equals 1/q minus 1/p, the Nemytskii operator is Fréchet differentiable from Lp to Lq. Its derivative is pointwise multiplication by the generator's partial derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi:L^p(E)\to L^q(E)\text{ is Fréchet differentiable, and }(\Phi'(y)h)(x)=\varphi_y(x,y(x))h(x)\text{ a.e. for all }y,h\in L^p(E).\)

children.title: Extended-Valued Integrands
children.top_down_role: Integrands representing pointwise restrictions and singular costs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Well-definedness of indicator-augmented integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sums \((+\infty)+(-\infty)\) and \((-\infty)+(+\infty)\) are undefined in standard extended-real arithmetic. Thus \(g+\delta_C\) is automatically well-defined when \(g\) is real-valued or never takes \(-\infty\); a general extended-valued \(g\) requires an explicit compatibility convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Indicator augmentation must avoid indeterminate sums of positive and negative infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g>-\infty\Rightarrow g+\delta_C\text{ is well-defined}.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Real Arithmetic Compatibility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fiberwise admissible domain encoded by finite values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an extended-valued integrand \(h\), define \(D(\omega)=\operatorname{dom}h_\omega=\{x\in X:h(\omega,x)<+\infty\}\). Thus finite values identify the effective domain, while \(+\infty\) excludes states from it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective domain of each fiber is the state multifunction encoded by finite integrand values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D(\omega)=\{x:h(\omega,x)<+\infty\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Effective-Domain Multifunction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-semicontinuity failure for an open feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=(0,1)\subset\mathbb R\), the indicator \(\delta_C\) is not lower semicontinuous at \(0\) or \(1\). Hence measurability without fiberwise closedness does not make a constraint indicator normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of an open constraint set is not lower semicontinuous at its boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta_{(0,1)}\text{ is not a normal integrand}.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Constraints Yield Nonnormal Indicators

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between measurable closed constraints and normal indicator integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be Polish and let \(C:\Omega\rightrightarrows X\) have nonempty values. Then \(\delta_C(\omega,x)=0\) for \(x\in C(\omega)\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise is a normal integrand if and only if \(C\) is closed-valued and Effros measurable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty constraint multifunction has a normal indicator exactly when it is closed-valued and measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta_C\text{ is normal}\iff C\text{ is closed-valued and Effros measurable}.
knowledge_statements.title: Normality of Constraint Indicators

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise constraints are represented by \(h=g+\delta_C\), where \(\delta_C\) takes the values \(0\) and \(+\infty\).

notation.meaning: Indicator integrand of the constraint multifunction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint representation by an extended-valued indicator integrand, with a real-valued base integrand so the sum is well-defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An extended-valued integrand is a map \(h:\Omega\times X\to\overline{\mathbb R}:=\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}\). For a multifunction \(C:\Omega\rightrightarrows X\), define \[\delta_C(\omega,x):=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C(\omega),\\+\infty,&x\notin C(\omega).\end{cases}\] If \(g:\Omega\times X\to\mathbb R\) is real-valued, then minimizing \(g(\omega,x)\) subject to \(x\in C(\omega)\) is represented pointwise by minimizing \(h(\omega,x):=g(\omega,x)+\delta_C(\omega,x)\). The value \(+\infty\) excludes infeasible states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real indicator that is zero on feasible states and positive infinity elsewhere converts a pointwise constrained problem with a real-valued objective into an unconstrained extended-valued expression.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Valued Integrands

children.title: Convex Normal Integrands
children.top_down_role: Normal integrands with fiberwise convex structure and dual representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fiberwise primal-dual subgradient certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\omega,x,x^*\), \(h_\omega(x)+h_\omega^*(x^*)\ge\langle x^*,x\rangle\). Equality holds exactly when \(x^*\in\partial h_\omega(x)\), equivalently when \(x\in\partial h_\omega^*(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel–Young equality exactly certifies a primal-dual subgradient pair in each fiber.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h_\omega(x)+h_\omega^*(x^*)=\langle x^*,x\rangle\iff x^*\in\partial h_\omega(x)\iff x\in\partial h_\omega^*(x^*).
knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel–Young Equality Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fiberwise Fenchel conjugation in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be a convex normal integrand whose fibers are proper. Then its fiberwise conjugate \(h^*(\omega,x^*)=\sup_x\{\langle x^*,x\rangle-h(\omega,x)\}\) is also a convex normal integrand with proper fibers, and \(h^{**}=h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fiberwise Fenchel conjugation preserves proper convex normal integrands, and biconjugation recovers the original fibers.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is a finite-dimensional convex normal integrand.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h^*\text{ is a proper convex normal integrand and }h^{**}=h.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugacy Preserves Convex Normality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the usual conjugate and subgradient package without properness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(h_\omega\equiv+\infty\), then \(h_\omega^*\equiv-\infty\). If \(h_\omega\) takes the value \(-\infty\), then \(h_\omega^*\equiv+\infty\). Thus the usual proper conjugacy and subgradient statements require proper fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Improper fibers make Fenchel conjugacy degenerate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h_\omega\text{ improper}\Rightarrow\text{the proper Fenchel duality package may degenerate}.
knowledge_statements.title: Improper-Fiber Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric representation of fiberwise convex subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-dimensional proper convex normal integrand, the multifunction \((\omega,x)\mapsto\partial h_\omega(x)\) has closed convex values and a measurable graph in \(\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fiberwise convex subdifferentials form a closed-convex-valued multifunction with measurable graph.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is a proper convex normal integrand on \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{(\omega,x,x^*):x^*\in\partial h_\omega(x)\}\text{ is measurable}.
knowledge_statements.title: Measurable Subdifferential Graph

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\) is a convex normal integrand when its fibers are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and its epigraph mapping is measurable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional proper convex normal-integrand convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integrand \(h:\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is a convex normal integrand when each fiber \(h_\omega:=h(\omega,\cdot)\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and the multifunction \(\omega\mapsto\operatorname{epi}h_\omega\) is measurable. Its fiberwise Fenchel conjugate is defined by \[h_\omega^*(x^*):=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}\{\langle x^*,x\rangle-h_\omega(x)\}.\] The normal-integrand framework supplies the measurable structure needed to treat these convex fibers and their conjugates parametrically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex normal integrand has measurable epigraphs and proper lower-semicontinuous convex fibers, with conjugates defined pointwise by Fenchel duality.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Normal Integrands

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the leaf, and the record clearly states its finite-dimensional proper-fiber convention. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal-integrand preservation under suprema, infima, and finite sums
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure properties of normal integrands under countable lattice operations and finite nonnegative aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{f_j:T\times\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\}_{j\in J}\) be normal integrands. If \(J\) is countable, then \(\sup_{j\in J}f_j\) is a normal integrand. If \(J\) is countable, then \(\inf_{j\in J}f_j\) is a normal integrand whenever it is lower semicontinuous in \(x\); in general, \(\operatorname{cl}_x(\inf_{j\in J}f_j)\) is a normal integrand. If \(J\) is finite and \(\lambda_j\ge0\), then \(\sum_{j\in J}\lambda_jf_j\) is a normal integrand. Moreover, if \(f_j:T\times\mathbb R^{n_j}\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are normal integrands with proper fibers \(f_j(t,\cdot)\), then \(f(t,x_1,\ldots,x_r)=\sum_{j=1}^r f_j(t,x_j)\) is a normal integrand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Countable pointwise suprema of normal integrands remain normal. Countable pointwise infima remain normal when fiberwise lower semicontinuous, and their lower-semicontinuous regularizations are always normal. Finite nonnegative sums are normal, including separable sums over distinct variables when every fiber is proper.
assumptions_latex: f_j:T\times\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\text{ is a normal integrand for every }j\in J
J\text{ is countable for the supremum and infimum assertions}
x\mapsto\inf_{j\in J}f_j(t,x)\text{ is lsc for the unregularized infimum assertion}
J\text{ is finite and }\lambda_j\in\mathbb R_+\text{ for weighted sums}
f_j(t,\cdot)\text{ is proper for the separate-variable sum}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_j f_j,\quad \operatorname{cl}_x\!\left(\inf_j f_j\right),\quad \sum_j\lambda_jf_j,\quad\text{and the stated unregularized special cases are normal integrands.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers finite or countable families of inequality and equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X:T\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed-valued and measurable, let \(I_1,I_2\) be finite or countable, let \(f_i\) be a normal integrand for \(i\in I_1\) and a Carathéodory integrand for \(i\in I_2\), and let \(\alpha_i:T\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be measurable. Define \(C(t)=\{x\in X(t)\mid f_i(t,x)\leq\alpha_i(t)\ (i\in I_1),\ f_i(t,x)=\alpha_i(t)\ (i\in I_2)\}\). Then \(C\) is closed-valued and measurable. Consequently, \(A=\{t\mid C(t)\neq\varnothing\}\) is measurable, and there exists a measurable selection \(x:A\to\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(x(t)\in C(t)\) for every \(t\in A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite or countable system of normal-integrand inequalities and Carathéodory-integrand equalities over a measurable closed-valued base set defines a closed-valued measurable feasible-set mapping. Its nonemptiness set is measurable and admits a measurable feasible selection.

\alpha_i\text{ is measurable for every }i\in I_1\cup I_2

children.title: Lattice-Envelope Construction Calculus
children.top_down_role: Pointwise extremum and envelope constructions for integrands.

children.title: Lattice Extremum Operations
children.top_down_role: Pointwise supremum and infimum constructions for measurable integrands.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive convexity-preservation result for lattice suprema.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every \(f_i(t,\cdot)\) is convex, then \[x\mapsto\sup_{i\in I}f_i(t,x)\] is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrary pointwise supremum of convex sections is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{i\in I}f_i(t,\cdot)\text{ is convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Preservation Under Suprema

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph Calculus for Pointwise Lattice Extrema
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph formulas for arbitrary suprema and finite minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any family \((f_i)_{i\in I}\), \[\operatorname{epi}\Bigl(\sup_{i\in I}f_i\Bigr)=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{epi}f_i.\] For \(f_1,\ldots,f_k\), \[\operatorname{epi}\Bigl(\min_{1\leq i\leq k}f_i\Bigr)=\bigcup_{i=1}^k\operatorname{epi}f_i.\] Consequently arbitrary suprema and finite minima of lower-semicontinuous sections are lower-semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise suprema correspond to epigraph intersections, while finite minima correspond to finite epigraph unions.
assumptions_latex: The functions take values in \(\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}(\sup_i f_i)=\bigcap_i\operatorname{epi}f_i,\qquad \operatorname{epi}(\min_{i\leq k}f_i)=\bigcup_{i\leq k}\operatorname{epi}f_i.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Calculus for Pointwise Lattice Extrema

assumptions_latex: \((T,\mathcal A)\) is a measurable space and \(X=\mathbb R^d\).
Each \(f_n:T\times X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is jointly measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_n f_n\) and \(\inf_n f_n\) are jointly measurable; if every section is lower semicontinuous, then \(\sup_n f_n(t,\cdot)\) and every finite minimum are lower semicontinuous.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Countable pointwise lattice operations on extended-real measurable integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sequence \((f_n)_{n\geq1}\), define the lattice extrema pointwise by \[f^{\vee}(t,x)=\sup_{n\geq1}f_n(t,x),\qquad f^{\wedge}(t,x)=\inf_{n\geq1}f_n(t,x).\] Both functions are \((\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(X))\)-measurable. If every \(f_n(t,\cdot)\) is lower semicontinuous, then \(f^{\vee}(t,\cdot)\) is lower semicontinuous. A finite pointwise minimum of lower-semicontinuous sections is also lower semicontinuous, whereas a countably infinite minimum need not be.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Countable pointwise suprema and infima preserve measurability. Suprema and finite minima preserve lower semicontinuity, but countably infinite minima may not.
knowledge_statements.title: Lattice Extremum Operations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the leaf and is mathematically standard, but no inspectable citation supports the preservation and failure claims.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convexity preservation under pointwise minima.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Suprema preserve convexity, whereas even finite minima generally do not.
assumptions_latex: Each function in the supremum family is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_i f_i\text{ is convex, while finite infima need not be convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Boundary for Lattice Extrema

children.title: Measurable Envelope Constructions
children.top_down_role: Envelope constructions retaining measurable-integrand structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure-theoretic lower envelopes modulo almost-everywhere equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every family \(\{f_i:i\in I\}\subset L^0(S;\overline{\mathbb R})\), there is an essential infimum \(\ell\), unique almost everywhere, characterized by \(\ell\leq f_i\) almost everywhere for every \(i\) and maximality among measurable common lower bounds. Moreover, some countable \(I_0\subset I\) satisfies \[\ell=\inf_{i\in I_0}f_i\quad\text{almost everywhere}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every measurable family has an essential infimum represented almost everywhere by a countable subfamily.
assumptions_latex: \((S,\Sigma,\nu)\) is a complete finite measure space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{i\in I}f_i=\inf_{i\in I_0}f_i\quad\nu\text{-almost everywhere for some countable }I_0\subset I.
knowledge_statements.title: Essential Infimum and Countable Representation

assumptions_latex: \((S,\Sigma,\nu)\) is a complete finite measure space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a measurable essential supremum \(h\), unique almost everywhere, and some countable \(I_0\subset I\) satisfies \(h=\sup_{i\in I_0}f_i\) almost everywhere.

notation.meaning: Space of measurable extended-real functions modulo almost-everywhere equality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure-theoretic upper envelopes, including reduction to a countable subfamily.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The measurable upper envelope of the family is its essential supremum \[h=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{i\in I}f_i,\] characterized by \(h\geq f_i\) almost everywhere for every \(i\in I\), and by \(h\leq g\) almost everywhere for every measurable common upper bound \(g\). Moreover, there exists a countable subset \(I_0\subset I\) such that \[h=\sup_{i\in I_0}f_i\quad\nu\text{-almost everywhere}.\] Thus an arbitrarily indexed measurable envelope has a countable measurable representative modulo null sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every family of measurable extended-real functions on a complete finite measure space has an essential supremum represented almost everywhere by a countable subfamily.
knowledge_statements.title: Measurable Envelope Constructions

children.title: Operation Preservation Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Minima Need Not Preserve Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp convexity boundary for lattice minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The functions \(f_1(x)=(x-1)^2\) and \(f_2(x)=(x+1)^2\) are convex, but \[h(x)=\min\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\}\] is not convex; indeed \(h(-1)=h(1)=0\) while \(h(0)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even the minimum of two finite continuous convex functions can fail to be convex.
assumptions_latex: The functions are defined on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_1,f_2\text{ are convex but }\min\{f_1,f_2\}\text{ is not convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Minima Need Not Preserve Convexity

assumptions_latex: Measurability is understood with respect to the stated Borel or Lebesgue sigma-fields.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uncountable suprema can destroy measurability, and countable infima can destroy lower semicontinuity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failures beyond countable measurability and finite lower-semicontinuous minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\subset\mathbb R\) be non-Lebesgue-measurable. Every singleton indicator \(\mathbf 1_{\{a\}}\) is measurable, but \[\sup_{a\in A}\mathbf 1_{\{a\}}=\mathbf 1_A\] is not measurable. Separately, each \(f_n=\delta_{\{1/n\}}\) is lower semicontinuous, while \[\inf_{n\geq1}f_n=\delta_{\{1/n:n\geq1\}}\] is not lower semicontinuous because its zero set is not closed. Hence arbitrary lattice operations require countability, closure, or measurable-envelope hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An uncountable supremum of measurable functions may be nonmeasurable, while a countable infimum of lower-semicontinuous functions may lose lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.title: Operation Preservation Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition associated with an optimal-control dynamics map and running cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \((t,y,\eta)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n\), define
\[
g(t,y,\eta)=\min\{f(t,y,\omega):(t,y,\omega)\in E,\ \varphi(t,y,\omega)=\eta\}.
\]
Thus \(g(t,y,\eta)\in\mathbb{R}_+\) when \(\eta\in\Gamma_{t,y}\), and \(g(t,y,\eta)=+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reduced cost at a time, state, and prescribed velocity is the minimum running cost among feasible controls producing that velocity. It is nonnegative on the admissible-speed set and equals positive infinity outside that set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(t,y,\eta)=\min\{f(t,y,\omega):(t,y,\omega)\in E,\ \varphi(t,y,\omega)=\eta\},\quad g\in\mathbb{R}_+\text{ on }\Gamma_{t,y},\quad g=+\infty\text{ off }\Gamma_{t,y}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation of normal-integrand structure under variable elimination and lower-semicontinuous regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:T\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be a normal integrand and define \(p(t,u)=\inf_x f(t,x,u)\). If \(u\mapsto p(t,u)\) is lower semicontinuous for every \(t\)—in particular, if \(f(t,x,u)\) is level-bounded in \(x\) locally uniformly in \(u\) for every \(t\)—then \(p\) is a normal integrand. Without this assumption, \(\bar p(t,u)=\operatorname{cl}_u p(t,u)\) is always a normal integrand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimum of a normal integrand over an eliminated variable is normal when the resulting fibers are lower semicontinuous; local-uniform level-boundedness in the eliminated variable is sufficient. In all cases, lower-semicontinuous regularization in the retained variable is normal.

u\mapsto p(t,u)\text{ is lsc for every }t\text{ for the unregularized conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\text{ is a normal integrand under the lsc hypothesis, and }\operatorname{cl}_u p\text{ is always a normal integrand.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence under convexity of the reduced cost integrand
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The preceding hypotheses of the optimal-control problem remain in force.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume the preceding hypotheses. If, for every \((t,y)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^n\), the function \(\eta\mapsto g(t,y,\eta)\) is convex on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with values in \(\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), then there exists at least one admissible optimal control. Equivalently, for each \((t,y)\), the set
\[
\{(\eta,a)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:\exists\omega\in E_{t,y},\ \varphi(t,y,\omega)=\eta,\ a\ge f(t,y,\omega)\}
\]
is convex. Its horizontal projection \(\Gamma_{t,y}\), the set of admissible velocities, is consequently convex and compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the preceding optimal-control hypotheses, pointwise convexity in velocity of the reduced cost guarantees existence of an admissible optimal control. This convexity is equivalent to convexity of the feasible velocity-cost epigraph; its projection, the admissible-speed set, is convex and compact.
assumptions_latex: \text{The preceding hypotheses of the optimal-control problem hold.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ at least one admissible optimal control};\qquad \Gamma_{t,y}\text{ is convex and compact for every }(t,y).

children.title: Integrand Composition
children.top_down_role: Integrands formed through measurable or continuous transformations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fiberwise convexity and properness under affine inner composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f(t,\cdot)\) is convex and \(\Phi(t,x)=A(t)x+b(t)\), then \(g(t,x)=f(t,\Phi(t,x))\) is convex in \(x\). If \(f(t,\cdot)\) is proper, then \(g(t,\cdot)\) is proper if and only if \(\operatorname{range}\Phi(t,\cdot)\cap\operatorname{dom}f(t,\cdot)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine inner composition preserves fiberwise convexity; properness additionally requires the affine range to meet the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(t,\cdot)=f(t,\Phi(t,\cdot))\) is convex, with the stated properness criterion.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Under Affine Integrand Composition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact fiberwise epigraph representation of composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g(t,x)=f(t,\Phi(t,x))\), \[\operatorname{epi}g_t=\{(x,r):(\Phi(t,x),r)\in\operatorname{epi}f_t\}=\Psi_t^{-1}(\operatorname{epi}f_t),\qquad \Psi_t(x,r)=(\Phi(t,x),r).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of a composed integrand is the inverse image of the original epigraph under the lifted inner mapping.
assumptions_latex: \(f_t:\mathbb R^m\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(\Phi_t:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^m\) are arbitrary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}g_t=\Psi_t^{-1}(\operatorname{epi}f_t)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraphical Pullback Representation

assumptions_latex: \(f:T\times\mathbb R^m\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is a normal integrand.
\(\Phi:T\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^m\) is measurable in \(t\) and continuous in \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The composition \(g(t,x)=f(t,\Phi(t,x))\) is a normal integrand.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition with a measurable-in-parameter, continuous-in-decision transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[g(t,x)=f\bigl(t,\Phi(t,x)\bigr).\] The map \((t,x)\mapsto(t,\Phi(t,x))\) is measurable, so \(g\) is jointly measurable. For every fixed \(t\), continuity of \(\Phi(t,\cdot)\) and lower semicontinuity of \(f(t,\cdot)\) imply that \(g(t,\cdot)\) is lower semicontinuous. Consequently \(g\) is a normal integrand on \(T\times\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composing a normal integrand with a Carathéodory transformation preserves joint measurability and lower semicontinuity, hence normality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The preservation property matches integrand composition, but the joint-measurability and normal-integrand conclusion lacks a cited theorem and precise locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normality under Carathéodory substitution, monotone scalar composition, and measurable parameter substitution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Each of the following defines a normal integrand: (i) \(f(t,x)=g(t,F(t,x))\) when \(g:T\times\mathbb R^m\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is a normal integrand and \(F:T\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is Carathéodory; (ii) \(f(t,x)=\theta(t,g(t,x))\) when \(g:T\times\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(\theta:T\times\mathbb R\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are normal integrands, \(\theta(t,\alpha)\) is nondecreasing in \(\alpha\), and \(\theta(t,\infty)=\sup_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\theta(t,\alpha)\), \(\theta(t,-\infty)=\inf_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\theta(t,\alpha)\); (iii) \(f(t,x)=g(t,x,u(t))\) when \(g:T\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is a normal integrand and \(u:T\to\mathbb R^m\) is measurable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal integrands remain normal after composition with a Carathéodory state mapping, after a fiberwise nondecreasing normal-integrand scalar transformation using the stated extended-value conventions, and after substituting a measurable parameter.
assumptions_latex: g\text{ is a normal integrand in each of the three constructions}
F:T\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\text{ is Carathéodory in case (i)}
\theta:T\times\mathbb R\to\overline{\mathbb R}\text{ is a normal integrand and is nondecreasing in its scalar argument in case (ii)}
u:T\to\mathbb R^m\text{ is measurable in case (iii)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is a normal integrand in each stated composition construction.}

children.title: Variable Marginalization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fiberwise convexity and properness under partial minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \((x,y)\mapsto f(t,x,y)\) is convex, then \(x\mapsto g(t,x)=\inf_y f(t,x,y)\) is convex, possibly taking the value \(-\infty\). If \(g_t(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\) and \(\operatorname{dom}g_t\neq\varnothing\), then \(g_t\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial minimization preserves convexity, while properness requires exclusion of minus infinity and a nonempty effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(t,\cdot)\) is convex, with properness under the stated additional conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal Epigraph as an Existential Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection formula and its attainment boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g(t,x)=\inf_y f(t,x,y)\), let \(P_t=\operatorname{proj}_{x,r}(\operatorname{epi}f_t)\). Always \(P_t\subseteq\operatorname{epi}g_t\). Equality holds if every finite value \(g(t,x)\) is attained; without attainment, \(\operatorname{epi}g_t\) may contain boundary points absent from \(P_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A marginal epigraph is the projection of the original epigraph when finite minima are attained; otherwise the projection can miss boundary points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_t\subseteq\operatorname{epi}g_t\), with equality under attainment of finite marginal values.

assumptions_latex: \((T,\mathcal A,\mu)\) is complete and sigma-finite, and \(f:T\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is a normal integrand.
For every \(t\), bounded \(x\)-sets and finite levels, the corresponding feasible \(y\)-level sets are bounded.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional inf-projection under local uniform level-boundedness in the eliminated variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[g(t,x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb R^m}f(t,x,y),\qquad M(t,x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb R^m}f(t,x,y).\] If \(f\) is locally uniformly level-bounded in \(y\) with respect to \(x\), then every section \(g(t,\cdot)\) is lower semicontinuous, and \(M(t,x)\) is nonempty and compact whenever \(g(t,x)\) is finite. On the completed sigma-field, the measurable inf-projection theorem makes \(g\) measurable; hence \(g\) is a normal integrand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normal integrand remains normal after minimizing out a variable when its level sets are locally uniformly bounded in that variable; finite minima are attained.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[g(x)=\inf\{f(y):Ay=x\}.\] Then, as an extended-real identity, \[g^*(x^*)=f^*(A^*x^*).\]

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The image-value function \(g(t,x)=\inf\{f(t,y):A(t)y=x\}\) is a normal integrand and has closed epigraphical images.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The image-based integrand is represented by \[g(t,x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb R^m}\bigl\{f(t,y)+\delta_{\{x\}}(A(t)y)\bigr\}=\inf\{f(t,y):A(t)y=x\}.\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{epi}g_t=\{(A(t)y,r):(y,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f_t\}.\] Under the stated constrained level-boundedness, this epigraphical image is closed, the infimum is attained whenever finite, and measurable marginalization yields a normal integrand \(g\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Decreasing Continuous Sections Can Lose Normality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp pointwise-limit failure for lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R\), let \[f_n(x)=\max\{0,1-n|x|\}.\] Then every \(f_n\) is continuous and \(f_n\downarrow\mathbf 1_{\{0\}}\) pointwise, but the limit is not lower-semicontinuous at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decreasing sequence of continuous sections can converge to an upward spike that is not lower-semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_n\downarrow\mathbf 1_{\{0\}},\quad \mathbf 1_{\{0\}}\text{ is not lower-semicontinuous}.
knowledge_statements.title: Decreasing Continuous Sections Can Lose Normality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Limits and the Lower-Semicontinuity Threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinction between measurable pointwise limits and normal-integrand limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For jointly measurable \(f_n:T\times\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), \(\liminf_n f_n\) and \(\limsup_n f_n\) are jointly measurable. If every section is lower-semicontinuous and \(f_n\uparrow f\), then \(f=\sup_n f_n\) is lower-semicontinuous sectionwise and hence is a normal integrand. A decreasing pointwise limit need not be lower-semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise lower and upper limits preserve measurability, while increasing—but not decreasing—limits of lower-semicontinuous sections automatically preserve normality.
assumptions_latex: For the normality conclusion, each \(f_n(t,\cdot)\) is lower-semicontinuous and \(f_n\uparrow f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \liminf_n f_n\text{ and }\limsup_n f_n\text{ are measurable, and }f_n\uparrow f\Longrightarrow f\text{ is a normal integrand}.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Limits and the Lower-Semicontinuity Threshold

assumptions_latex: \((T,\mathcal A,\mu)\) is complete and sigma-finite, and \(X=\mathbb R^d\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The epigraphical lower and upper limits are normal integrands; when equal, their common value is the measurable epi-limit.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential epigraphical limits of finite-dimensional normal integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\bigl(\operatorname{e\!\!-\!liminf}_{n}f_n\bigr)(t,x)=\sup_{\rho>0}\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{y\in B_\rho(x)}f_n(t,y),\] \[\bigl(\operatorname{e\!\!-\!limsup}_{n}f_n\bigr)(t,x)=\sup_{\rho>0}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\inf_{y\in B_\rho(x)}f_n(t,y).\] On the completed sigma-field these functions are measurable, and their sections are lower semicontinuous; hence they are normal integrands. If the two expressions coincide, their common value is the epi-limit of \((f_n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epigraphical lower and upper limits of a sequence of normal integrands remain measurable and lower semicontinuous; equality defines the measurable epi-limit.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure under replacement on measurable finite-measure sets by bounded measurable functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A space \(\mathcal X\) of measurable functions \(x:T\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is decomposable relative to a measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathcal A\) if, for every \(x_0\in\mathcal X\), every \(A\in\mathcal A\) with \(\mu(A)<\infty\), and every bounded measurable \(x_1:A\to\mathbb{R}^n\), the function \(x:T\to\mathbb{R}^n\) defined by \(x=x_1\) on \(A\) and \(x=x_0\) on \(T\setminus A\) belongs to \(\mathcal X\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interchange of Supremum and Integration over Measurable Selections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Carathéodory integrands optimized over measurable closed-valued pointwise constraints and essentially bounded selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) be open. Let \(\varphi:\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be measurable in \(x\) for every fixed \(p\) and continuous in \(p\) for every fixed \(x\). Let \(P:\Omega\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) be measurable and closed-valued, and define \[\Sigma:=\left\{p\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^n):p(x)\in P(x)\text{ a.e. and }\int_\Omega\varphi(x,p(x))\,dx\text{ is well defined in }\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\right\}.\] If \(\Sigma\neq\varnothing\), then \(\int_\Omega\sup_{q\in P(x)}\varphi(x,q)\,dx\) is well defined in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), and \[\int_\Omega\sup_{q\in P(x)}\varphi(x,q)\,dx=\sup_{p(\cdot)\in\Sigma}\int_\Omega\varphi(x,p(x))\,dx,\] where both sides may equal \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated integrand and measurable closed-valued pointwise constraint, if at least one admissible essentially bounded selection has a well-defined integral, then the integral of the pointwise supremum equals the supremum of the integrals over all such selections; both sides may be positive infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \int_\Omega\sup_{q\in P(x)}\varphi(x,q)\,dx=\sup_{p(\cdot)\in\Sigma}\int_\Omega\varphi(x,p(x))\,dx\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be the set of measurable real-valued functions having finite range. Then \(D\) is closed under binary, hence finite, measurable pasting. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the measurable pasting by \[(u\oplus_Av)(t)=\begin{cases}u(t),&t\in A,\\v(t),&t\notin A.\end{cases}\] Then \(u\oplus_Av\) is strongly measurable. A set \(D\) of measurable functions is decomposable precisely when \(u,v\in D\) and \(A\in\mathcal A\) imply \(u\oplus_Av\in D\). For every measurable integrand \(f\), whenever the extended integrals are well defined, \[\int_T f(t,(u\oplus_Av)(t))\,d\mu=\int_A f(t,u(t))\,d\mu+\int_{T\setminus A}f(t,v(t))\,d\mu.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pasting two measurable decisions on complementary measurable sets preserves measurability; decomposable spaces are exactly those closed under this localization operation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral vectors attained by arbitrary measurable decisions on the Lebesgue interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $S\subseteq\mathbb R$ be Lebesgue measurable, and for $i=1,\ldots,m$ let $F_i:S\times[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be Lebesgue integrable. Then $X=\{\psi(x):x\in\Gamma\}$ is convex in $\mathbb R^m$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The set of finite-dimensional integral vectors attainable by measurable decisions taking values in a measurable subset of the real line is convex.

children.top_down_role: Measure-space distinctions affecting localization, selection, and convexification.

children.title: Atomic Measure-Space Regimes
children.top_down_role: Localization and selection behavior on measure spaces with atoms.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral functionals reduce to coordinate sums on countably atomic spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\Omega=\bigsqcup_{k\geq1}A_k\) modulo null sets, where each \(A_k\) is a finite-measure atom, and let \(u=x_k\) almost everywhere on \(A_k\). Whenever the extended sum is defined, \[\int_\Omega f(\omega,u(\omega))\,d\mu=\sum_{k\geq1}\int_{A_k}f(\omega,x_k)\,d\mu.\] If \(f(\omega,x)=\phi_k(x)\) almost everywhere on \(A_k\), this becomes \(\sum_k\mu(A_k)\phi_k(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a countably atomic space, a measurable decision is represented by atomic coordinates and its integral functional by a coordinate sum.
assumptions_latex: The space is covered modulo null sets by countably many finite-measure atoms \(A_k\).
The decision has essential value \(x_k\) on each atom.
The resulting extended series is defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The integral decomposes into the displayed sum over atoms.
knowledge_statements.title: Countable Atomic Integral Representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurable maps cannot vary essentially inside a finite-measure atom when the range is separable metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a \(\mu\)-atom with \(0<\mu(A)<\infty\), and let \(X\) be a separable metric space. Every Borel-measurable map \(u:A\to X\) is equal almost everywhere on \(A\) to a constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable-metric-valued measurable decision is essentially constant on each finite-measure atom.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x_A\in X\) such that \(u=x_A\) almost everywhere on \(A\).

notation.meaning: Essential value of u on atom A

knowledge_statements.title: Essential Constancy on an Atom

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The measure space is purely atomic precisely when every measurable set of positive measure contains a \(\mu\)-atom.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard measure-theoretic notion of pure atomicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(A\in\Sigma\) is a \(\mu\)-atom if \(\mu(A)>0\) and every \(B\in\Sigma\) with \(B\subseteq A\) satisfies \(\mu(B)=0\) or \(\mu(A\setminus B)=0\). The measure space \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) is purely atomic if every \(E\in\Sigma\) with \(\mu(E)>0\) contains a \(\mu\)-atom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atomic regime is one in which every positive-measure event contains an indivisible positive-measure event.

children.title: Nonatomic Measure-Space Regimes
children.top_down_role: Localization, selection, and convexification behavior without atoms.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational localization consequence of finite nonatomicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mu\) is finite and nonatomic, then for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a finite measurable partition \(\Omega=A_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup A_m\) such that \(\mu(A_i)\leq\varepsilon\) for every \(i\). More generally, every finite list of nonnegative numbers summing to \(\mu(E)\) is realized by a measurable partition of \(E\) with those cell measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite nonatomic space admits partitions into arbitrarily small pieces and partitions with prescribed finite cell measures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite measurable partitions with arbitrarily small or prescribed cell measures exist.
knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrarily Fine Measurable Partitions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Divisibility of Nonatomic Finite Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact prescribed-measure divisibility on a finite nonatomic measure space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mu\) is finite and nonatomic, then for every \(E\in\Sigma\) and every \(\alpha\in[0,\mu(E)]\), there exists \(B\in\Sigma\), \(B\subseteq E\), such that \(\mu(B)=\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every measurable set in a finite nonatomic space contains measurable subsets of every prescribed intermediate measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists B\in\Sigma\) with \(B\subseteq E\) and \(\mu(B)=\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Divisibility of Nonatomic Finite Measures

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The space is nonatomic exactly when each positive-measure set has a measurable subset of strictly intermediate measure.

No supplied locator directly supports this definition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States nonatomicity through measurable divisibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The measure space \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) is nonatomic if it has no \(\mu\)-atoms. Equivalently, for every \(E\in\Sigma\) with \(0<\mu(E)<\infty\), there exists \(B\in\Sigma\), \(B\subset E\), such that \(0<\mu(B)<\mu(E)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonatomic regime allows every finite positive-measure event to be split into two positive-measure parts.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonatomic Measure-Space Regimes

children.title: Mixed Measure-Space Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structures combining atomic and nonatomic components.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Only the atomic component can retain finite-dimensional nonconvex selection effects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the finite-dimensional Aumann convexification hypotheses on \(\Omega_n\), \[\int_{\Omega_n}F\,d\mu=\int_{\Omega_n}\operatorname{co}F\,d\mu.\] Consequently, \[\int_\Omega F\,d\mu=\int_{\Omega_a}F\,d\mu+\int_{\Omega_n}\operatorname{co}F\,d\mu,\] and any gap between \(\int_\Omega F\,d\mu\) and \(\int_0mega\operatorname{co}F\,d\mu\) is generated by the atomic component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a mixed space, finite-dimensional integration convexifies the nonatomic component, while any remaining convexification gap comes from the atoms.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^d\) satisfies the measurable, nonempty closed-valued, integrably bounded Aumann hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finite-dimensional convexification gap is localized to \(\Omega_a\).
knowledge_statements.title: Localization of the Convexification Gap

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral Splitting Across Atomic and Nonatomic Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive decomposition of scalar and Aumann integrals over the mixed-space partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an atomic–nonatomic decomposition \(\Omega=\Omega_a\sqcup\Omega_n\) modulo null sets and any integrable scalar function \(h\), \[\int_\Omega h\,d\mu=\int_{\Omega_a}h\,d\mu+\int_{\Omega_n}h\,d\mu.\] If \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^d\) is measurable with nonempty closed values and an integrable bound, then \[\int_\Omega F\,d\mu=\int_{\Omega_a}F\,d\mu+\int_{\Omega_n}F\,d\mu,\] where the last addition is Minkowski addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrals on a mixed space split into atomic and nonatomic contributions; Aumann integrals split by Minkowski addition.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega_a,\Omega_n\) form the atomic–nonatomic decomposition modulo null sets.
\(h\) is integrable, or \(F\) is measurable with nonempty closed values and an integrable bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scalar and Aumann integrals split over \(\Omega_a\) and \(\Omega_n\).

notation.meaning: Minkowski addition in the set-valued formula

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Splitting Across Atomic and Nonatomic Components

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Up to null sets, \(\Omega\) decomposes into a purely atomic component and a nonatomic component.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard atomic–nonatomic decomposition for sigma-finite measure spaces
A directly supporting decomposition theorem and locator are still required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The decomposition is understood modulo measurable null sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist disjoint measurable sets \(\Omega_a,\Omega_n\in\Sigma\) such that \(\mu\bigl(\Omega\setminus(\Omega_a\cup\Omega_n)\bigr)=0\), the restricted space \((\Omega_a,\Sigma|_{\Omega_a},\mu|_{\Omega_a})\) is purely atomic, and \((\Omega_n,\Sigma|_{\Omega_n},\mu|_{\Omega_n})\) is nonatomic. This decomposition is unique modulo \(\mu\)-null sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sigma-finite mixed space splits, modulo null sets, into uniquely determined atomic and nonatomic components.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Measure-Space Regimes

children.title: Convexification Regime Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dependence of convexification effects on the measure-space decomposition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary nonatomicity does not ensure convex vector-measure ranges in infinite-dimensional Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On Lebesgue \([0,1]\), define the \(L^1([0,1])\)-valued vector measure \(m(A)=\mathbf1_A\). It is countably additive and absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, but its range \(\{\mathbf1_A:A\in\Sigma\}\) is not convex; for example, \(\tfrac12\mathbf1_{[0,1]}\) is not in the range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonatomic measure can have a nonconvex vector-measure range when the range space is infinite dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ordinary nonatomicity alone does not extend Lyapunov convexity to arbitrary infinite-dimensional ranges.
knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Dimensional Lyapunov Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convexification of integrals of measurable selections on a finite nonatomic space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a complete finite nonatomic measure space, and let \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^d\) be measurable with nonempty closed values and an integrable bound. Then its Aumann integral is convex and \[\int_\Omega F(\omega)\,d\mu=\int_\Omega\operatorname{co}F(\omega)\,d\mu.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonatomic integration exactly convexifies integrably bounded finite-dimensional measurable multifunctions.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^d\) is measurable and has nonempty closed values.
There is \(g\in L^1(\mu)\) with \(\sup_{x\in F(\omega)}\|x\|\leq g(\omega)\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\int F\,d\mu\) is convex and equals \(\int\operatorname{co}F\,d\mu\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Aumann Convexification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-measure form of the finite-dimensional nonatomic convexification principle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mu\) is finite and nonatomic and \(m:\Sigma\to\mathbb R^d\) is a finite countably additive vector measure with \(m\ll\mu\), then \(\{m(A):A\in\Sigma\}\) is compact and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The range of a finite-dimensional vector measure absolutely continuous with respect to a finite nonatomic measure is compact and convex.
assumptions_latex: \(m:\Sigma\to\mathbb R^d\) is finite, countably additive, and absolutely continuous with respect to \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{m(A):A\in\Sigma\}\) is compact and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Lyapunov Convexity

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) is a finite nonatomic measure space.
\(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^d\) is measurable, nonempty-valued, and integrably bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Aumann integral satisfies \(\int F\,d\mu=\int \operatorname{co}F\,d\mu\) and is convex; this can fail on an atom.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-dimensional Aumann–Lyapunov convexification principle and its atomic counterexample
An authoritative theorem locator is required for the precise hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convexification boundary for integrals of measurable selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mu\) is nonatomic, then the Aumann integral of \(F\) is convex and obeys \[\int_\Omega F(\omega)\,d\mu=\int_\Omega \operatorname{co}F(\omega)\,d\mu.\] Nonatomicity is essential: if \(\Omega=A\) is a single atom and \(F(\omega)=\{0,1\}\), then \(\int_A F\,d\mu=\{0,\mu(A)\}\), whereas \(\int_A\operatorname{co}F\,d\mu=[0,\mu(A)]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonatomic integration convexifies finite-dimensional selections; a single atom can preserve nonconvexity and destroy the convexification identity.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexification Regime Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and finite-dimensional atomic counterexample fit the leaf, but the convexity and convexification theorem needs an authoritative locator supporting its exact measurability and boundedness hypotheses.

children.title: Range-Space Measurability Regimes
children.top_down_role: Separability and related range-space conditions governing measurable representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of weak-to-strong measurability in a nonseparable Hilbert range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I=[0,1]\) with completed Lebesgue measure, let \(X=\ell^2(I)\), and define \(f(t)=e_t\). Then \(x^*\circ f\) is measurable for every \(x^*\in X^*\), but \(f\) is not essentially separably valued and therefore is not strongly measurable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The uncountable coordinate-vector map into a nonseparable Hilbert space is weakly measurable but not strongly measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak measurability does not imply strong measurability without essential separability.

notation.meaning: Coordinate unit vector indexed by t

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separable Reduction for Strongly Measurable Decisions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Every strongly measurable Banach-valued decision lives almost surely in a separable closed subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:\Omega\to X\) is strongly measurable, then there exists a separable closed subspace \(X_0\subseteq X\) such that \(f(\omega)\in X_0\) for almost every \(\omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong measurability always yields an essentially separable closed range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\omega)\in X_0\) almost everywhere for some separable closed \(X_0\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.title: Separable Reduction for Strongly Measurable Decisions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: In a separable Banach range, essential separability in Pettis measurability is automatic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a separable Banach space. A map \(f:\Omega\to X\) is strongly measurable if and only if \(x^*\circ f\) is measurable for every \(x^*\in X^*\), with measurability understood on the completed measure space when necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For separable Banach ranges, weak and strong measurability coincide.
assumptions_latex: The measure space is complete, or measurability is interpreted after completion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is strongly measurable}\iff x^*\circ f\text{ is measurable for every }x^*\in X^*.
knowledge_statements.title: Separable-Range Simplification

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(f:\Omega\to X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \(f\) is strongly measurable exactly when it is weakly measurable and essentially separably valued.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integrable Lipschitz domination of directional support integrands
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verification that directional support functions associated with pointwise generalized gradients satisfy the measurability and Lipschitz hypotheses needed for an integral-functional result.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \widehat f_t(v):=f_t^\circ(x(t);v)=\sigma_{\partial f_t(x(t))}(v). Suppose t\mapsto\widehat f_t(v) is measurable for every v and that, under Hypothesis A or B, \partial f_t(x(t)) is bounded by an integrable function r(t) (with r=k under A and r(t)=c[1+\|x(t)\|_Y^{p-1}] under B). Then \widehat f_t is globally Lipschitz with constant r(t), \int_T\widehat f_t(0)\,\mu(dt)=0 is defined, and the family satisfies the required measurable, integrably dominated Lipschitz hypotheses at the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke directional derivative at the state x(t) is the support function of the pointwise generalized-gradient set. An integrable bound on that set makes this support function globally Lipschitz with an integrable modulus; together with pointwise measurability and its zero value at the origin, this verifies the integral-functional hypotheses.
assumptions_latex: r=k\text{ under Hypothesis A, or }r(t)=c\bigl(1+\|x(t)\|_Y^{p-1}\bigr)\text{ under Hypothesis B}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inheritance of pointwise convexity by the integral functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\mapsto f(\omega,x)\) is convex for almost every \(\omega\), then for \(u,v\in L^p(\Omega;X)\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), whenever the displayed extended integrals are well defined, \[I_f(\lambda u+(1-\lambda)v)\le\lambda I_f(u)+(1-\lambda)I_f(v).\] Consequently, \(I_f\) and its effective domain are convex.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurability criterion for Banach-valued Bochner decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A map \(u:\Omega\to X\) is strongly measurable if and only if it is weakly measurable and essentially separably valued: some separable subspace \(X_0\subset X\) contains \(u(\omega)\) almost everywhere. In particular, for separable \(X\), weak and strong measurability coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong measurability equals weak measurability plus essential separable valuedness; for separable Banach spaces, weak measurability suffices.
assumptions_latex: The measure space is complete, or measurability is understood with respect to its completion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\text{ strongly measurable}\iff u\text{ weakly measurable and essentially separably valued}.\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary of the standard extended-expectation convention, with a concrete probability-space example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a measurable extended-real random variable \(Y\), the standard extended expectation \(\mathbb E[Y]=\mathbb E[Y^+]-\mathbb E[Y^-]\) is defined only when at least one of \(\mathbb E[Y^+]\) and \(\mathbb E[Y^-]\) is finite. For example, on \(\mathbb N\) with \(\mathbb P(\{n\})=6/(\pi^2n^2)\), the random variable \(Y(n)=(-1)^n n\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[Y^+]=\mathbb E[Y^-]=+\infty\), so \(\mathbb E[Y]\) is undefined.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\mathbb E[Y^+]=\mathbb E[Y^-]=+\infty\), then \(\mathbb E[Y]\) has no standard extended-real value.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-Boundary Variational Problem for a Surface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulation for two independent variables; the extract notes that analogous formulations extend to more independent variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\subset\mathbb{R}^2\) be a closed region with boundary \(\Gamma\), and let \(F(x,y,z,p,q)\) have continuous first and second partial derivatives with respect to all its arguments. Define
\[
J[z]=\iint_R F(x,y,z,z_x,z_y)\,dx\,dy.
\]
The fixed-boundary variational problem is to seek a function \(z(x,y)\) whose first and second derivatives are continuous in \(R\), which takes prescribed values on \(\Gamma\), and for which \(J[z]\) has an extremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a sufficiently smooth integrand, the fixed-boundary surface variational problem seeks a function with continuous derivatives through order two, prescribed boundary values, and an extremal value of the integral depending on the function and its first partial derivatives.
assumptions_latex: R\subset\mathbb{R}^2\text{ is a closed region with boundary }\Gamma.
F\text{ has continuous first and second partial derivatives in all its arguments}.
z\text{ and its first and second derivatives are continuous in }R.
z|_\Gamma\text{ equals the prescribed boundary data}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J[z]=\iint_R F(x,y,z,z_x,z_y)\,dx\,dy\text{ is required to have an extremum at }z.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-variable form using twice continuously differentiable variations that vanish on the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\subset\mathbb{R}^2\) be a closed region with boundary \(\Gamma\), and let \(\alpha\) be continuous in \(R\). If
\[
\iint_R \alpha(x,y)h(x,y)\,dx\,dy=0
\]
for every function \(h\) whose first and second derivatives are continuous in \(R\) and which satisfies \(h|_\Gamma=0\), then \(\alpha(x,y)=0\) everywhere in \(R\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional stationarity equation for a finite-order variational integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[J(u)=\int_\Omega f(x,j^ku)\,dx.\]
If f is differentiable in every jet variable, the coefficient fields f_{D^\alpha u}(x,j^ku) are locally integrable, and u is stationary under all \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^m), then
\[\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}(-1)^{|\alpha|}D^\alpha\!\left(f_{D^\alpha u}(x,j^ku)\right)=0
\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Omega;\mathbb R^m).\]
With sufficient smoothness this holds pointwise and has order at most 2k.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An order-k stationary integral satisfies the Euler–Poisson system obtained by applying the formal adjoint to each jet derivative.

Each first-variation coefficient is locally integrable.
u is stationary under compactly supported smooth outer variations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative, local, and global finite perimeter
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a Lebesgue-measurable set through the variation of its characteristic function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be Lebesgue measurable and let $D\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be open. Its perimeter relative to $D$ is $P_D(\Omega):=\|\nabla\chi_\Omega\|_{M^1(D)^N}$. It has finite perimeter relative to $D$ when $P_D(\Omega)<\infty$. It has locally finite perimeter when $\chi_\Omega\in\mathrm{BV}(D)$ for every bounded open $D\subset\mathbb{R}^N$, equivalently $\chi_\Omega\in\mathrm{BV}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^N)$, and it has finite perimeter when $\chi_\Omega\in\mathrm{BV}(\mathbb{R}^N)$. The class $\mathrm{BX}(D)$ consists of measurable characteristic functions having finite measure and finite relative perimeter in $D$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perimeter of a measurable set relative to an open set D is the total variation of the distributional gradient of its characteristic function on D. Local and global finite perimeter mean that this characteristic function is respectively locally BV or BV on all of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_D(\Omega)=\|\nabla\chi_\Omega\|_{M^1(D)^N};\quad \Omega\text{ has locally finite perimeter}\iff\chi_\Omega\in\mathrm{BV}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^N);\quad \Omega\text{ has finite perimeter}\iff\chi_\Omega\in\mathrm{BV}(\mathbb{R}^N).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes both bounded-holdall and local Euclidean-space forms; χ_{∂A} denotes the indicator of the boundary and the norms are total variations of the corresponding derivative measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(i) Let D\subset\mathbb{R}^N be a nonempty bounded open Lipschitz holdall, and let A\subset\overline D with \partial A\neq\varnothing. If \nabla b_A\in\mathrm{BV}(D)^N, then
\[
\|\nabla\chi_{\partial A}\|_{M^1(D)}\le 2\|D^2b_A\|_{M^1(D)},\qquad \chi_{\partial A}\in\mathrm{BV}(D),
\]
and \partial A has finite perimeter relative to D. (ii) For every A\subset\mathbb{R}^N with \partial A\neq\varnothing,
\[
\nabla b_A\in\mathrm{BV}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^N)^N\implies\chi_{\partial A}\in\mathrm{BV}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^N),
\]
and \partial A has locally finite perimeter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a bounded Lipschitz holdall, BV regularity of the oriented-distance gradient makes the boundary indicator a BV function, bounds its variation by twice the variation of the distance function's second derivative, and gives the boundary finite relative perimeter. The corresponding local BV hypothesis implies locally finite perimeter in Euclidean space.
assumptions_latex: D\subset\mathbb{R}^N\text{ is nonempty, bounded, open, and Lipschitz}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|\nabla\chi_{\partial A}\|_{M^1(D)}\le2\|D^2b_A\|_{M^1(D)},\quad\chi_{\partial A}\in\mathrm{BV}(D),\quad P(\partial A;D)<\infty;\qquad \chi_{\partial A}\in\mathrm{BV}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^N),\quad \partial A\text{ has locally finite perimeter}.
