knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded variation, variation, and local BV
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For scalar integrable functions on open subsets of an ambient domain; the test-function class is retained exactly as extracted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\omega\subset\Omega\) be open and \(f\in L^1(\omega)\). Then \(f\in BV(\omega)\) if there exists \(C>0\) such that \(\left|\int_\omega f\,\partial_{x_i}\zeta\,dx\right|\le C\|\zeta\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,N\) and every \(\zeta\in C^\infty(\Omega)\). Its variation is \(V_\omega f=\sup\left\{\sum_{i=1}^N\int_\omega f\,\partial_{x_i}\zeta_i\,dx:\zeta_i\in C^\infty(\Omega),\ \sum_{i=1}^N\zeta_i^2\le1\right\}\). Finally, \(f\in BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)\) if \(V_\omega f<\infty\) for every open \(\omega\) with \(\omega\subset\overline\omega\subset\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrable function is BV when its coordinate distributional derivatives obey the stated uniform bounds on smooth test functions. Its variation is the given supremum over smooth vector test fields, and it is locally BV when this variation is finite on every relatively compact open subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\in BV(\omega)\) under the stated derivative bounds, with \(V_\omega f\) and \(BV_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)\) defined as above.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded variation on an open Euclidean domain, defined through the distributional gradient as a bounded vector measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $D\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be open. A function $f\in L^1(D)$ has bounded variation when its distributional gradient, defined by $\langle
abla f,\varphiangle=-\int_D f\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx$, belongs to $M^1(D)^N$. Thus $\mathrm{BV}(D)=\{f\in L^1(D):
abla f\in M^1(D)^N\}$, with $\|f\|_{\mathrm{BV}(D)}=\|f\|_{L^1(D)}+\|
abla f\|_{M^1(D)^N}$; equipped with this norm, $\mathrm{BV}(D)$ is a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an open set D, a function is of bounded variation when it is integrable and its distributional gradient is a bounded vector measure. The BV norm is the sum of its L1 norm and the total-variation norm of its gradient measure, and BV(D) is complete in this norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in\mathrm{BV}(D)\iff \nabla f\in M^1(D)^N,\qquad \mathrm{BV}(D)\text{ is Banach under }\|f\|_{L^1(D)}+\|\nabla f\|_{M^1(D)^N}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: State-Dependent Jump Energies Require Two Traces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the single-representative polar formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A generic state-dependent singular formula cannot evaluate the jump part solely at a single value \(u^*\): on \(J_u\), the canonical data are the two traces \(u^+,u^-\) and the oriented normal \(
u_u\). Consequently a general state-dependent jump contribution requires a surface density depending on both traces, with orientation symmetry \(g(x,a,b,
u)=g(x,b,a,-
u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a jump there is no canonical single state value; general state-dependent jump energy must use both traces.
assumptions_latex: \(u\in BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) has a nontrivial jump part.
The singular density depends on the state value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A generic jump term is not determined by }u^*\text{ and }dD^ju/d|D^ju|\text{ alone}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(D^su=D^ju+D^cu\) and positively one-homogeneous \(g(x,z)\), \[\int g\!\left(x,\frac{dD^su}{d|D^su|}\right)d|D^su|=\int_{J_u}g\bigl(x,(u^+-u^-)\otimes\nu_u\bigr)d\mathcal H^{d-1}+\int g\!\left(x,\frac{dD^cu}{d|D^cu|}\right)d|D^cu|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Value-independent singular energy splits into jump and Cantor contributions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal E_s(u)=\mathcal E_j(u)+\mathcal E_c(u).

notation.meaning: Jump and Cantor parts of the derivative.

knowledge_statements.title: Jump–Cantor Splitting of Singular Energy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Homogeneous Energy of a Singular Measure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-independent polar representation of singular derivative energy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite vector-valued Radon measure \(\mu\) and a Borel positively one-homogeneous density \(g(x,z)\), define \[\Phi_g(\mu):=\int_\Omega g\!\left(x,\frac{d\mu}{d|\mu|}\right)d|\mu|.\] If \(\mu_1\perp\mu_2\), then \(\Phi_g(\mu_1+\mu_2)=\Phi_g(\mu_1)+\Phi_g(\mu_2)\), whenever these integrals are defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-homogeneous density evaluates a singular measure through its polar direction and is additive over mutually singular components.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a finite vector-valued Radon measure.
\(g\) is Borel and positively one-homogeneous in its second argument.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu_1\perp\mu_2\Longrightarrow\Phi_g(\mu_1+\mu_2)=\Phi_g(\mu_1)+\Phi_g(\mu_2).
knowledge_statements.title: One-Homogeneous Energy of a Singular Measure

assumptions_latex: \(u\in BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) and \(D^s u\) is the singular part of \(Du\).
The strong recession function \(f^\infty(x,y,z)=\lim_{t\to\infty}f(x,y,tz)/t\) exists for the relevant arguments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{sing}}(u)=\int_\Omega f^\infty\!\left(x,u^*(x),\frac{dD^s u}{d|D^s u|}(x)\right)d|D^s u|(x)\).

notation.meaning: Singular part and its total variation measure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic singular-measure term; jump-specific representatives may require a refined formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Writing the polar decomposition as \(D^s u=\frac{dD^s u}{d|D^s u|}|D^s u|\), the singular-derivative energy associated with the strong recession density is \[\mathcal F_{\mathrm{sing}}(u):=\int_\Omega f^\infty\!\left(x,u^*(x),\frac{dD^s u}{d|D^s u|}(x)\right)d|D^s u|(x).\] Thus the singular part is measured against \(|D^s u|\), while its polar vector supplies the direction argument of \(f^\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The singular energy integrates the recession density at the polar direction of the singular derivative, using the singular derivative's total variation as measure.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Derivative Energies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied, and the displayed generic formula is not reliable without substantially sharper hypotheses. For integrands depending on the value variable, the jump contribution generally cannot be represented simply by evaluating the recession density at a single precise representative u^*, which is not canonically defined on the jump set.

children.title: Derivative-Decomposition Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interaction between bulk and singular contributions in BV representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical refinement of the singular derivative interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), \[Du=\nabla u\,\mathcal L^d+(u^+-u^-)\otimes\nu_u\,\mathcal H^{d-1}\!\llcorner J_u+D^cu.\] Thus \(D^su=D^ju+D^cu\), with jump and Cantor parts mutually singular; \(u\in SBV\) exactly when \(D^cu=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The singular derivative separates further into jump and Cantor parts, and SBV excludes the Cantor part.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D^su=D^ju+D^cu,\qquad D^ju=(u^+-u^-)\otimes\nu_u\,\mathcal H^{d-1}\!\llcorner J_u.
knowledge_statements.title: Jump–Cantor Refinement

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe energy decomposition for a prescribed gradient density and one-homogeneous singular density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x,z)\) and a positively one-homogeneous Borel density \(g(x,z)\) define the displayed integrals. Then the derivative-decomposed energy is \[\mathcal F(u)=\int_\Omega f(x,\nabla u)\,dx+\int_\Omega g\!\left(x,\frac{dD^su}{d|D^su|}\right)d|D^su|=\mathcal F_{\mathrm{bulk}}(u)+\mathcal F_{\mathrm{sing}}(u).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For value-independent densities, the Lebesgue decomposition of the derivative directly induces bulk and singular energy components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F=\mathcal F_{\mathrm{bulk}}+\mathcal F_{\mathrm{sing}}.

notation.meaning: Polar direction of the singular derivative.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-Independent Bulk–Singular Energy Interface

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lebesgue Decomposition of a BV Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure-theoretic interface separating absolutely continuous and singular derivative components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), \[Du=\nabla u\,\mathcal L^d+D^su,\qquad D^su\perp\mathcal L^d,\] uniquely, and \(|Du|=|\nabla u|\,\mathcal L^d+|D^su|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A BV derivative uniquely separates into an ordinary-gradient part and a singular measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Du=\nabla u\,\mathcal L^d+D^su,\quad D^su\perp\mathcal L^d.

notation.meaning: Part of \(Du\) singular with respect to Lebesgue measure.

knowledge_statements.title: Lebesgue Decomposition of a BV Derivative

assumptions_latex: The bulk and singular integrals displayed below are well defined.
\(Du=\nabla u\,\mathcal L^d+D^s u\) is the Lebesgue decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F(u)=\mathcal F_{\mathrm{bulk}}(u)+\mathcal F_{\mathrm{sing}}(u)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface between the Lebesgue decomposition of \(Du\) and the energy decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The derivative-measure decomposition induces the energy interface \[Du=\nabla u\,\mathcal L^d+D^s u,\qquad \mathcal F(u)=\int_\Omega f(x,u,\nabla u)\,dx+\int_\Omega f^\infty\!\left(x,u^*,\frac{dD^s u}{d|D^s u|}\right)d|D^s u|.\] Equivalently, \(\mathcal F=\mathcal F_{\mathrm{bulk}}+\mathcal F_{\mathrm{sing}}\). The mutually singular measures \(\mathcal L^d\) and \(|D^s u|\) determine which density acts on each derivative component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lebesgue decomposition of a BV derivative separates the functional into an ordinary-gradient bulk integral and a recession-density singular integral.
knowledge_statements.title: Derivative-Decomposition Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the interface leaf, but the asserted energy decomposition inherits the unresolved value-dependent singular formula and lacks the hypotheses and citation needed for an integral-representation statement.

children.title: Recession-Energy Components
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic density structures associated with singular derivative energy.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radial recession convention when the asymptotic limit exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a density \(f(x,y,z)\), its strong recession function in the last variable is \[f^\infty(x,y,z):=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\frac{f(x,y,tz)}{t},\] whenever this limit exists. It is positively one-homogeneous in \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strong recession density is the asymptotic linear rate along a fixed gradient direction.
assumptions_latex: The displayed limit exists for every relevant \((x,y,z)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^\infty(x,y,\lambda z)=\lambda f^\infty(x,y,z)\quad(\lambda>0).

notation.meaning: Strong recession function in the last variable.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Recession Function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robust limsup convention when a strong radial limit may fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R\) with at most linear growth, define \[f^{\#}(z):=\limsup_{\substack{z'\to z\\t\to+\infty}}\frac{f(tz')}{t}.\] This function is positively one-homogeneous and upper semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The upper recession function records robust asymptotic linear growth under directional perturbations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^{\#}(\lambda z)=\lambda f^{\#}(z)\quad(\lambda>0).
knowledge_statements.title: Upper Recession Function

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Support Representation of Convex Recession
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate-domain representation for a proper closed convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f\), its recession function is the support function of the effective domain of its Fenchel conjugate: \[f^\infty(z)=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f^*}(z)=\sup_{z^*\in\operatorname{dom}f^*}\langle z^*,z\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex function's recession rate is the support function of the domain of its conjugate.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^N\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^\infty=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f^*}.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Support Representation of Convex Recession

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Recession Limits Can Fail under Linear Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between radial limits and robust upper recession envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(s)=|s|\bigl(2+\sin(\log(1+|s|))\bigr)\), the quotient \(f(t)/t\) oscillates as \(t\to\infty\). Hence \(f^\infty(1)\) does not exist, while \(f^{\#}(1)=3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear growth alone does not guarantee a strong recession limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{t\to\infty}f(t)/t\text{ does not exist},\qquad f^{\#}(1)=3.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Recession Limits Can Fail under Linear Growth

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Base-point-independent recession limit for proper closed convex densities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:\mathbb R^N\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex and \(z_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), then \[f^\infty(z)=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{f(z_0+tz)-f(z_0)}{t}=\sup_{t>0}\frac{f(z_0+tz)-f(z_0)}{t}.\] The value is independent of \(z_0\), and \(f^\infty\) is convex and positively one-homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed convex density, the recession rate exists, is base-point independent, convex, and one-homogeneous.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^\infty(z)=\sup_{t>0}[f(z_0+tz)-f(z_0)]/t.

notation.meaning: Arbitrary base point in the effective domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Recession Formula

assumptions_latex: \(f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^{m\times d}\to\mathbb R\) has at most linear growth in its last variable.
The displayed limit exists for every relevant \((x,y,z)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^\infty(x,y,z)=\lim_{t\to\infty}f(x,y,tz)/t\), and \(f^\infty(x,y,\lambda z)=\lambda f^\infty(x,y,z)\) for \(\lambda>0\).

notation.meaning: Strong recession function of the gradient variable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong recession function, rather than the upper recession function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The strong recession function of \(f\) in its last variable is \[f^\infty(x,y,z):=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\frac{f(x,y,tz)}{t}.\] Whenever this limit exists, it is positively one-homogeneous in \(z\): for every \(\lambda>0\), \[f^\infty(x,y,\lambda z)=\lambda f^\infty(x,y,z).\] In linear-growth integral representations, this asymptotic density evaluates derivative components that are singular with respect to Lebesgue measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession density is the linear-rate limit of the integrand along large gradient directions; it is positively one-homogeneous and governs singular derivative energy.
knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Energy Components

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and positive one-homogeneity calculation fit the topic, but no source is given for the selected strong-recession convention or for the claim that this density governs singular derivative components in the intended BV representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance under simultaneous reversal of jump traces and normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because \((u^+,u^-,
u_u)\) and \((u^-,u^+,-
u_u)\) describe the same unoriented jump, an orientation-independent surface density satisfies \[g(x,a,b,
u)=g(x,b,a,-
u).\]

assumptions_latex: The jump set is geometrically unoriented.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(x,a,b,\nu)=g(x,b,a,-\nu).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order bulk–surface architecture with an unknown jump set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(u\in SBV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), a free-discontinuity functional has the form \[\mathcal F(u)=\int_\Omega f(x,u,
abla u)\,dx+\int_{J_u}g(x,u^+,u^-,\nu_u)\,d\mathcal H^{d-1},\] whenever the integrals are defined. The jump set \(J_u\) is part of the unknown rather than prescribed in advance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A free-discontinuity functional combines bulk energy with surface energy on the unknown jump set.
assumptions_latex: The bulk and surface integrands are measurable and the displayed integrals are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F(u)=\int_\Omega f(x,u,\nabla u)\,dx+\int_{J_u}g(x,u^+,u^-,\nu_u)\,d\mathcal H^{d-1}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical scalar free-discontinuity model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For data \(h\in L^2(\Omega)\) and \(\alpha,\beta>0\), the extended-real Mumford–Shah functional is \[MS(u)=\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2\,dx+\alpha\int_\Omega|u-h|^2\,dx+\beta\mathcal H^{d-1}(J_u),\] on those \(u\in SBV(\Omega)\) for which the terms are finite, and \(+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mumford–Shah penalizes smooth variation, data mismatch, and the area of the unknown jump set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: MS(u)=\int|\nabla u|^2dx+\alpha\int|u-h|^2dx+\beta\mathcal H^{d-1}(J_u).

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is open and \(u\in SBV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\).
\(f\) is a bulk density and \(g\) is a surface density for which both displayed integrals are defined.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of Minimizers for the Generalized Bolza Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct-method existence under endpoint coercivity, lower semicontinuity, velocity convexity, and superlinear velocity growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
\Lambda(x)=l(x(S),x(T))+\int_S^T L(t,x(t),\dot x(t))\,dt,
\qquad x\in W^{1,1}([S,T];\mathbb R^n).
\]
Assume that $l$ is lower semicontinuous and there is a lower semicontinuous $l^0:\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R$ with $l^0(r)\to+\infty$ such that either $l^0(|x_0|)\le l(x_0,x_1)$ for all $x_0,x_1$ or $l^0(|x_1|)\le l(x_0,x_1)$ for all $x_0,x_1$. Assume also that $L$ is product measurable, $(x,v)\mapsto L(t,x,v)$ is lower semicontinuous for every $t$, and $v\mapsto L(t,x,v)$ is convex with nonempty effective domain for every $(t,x)$. Finally, suppose that for some $\alpha\ge0$ and lower semicontinuous convex $\theta:\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R_+$,
\[
L(t,x,v)\ge\theta(|v|)-\alpha|x|,
\qquad \lim_{r\to+\infty}\frac{\theta(r)}r=+\infty.
\]
Then the generalized Bolza problem has a minimizer. Under the stated convention, if $\Lambda\equiv+\infty$, every arc is a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized Bolza problem has a minimizer if the endpoint cost is lower semicontinuous and coercive in at least one endpoint, while the integrand is measurable, lower semicontinuous, convex with nonempty domain in velocity, and has superlinear velocity growth up to a linear state term. The source convention treats every arc as minimizing when all costs are infinite.
assumptions_latex: \exists l^0:\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R\text{ lower semicontinuous with }\lim_{r\to+\infty}l^0(r)=+\infty
\bigl[\forall x_0,x_1,\ l^0(|x_0|)\le l(x_0,x_1)\bigr]\lor\bigl[\forall x_0,x_1,\ l^0(|x_1|)\le l(x_0,x_1)\bigr]
L\text{ is }\mathcal L([S,T])\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n)\text{-measurable}
\exists\alpha\ge0,\ \exists\theta:\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R_+\text{ lower semicontinuous and convex such that }L(t,x,v)\ge\theta(|v|)-\alpha|x|
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^*\in W^{1,1}([S,T];\mathbb R^n)\text{ minimizing }\Lambda;\quad \Lambda\equiv+\infty\implies\text{every arc is regarded as minimizing}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise reduction of unconstrained normal-integrand minimization over a decomposable measurable-function space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu\) be a \(\sigma\)-finite measure on \(\mathcal A\), let \(\mathcal X\) be a space of measurable functions \(T\to\mathbb{R}^n\) decomposable relative to \(\mu\), and let \(f:T\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be a normal integrand. If \(I_f\not\equiv+\infty\) on \(\mathcal X\), then \[\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\int_T f(t,x(t))\,\mu(dt)=\int_T\inf_{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(t,u)\,\mu(dt).\] If this common value is also greater than \(-\infty\), then, for every \(\bar x\in\mathcal X\), \[\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}I_f[x]\iff \bar x(t)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(t,u)\quad\text{for }\mu\text{-almost every }t.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a normal integrand over a decomposable measurable-function space and a sigma-finite measure, the infimum of the integral equals the integral of the pointwise infimum, provided the integral functional is not identically positive infinity. If the common value is not negative infinity, a function is a global minimizer exactly when it minimizes the integrand pointwise almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in\mathcal X}I_f[x]=\int_T\inf_{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(t,u)\,\mu(dt);\quad\text{if the common value is greater than }-\infty,\;\bar x\in\arg\min_{x\in\mathcal X}I_f[x]\iff\bar x(t)\in\arg\min_{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(t,u)\;\mu\text{-a.e.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized Bolza Problem and Extended-Valued Constraint Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the generalized Bolza functional on W^{1,1} and its representation of differential-inclusion and endpoint constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an interval $[S,T]$, extended-valued functions $l:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ and $L:[S,T]\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ define the generalized Bolza problem
\[
\min_{x\in W^{1,1}([S,T];\mathbb R^n)}\Lambda(x),\qquad \Lambda(x):=l(x(S),x(T))+\int_S^T L(t,x(t),\dot x(t))\,dt.
\]
If $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),\dot x(t))$ is measurable and minorized by an integrable function for every $x\in W^{1,1}$, then $\Lambda$ is well defined with values in $\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. Differential-inclusion and endpoint constraints can be encoded by
\[
L(t,x,v)=\begin{cases}0,&v\in F(t,x),\\+\infty,&v\notin F(t,x),\end{cases}\qquad
l(x_0,x_1)=\begin{cases}g(x_0,x_1),&(x_0,x_1)\in C,\\+\infty,&(x_0,x_1)\notin C.\end{cases}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized Bolza problem minimizes an extended-valued endpoint cost plus an integral cost over W^{1,1} arcs. Measurability and an integrable lower bound make the functional well defined. Infinite endpoint or integrand values can encode endpoint constraints and differential inclusions.
assumptions_latex: t\mapsto L(t,x(t),\dot x(t))\text{ is measurable and minorized by an integrable function for every }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Lambda(x)=l(x(S),x(T))+\int_S^T L(t,x(t),\dot x(t))\,dt\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\},\quad\text{and constraints may be encoded through }+\infty\text{-valued terms}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dirichlet solution convergence under complementary-distance convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives unconditional convergence on intersected domains, subsequential weak convergence on the original sequence, and strong continuity at stable domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $D\subset\mathbb R^N$ be bounded, open, and nonempty. For every open $U\subset D$, let $y(U)\in H_0^1(U;D)$ solve the classical Dirichlet problem. If open sets $\Omega_n,\Omega\subset D$ satisfy
\[
d_{\complement\Omega_n}\to d_{\complement\Omega}\quad\text{in }C(\overline D),
\]
then
\[
y(\Omega_n\cap\Omega)\to y(\Omega)\quad\text{strongly in }H_0^1(D).
\]
Moreover, some subsequence satisfies
\[
y(\Omega_{n_k})\rightharpoonup y_0\quad\text{weakly in }H_0^1(D),
\]
where $y_0\in H_\diamond^1(\Omega;D)$ solves the variational equation against every test function in $H_0^1(\Omega;D)$ and need not be unique in $H_\diamond^1(\Omega;D)$. If $H_0^1(\Omega;D)=H_\diamond^1(\Omega;D)$, then the solution map $d_{\complement\Omega}\mapsto y(\Omega)$ is strongly continuous into $H_0^1(D)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform convergence of the distance functions to the complementary domains implies strong convergence of the solutions on the intersected domains. The solutions on the unmodified domains have a weakly convergent subsequence whose limit lies in the relaxed Sobolev space and satisfies the classical variational equation on the classical test space, although that relaxed-space limit may not be unique. At stable domains, the classical solution map is strongly continuous.
assumptions_latex: D\subset\mathbb R^N\text{ is bounded, open, and nonempty}
y(U)\in H_0^1(U;D)\text{ solves the classical Dirichlet problem for each open }U\subset D
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y(\Omega_n\cap\Omega)\to y(\Omega)\text{ strongly, and a subsequence }y(\Omega_{n_k})\rightharpoonup y_0\in H_\diamond^1(\Omega;D);\ H_0^1(\Omega;D)=H_\diamond^1(\Omega;D)\Rightarrow d_{\complement\Omega}\mapsto y(\Omega)\text{ is strongly continuous.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical, relaxed, and overrelaxed Dirichlet spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines two measurable-domain Sobolev relaxations, their relation to the classical space, and the corresponding uniformly elliptic variational problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a bounded open set $D\subset\mathbb R^N$ and measurable $\Omega\subset D$, define
\[
H_\diamond^1(\Omega;D)=\{\varphi\in H_0^1(D):(1-\chi_\Omega)\varphi=0\ \text{a.e. in }D\},
\]
\[
H_\bullet^1(\Omega;D)=\{\varphi\in H_0^1(D):(1-\chi_\Omega)\nabla\varphi=0\ \text{a.e. in }D\}.
\]
These are closed subspaces with $H_\diamond^1(\Omega;D)\subset H_\bullet^1(\Omega;D)$; if $\Omega$ is open, then
\[
H_0^1(\Omega;D)\subset H_\diamond^1(\Omega;D)\subset H_\bullet^1(\Omega;D),
\]
and the inclusions may be strict. If $f\in H^{-1}(D)$ and $A\in L^\infty(D;\mathcal L(\mathbb R^N,\mathbb R^N))$ is symmetric with $\alpha I\le A\le\beta I$ for $0<\alpha\le\beta$, the classical, relaxed, and overrelaxed solutions are respectively the elements of these three spaces satisfying
\[
\int_D A\nabla y\cdot\nabla\varphi\,dx=\langle f,\varphi\rangle
\]
for every test function in the same space. The relaxed spaces depend only on the a.e.-equivalence class of $\Omega$ and therefore do not detect measure-zero cracks. By convention the solution for $\Omega=\varnothing$ is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relaxed space consists of ambient zero-trace Sobolev functions that vanish almost everywhere outside the measurable domain, while the overrelaxed space only requires their gradients to vanish there. For open domains the classical zero-trace space is contained in the relaxed space, which is contained in the overrelaxed space, and either inclusion can be strict. A symmetric uniformly elliptic coefficient and a load in the ambient dual define corresponding variational Dirichlet problems on each space. The relaxed spaces depend only on the domain up to null sets and ignore measure-zero cracks.
assumptions_latex: D\subset\mathbb R^N\text{ is bounded and open}
\Omega\subset D\text{ is measurable; it is open when }H_0^1(\Omega;D)\text{ is compared}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H_0^1(\Omega;D)\subset H_\diamond^1(\Omega;D)\subset H_\bullet^1(\Omega;D)\text{ for open }\Omega,\text{ with the associated variational problems defined on these spaces.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a function space with trace map \(T:X\to Y(\partial\Omega)\), and let \(R_\Gamma:Y(\partial\Omega)\to Y(\Gamma)\) denote restriction to a specified boundary portion \(\Gamma\). For prescribed data \(h\in Y(\Gamma)\), define \[\mathcal A_{\Gamma,h}:=\{u\in X:R_\Gamma Tu=h\}.\] The choice \(\Gamma=\partial\Omega\) gives the full-trace class; a proper \(\Gamma\) gives a partial-trace class. Sobolev and \(BV\) variants arise by selecting their respective ambient spaces and trace maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trace-class variant fixes an ambient trace theory and prescribes the trace on all or part of the boundary.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The class \(\mathcal A_{\Gamma,h}\) is nonempty exactly when \(h\in\operatorname{ran}(R_\Gamma T)\). If \(u_h\in X\) satisfies \(R_\Gamma Tu_h=h\) and \(T\) and \(R_\Gamma\) are linear, then \[\mathcal A_{\Gamma,h}=u_h+\ker(R_\Gamma T).\] Thus arbitrary data in a larger boundary space cannot be presumed feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prescribed trace data are feasible exactly when they lie in the restricted trace range; a nonempty linear trace class is an affine translate of the zero-trace class.

\(K:\Omega\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) has measurable graph and nonempty values.
\(X\) is a space of measurable maps \(u:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal K=\{u\in X:u(x)\in K(x)\text{ for }\mu\text{-a.e. }x\in\Omega\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-distance characterization for closed-valued pointwise constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K(x)\) is nonempty and closed almost everywhere and \(r_u(x):=\operatorname{dist}(u(x),K(x))\) is measurable, then \(u\in\mathcal K\) if and only if \(r_u=0\) almost everywhere. If \(r_u\in L^p\), this is equivalent to \(\|r_u\|_{L^p}=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise feasibility is equivalent to vanishing distance from the feasible fiber almost everywhere.
assumptions_latex: \(K(x)\) is nonempty and closed almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\in\mathcal K\Longleftrightarrow r_u=0\ \mu\text{-a.e.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural locality of pointwise admissible classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X\) is stable under measurable pasting, then for \(u,v\in\mathcal K\) and \(A\in\mathcal A\), \(\mathbf1_Au+\mathbf1_{A^c}v\in\mathcal K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise-feasible maps may be pasted along a measurable set without losing feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf1_Au+\mathbf1_{A^c}v\in\mathcal K.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fiberwise Convexity of the Admissible Class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity inherited from almost-everywhere convex fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K(x)\) is convex almost everywhere and the ambient space is linear, then \(\mathcal K\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex feasible fibers induce a convex admissible class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u,v\in\mathcal K,\ \theta\in[0,1]\Longrightarrow\theta u+(1-\theta)v\in\mathcal K.
knowledge_statements.title: Fiberwise Convexity of the Admissible Class

children.title: Unilateral Constraints
children.top_down_role: Admissible classes subject to one-sided restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Unilateral Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar one-sided obstacle constraints imposed almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a measurable lower obstacle \(\psi:\Omega\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), the lower unilateral admissible class is \[\mathcal K_{\psi}:=\left\{u\in X:u(x)\geq\psi(x)\text{ for }\mu\text{-almost every }x\in\Omega\right\}.\] Similarly, a measurable upper obstacle \(\phi\) defines \(\mathcal K^{\phi}:=\{u\in X:u(x)\leq\phi(x)\text{ for }\mu\text{-almost every }x\in\Omega\}\). These are pointwise constraints with feasibility intervals \([\psi(x),+\infty)\) and \(( -\infty,\phi(x)]\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unilateral constraint requires a scalar-valued function to remain above a lower obstacle or below an upper obstacle almost everywhere.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an ordered space of measurable real-valued functions on the measure space \((\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal K_{\psi}=\{u\in X:u(x)\geq\psi(x)\text{ for }\mu\text{-a.e. }x\in\Omega\}\), and \(\mathcal K^{\phi}=\{u\in X:u(x)\leq\phi(x)\text{ for }\mu\text{-a.e. }x\in\Omega\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric Projection onto a Unilateral Obstacle Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit L2 projection for lower and upper scalar obstacles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\psi\in L^2(\Omega)\) and \(K_\psi=\{u\in L^2:u\ge\psi\ \mu\text{-a.e.}\}\), \(P_{K_\psi}v=v\vee\psi\). For \(\phi\in L^2(\Omega)\) and \(K^\phi=\{u:u\le\phi\ \mu\text{-a.e.}\}\), \(P_{K^\phi}v=v\wedge\phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a lower obstacle clips upward; projection onto an upper obstacle clips downward.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{K_\psi}v=v\vee\psi,\qquad P_{K^\phi}v=v\wedge\phi.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal-Cone Complementarity for a Lower Obstacle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual contact-set characterization in L2.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in K_\psi\subset L^2(\Omega)\), \(\xi\in N_{K_\psi}(u)\) if and only if \(\xi\le0\) almost everywhere and \(\xi=0\) almost everywhere on \(\{u>\psi\}\). Equivalently, \(\xi\le0\) and \(\xi(u-\psi)=0\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normal to a lower-obstacle set is nonpositive and supported on the contact set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \xi\in N_{K_\psi}(u)\Longleftrightarrow \xi\le0\ \mu\text{-a.e.},\ \xi(u-\psi)=0\ \mu\text{-a.e.}
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Complementarity for a Lower Obstacle

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Almost-everywhere feasibility is invariant under changing representatives: if \(u=v\) \(\mu\)-almost everywhere, then \[u(x)\in K(x)\text{ for }\mu\text{-almost every }x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v(x)\in K(x)\text{ for }\mu\text{-almost every }x.\] Consequently, the admissible class is well defined on spaces such as \(L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), whose elements are equivalence classes modulo null sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Almost-everywhere feasibility does not depend on the chosen representative of an equivalence class of measurable functions.

children.title: Constraint-Closure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Sequential-closure issues for pointwise or unilateral admissible sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Closure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure threshold for constant closed convex pointwise value sets in finite-measure \(L^p\) spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K\subset\mathbb R^m\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, then \[\mathcal K:=\left\{u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m):u(x)\in K\text{ for }\mu\text{-almost every }x\right\}\] is convex, strongly closed, and weakly closed in \(L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\). Closedness of \(K\) cannot in general be omitted: if \(K=(0,+\infty)\subset\mathbb R\) and \(0<\mu(\Omega)<\infty\), the feasible constant functions \(u_n(x)=1/n\) converge strongly in \(L^p(\Omega)\) to the infeasible zero function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex pointwise value set yields a strongly and weakly closed convex feasible class. Without closedness of the value set, even constant feasible functions can converge strongly to an infeasible limit.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)\) is a measure space with \(0<\mu(\Omega)<\infty\).
\(K\subset\mathbb R^m\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal K=\{u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m):u(x)\in K\ \mu\text{-a.e.}\}\) is convex, strongly closed, and weakly closed; nonclosed \(K\) need not yield a strongly closed feasible class.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonconvex Values Need Not Give Weak Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-closure failure for a closed nonconvex value set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\Omega=(0,1)\), let \(K=\{-1,1\}\) and let \((r_n)\) be the Rademacher functions. Then \(r_n\in\mathcal K\) and \(r_n\rightharpoonup0\) in \(L^2(0,1)\), whereas \(0\notin\mathcal K\). Thus \(\mathcal K\) is strongly closed but not weakly closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed nonconvex pointwise values can produce a strongly closed class that is not weakly closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_n\rightharpoonup0\text{ in }L^2,\quad r_n\in\mathcal K,\quad0\notin\mathcal K.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Closure for Closed-Valued Pointwise Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong sequential closure for variable closed-valued constraints in finite-dimensional-valued Lp spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(1\le p<\infty\) and let \(K:\Omega\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) have closed values. Then \(\mathcal K:=\{u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m):u(x)\in K(x)\ \mu\text{-a.e.}\}\) is strongly closed in \(L^p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed pointwise feasible values yield a strongly closed admissible class in Lp.
assumptions_latex: \(K(x)\subset\mathbb R^m\) is closed for almost every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u_n\in\mathcal K,\ u_n\to u\text{ in }L^p\Longrightarrow u\in\mathcal K.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Closure for Closed-Valued Pointwise Constraints

children.title: Differential Constraints
children.top_down_role: Admissible fields restricted by differential operators or inclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Differential Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sobolev fields subject to an almost-everywhere differential inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d,m,q\in\mathbb N\), \(k\in\mathbb N_0\), \(1\le p\le\infty\), and let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) be open. Given a differential operator \(A:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\to L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^q)\) of order at most \(k\) and a multifunction \(K:\Omega\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^q\) with measurable graph, the differentially constrained admissible class is
\[
\mathcal A_{A,K}:=\bigl\{u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m):(Au)(x)\in K(x)\text{ for almost every }x\in\Omega\bigr\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differential constraint admits the Sobolev fields whose image under the specified differential operator belongs almost everywhere to the prescribed measurable multifunction.
assumptions_latex: \(A:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\to L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^q)\) is a differential operator of order at most \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A_{A,K}=\{u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m):(Au)(x)\in K(x)\text{ for a.e. }x\in\Omega\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong and weak closedness for continuous linear operator constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be Banach spaces and let \(A:X\to Y\) be bounded and linear. Then \(\ker A\) is a norm-closed linear subspace of \(X\) and is therefore weakly closed. More generally, \(A^{-1}(C)\) is norm closed when \(C\subset Y\) is norm closed and weakly closed when \(C\) is weakly closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kernels of continuous linear differential operators are strongly and weakly closed, and inverse-image constraints inherit the corresponding closedness from their target sets.
assumptions_latex: For the inverse-image variants, \(C\subset Y\) is norm closed or weakly closed, respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker A\) is norm and weakly closed; \(A^{-1}(C)\) inherits norm or weak closedness from \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Standing regularity assumptions for Banach-space optimal control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hypotheses imposed near a fixed optimal trajectory and its terminal state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed optimal pair \((\bar u,\bar x)\), assume that \(X\) is Banach; \(U\) is a Souslin subset of a complete separable metric space; and an open set \(O\subset X\) contains \(\bar x(t)\) for every \(t\in[a,b]\). On \(O\times U\), the mapping \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable in \(x\); both \(f(x,u,t)\) and \(\nabla_xf(x,u,t)\) are continuous in \((x,u)\), measurable in \(t\), and norm-bounded by a summable function uniformly for \(x\in O\), \(u\in U\), and almost every \(t\). Every \(\varphi_i\), \(i=0,\ldots,m+r\), is continuous near \(\bar x(b)\), and the equality-constraint functions \(\varphi_i\), \(i=m+1,\ldots,m+r\), are Fréchet differentiable at \(\bar x(b)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The state space is Banach, the control set is Souslin in a complete separable metric space, and the dynamics and their state derivative satisfy continuity, measurability, and uniform integrable-bound conditions near the optimal trajectory. All endpoint functions are locally continuous, while equality-constraint functions are Fréchet differentiable at the optimal endpoint.
assumptions_latex: U\text{ is a Souslin subset of a complete separable metric space}
f\text{ is Fréchet differentiable in }x\text{ on }O
f,\nabla_xf\text{ are continuous in }(x,u),\text{ measurable in }t,\text{ and integrably norm-bounded}
\varphi_i\text{ is continuous near }\bar x(b)\quad(0\leq i\leq m+r)
\varphi_i\text{ is Fréchet differentiable at }\bar x(b)\quad(m+1\leq i\leq m+r)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{These are the standing hypotheses for the subsequent maximum-principle results.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Admissible, feasible, and optimal control-trajectory pairs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint-constrained control with state arcs defined through a Bochner-integral equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((u,x)\) is admissible when \(u\) is measurable, \(u(t)\in U\) for almost every \(t\in[a,b]\), and \[x(t)=x_0+\int_a^t f(x(s),u(s),s)\,ds\qquad(t\in[a,b])\] in the Bochner sense. It is feasible when additionally \(\varphi_i(x(b))\leq0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(\varphi_i(x(b))=0\) for \(i=m+1,\ldots,m+r\). A feasible pair \((\bar u,\bar x)\) is globally optimal if \(\varphi_0(\bar x(b))\leq\varphi_0(x(b))\) for every feasible \((u,x)\). It is a strong local minimizer if this inequality holds for every feasible \((u,x)\) satisfying \(\|x(t)-\bar x(t)\|<\varepsilon\) for all \(t\in[a,b]\), for some \(\varepsilon>0\). Every integral solution is absolutely continuous; its almost-everywhere differentiability and satisfaction of the differential equation follow when \(X\) has the Radon--Nikodým property, which is not assumed in the formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Admissibility requires a measurable pointwise-feasible control and its Bochner-integral state trajectory. Feasibility adds the endpoint inequalities and equalities. Global and strong-local optimality compare terminal costs over all feasible pairs or over feasible pairs with uniformly close state trajectories. The integral formulation does not require the Radon–Nikodým property.
assumptions_latex: \{(u,x): (u,x)\text{ is admissible and satisfies the endpoint constraints}\}\neq\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (u,x)\text{ is feasible}\iff (u,x)\text{ is admissible},\ \varphi_i(x(b))\leq0\ (1\leq i\leq m),\ \varphi_i(x(b))=0\ (m+1\leq i\leq m+r).

children.title: Global Constraint Classes

children.title: Integral Constraints
children.top_down_role: Admissible classes restricted by subsidiary integral quantities.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional moment constraints imposed on an infinite-dimensional decision field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m,r,s\in\mathbb N\). An integral constraint is a global feasibility requirement obtained by integrating functions of a decision field. For a class \(X\) of measurable maps \(u:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m\), its standard mixed form is
\[
\mathcal A:=\left\{u\in X:\int_\Omega g(\omega,u(\omega))\,d\mu\le 0,\quad\int_\Omega h(\omega,u(\omega))\,d\mu=0\right\},
\]
where the vector inequality is componentwise and the displayed integrals are finite. This aggregate condition does not require \(g(\omega,u(\omega))\le0\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral constraints impose integrated equalities or componentwise inequalities on aggregate moments of a measurable field, rather than requiring pointwise feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) is a finite measure space and \(m,r,s\in\mathbb N\).
\(X\) is a class of measurable maps from \(\Omega\) to \(\mathbb R^m\).
\(g:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^r\) and \(h:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^s\) are \(\Sigma\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\)-measurable.
For every \(u\in X\), the components of \(g(\cdot,u(\cdot))\) and \(h(\cdot,u(\cdot))\) are integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A=\{u\in X:\int_\Omega g(\omega,u(\omega))\,d\mu\le0,\ \int_\Omega h(\omega,u(\omega))\,d\mu=0\}\), with vector inequalities interpreted componentwise.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space of admissible fields.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A_Q=T^{-1}(Q)=\{u\in X:T(u)\in Q\}\).

notation.meaning: Chosen homotopy, degree, winding, or homology invariant.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global feasibility specified by a chosen homotopy-invariant quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a particular topological invariant \(T\), such as a homotopy class, degree, winding number, or induced homology class, on the field space \(X\). A topological constraint with allowed values \(Q\subset Y\) defines
\[
\mathcal A_Q:=T^{-1}(Q)=\{u\in X:T(u)\in Q\}.
\]
The invariant and its domain are part of the constraint data: the expression is meaningful only where \(T(u)\) is defined, including any continuity, trace, or nonvanishing requirements needed by that invariant. Feasibility is global because fields agreeing locally may still have different values of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A topological constraint admits fields whose specified homotopy, degree, winding, or homology invariant lies in a prescribed set.
knowledge_statements.title: Topological Constraints

children.title: Coupled Global Constraints
children.top_down_role: Problem classes combining integral restrictions with global geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Global Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global constraints jointly linking several fields or components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\in\mathbb N\), let \(X_i\) be a decision-field space for each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and let \(Z\) be a target space. Given a joint constraint mapping \(G:\prod_{i=1}^mX_i\to Z\) and an admissible set \(C\subset Z\), the coupled feasible class is
\[
\mathcal A:=\left\{(u_1,\ldots,u_m)\in\prod_{i=1}^mX_i:G(u_1,\ldots,u_m)\in C\right\}.
\]
The constraint is coupled when membership cannot in general be determined by testing each component independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coupled global constraint tests a tuple of fields through one joint mapping, so feasibility generally cannot be determined component by component.
assumptions_latex: \(X_i\) is a decision-field space for each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\).
\(Z\) is a target space and \(G:\prod_{i=1}^mX_i\to Z\) is a joint constraint mapping.
\(C\subset Z\) is the admissible target set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A=\{(u_1,\ldots,u_m)\in\prod_{i=1}^mX_i:G(u_1,\ldots,u_m)\in C\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General stability criterion for a global constraint under a selected convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be topological spaces, let \(G:X\to Y\) be sequentially continuous, and let \(C\subset Y\) be sequentially closed. Then \(G^{-1}(C)\) is sequentially closed in \(X\). The same statement applies to strong or weak sequential convergence after equipping \(X\) and \(Y\) with the corresponding topologies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global feasible class is sequentially closed when its constraint map is sequentially continuous and its target set is sequentially closed in the chosen topologies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G^{-1}(C)\) is sequentially closed in \(X\).

notation.meaning: Global feasible class defined by the constraint mapping.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonclosed Equality Level of a Lower-Semicontinuous Constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary sharp counterexample to equality-level closure under lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(G:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \(G(0)=0\) and \(G(x)=1\) for \(x\ne0\). Then \(G\) is lower semicontinuous, but \(\{x:G(x)=1\}=\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-semicontinuous global constraint can have a nonclosed nonminimal equality level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is lower semicontinuous but \(\{G=1\}\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Equality Level of a Lower-Semicontinuous Constraint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure distinction between inequality and equality global constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(G:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous, then \(\{u:G(u)\le c\}\) is closed for every \(c\in\mathbb R\). Lower semicontinuity alone does not imply closedness of \(\{G=c\}\) or \(\{G\ge c\}\); continuity, or appropriate upper-semicontinuity in addition, is needed for those conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower semicontinuity closes global sublevel inequalities but does not by itself close equality levels or superlevels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{G\le c\}\) is closed, while closedness of \(\{G=c\}\) and \(\{G\ge c\}\) does not follow from lower semicontinuity alone.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Semicontinuity Closes Only Sublevels

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The equality set \(\{u\in X:G(u)=\pi\}\) is not weakly sequentially closed.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-closure failure for a nonlinear integral equality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(u_n(x)=\sin(nx)\) for \(x\in(0,2\pi)\). Then \(u_n\rightharpoonup0\) in \(L^2(0,2\pi)\), while
\[
G(u_n)=\int_0^{2\pi}|\sin(nx)|^2\,dx=\pi
\]
for every \(n\), but \(G(0)=0\). Consequently,
\[
\{u\in L^2(0,2\pi):G(u)=\pi\}
\]
is not weakly sequentially closed. Thus weak lower semicontinuity of a nonlinear integral functional ensures closure of sublevel inequalities, but does not by itself ensure weak closure of its nonminimal equality levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oscillations can preserve a nonlinear integral equality along a weakly convergent sequence while the weak limit violates that equality.
knowledge_statements.title: Global-Constraint Closure Boundaries

children.title: Infimum–Integration Interchange
children.top_down_role: Interchange for decomposable decision spaces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal one-sided comparison and exactness certificate preceding any measurable-selection theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal X\) be any class of measurable decisions for which the displayed integrals are well defined, and set
\[
m(\omega):=\inf_{z\in E}f(\omega,z).
\]
If \(m\) is measurable, then
\[
\int_\Omega m\,d\mu
\le
\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\int_\Omega f(\omega,x(\omega))\,d\mu.
\]
Whenever both sides are finite, the interchange gap
\[
\Delta:=\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\int_\Omega f(\omega,x(\omega))\,d\mu-\int_\Omega m\,d\mu
\]
is nonnegative, and \(\Delta=0\) exactly when infimum-integration interchange holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The integral of the pointwise infimum is always a lower bound on the best admissible integral value; their finite nonnegative difference measures exactness or failure of interchange.
assumptions_latex: The extended integrals are well defined; both sides are finite when \(\Delta\) is formed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \int_\Omega m\,d\mu\le\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\int_\Omega f(\omega,x(\omega))\,d\mu,\qquad \Delta\ge0.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative Infimum–Integration Gap

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General interchange theorem over the full decomposable class of measurable decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a complete finite measure space, let \(E\) be Polish, and let \(f:\Omega\times E\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be a normal integrand. Set
\[
\mathcal X:=L^0(\Omega;E),\qquad m(\omega):=\inf_{z\in E}f(\omega,z).
\]
Assume \(m^-\in L^1(\mu)\) and that some \(x_0\in\mathcal X\) satisfies \(f(\cdot,x_0(\cdot))^+\in L^1(\mu)\). Then \(m\) is measurable, measurable \(\varepsilon\)-minimizers exist, and
\[
\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\int_\Omega f(\omega,x(\omega))\,d\mu
=
\int_\Omega m(\omega)\,d\mu.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a normal integrand over all measurable decisions, integrable lower control and one finite competitor allow minimization and integration to interchange.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) is complete and finite; \(E\) is Polish.
\(m^-\in L^1\) and one admissible cost has integrable positive part.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in L^0(\Omega;E)}\int_\Omega f(\omega,x(\omega))\,d\mu=\int_\Omega\inf_{z\in E}f(\omega,z)\,d\mu.

notation.meaning: Full decomposable class of measurable E-valued decisions

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Integrand Infimum–Integration Interchange

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) is a complete finite measure space and \(E\) is a Polish space.
\(f:\Omega\times E\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is a normal integrand.
The measurable-selection class \(\mathcal X\) is decomposable and satisfies the stated integrability bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\int_\Omega f(\omega,x(\omega))\,d\mu=\int_\Omega\inf_{z\in E}f(\omega,z)\,d\mu\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-integrand interchange over a decomposable measurable-selection class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m(\omega):=\inf_{z\in E}f(\omega,z)\). Assume \(m\) is measurable, \(m^-\in L^1(\mu)\), and there exists \(x_0\in\mathcal X\) with \(f(\cdot,x_0(\cdot))^+\in L^1(\mu)\). Assume also that \(\mathcal X\) contains every measurable selection needed to paste finite-valued competitors along measurable sets. Then
\[
\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\int_\Omega f(\omega,x(\omega))\,d\mu
=
\int_\Omega m(\omega)\,d\mu.
\]
Both sides are interpreted as extended-real integrals without an indeterminate difference of infinities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a normal integrand and a sufficiently rich decomposable selection space, minimizing the integral equals integrating the pointwise infimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Infimum–Integration Interchange

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is an interchange theorem in the correct container, but no authoritative locator is supplied and the phrase describing selections needed to paste competitors is not a precise theorem hypothesis. The exact richness and integrability conditions require source certification.

children.title: Selection-Attainment Interchange Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Measurable-selection routes between pointwise and integral minimizers.

children.title: Selection-Based Interchange
children.top_down_role: Measurable-selection routes connecting pointwise choices to integral optimization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact measurable selection when the pointwise minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) be the completion of a \(\sigma\)-finite standard Borel measure space, let \(E\) be Polish, and let \(f:\Omega\times E\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be a normal integrand. If \(M(\omega)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in E}f(\omega,z)\) is nonempty almost everywhere, then there is a \(\Sigma\)-measurable selection \(x^*\) such that \(x^*(\omega)\in M(\omega)\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a normal integrand on a completed standard Borel measure space, nonempty pointwise argmin sets admit a measurable exact minimizing selection.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) is the completion of a \(\sigma\)-finite standard Borel measure space.
\(E\) is Polish and \(f\) is a normal integrand.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x^*\text{ measurable with }x^*(\omega)\in M(\omega)\text{ a.e.}\)
knowledge_statements.title: Measurable Exact-Argmin Selection

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) is complete and finite, and \(E\) is Polish.
\(f:\Omega\times E\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is a normal integrand with measurable pointwise infimum \(m\).
The admissible class contains the measurable selections constructed below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), a measurable \(x_\varepsilon\) exists with \(f(\omega,x_\varepsilon(\omega))\le m(\omega)+\varepsilon\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interchange realized by measurable approximate minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(m(\omega):=\inf_{z\in E}f(\omega,z)\). For each \(\varepsilon>0\), define the approximate argmin multifunction
\[
M_\varepsilon(\omega):=\{z\in E:f(\omega,z)\le m(\omega)+\varepsilon\}.
\]
Under the stated normal-integrand hypotheses, \(M_\varepsilon\) has a measurable graph and nonempty values, hence admits a measurable selection \(x_\varepsilon\) satisfying
\[
f(\omega,x_\varepsilon(\omega))\le m(\omega)+\varepsilon
\]
for almost every \(\omega\). If the relevant functions are integrable, then \(\int f(\omega,x_\varepsilon(\omega))\,d\mu\le\int m\,d\mu+\varepsilon\mu(\Omega)\), which yields interchange as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Measurable selections from approximate pointwise argmin sets produce admissible fields whose integral values converge to the integrated pointwise infimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Based Interchange

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asserted nonemptiness of M_epsilon fails when the pointwise infimum is minus infinity but is not attained. A finite-valued pointwise infimum or a different approximate-selection formulation is required. An authoritative measurable-selection locator is also absent, and the result functions as a theorem rather than merely a representation.

children.title: Attainment Transfer
children.top_down_role: Passage between pointwise attainment and attainment of integral minima.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise-optimality certificate using a well-defined nonnegative gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m(\omega)=\inf_z f(\omega,z)\). Suppose \(m\) and \(f(\cdot,\bar x(\cdot))\) are finite almost everywhere and \(h:=f(\cdot,\bar x(\cdot))-m\) is measurable and nonnegative. If \(\int_\Omega h\,d\mu=0\), then \(h=0\) almost everywhere and \(\bar x(\omega)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_z f(\omega,z)\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate minimizes pointwise almost everywhere when its well-defined nonnegative pointwise gap has integral zero.
assumptions_latex: h:=f(\cdot,\bar x(\cdot))-m\text{ is measurable, nonnegative, and }\int_\Omega h\,d\mu=0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x(\omega)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_z f(\omega,z)\quad\text{a.e.}
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Gap Certificate for Pointwise Attainment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of integral and pointwise attainment under interchange and finite integrability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m(\omega)=\inf_{z\in E}f(\omega,z)\). Assume \(m\in L^1(\Omega)\) and \[\inf_{y\in\mathcal X}\int_\Omega f(\omega,y(\omega))\,d\mu=\int_\Omega m\,d\mu.\] If \(x\in\mathcal X\) and \(f(\cdot,x(\cdot))\in L^1(\Omega)\), then \[x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathcal X}\int_\Omega f(\omega,y(\omega))\,d\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x(\omega)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in E}f(\omega,z)\ \text{a.e.}\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With finite integrable pointwise and candidate costs and valid infimum–integration interchange, integral minimization is equivalent to pointwise minimization almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ minimizes the integral}\iff f(\omega,x(\omega))=m(\omega)\text{ a.e.}
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Valued Two-Way Attainment Transfer

assumptions_latex: The hypotheses of infimum–integration interchange hold for \(f\) and \(\mathcal X\).
The pointwise argmin multifunction \(M(\omega)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in E}f(\omega,z)\) has nonempty values almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\) minimizes the integral, and any integral minimizer belongs to \(M(\omega)\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer between pointwise measurable attainment and integral attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m(\omega):=\inf_{z\in E}f(\omega,z)\). If \(x^*(\omega)\in M(\omega)\) almost everywhere, then
\[
\int_\Omega f(\omega,x^*(\omega))\,d\mu=\int_\Omega m(\omega)\,d\mu=
\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\int_\Omega f(\omega,x(\omega))\,d\mu,
\]
so \(x^*\) attains the integral infimum. Conversely, if \(\bar x\in\mathcal X\) attains that infimum and the nonnegative gap \(f(\cdot,\bar x(\cdot))-m\) is measurable and integrable, then its integral is zero; hence \(\bar x(\omega)\in M(\omega)\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A measurable pointwise minimizer attains the integral minimum; conversely, an integral minimizer must minimize pointwise almost everywhere when its gap is integrable.
knowledge_statements.title: Attainment Transfer

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The attainment-transfer theorem fits the leaf and its converse includes an appropriate integrable-gap condition, but it depends on an uncited interchange theorem and requires a source fixing the extended-real integrability hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed positive-infinity failure example; deferred to the sibling devoted to nonattainment boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega=(0,\infty)\), \(E=\{0,1\}\), \(f(\omega,0)=1\), and \(f(\omega,1)=2\). Every measurable selection has integral value \(+\infty\), although \(x\equiv1\) is nowhere pointwise minimizing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every integral value is positive infinity, extended-real argmin membership need not imply pointwise minimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\equiv1\text{ has integral value }+\infty\text{ but is nowhere pointwise minimizing}.
knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Value Attainment Does Not Transfer

intermediate_metadata.reason: The local inventory consists of the finite-valued two-way transfer theorem and the accepted zero-gap certificate. Selection construction is excluded to Selection-Based Interchange, while positive-infinity and other obstruction families are excluded to Nonattainment Boundaries.

children.title: Nonattainment Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Obstructions to transferring pointwise or integral minimizers.

assumptions_latex: The decision class is \(\mathcal X=L^0(\Omega;\mathbb R)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\int_\Omega e^{x(\omega)}\,d\mu=0\), but no \(x\in\mathcal X\) attains this value.

notation.meaning: Class of finite real-valued measurable decisions modulo almost-everywhere equality.
Positive integrand with unattained pointwise infimum.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interchange can hold even though neither pointwise nor integral minima are attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\omega\),
\[
\inf_{z\in\mathbb R}e^z=0,
\]
but no finite \(z\in\mathbb R\) attains the infimum. The constant decisions \(x_n(\omega)=-n\) satisfy
\[
\int_\Omega e^{x_n(\omega)}\,d\mu=e^{-n}\downarrow0.
\]
Therefore the infimum of the integral equals the integral of the pointwise infimum and is zero. Nevertheless, for every finite real-valued measurable \(x\), the function \(e^{x(\omega)}\) is strictly positive almost everywhere, so its integral cannot equal zero. Thus interchange alone does not imply attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the exponential integrand, constant decisions tending to negative infinity approach value zero, but no finite measurable decision attains zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonattainment Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exponential example correctly exhibits nonattainment, but it has no citation or explicit standard-field rationale. Moreover, counterexample is not among the permitted record content kinds; failure_boundary is the fitting terminal role.

children.title: Conditioned-Parametric Interchange Family
children.top_down_role: Interchange in conditioned, nested, and parameterized settings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interchange of the Order of Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality of joint and iterated infima, together with both corresponding argmin decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimum over a product space equals either iterated infimum. A pair is a joint minimizer exactly when one component minimizes the corresponding partial-infimum function and the other minimizes the resulting fiber problem, in either order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x,u}f(x,u)=\inf_u p(u)=\inf_x q(x)\quad\text{with the stated two argmin decompositions}

source_evidence.locator: Max and Min / I. Auxiliary Facts and Principles / Proposition 1.35

source_refs.locator: Max and Min / I. Auxiliary Facts and Principles / Proposition 1.35

knowledge_statements.title: Interchange of the Order of Minimization

source_witnesses.locator: Max and Min / I. Auxiliary Facts and Principles / Proposition 1.35
