children.title: Conditional Interchange
children.top_down_role: Interchange relative to conditioning structures or sub-sigma-algebras.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional Interchange Through a Conditional Normal Integrand
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional optimization when the original data need not be measurable with respect to the conditioning sigma-algebra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\Omega\times E\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) admit a conditional normal-integrand representative \(h\) such that
\[
h(\omega,z)=\mathbb E[f(\cdot,z)\mid\mathcal G](\omega)
\]
and
\[
\mathbb E[f(\cdot,x(\cdot))\mid\mathcal G]=h(\cdot,x(\cdot))
\]
for every admissible \(\mathcal G\)-measurable decision \(x\). If \(h\) has measurable \(\varepsilon\)-minimizers, then
\[
\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{x\in L^0(\mathcal G;E)}\mathbb E[f(\cdot,x)\mid\mathcal G]
=
\inf_{z\in E}h(\cdot,z)
\quad\text{a.s.}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional optimization reduces to pointwise minimization of the conditional expected integrand under the stated substitution and selection hypotheses.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is Polish and \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb P)\) is complete.
\(h\) is a \(\mathcal G\)-normal integrand satisfying the displayed substitution identity.
The conditional expectations share an integrable lower bound and measurable approximate minimizers exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{x\in L^0(\mathcal G;E)}\mathbb E[f(\cdot,x)\mid\mathcal G]=\inf_{z\in E}h(\cdot,z)\quad\text{a.s.}
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Interchange Through a Conditional Normal Integrand

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-space failure when decisions cannot observe the information needed for pointwise minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega=\{0,1\}\) with equal probabilities, let \(\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}\), let \(E=\{0,1\}\), and set \(f(\omega,z)=\mathbf1_{\{z\ne\omega\}}\). Every \(\mathcal G\)-measurable decision is constant, so
\[
\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{x\in L^0(\mathcal G;E)}\mathbb E[f(\cdot,x)\mid\mathcal G]=\tfrac12,
\]
whereas
\[
\mathbb E[\inf_{z\in E}f(\cdot,z)\mid\mathcal G]=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision unable to observe the state incurs error one half even though statewise pointwise minimization has zero cost.
assumptions_latex: The state and action sets each contain two points with equal state probabilities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{x\in L^0(\mathcal G;E)}\mathbb E[f(\cdot,x)\mid\mathcal G]=\tfrac12>0=\mathbb E[\inf_zf(\cdot,z)\mid\mathcal G].
knowledge_statements.title: Information-Mismatch Conditional Gap

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct conditional interchange when the data and decisions use the conditioning sigma-algebra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb P)\) be complete, \(\mathcal G\subset\Sigma\), and let \(E\) be Polish. Let \(f:\Omega\times E\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be a \(\mathcal G\)-normal integrand with an integrable lower bound and at least one \(\mathcal G\)-measurable decision of integrable cost. Then \(m(\omega):=\inf_{z\in E}f(\omega,z)\) is \(\mathcal G\)-measurable, measurable \(\varepsilon\)-minimizers exist, and
\[
\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{x\in L^0(\mathcal G;E)}
\mathbb E[f(\cdot,x(\cdot))\mid\mathcal G]
=m
\quad\text{a.s.}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For adapted normal-integrand data, conditional optimization over adapted decisions equals pointwise minimization almost surely.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb P)\) is complete and \(E\) is Polish.
A common integrable lower bound and one integrable admissible cost are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{x\in L^0(\mathcal G;E)}\mathbb E[f(\cdot,x)\mid\mathcal G]=\inf_{z\in E}f(\cdot,z)\quad\text{a.s.}

notation.meaning: Almost-everywhere classes of G-measurable E-valued decisions

knowledge_statements.title: Adapted Conditional Interchange

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb P)\) is a complete probability space with \(\mathcal G\subset\Sigma\).
\(E\) is Polish and \(f:\Omega\times E\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is \(\mathcal G\otimes\mathcal B(E)\)-measurable and lower semicontinuous in its second argument.
Conditional expectations are well defined by a common integrable lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{x\in L^0(\mathcal G;E)}\mathbb E[f(\cdot,x)\mid\mathcal G]=\inf_{z\in E}f(\cdot,z)\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interchange for decisions measurable with respect to the conditioning information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(m(\omega):=\inf_{z\in E}f(\omega,z)\), which is \(\mathcal G\)-measurable under the stated hypotheses. Because \(f(\cdot,x(\cdot))\) is already \(\mathcal G\)-measurable for every \(x\in L^0(\mathcal G;E)\), one has \(\mathbb E[f(\cdot,x)\mid\mathcal G]=f(\cdot,x)\) almost surely. Measurable approximate minimizers then give
\[
\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{x\in L^0(\mathcal G;E)}
\mathbb E[f(\cdot,x(\cdot))\mid\mathcal G]
=m
\quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
Thus conditioning and optimization interchange when both the data and admissible decisions use exactly the information in \(\mathcal G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When both the integrand and decisions are measurable with respect to the conditioning information, conditional optimization reduces almost surely to pointwise minimization.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Interchange

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional formula is plausible when the data and decisions are both G-measurable, but no source certifies measurability of the pointwise infimum, existence of approximate selectors, or the extended conditional expectations under the stated generality.

children.title: Parametric Interchange
children.top_down_role: Interchange for families indexed by external parameters.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General fixed-parameter interchange with an explicit common measurable-decision class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) be complete and finite, let \(P,E\) be Polish, and let
\[
\mathcal X:=L^0(\Omega;E).
\]
Suppose that, for every fixed \(p\in P\), \(f_p(\omega,z):=f(\omega,p,z)\) is a normal integrand, its pointwise value \(v(\omega,p):=\inf_zf(\omega,p,z)\) has integrable negative part, and some \(x_p\in\mathcal X\) has integrable positive cost. Then
\[
V(p):=\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\int_\Omega f(\omega,p,x(\omega))\,d\mu
=
\int_\Omega v(\omega,p)\,d\mu
\quad\text{for every }p\in P.
\]
The assertion is parameterwise and does not imply continuity or uniform convergence in \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each fixed external parameter, normal-integrand interchange gives the integral of the pointwise parametric value, without any parameter-uniform conclusion.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) is complete and finite; \(P,E\) are Polish.
For every fixed \(p\), \(f_p\) is a normal integrand with the stated integrability bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V(p)=\int_\Omega\inf_{z\in E}f(\omega,p,z)\,d\mu\quad\forall p\in P.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise-in-Parameter Interchange

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(E\) are Polish spaces, and \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) is complete and finite.
\(f:\Omega\times P\times E\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is jointly measurable and lower semicontinuous in \((p,z)\).
For every \(p\in P\), the admissible selection class is decomposable and the interchange integrability conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(p\in P\), \(V(p)=\int_\Omega v(\omega,p)\,d\mu\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise-in-parameter representation of an integral value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(p\in P\), define
\[
v(\omega,p):=\inf_{z\in E}f(\omega,p,z),
\qquad
V(p):=\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\int_\Omega f(\omega,p,x(\omega))\,d\mu.
\]
If the normal-integrand, decomposability, and integrability hypotheses hold for each fixed \(p\), then
\[
V(p)=\int_\Omega v(\omega,p)\,d\mu
\quad\text{for every }p\in P.
\]
This is a pointwise-in-parameter assertion. Continuity, differentiability, or locally uniform convergence of \(V\) requires additional hypotheses uniform in \(p\) and does not follow from the displayed identity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each fixed parameter, the integral value function equals the integral of the pointwise parametric value, without implying uniformity across parameters.
knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Interchange

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise-in-parameter identity fits the leaf and appropriately avoids uniformity claims, but the symbol X is not explicitly introduced and no source fixes the parameterwise decomposability and integrability hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Integral Modulus Transfers to Parametric Values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-continuity result whose primary home is parametric integral sensitivity rather than fixed-parameter interchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a common admissible class and \(V(p):=\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\int_\Omega f(\omega,p,x(\omega))\,d\mu\). If \(\sup_{z\in E}|f(\omega,p,z)-f(\omega,p_0,z)|\le h_p(\omega)\) with \(h_p\in L^1\), then \(|V(p)-V(p_0)|\le\int h_p\,d\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision-uniform integral modulus yields continuity of a parametric value function, but this is sensitivity rather than the interchange identity owned by this leaf.
assumptions_latex: The admissible class is common near \(p_0\).
The displayed integrable uniform modulus holds.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Integral Modulus Transfers to Parametric Values

intermediate_metadata.reason: This leaf owns the fixed-parameter interchange identity for externally indexed families. Conditional and nested interchange are excluded as siblings; parameter-uniform failure belongs to Uniformity Failure Boundaries, and value continuity or differentiation belongs to Parametric Integral Sensitivity. The local foundational theorem remains missing.

children.title: Nested Interchange
children.top_down_role: Interchange across multiple levels of integration or optimization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact nested interchange for additively separated decisions on finite product measure spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Omega,\mu)\) and \((S,\nu)\) be finite measure spaces and
\[
f(\omega,s,x,y)=a(\omega,x)+b(s,y).
\]
If the measurable decision classes for \(x:\Omega\to E\) and \(y:S\to F\) admit their ordinary infimum-integral interchanges, then
\[
\inf_{x,y}\int_\Omega\int_S f(\omega,s,x(\omega),y(s))\,d\nu\,d\mu
=
\nu(S)\int_\Omega\inf_{z\in E}a(\omega,z)\,d\mu
+
\mu(\Omega)\int_S\inf_{w\in F}b(s,w)\,d\nu.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For additively separated levels, nested optimization and integration split into two independently interchanged pointwise problems.
assumptions_latex: The extended integrals have no \(+\infty-\infty\) ambiguity.
Each level admits measurable approximate minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x,y}\iint f=\nu(S)\int\inf_z a+\mu(\Omega)\int\inf_w b.
knowledge_statements.title: Separable Two-Level Interchange Factorization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General joint interchange on a product measure space with order-independent evaluation under Fubini conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((S,\mathcal T,\nu)\) be complete finite measure spaces, let \(E\) be Polish, and let \(f:\Omega\times S\times E\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be a normal integrand for the completed product sigma-algebra. Put \(m(\omega,s):=\inf_{z\in E}f(\omega,s,z)\). Assume \(m^-\in L^1(\mu\otimes\nu)\) and that some jointly measurable decision has integrable positive cost. Then, over all jointly measurable \(x:\Omega\times S\to E\),
\[
\inf_x\int_{\Omega\times S}f(\omega,s,x(\omega,s))\,d(\mu\otimes\nu)
=
\int_{\Omega\times S}m\,d(\mu\otimes\nu).
\]
If \(m\) is integrable, Fubini's theorem gives
\[
\int_\Omega\int_Sm\,d\nu\,d\mu
=
\int_S\int_\Omega m\,d\mu\,d\nu.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint measurable optimization on a product space reduces to the product integral of the pointwise infimum, whose two iterated evaluations agree under Fubini integrability.
assumptions_latex: Both measure spaces are complete and finite, and \(E\) is Polish.
\(f\) is a normal integrand on the completed product space.
\(m^-\) is integrable and one jointly measurable decision has integrable positive cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\inf_x\int f\,d(\mu\otimes
u)=\int m\,d(\mu\otimes
u),\quad \int\!\int m\,d
u d\mu=\int\!\int m\,d\mu d
u.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Space Nested Interchange

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) and \((S,\mathcal T,\nu)\) are complete finite measure spaces, and \(E\) is Polish.
\(f:\Omega\times S\times E\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is a normal integrand on the product space.
The joint and iterated measurable-selection classes are decomposable and satisfy common integrability bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The joint infimum equals both iterated integrals of the pointwise infimum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successive optimization–integration interchange on a product measure space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m(\omega,s):=\inf_{z\in E}f(\omega,s,z)\). Under the stated selection and integrability hypotheses, infimum–integration interchange on the product space and Fubini's theorem give
\[
\inf_x\int_\Omega\int_S f(\omega,s,x(\omega,s))\,d\nu(s)\,d\mu(\omega)
=
\int_\Omega\int_S m(\omega,s)\,d\nu(s)\,d\mu(\omega)
\]
and
\[
\int_\Omega\int_S m\,d\nu\,d\mu
=
\int_S\int_\Omega m\,d\mu\,d\nu.
\]
Thus the joint interchange may be evaluated in either integration order, provided joint measurability and the hypotheses for both iterated interchanges are preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a product measure space, joint minimization and integration can be interchanged successively, and either integration order gives the same value under Fubini conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested Interchange

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nested-interchange role is appropriate, but the domain of inf_x is undefined and the common bounds needed both for extended-real Fubini interchange and for joint versus iterated measurable selections are not stated precisely or sourced.

children.title: Uniformity Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Loss of interchange under inadequate parameter uniformity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Decision-Uniform Integrable Domination Restores Parameter Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient uniformity condition for passing parameter limits through integration and infimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a common admissible class \(\mathcal X\), set
\[
d_p(\omega):=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|f(\omega,p,x(\omega))-f(\omega,p_0,x(\omega))|.
\]
Assume \(d_p\) is measurable, \(d_p\to0\) almost everywhere, and \(d_p\le 2g\) for some \(g\in L^1\). Then, for \(F_p(x):=\int f(\omega,p,x(\omega))\,d\mu\),
\[
\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|F_p(x)-F_{p_0}(x)|\le\int d_p\,d\mu\to0,
\]
and consequently \(\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}F_p(x)\to\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}F_{p_0}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A measurable decision-uniform difference dominated in L1 permits the parameter limit to pass through integration and infimization.
assumptions_latex: \(d_p\) is measurable, converges almost everywhere to zero, and is dominated by \(2g\) with \(g\in L^1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|F_p(x)-F_{p_0}(x)|\to0\quad\text{and}\quad\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}F_p(x)\to\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}F_{p_0}(x).
knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Uniform Integrable Domination Restores Parameter Stability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moving Minimizers Defeat Pointwise Parameter Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of passage through infimization when convergence is not uniform over decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the measure space consist of one point, let \(E=\mathbb N\), and define
\[
f_n(z):=-\mathbf 1_{\{n\}}(z),\qquad f(z):=0.
\]
For every fixed \(z\in\mathbb N\), \(f_n(z)\to f(z)\), but
\[
\inf_{z\in E}f_n(z)=-1\quad\text{for every }n,
\qquad
\inf_{z\in E}f(z)=0.
\]
Thus pointwise parameter convergence does not pass through infimization when the minimizing decision moves with the parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative well moving through the decision set disappears pointwise but keeps every parametric infimum equal to minus one.
assumptions_latex: The parameter is the sequence index \(n\).
The decision set is the countable discrete space \(\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_n(z)\to0\ \forall z,\qquad \lim_n\inf_z f_n(z)=-1<0=\inf_z\lim_n f_n(z).
knowledge_statements.title: Moving Minimizers Defeat Pointwise Parameter Convergence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter-limit failure after integration caused specifically by concentration and absent uniform integrability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T=\mathbb N\) with \(\mu(\{k\})=2^{-k}\), and define
\[
g_n(k):=2^n\mathbf1_{\{n\}}(k).
\]
For every fixed \(k\), \(g_n(k)\to0\), but
\[
\int_Tg_n\,d\mu=1\quad\text{for every }n.
\]
Moreover, for every \(K>0\), choosing \(n\) with \(2^n>K\) gives
\[
\int_{\{g_n>K\}}g_n\,d\mu=1,
\]
so \(\{g_n\}\) is not uniformly integrable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unit mass moves to atoms of vanishing measure, producing pointwise convergence to zero while every integral stays one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_n\to0\ \text{pointwise},\qquad \int g_n\,d\mu=1,\qquad \{g_n\}\ \text{is not uniformly integrable}.
knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Concentration Without Uniform Integrability

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_\theta(t)\to0\) for every \(t\in(0,1)\) as \(\theta\downarrow0\), but \(\int_T g_\theta\,d\mu=1\) for every \(\theta\in\Theta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concentration example marking failure of parameter-uniform integral passage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=(0,1)\) with Lebesgue measure \(\mu\), and, for \(\theta\in(0,1]\), define \(g_\theta(t)=\theta^{-1}\mathbf 1_{(0,\theta)}(t)\). For every \(t\in(0,1)\), one has \(g_\theta(t)\to0\) as \(\theta\downarrow0\), whereas \(\int_T g_\theta(t)\,d\mu(t)=1\) for every \(\theta\in(0,1]\). Thus pointwise parameter convergence does not justify passage through integration. The obstruction is concentration: \(\{g_\theta:\theta\in(0,1]\}\) is not uniformly integrable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Concentrating unit-mass densities converge pointwise to zero while their integrals remain one, so pointwise parameter convergence alone does not justify passage through integration.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniformity Failure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global-Parameter and Pointwise-Parameter Optimization Need Not Interchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-scope mismatch rather than failure of parameter-uniform convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_1=(0,\tfrac12)\), \(A_2=(\tfrac12,1)\), and \(g_i=\mathbf1_{A_i}\). Then \(\sup_i\int_0^1g_i=\tfrac12<1=\int_0^1\sup_i g_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single global parameter cannot reproduce a pointwise-varying parameter choice, but this does not diagnose inadequate uniformity across a parameter limit.
assumptions_latex: The parameter is one global element of \(\{1,2\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_i\int g_i<\int\sup_i g_i.
knowledge_statements.title: Global-Parameter and Pointwise-Parameter Optimization Need Not Interchange

intermediate_metadata.reason: This leaf owns failures caused by inadequate parameter-uniform control and positive conditions repairing them. The accepted record covers decision-uniform dominated convergence. Conditional, parametric, and nested identities remain in their sibling leaves; the global-versus-pointwise decision example was deferred as misplaced. A genuine uniform-integrability counterexample remains required.

children.title: Interchange Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Obstructions from measurability, decomposability, or integral-control failures.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral-control boundary excluding indeterminate extended-real integrals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a measurable extended-real function \(g\), the Lebesgue integral \(\int g\,d\mu\) is undefined when \(\int g^+\,d\mu=\int g^-\,d\mu=+\infty\). Consequently, an infimum–integration identity is not well formed unless every integral appearing in it avoids this indeterminate case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interchange cannot be asserted when either side requires an undefined infinity-minus-infinity integral.
assumptions_latex: For a relevant integrand composition or pointwise value, both positive and negative parts have infinite integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\int g\,d\mu\) is undefined, so the proposed interchange equality is not a mathematical identity.

notation.meaning: Positive and negative parts of the measurable function.

knowledge_statements.title: Undefined Extended-Integral Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the standard interchange mechanism when values or near-minimizers cannot be measured.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m(\omega)=\inf_{z\in E}f(\omega,z)\). If \(m\) is not measurable, its ordinary Lebesgue integral is unavailable. If measurable near-argmin selections cannot be formed in the admissible class, the standard construction of integral competitors from pointwise near-minimizers also fails. These obstructions do not logically preclude accidental equality in a particular example, but they invalidate the usual interchange theorem and proof mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonmeasurable pointwise value or unavailable measurable near-minimizers defeats the standard interchange theorem, though equality may still occur accidentally.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\Omega\times E\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is an extended-real integrand.
The required value measurability or measurable-selection hypothesis fails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The standard measurable-selection interchange theorem is inapplicable.
knowledge_statements.title: Measurability and Selection Obstructions

assumptions_latex: The admissible class \(\mathcal C\) consists of measurable functions that are constant almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{u\in\mathcal C}\int_0^1 (u(t)-t)^2\,dt=1/12>0=\int_0^1\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}(x-t)^2\,dt\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure caused by a nondecomposable admissible selection class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(T=(0,1)\), let \(f(t,x)=(x-t)^2\), and let \(\mathcal C\) be the set of measurable functions that are constant almost everywhere. Then \(\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}f(t,x)=0\) for every \(t\in T\), attained pointwise at \(x=t\). However, \(\inf_{u\in\mathcal C}\int_0^1 f(t,u(t))\,dt=\inf_{c\in\mathbb R}\int_0^1(c-t)^2\,dt=1/12\), while \(\int_0^1\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}f(t,x)\,dt=0\). Hence infimum-integration interchange can fail when the admissible class is not decomposable under measurable pasting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting selections to constants prevents pointwise minimizers from being pasted, producing a strict gap between the integral infimum and the integral of pointwise infima.
knowledge_statements.title: Interchange Failure Boundaries

children.title: Integral Conjugacy
children.top_down_role: Dual representations assembled from pointwise conjugate integrands.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit nonsingular integral-conjugacy model on a reflexive Lebesgue space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(1<p<\infty\), \(q=p/(p-1)\), and let \(a\in L^\infty(T)\) satisfy \(a\ge\alpha>0\) almost everywhere. For
\[
I(x)=\int_T\frac{a(t)}p|x(t)|^p\,d\mu(t),
\]
the conjugate under the \(L^p\)-\(L^q\) pairing is
\[
I^*(y)=\int_T\frac{a(t)^{1-q}}q|y(t)|^q\,d\mu(t).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a weighted p-power integral is the integral of the reciprocal-weighted q-power conjugate.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Power Integral Conjugacy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duality-gap certificate under an established integral-conjugacy identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume \(I_f(x)=\int_T f(t,x(t))\,d\mu\) and \(I_f^*(y)=\int_T f^*(t,y(t))\,d\mu\), with all displayed expressions well defined. Then
\[
I_f(x)+I_f^*(y)-\langle x,y\rangle
=\int_T\bigl(f(t,x(t))+f^*(t,y(t))-\langle x(t),y(t)\rangle\bigr)\,d\mu\ge0.
\]
If this integral is finite, it vanishes exactly when \(y(t)\in\partial f(t,x(t))\) for almost every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under integral conjugacy, the global Fenchel gap is the integral of the nonnegative pointwise gaps and vanishes exactly at pointwise Fenchel equality.
assumptions_latex: The integral-conjugacy identity holds for the specified primal-dual pairing.
The extended-real expressions contain no indeterminate difference.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I_f(x)+I_f^*(y)-\langle x,y\rangle=\int_T\bigl(f(t,x(t))+f^*(t,y(t))-\langle x(t),y(t)\rangle\bigr)\,d\mu\ge0.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral Fenchel-Gap Decomposition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugacy Failure on a Nondecomposable Decision Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-atomic example showing that restriction of the primal space introduces annihilator duals absent from the pointwise conjugates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T=\{1,2\}\) have equal positive masses, let \(X=\{(c,c):c\in\mathbb R\}\), and extend the zero functional on \(X\) to the ambient space as \(J=\delta_X\). Then
\[
J^*(y)=\begin{cases}0,&\int_Ty\,d\mu=0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
For the pointwise integrand \(f(t,z)=0\), however, \(f^*(t,y(t))=\delta_{\{0\}}(y(t))\). Hence every nonzero zero-mean \(y\) satisfies
\[
J^*(y)=0<\int_Tf^*(t,y(t))\,d\mu=+\infty.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting decisions to constant functions creates a global annihilator, so the conjugate is not the integral of the pointwise conjugates.
assumptions_latex: The primal decision space is the constant-function subspace on a two-atom measure space.
The restricted functional is represented in the ambient space by its indicator extension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists y\ne0:\ \int_Ty\,d\mu=0,\quad J^*(y)=0<\int_Tf^*(t,y(t))\,d\mu=+\infty.

notation.meaning: Annihilator of the restricted primal subspace
Ambient extension of the zero functional on the constant-function subspace

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugacy Failure on a Nondecomposable Decision Space

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Normal-Integrand Conjugacy on Reflexive Lebesgue Spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General density-dual conjugacy theorem for a convex integral functional on \(L^p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) be complete and \(\sigma\)-finite, let \(1<p<\infty\), and put \(q=p/(p-1)\). Let \(f:T\times\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a proper convex normal integrand. Suppose \(I_f(x):=\int_Tf(t,x(t))\,d\mu\) is proper on \(L^p\) and is norm-continuous at some point of its effective domain. Under the \(L^p\)-\(L^q\) pairing,
\[
I_f^*(y)=\int_T f^*(t,y(t))\,d\mu
\qquad(y\in L^q).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex normal-integrand functional that is continuous at a domain point has a conjugate equal to the integral of the fiber conjugates.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a proper convex normal integrand.
\(I_f\) is proper and norm-continuous at a point of its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I_f^*(y)=\int_Tf^*(t,y(t))\,d\mu\quad\forall y\in L^q.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Normal-Integrand Conjugacy on Reflexive Lebesgue Spaces

assumptions_latex: \(f:T\times\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a proper convex normal integrand.
\(I_f\) is proper on \(L^p(T;\mathbb R^d)\) and continuous at some point of its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_f^*(y)=\int_T f^*(t,y(t))\,d\mu(t)\) for every \(y\in L^q(T;\mathbb R^d)\).

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the fiber integrand

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reflexive \(L^p\)-space conjugacy without singular dual functionals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) be \(\sigma\)-finite, let \(1<p<\infty\), and put \(q=p/(p-1)\). Let \(f:T\times\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a proper convex normal integrand such that \(I_f\) is proper on \(L^p(T;\mathbb R^d)\) and continuous at some point of its effective domain. Under the pairing \(\langle x,y\rangle=\int_T\langle x(t),y(t)\rangle\,d\mu(t)\), its Fenchel conjugate satisfies \(I_f^*(y)=\int_T f^*(t,y(t))\,d\mu(t)\) for every \(y\in L^q(T;\mathbb R^d)\), with the extended-integral convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated continuity qualification, conjugating a convex integral functional on reflexive Lp equals integrating its pointwise conjugates over the Lq dual.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral Conjugacy

children.title: Integral Subdifferential Formulas
children.top_down_role: Subgradient and singular-subgradient representation families for integral functionals.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit convex subdifferential formula on a reflexive Lebesgue space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(1<p<\infty\), let \(a\in L^\infty(T)\) satisfy \(a\ge0\), and define
\[
I(x)=\int_T\frac{a(t)}p|x(t)|^p\,d\mu(t).
\]
Then \(I\) is Fréchet differentiable on \(L^p(T;\mathbb R^d)\) and
\[
\partial I(x)=\{a|x|^{p-2}x\}\subset L^q(T;\mathbb R^d).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subgradient of a weighted p-power integral is the pointwise weighted duality map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial I(x)=\{a|x|^{p-2}x\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Power Integral Subgradient

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex minimizer certificate conditional on the nonsingular integral-subgradient formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(I_f\) is proper convex and, at \(x\), its subdifferential satisfies
\[
y\in\partial I_f(x)\iff y(t)\in\partial f(t,x(t))\quad\text{a.e.}
\]
for dual densities \(y\). Then
\[
x\in\operatorname*{argmin}I_f
\iff 0\in\partial I_f(x)
\iff 0\in\partial f(t,x(t))\ \text{a.e.}
\iff x(t)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_z f(t,z)\ \text{a.e.}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the exact density subgradient formula, global convex optimality is equivalent to pointwise optimality almost everywhere.
assumptions_latex: The displayed nonsingular integral-subgradient formula holds at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname*{argmin}I_f\iff x(t)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_z f(t,z)\quad\text{a.e.}
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Certificate for Integral Minimizers

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary showing that density formulas do not describe the full dual of \(L^\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) be nonatomic, let \(X=L^\infty(T)\), and set
\[
C:=\{x\in L^\infty:x\le0\ \text{a.e.}\},\qquad I=\delta_C.
\]
With the full dual \((L^\infty)^*=ba\),
\[
\partial I(0)=N_C(0)=ba_+.
\]
Consequently, positive purely finitely additive functionals are subgradients at zero although they admit no \(L^1\)-density representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full L-infinity subdifferential can contain positive purely finitely additive functionals invisible to pointwise L1-density formulas.
assumptions_latex: The full Banach dual \((L^\infty)^*=ba\) is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial I(0)=ba_+\supsetneq L^1_+.

notation.meaning: Positive bounded finitely additive dual functionals

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Full-Dual Subgradients on L-Infinity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex density-valued subdifferential formula under established integral conjugacy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(1<p<\infty\), \(q=p/(p-1)\), and let \(f\) define a proper convex integral functional \(I_f\) on \(L^p(T;\mathbb R^d)\). If
\[
I_f^*(y)=\int_Tf^*(t,y(t))\,d\mu
\quad(y\in L^q),
\]
then, for \(x\in\operatorname{dom}I_f\) and \(y\in L^q\) with finite conjugate value,
\[
y\in\partial I_f(x)
\iff
y(t)\in\partial f(t,x(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under integral conjugacy, a dual density is a subgradient of the integral functional exactly when it is a pointwise subgradient almost everywhere.
assumptions_latex: The relevant primal and conjugate values are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y\in\partial I_f(x)\iff y(t)\in\partial f(t,x(t))\ \text{a.e.}

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential in the Lp-Lq pairing

knowledge_statements.title: Almost-Everywhere Integral Subgradient Formula

assumptions_latex: \(1<p<\infty\), \(q=p/(p-1)\), and the stated integral-conjugacy identity holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\in\partial I_f(x)\iff y(t)\in\partial f(t,x(t))\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(t\in T\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex \(L^p\)-\(L^q\) subgradient formula in the nonsingular dual regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(1<p<\infty\), put \(q=p/(p-1)\), and suppose the conjugacy identity \(I_f^*(y)=\int_T f^*(t,y(t))\,d\mu(t)\) holds for the proper convex normal integrand \(f\) defining \(I_f\) on \(L^p(T;\mathbb R^d)\). For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}I_f\) and \(y\in\operatorname{dom}I_f^*\subset L^q(T;\mathbb R^d)\), one has \(y\in\partial I_f(x)\) if and only if \(y(t)\in\partial f(t,x(t))\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(t\in T\). Equivalently, the integral Fenchel equality holds exactly when the pointwise Fenchel equality holds almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the integral-conjugacy identity, a dual density is an integral-functional subgradient exactly when it is a pointwise subgradient of the integrand almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral Subdifferential Formulas

children.title: Singular Dual Components
children.top_down_role: Dual components not representable by ordinary integrable densities.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concentration Characterization of a Singular Functional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational characterization of singular finitely additive functionals relative to the base measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A functional \(v_s\in(L^\infty(\mu))^*\), represented by a bounded finitely additive measure vanishing on \(\mu\)-null sets, is singular relative to \(\mu\) when there are measurable sets \(A_n\) with \(\mu(A_n)\downarrow0\) such that \(v_s(x\mathbf1_{\Omega\setminus A_n})=0\) for every \(x\in L^\infty(\mu)\) and every \(n\). Thus it is concentrated on sets of arbitrarily small \(\mu\)-measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular dual functional is concentrated on measurable sets whose base-measure sizes tend to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(v_s\) is represented by a bounded finitely additive measure that vanishes on \(\mu\)-null sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists A_n\in\Sigma:\mu(A_n)\downarrow0\text{ and }v_s(x\mathbf1_{\Omega\setminus A_n})=0\ \forall x,n.\)

notation.meaning: Measurable concentration sets of vanishing base measure.

knowledge_statements.title: Concentration Characterization of a Singular Functional

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Absence of Singular Components for Reflexive Lebesgue Exponents
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Function-space boundary separating density duals from the \(L^\infty\) singular phenomenon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(1<p<\infty\), \(q=p/(p-1)\), and let the range be finite-dimensional. Every continuous linear functional on \(L^p(\mu;\mathbb R^d)\) has the form \(x\mapsto\int\langle y,x\rangle\,d\mu\) for a unique \(y\in L^q(\mu;\mathbb R^d)\). Hence no nonzero purely finitely additive singular summand occurs in this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For reflexive Lebesgue exponents, all dual variables are integrable densities; the extra singular summand is an L-infinity-dual phenomenon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((L^p(\mu;\mathbb R^d))^*=L^q(\mu;\mathbb R^d)\), with no purely finitely additive summand.
knowledge_statements.title: Absence of Singular Components for Reflexive Lebesgue Exponents

assumptions_latex: The primal space is \(L^\infty(T;\mathbb R^d)\), formed modulo \(\mu\)-almost-everywhere equality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(v\in(L^\infty(T;\mathbb R^d))^*\) decomposes uniquely as \(v=v_a+v_s\), where \(v_a(x)=\int_T\langle y(t),x(t)\rangle\,d\mu(t)\) for some \(y\in L^1(T;\mathbb R^d)\), and \(v_s\) is purely finitely additive.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Yosida-Hewitt-type dual decomposition relevant to integral functionals on \(L^\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a finite measure space, and form \(L^\infty(T;\mathbb R^d)\) modulo \(\mu\)-almost-everywhere equality. Each continuous linear functional \(v\in(L^\infty(T;\mathbb R^d))^*\) has a unique Yosida-Hewitt decomposition \(v=v_a+v_s\). The countably additive component has a density \(y\in L^1(T;\mathbb R^d)\) and acts by \(v_a(x)=\int_T\langle y(t),x(t)\rangle\,d\mu(t)\). The component \(v_s\) is purely finitely additive and, unless zero, cannot be represented by an \(L^1\) density. Consequently, dual representations of integral functionals on \(L^\infty\) may require a singular term beyond the integral of pointwise conjugates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of L-infinity decomposes into a density-representable countably additive part and a purely finitely additive singular part, so integrable densities need not exhaust integral-functional dual variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular Dual Components

children.title: Parametric Integral Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Value and solution sensitivity for parameter-dependent integral functionals.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for ordinary differentiability when active minimizers have different parameter slopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a one-point probability space, let \(X=\{-1,1\}\) and \(f(t,x,\theta)=x\theta\). Then \(\varphi(\theta)=\min_{x\in X}x\theta=-|\theta|\). Both decisions minimize at \(\theta=0\), but their parameter slopes are \(-1\) and \(1\); hence \(\varphi\) is not differentiable at zero, although \(\varphi'(0;h)=-|h|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Competing minimizers with different parameter slopes can make the integral value function nondifferentiable.
assumptions_latex: The probability space has one atom of mass one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varphi(\theta)=-|\theta|\) is not differentiable at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Nondifferentiability from Competing Integral Minimizers

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional solution sensitivity obtained from the integrated stationarity system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x,	heta)=\int_T f(t,x,	heta)\,d\mu(t)\) be \(C^2\) near \(( ar x, ar	heta)\), with its first and second derivatives represented by differentiation under the integral. If \(
abla_xF( ar x, ar	heta)=0\) and \(H=
abla^2_{xx}F( ar x, ar	heta)\) is positive definite, then a neighborhood of \( ar	heta\) admits a unique \(C^1\) stationary branch \(x(	heta)\) near \( ar x\); its points are strict local minimizers and \[Dx( ar	heta)=-H^{-1}
abla^2_{x	heta}F( ar x, ar	heta)=-\left(\int_T
abla^2_{xx}f(t, ar x, ar	heta)\,d\muight)^{-1}\left(\int_T
abla^2_{x	heta}f(t, ar x, ar	heta)\,d\muight).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite integrated Hessian gives a unique differentiable local-minimizer branch with derivative determined by integrated Hessian blocks.
assumptions_latex: The decision and parameter spaces are finite-dimensional.
\(F\) is \(C^2\) locally and differentiation through the integral is valid through second order.
\(\nabla_xF(\bar x,\bar\theta)=0\) and \(\nabla^2_{xx}F(\bar x,\bar\theta)\) is positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Dx(\bar\theta)=-[\nabla^2_{xx}F(\bar x,\bar\theta)]^{-1}\nabla^2_{x\theta}F(\bar x,\bar\theta).\)
knowledge_statements.title: Differentiable Local-Minimizer Branch

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Danskin directional sensitivity after differentiation under the integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(F(x,	heta)=\int_T f(t,x,	heta)\,d\mu(t)\), \(\varphi(	heta)=\min_{x\in X}F(x,	heta)\), and \(S( ar	heta)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}F(x, ar	heta)\). If \(X\) is compact, \(F\) is continuous locally, and an integrable local bound permits \(
abla_	heta F(x, ar	heta)=\int_T
abla_	heta f(t,x, ar	heta)\,d\mu(t)\) continuously in \(x\), then \[\varphi'( ar	heta;h)=\min_{x\in S( ar	heta)}\int_T\langle
abla_	heta f(t,x, ar	heta),hangle\,d\mu(t).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With multiple minimizers, the directional value derivative is the smallest integrated parameter slope among active minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is compact and the integral objective is continuous near the reference parameter.
Parameter differentiation under the integral is valid with an integrable local dominating function.
The resulting parameter gradient is continuous in the decision on the active compact set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varphi'(\bar\theta;h)=\min_{x\in S(\bar\theta)}\int_T\langle\nabla_\theta f(t,x,\bar\theta),h\rangle\,d\mu.\)

notation.meaning: Integral minimizers at the reference parameter.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Minimizer Integral Envelope Formula

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a compact metric space, \(\Theta\subset\mathbb R^k\) is open, and \(\bar\theta\in\Theta\).
For almost every \(t\), \((x,\theta)\mapsto f(t,x,\theta)\) is continuous and \(\theta\mapsto f(t,x,\theta)\) is differentiable near \(\bar\theta\).
There exists \(m\in L^1(T)\) such that \(\|\nabla_\theta f(t,x,\theta)\|\le m(t)\) for every \(x\in X\) and all \(\theta\) near \(\bar\theta\), almost everywhere.
The map \((x,\theta)\mapsto\int_T f(t,x,\theta)\,d\mu(t)\) is finite and continuous near \(X\times\{\bar\theta\}\), and its minimizer at \(\bar\theta\) is unique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(h\in\mathbb R^k\), \(\varphi'(\bar\theta;h)=\int_T\langle\nabla_\theta f(t,\bar x,\bar\theta),h\rangle\,d\mu(t)\), where \(\bar x\) is the unique minimizer at \(\bar\theta\).

notation.meaning: unique optimizer at the reference parameter

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite-dimensional dominated directional-envelope formula for the value function; solution-map sensitivity is outside this record.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a compact metric space, let \(\Theta\subset\mathbb R^k\) be open, and define \(\varphi(\theta)=\min_{x\in X}\int_T f(t,x,\theta)\,d\mu(t)\). Assume that for almost every \(t\), the map \((x,\theta)\mapsto f(t,x,\theta)\) is continuous and \(\theta\mapsto f(t,x,\theta)\) is differentiable near \(\bar\theta\). Assume also that \(\|\nabla_\theta f(t,x,\theta)\|\le m(t)\) for every \(x\in X\) and every \(\theta\) near \(\bar\theta\), almost everywhere, for some \(m\in L^1(T)\), and that \((x,\theta)\mapsto\int_T f(t,x,	heta)\,d\mu(t)\) is finite and continuous near \(X\times\{\bar\theta\}\). If the minimizer \(\bar x\) at \(\bar\theta\) is unique, then for every \(h\in\mathbb R^k\), \(\varphi'(\bar\theta;h)=\int_T\langle\nabla_\theta f(t,\bar x,\bar\theta),h\rangle\,d\mu(t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a compact decision set, dominated parameter derivatives, and a unique optimizer at the reference parameter, the directional derivative of the value equals the integral of the parameter derivative evaluated at that optimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Integral Sensitivity

children.title: Fatou-Type Passage

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\int_T\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n(t)\,d\mu(t)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_T f_n(t)\,d\mu(t)\).

notation.meaning: almost-everywhere pointwise limit when it exists

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Fatou lower-bound passage for nonnegative measurable functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a measure space, and let \(f_n:T\to[0,+\infty]\) be measurable for every \(n\ge1\). Then \(\int_T\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n(t)\,d\mu(t)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_T f_n(t)\,d\mu(t)\). In particular, if \(f_n(t)\to f(t)\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(t\), then \(\int_T f\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_T f_n\,d\mu\), with both sides in \([0,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative measurable functions, the integral of the pointwise lower limit does not exceed the lower limit of the integrals; this applies in particular to an almost-everywhere limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Fatou-Type Passage

children.title: Integrable Lower-Bound Regimes
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound structures compatible with integral limit passage.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shifted Fatou Lemma for Pointwise Lower Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General liminf form under a common integrable lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a measure space. If measurable \(f_n:T\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) satisfy \(f_n\geq g\) almost everywhere for every \(n\), where \(g\in L^1(T)\), then \[\int_T\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_Tf_n\,d\mu.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common integrable lower bound yields Fatou's inequality for the full pointwise lower limit without requiring pointwise convergence.
assumptions_latex: There is \(g\in L^1(T)\) with \(f_n\geq g\) almost everywhere for every \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \int_T\liminf_n f_n\,d\mu\leq\liminf_n\int_Tf_n\,d\mu.
knowledge_statements.title: Shifted Fatou Lemma for Pointwise Lower Limits

assumptions_latex: \(f_n:T\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is measurable for every \(n\), and \(f_n\to f\) almost everywhere.
There exists \(g\in L^1(T)\) such that \(f_n\ge g\) almost everywhere for every \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\int_T f\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_T f_n\,d\mu\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shifted Fatou lemma under a common integrable lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a measure space. Suppose that measurable functions \(f_n:T\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) converge to \(f\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(t\), and that there exists \(g\in L^1(T)\) such that \(f_n(t)\ge g(t)\) for almost every \(t\) and every \(n\). Then \(f(t)\ge g(t)\) almost everywhere and \(\int_T f\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_T f_n\,d\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An almost-everywhere convergent sequence with a common integrable lower bound satisfies the Fatou lower-limit inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrable Lower-Bound Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral convergence and lower bounds under uniform integrability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preserves the distinct hypotheses for the lower-semicontinuity conclusion, continuous-integrand convergence, converse criterion, and p-growth characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mu_n\to\mu\) narrowly in \(\mathcal P(X)\). If \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is continuous, \(g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous, and \(|f|\) and \(g^-\) are uniformly integrable with respect to \(\{\mu_n:n\in\mathbb N\}\), then
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_X g\,d\mu_n\ge \int_X g\,d\mu>-\infty,
\qquad
\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_X f\,d\mu_n=\int_X f\,d\mu.
\]
Conversely, if \(f:X\to[0,+\infty)\) is continuous and \(\mu_n\)-integrable and
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\int_X f\,d\mu_n\le \int_X f\,d\mu<+\infty,
\]
then \(f\) is uniformly integrable with respect to \(\{\mu_n\}\). In particular, for \(p>0\), \(\{\mu_n\}\) has uniformly integrable \(p\)-moments if and only if
\[
\int_X h\,d\mu_n\to\int_X h\,d\mu
\]
for every continuous \(h:X\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(|h(x)|\le A+B d(x,\bar x)^p\) for some \(A,B\ge0\) and \(\bar x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For narrowly convergent probability measures, uniform integrability of the negative part of a lower-semicontinuous integrand yields a finite lower bound, while uniform integrability of the absolute value of a continuous integrand yields convergence of its integrals. The stated finite limsup condition gives a converse for nonnegative continuous integrands. Uniformly integrable p-moments are equivalent to convergence against every continuous function of p-growth.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(\mu_n,\mu\in\mathcal P(X)\).
For the forward conclusions, \(f\) is continuous, \(g\) is lower semicontinuous, and \(|f|\) and \(g^-\) are uniformly integrable with respect to \(\{\mu_n\}\).
For the converse, \(f\ge0\) is continuous and \(\mu_n\)-integrable, and the stated limsup is bounded by the finite integral \(\int_X f\,d\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_X g\,d\mu_n\ge\int_X g\,d\mu>-\infty,\qquad \int_X f\,d\mu_n\to\int_X f\,d\mu,\text{ together with the stated converse and }p\text{-growth equivalence.}

children.title: Negative-Part Control
children.top_down_role: Uniform control of negative contributions in varying integrands.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative-Part Fatou Passage under Convergence in Measure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence-in-measure variant on a finite measure space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a finite measure space. Suppose \(f_n:T\to\mathbb R\) are integrable, \(f_n\to f\) in measure, and \(\{f_n^-:n\geq1\}\) is uniformly integrable. Then \(f^-\in L^1(T)\) and \[\int_Tf\,d\mu\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_Tf_n\,d\mu.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform integrability of negative parts yields the Fatou lower bound under convergence in measure as well as under almost-everywhere convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^-\in L^1(T),\qquad\int_Tf\,d\mu\leq\liminf_n\int_Tf_n\,d\mu.
knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Part Fatou Passage under Convergence in Measure

assumptions_latex: Each \(f_n:T\to\mathbb R\) is integrable, and \(f_n\to f\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^-\in L^1(T)\) and \(\int_T f\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_T f_n\,d\mu\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized Fatou passage on a finite measure space controlled by uniform integrability of the negative parts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a finite measure space, and let \(f_n:T\to\mathbb R\) be integrable measurable functions such that \(f_n\to f\) almost everywhere. Define \(f_n^-=
\max\{-f_n,0\}\). Assume that \(\{f_n^-:n\ge1\}\) is uniformly integrable, meaning that \(\lim_{K\to\infty}\sup_n\int_{\{f_n^->K\}}f_n^-\,d\mu=0\). Then \(f^-\in L^1(T)\) and \(\int_T f\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_T f_n\,d\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite measure space, uniform integrability of the negative parts prevents escaping negative mass and yields the generalized Fatou lower-limit inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Part Control

children.title: Lower-Bound Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Loss of semicontinuity when lower control degenerates.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(f_n\to0\) almost everywhere, \(0=\int_T0\,dt>\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_T f_n\,dt=-1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concentrating negative mass violates Fatou passage without lower-bound control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(T=(0,1)\) with Lebesgue measure, set \(f_n(t)=-n\mathbf 1_{(0,1/n)}(t)\). Then \(f_n(t)\to0\) for every \(t\in(0,1)\), but \(\int_0^1 f_n(t)\,dt=-1\) for every \(n\ge1\). Consequently, for the almost-everywhere limit \(f=0\), one has \(\int_0^1 f(t)\,dt=0>-1=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_0^1 f_n(t)\,dt\). The negative parts are not uniformly integrable, and the sequence has no common integrable lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative mass concentrating on shrinking sets can disappear pointwise while retaining fixed integral mass, reversing the desired Fatou inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bound Failure Regimes

children.title: Equiintegrability Regimes
children.top_down_role: Uniform-integrability structures governing passage under integration.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar L1 characterization on a finite measure space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a finite measure space. A set \(\mathcal F\subset L^1(T)\) is relatively compact for \(\sigma(L^1,L^\infty)\) if and only if it is equiintegrable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite measure space, equiintegrability is equivalent to relative weak compactness in L1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F\text{ is relatively weakly compact in }L^1(T)\iff\mathcal F\text{ is equiintegrable}.

notation.meaning: weak topology on L1 induced by L-infinity

knowledge_statements.title: Dunford–Pettis Weak-Compactness Characterization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: L1 passage characterized by convergence in measure plus equiintegrability on a finite measure space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a finite measure space and let \(f_n,f\in L^1(T)\). Then \(f_n\to f\) in \(L^1(T)\) if and only if \(f_n\to f\) in measure and \(\{f_n:n\geq1\}\) is equiintegrable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite measure space, convergence in measure together with equiintegrability is exactly L1 convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_n\to f\text{ in }L^1\iff f_n\to f\text{ in measure and }\{f_n\}\text{ is equiintegrable}.

notation.meaning: integral convergence of the absolute difference

knowledge_statements.title: Vitali Convergence Theorem

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Superlinear integral characterization on a finite measure space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a finite measure space and \(\mathcal F\subset L^1(T)\). The family \(\mathcal F\) is equiintegrable if and only if there exists an increasing convex function \(\Phi:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty)\) such that \(\Phi(r)/r\to+\infty\) and \(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\int_T\Phi(|f|)\,d\mu<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equiintegrability is equivalent to a uniform integral bound through some convex superlinear gauge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F\text{ is equiintegrable}\iff\exists\Phi:\ \Phi(r)/r\to\infty,\ \sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\int_T\Phi(|f|)\,d\mu<\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: de la Vallée Poussin Criterion

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\) is equiintegrable exactly when it is uniformly bounded in \(L^1\) and its integrals are uniformly absolutely continuous; equivalently, its large-value tails vanish uniformly.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform absolute-continuity definition and tail characterization on a finite measure space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a finite measure space. A family \(\mathcal F\subset L^1(T)\) is equiintegrable if \(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\int_T|f|\,d\mu<\infty\) and, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(\delta>0\) such that, for every \(A\in\Sigma\), \(\mu(A)<\delta\) implies \(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\int_A|f|\,d\mu<\varepsilon\). On a finite measure space this is equivalent to \(\lim_{K\to\infty}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\int_{\{|f|>K\}}|f|\,d\mu=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite measure space, equiintegrability means uniformly bounded L1 mass together with uniform absolute continuity of the integrals, equivalently uniformly vanishing large-value tails.
knowledge_statements.title: Equiintegrability Regimes

children.title: Convex-Integrand Weak Semicontinuity
children.top_down_role: Weak semicontinuity families supported by fiberwise convexity.

assumptions_latex: \(f:T\times\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a convex normal integrand.
There exist \(a\in L^1(T)\) and \(b\in L^q(T;\mathbb R^d)\) such that \(f(t,z)\ge a(t)+\langle b(t),z\rangle\) for almost every \(t\) and every \(z\in\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\) in \(L^p(T;\mathbb R^d)\), then \(I_f(x)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}I_f(x_n)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential weak lower semicontinuity on reflexive \(L^p\) under an affine integrable minorant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a measure space, let \(1<p<\infty\), and set \(q=p/(p-1)\). Suppose \(f:T\times\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a convex normal integrand and admits the affine minorant \(f(t,z)\ge a(t)+\langle b(t),z\rangle\) for almost every \(t\in T\) and every \(z\in\mathbb R^d\), where \(a\in L^1(T)\) and \(b\in L^q(T;\mathbb R^d)\). Then \(I_f(x)=\int_T f(t,x(t))\,d\mu(t)\) is sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous on \(L^p(T;\mathbb R^d)\): if \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\), then \(I_f(x)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}I_f(x_n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fiberwise convexity and an integrable affine lower bound make the integral functional sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous on reflexive Lp.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Integrand Weak Semicontinuity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General Banach-space principle proposed as a local record, but its canonical home is general convex functional analysis rather than this integral-functional leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(I:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, convex, and norm-lower-semicontinuous. Then \(I\) is weakly lower-semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper convex norm-lower-semicontinuous functional on a Banach space is weakly lower-semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_\alpha\rightharpoonup x\Longrightarrow I(x)\leq\liminf_\alpha I(x_\alpha).
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Strong-to-Weak Lower Semicontinuity Principle

intermediate_metadata.reason: The locally owned inventory is the convex-normal-integrand weak-liminf theorem under an affine integrable minorant. The proposed general Banach-space convex-functional principle was deferred because its canonical home is broader convex analysis. Fatou passage, equiintegrability, and state-integral failures are excluded to their sibling scopes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint lower semicontinuity and fiberwise convexity, measurable composition, an integrable affine lower bound, and closed admissibility constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume: (a) \(F(x,\cdot,\cdot)\) is lower semicontinuous in \((u,z)\) and convex in \(z\); (b) for every measurable \(u:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{\ell}\) satisfying \((x,u(x))\in Q\) a.e. and every measurable \(z:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^n\), the function \(x\mapsto F(x,u(x),z(x))\) is measurable; (c) there exist \(\alpha\in L^1(\Omega)\) and \(\beta\in L^{\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^n)\) such that \(F(x,u,z)\geq\alpha(x)+\langle\beta(x),z\rangle\) for all \((x,u)\in Q\) and \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\); and (d) \(Q\) is closed in \(\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^{\ell}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The semicontinuity hypothesis requires lower semicontinuity in the decision variables, convexity in the weakly convergent variable, measurability along every admissible measurable pair, a uniform integrable affine lower bound in that variable, and closedness of the admissibility set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conditions (a)--(d) constitute the convex-integrand integral-semicontinuity hypothesis.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral semicontinuity under almost-everywhere and weak convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower semicontinuity of the source-defined integral functional under Hypothesis 6.37.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume Hypothesis 6.37. Let \((u_i)\) be measurable functions satisfying \((x,u_i(x))\in Q\) almost everywhere and converging almost everywhere to \(u_*\). If \(r>1\) and \(z_i\rightharpoonup z_*\) in \(L^r(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^n)\), then \[J(u_*,z_*)\leq\liminf_{i\to\infty}J(u_i,z_i).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the preceding integral-semicontinuity hypothesis, almost-everywhere convergence of admissible u-components and weak L-r convergence of z-components imply the lower-limit inequality for the associated integral functional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J(u_*,z_*)\leq\liminf_{i\to\infty}J(u_i,z_i).

children.title: State-Integral Semicontinuity Failures
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by negative-part escape, concentration, or inadequate topology.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak lower-semicontinuity failure caused by unresolved state oscillations and a nonconvex integrand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega=(0,1)\), let \((r_n)\) be the Rademacher functions, and set \(f(s)=(1-s^2)^2\) and \(I(u)=\int_\Omega f(u(x))\,dx\), with the integral interpreted as extended-valued on \(L^2(\Omega)\). Then \(r_n\rightharpoonup0\) in \(L^2(\Omega)\), but \(I(r_n)=0\) for every \(n\), whereas \(I(0)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weakly vanishing oscillations can have strictly less energy than their weak limit when the state integrand is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_n\rightharpoonup0\text{ in }L^2(\Omega),\qquad I(0)=1>0=\liminf_{n\to\infty}I(r_n).
knowledge_statements.title: Oscillatory Weak-Semicontinuity Failure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative-Energy Escape on an Unbounded Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak lower-semicontinuity failure caused by translation of negative energy to spatial infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(1<p<\infty\), \(\Omega=\mathbb R\), \(u_n=\mathbf 1_{(n,n+1)}\), and \(I(u)=-\int_{\mathbb R}|u(x)|^p\,dx\). Then \(u_n\rightharpoonup0\) in \(L^p(\mathbb R)\), while \(I(u_n)=-1\) for every \(n\) and \(I(0)=0\). Hence \(I\) is not sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translating a fixed negative-energy profile to infinity gives weak convergence to zero while its negative integral energy remains unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u_n\rightharpoonup0\text{ in }L^p(\mathbb R),\qquad I(0)=0>-1=\liminf_{n\to\infty}I(u_n).

notation.meaning: State integral with an uncontrolled negative part

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Energy Escape on an Unbounded Domain

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_n\to0\) in \(L^1(\Omega)\) and in measure, but \(I(0)=0>\liminf_{n\to\infty}I(u_n)=-1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure caused by concentration of an uncontrolled negative part.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u_n=\sqrt n\,\mathbf 1_{(0,1/n)}\). Then \(\|u_n\|_{L^1(\Omega)}=n^{-1/2}\to0\), so \(u_n\to0\) strongly in \(L^1(\Omega)\) and in measure. Nevertheless, \[I(u_n)=\int_0^1-u_n(x)^2\,dx=-1,\qquad I(0)=0.\] Thus \(I\) is not sequentially lower semicontinuous for either convergence. The negative parts \(f(u_n)^-=u_n^2\) concentrate on shrinking sets and are not uniformly integrable, preventing a Fatou-type lower-bound passage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong L1 convergence does not ensure lower semicontinuity when the integrand's negative part concentrates without uniform-integrability control.
knowledge_statements.title: State-Integral Semicontinuity Failures

children.title: Scalar Convexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Convex-gradient criteria for scalar weak lower semicontinuity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit scalar weak-lower-semicontinuity failure generated by fine gradient oscillations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\Omega=(0,1)\), let \(f(z)=(z^2-1)^2\). There are piecewise-affine \(u_j\in W^{1,4}_0(0,1)\) whose derivatives alternate with equal proportions between \(-1\) and \(1\) on cells of vanishing size, such that \(u_j\rightharpoonup0\) in \(W^{1,4}(0,1)\), while \[\int_0^1 f(u_j'(x))\,dx=0<1=\int_0^1f(0)\,dx.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fine oscillations between the wells of a nonconvex scalar density violate weak lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\mapsto\int_0^1f(u')\,dx\) is not sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous at zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Double-Well Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity complementing scalar convex-integral lower-semicontinuity sufficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a bounded Lipschitz domain, \(1<p<\infty\), and let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuous with \(|f(z)|\le C(1+|z|^p)\). If \[I(u)=\int_\Omega f(\nabla u(x))\,dx\] is sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous on \(W^{1,p}(\Omega)\), then \(f\) is convex. Together with the immutable sufficiency result, weak lower semicontinuity is equivalent to convexity in this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For continuous autonomous scalar-gradient integrands with finite p-growth, sequential weak lower semicontinuity is equivalent to convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous on \(W^{1,p}(\Omega)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Necessity of Convexity

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) is bounded and open, and \(1<p<\infty\).
\(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is convex, continuous, and satisfies \(|f(z)|\le C(1+|z|^p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The functional \(I(u)=\int_\Omega f(\nabla u(x))\,dx\) is sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous on \(W^{1,p}(\Omega)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Autonomous scalar first-order integral functionals with standard finite \(p\)-growth.

children.title: Morrey Quasiconvexity

children.title: Quasiconvex Integrands
children.top_down_role: The principal vectorial lower-semicontinuity class.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cell representation of the largest quasiconvex minorant in the standard finite continuous coercive regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) be finite and continuous with standard coercive \(p\)-growth. Its quasiconvex envelope is characterized by \[Qf(F)=\inf_{\varphi\in W^{1,\infty}_0(Q;\mathbb R^m)}\frac1{|Q|}\int_Q f(F+\nabla\varphi(x))\,dx.\] Under these hypotheses, \(Qf\) is the largest quasiconvex function not exceeding \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing cell energy over zero-boundary gradient perturbations produces the largest quasiconvex minorant.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is finite and continuous with standard coercive \(p\)-growth.
\(Q\) is a bounded Lipschitz reference cell.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed cell formula defines the largest quasiconvex minorant \(Qf\).
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvex Envelope by Cell Relaxation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between quasiconvexity and weak lower semicontinuity for nonnegative autonomous gradient densities with p-growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be bounded and Lipschitz, \(1<p<\infty\), and let \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to[0,\infty)\) be continuous with \[f(\xi)\le C(1+|\xi|^p).\] Then \[I(u)=\int_\Omega f(\nabla u)\,dx\] is sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous on \(W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) if and only if \(f\) is quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous nonnegative autonomous density with p-growth, Morrey quasiconvexity is exactly the condition for sequential weak lower semicontinuity of its gradient integral.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuous, nonnegative, and has an upper \(p\)-growth bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\) is sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous exactly when \(f\) is quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.title: Morrey Weak Lower-Semicontinuity Criterion

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is Borel measurable and locally integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is quasiconvex precisely when the displayed averaged-gradient inequality holds for every matrix and compactly supported smooth perturbation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Morrey quasiconvexity for finite autonomous first-order integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The integrand \(f\) is quasiconvex if, for every \(F\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and every \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)\), \[f(F)\le \frac1{|Q|}\int_Q f\bigl(F+\nabla\varphi(x)\bigr)\,dx.\] Equivalently, the affine map with gradient \(F\) cannot have its energy lowered by a zero-boundary oscillatory perturbation on a bounded Lipschitz reference domain. Under customary continuity and \(p\)-growth hypotheses, this condition is the central vectorial criterion for sequential weak lower semicontinuity of autonomous gradient integrals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasiconvex integrand assigns no lower average energy to any compactly supported gradient oscillation around a constant matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvex Integrands

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed inequality is the standard quasiconvexity condition, but local integrability of a merely Borel integrand does not transparently ensure every composed integral is defined. A source is required to settle the intended definition variant and the added equivalence and lower-semicontinuity claims.
