children.title: Quasiconvexity Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Failure of weaker convexity notions to guarantee vectorial semicontinuity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weakly convergent energy-lowering sequences arising from a failed quasiconvexity test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to[0,\infty)\) be continuous with \(p\)-growth. If for some \(F\) and \(\varphi\in W^{1,\infty}_0(Q;\mathbb R^m)\), \[\int_Q f(F+\nabla\varphi)\,dx<|Q|f(F),\] then there exists a sequence \(u_j\rightharpoonup \ell_F\) in \(W^{1,p}(Q;\mathbb R^m)\), with the same boundary trace as \(\ell_F(x)=Fx\), such that \[\limsup_{j\to\infty}\int_Qf(\nabla u_j)\,dx<\int_Qf(F)\,dx.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure of one quasiconvexity cell test yields a weakly convergent sequence whose energy lies strictly below that of its affine limit.
assumptions_latex: The displayed zero-boundary quasiconvexity test fails at \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The associated gradient integral is not sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous at \(\ell_F\).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonquasiconvexity Produces Weak-LSC Failure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Collapse in Scalar and One-Dimensional Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimensional boundary for strict separation between rank-one convexity and quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(m=1\) or \(n=1\), every matrix difference has rank at most one. Hence, for finite continuous integrands on \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \[\text{rank-one convexity}\iff\text{convexity}\iff\text{quasiconvexity}.\] Strict rank-one-convex versus quasiconvex separation therefore requires \(m,n\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank-one convexity and quasiconvexity coincide for scalar-valued maps or one-dimensional domains; strict separation is genuinely vectorial and multidimensional.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is finite and continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rank-one convexity, convexity, and quasiconvexity are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Collapse in Scalar and One-Dimensional Regimes

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rank-one convexity alone does not imply Morrey quasiconvexity and therefore cannot by itself guarantee weak lower semicontinuity of vectorial gradient integrals.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Šverák-type separation in a genuinely vectorial matrix space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a finite rank-one convex function \(f:\mathbb R^{3\times2}\to\mathbb R\) that is not quasiconvex. Thus, although \(t\mapsto f(F+t(a\otimes b))\) is convex for every \(F\in\mathbb R^{3\times2}\), \(a\in\mathbb R^3\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^2\), there are \(F\) and \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty((0,1)^2;\mathbb R^3)\) for which \[f(F)>\int_{(0,1)^2}f(F+\nabla\varphi(x))\,dx.\] Hence testing only simple rank-one laminations misses more complicated gradient microstructures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In vectorial dimensions, rank-one convexity is strictly weaker than quasiconvexity and does not suffice for weak lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvexity Failure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated 3-by-2 separation is a source-dependent Šverák-type result. Its exact finiteness, regularity, and implications for weak lower semicontinuity require a specific counterexample citation.

children.title: Polyconvexity
children.top_down_role: Minor-based sufficient structure for vectorial semicontinuity and existence.

children.title: Minor-Based Representations
children.top_down_role: Convex representations through gradient minors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic behavior of minor coordinates along rank-one lines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(a\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^n\), every minor coordinate is affine along \(F+t(a\otimes b)\). Thus every selected minor \(D_k\) satisfies \[D_k(F+t(a\otimes b))=D_k(F)+t\beta_k\] for some constant \(\beta_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every matrix minor varies affinely along a rank-one line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each coordinate of \(M(F+t(a\otimes b))\) is affine in \(t\).
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-One Affinity of Minors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-hyperplane form for a proper lower-semicontinuous convex representative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f=g\circ M\), where \(g:\mathbb R^N\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Then \[f(F)=\sup_{(p,c)\in\mathcal A}\bigl\{\langle p,M(F)\rangle+c\bigr\},\qquad \mathcal A=\{(p,c):\langle p,z\rangle+c\le g(z)\ \forall z\}.\] Conversely, every pointwise supremum of affine functions of the full minor vector is polyconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex minor representation is equivalently a supremum of minor-affine functions.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) has the displayed supremal representation by affine combinations of minors.

notation.meaning: Affine minorants of the convex representative

knowledge_statements.title: Supporting Minor-Affine Representation
Minor-Based Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued polyconvexity through all gradient minors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=\min\{m,n\}\), let \(M_k(F)\) denote the vector of all \(k\times k\) minors of \(F\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and set \(M(F)=(M_1(F),\ldots,M_r(F))\in\mathbb R^N\), where \(N=\sum_{k=1}^r\binom{m}{k}\binom{n}{k}\). The integrand \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is polyconvex if there exists a convex function \(g:\mathbb R^N\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) such that \[f(F)=g(M(F))\qquad\text{for every }F\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}.\] Here \(M_1(F)=F\), and when \(m=n\), the highest-order minor is \(\det F\). Lower semicontinuity of \(g\) is an additional regularity condition, not part of this basic representation definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyconvex density is a convex function of the full vector of matrix minors; lower semicontinuity of the representing convex function is an additional condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is polyconvex exactly when it admits a convex representation in the full vector of minors.

notation.meaning: Vector of all minors of orders one through \(r\)

children.title: Determinant-Sensitive Regimes
children.top_down_role: Polyconvex structures coupled to orientation and determinant behavior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Continuity Threshold for the Determinant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sobolev regime in which determinant minors pass to weak limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u_j\rightharpoonup u\) in \(W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^n)\) with \(p\ge n\). Then \[\det\nabla u_j\to\det\nabla u\] in distributions. If \(p>n\), the determinants are bounded in \(L^{p/n}\) and converge weakly in that space. At \(p=n\), the general conclusion is distributional; stronger \(L^1\)-type convergence requires additional equiintegrability. Below this regime, concentration can obstruct passage to the limit without extra control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At and above the natural Sobolev threshold, determinants pass to weak limits distributionally; stronger weak Lebesgue convergence holds above the endpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Determinants converge distributionally, and weakly in \(L^{p/n}\) when \(p>n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Continuity Threshold for the Determinant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-semicontinuity boundary between nonnegative and strictly positive determinant constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: As functions of the determinant coordinate, \[\iota_{[0,\infty)}\ \text{is convex and lower semicontinuous},\qquad \iota_{(0,\infty)}\ \text{is convex but not lower semicontinuous at }0.\] In particular, for \(F_j=\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,j^{-1})\to F=\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,0)\), the strict-orientation indicator has value \(0\) at every \(F_j\) and \(+\infty\) at \(F\). A lower-semicontinuous strict-orientation model may instead use a convex barrier \(h\) with \[h(d)=+\infty\ (d\le0),\qquad h(d)\to+\infty\quad(d\downarrow0).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative-determinant constraint is closed, while the bare positive-determinant indicator is not lower semicontinuous; strict orientation requires a barrier blowing up near zero.
assumptions_latex: The determinant is a coordinate of the full minor map.
Indicators equal zero on their constraint set and positive infinity outside.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Closed orientation constraints are lower semicontinuous, whereas strict positivity requires a blow-up barrier to obtain a lower-semicontinuous density.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Versus Strict Orientation Constraint

assumptions_latex: \(g:\mathbb R^N\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The density \(f(F)=g(M(F))+\iota_{(0,\infty)}(\det F)\) is extended-valued polyconvex and enforces positive orientation.

notation.meaning: Indicator taking zero on the set and positive infinity outside

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued orientation constraint expressed in the determinant coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[f(F)=g(M(F))+\iota_{(0,\infty)}(\det F),\] where \(\iota_{(0,\infty)}(d)=0\) for \(d>0\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise. Because the positivity constraint is convex in the scalar determinant coordinate, this formula is a polyconvex representation and gives finite energy only to orientation-preserving matrices. Weak lower semicontinuity of the associated integral additionally requires growth and integrability assumptions ensuring the relevant minors behave continuously under the chosen weak Sobolev convergence; these assumptions cannot be omitted merely from polyconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Determinant constraints fit polyconvex representations, but weak lower semicontinuity also depends on growth and weak continuity of the minors.
knowledge_statements.title: Determinant-Sensitive Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-determinant indicator is convex as a function of the determinant coordinate and therefore gives a standard polyconvex constraint, but it is not lower semicontinuous at determinant zero. A source is needed to distinguish basic polyconvexity from the stronger lower-semicontinuity regime.

children.title: Rank-One Lamination Geometry
children.top_down_role: Rank-one directional geometry and laminated oscillation structures.

children.title: Rank-One Directional Geometry
children.top_down_role: Directional behavior along rank-one connected matrix states.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Twice-differentiable characterization of rank-one convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^{m\times n})\). Then \(f\) is rank-one convex if and only if \[D^2f(F)[a\otimes b,a\otimes b]\ge0\] for every \(F\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(a\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A twice continuously differentiable integrand is rank-one convex exactly when its Hessian is nonnegative in every rank-one direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is rank-one convex exactly when its Hessian is nonnegative on all \(a\otimes b\).

notation.meaning: Hessian quadratic form at \(F\) in direction \(H\)

knowledge_statements.title: Legendre–Hadamard Rank-One Condition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact compatibility criterion for two constant gradients across a planar interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a continuous piecewise-affine map have gradients \(F^+\) and \(F^-\) on the two sides of a planar interface with nonzero normal \(\nu\). Continuity across the interface holds exactly when \[F^+-F^-=a\otimes\nu\] for some \(a\in\mathbb R^m\). Conversely, every jump of this form admits a continuous two-phase affine construction across that interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two constant gradients meet continuously across a planar interface exactly when their jump is a tensor product with the interface normal.
assumptions_latex: The map is continuous and affine on each side of a planar interface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^+-F^-=a\otimes\nu\) for some \(a\), and this condition is sufficient.

notation.meaning: Nonzero normal to the planar interface

knowledge_statements.title: Hadamard Jump Compatibility

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The segment joining \(F\) and \(G\) is a rank-one segment exactly when \(G-F=a\otimes b\) for nonzero vectors \(a,b\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of first-order compatible two-phase gradient mixtures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Matrices \(F\) and \(G\) are rank-one connected when \(\operatorname{rank}(G-F)=1\), equivalently \(G-F=a\otimes b\) for some nonzero \(a\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^n\). A continuous function \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is rank-one convex when, for every such pair and every \(t\in[0,1]\), \[f((1-t)F+tG)\le(1-t)f(F)+t f(G).\] Rank-one directions are precisely the jump-compatible directions for piecewise-affine gradients across planar interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank-one directions connect matrix phases whose difference is a tensor product and which can form compatible planar gradient mixtures.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-One Directional Geometry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Realization of finite splitting data by homogeneous piecewise-affine gradient oscillations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu=\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i\delta_{F_i}\) be a finite-order laminate with barycenter \(F\), and let \(Q\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a cube. There are piecewise-affine maps \(u_j:Q\to\mathbb R^m\) with \(u_j(x)=Fx\) on \(\partial Q\), \(u_j\to(x\mapsto Fx)\) uniformly, and uniformly bounded gradients such that \[(\nabla u_j)_\#\bigl(|Q|^{-1}\mathcal L^n\!\restriction_Q\bigr)\rightharpoonup^*\mu.\] Equivalently, \[\frac1{|Q|}\int_Q\psi(\nabla u_j(x))\,dx\to\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i\psi(F_i)\] for every continuous \(\psi:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite laminate is generated by fine compatible piecewise-affine gradient oscillations having the prescribed phase fractions and affine boundary value.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a finite-order laminate with barycenter \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Affine-boundary piecewise-affine gradients generate \(\mu\) as a homogeneous gradient Young measure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous laminate measures generated by compatible sequential splittings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Begin with \(\delta_F\). Replace an atom \(\lambda\delta_A\) by \(\lambda[\theta\delta_B+(1-\theta)\delta_C]\), where \(0<\theta<1\), \(A=\theta B+(1-\theta)C\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(B-C)=1\). Each replacement preserves total mass and barycenter. Measures obtainable after finitely many replacements are finite-order laminates; compactly supported weak-star limits of such measures are laminates. Consequently every continuous rank-one convex \(h\) satisfies the Jensen inequality \[h(\bar\mu)\le\int h(F)\,d\mu(F).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Laminate measures encode microstructures built through successive compatible rank-one phase splittings while preserving their average gradient.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Plane-Stress Conjugate Energy and Optimal Rank-1 Laminate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-dimensional stress with one zero and two nonzero principal stresses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a three-dimensional stress \(\sigma\) have eigenvalues \(\sigma_1=0\), \(\sigma_2\neq0\), and \(\sigma_3\neq0\). Then
\[
g^*(\sigma)=\frac{\sigma_2^2+\sigma_3^2}{2\mu}-\frac{\lambda}{2\mu(2\mu+3\lambda)}(\sigma_2+\sigma_3)^2.
\]
Optimality is achieved by a rank-1 sequential laminate in the direction of an eigenvector corresponding to \(\sigma_1=0\), with
\[
(m_1,m_2,m_3)=(1,0,0).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a three-dimensional plane stress with one zero and two nonzero eigenvalues, the conjugate energy has the stated quadratic formula. It is attained by a rank-1 laminate directed along an eigenvector associated with the zero eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g^*(\sigma)=\frac{\sigma_2^2+\sigma_3^2}{2\mu}-\frac{\lambda(\sigma_2+\sigma_3)^2}{2\mu(2\mu+3\lambda)}\), attained by the rank-1 laminate in the zero-eigenvalue direction with \((m_1,m_2,m_3)=(1,0,0)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementary-energy lower bound for the void case, under the notation and hypotheses defining the G-closure and nonlocal term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_p\in\mathcal M_N^s\), \(A^*\in G_\theta\), and let the constituent \(A=0\). Then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^p A^{*-1}\sigma_i:\sigma_i\geq \sum_{i=1}^p B^{-1}\sigma_i:\sigma_i+\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}g^*(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_p),
\]
where
\[
g^*(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_p)=\max_{(\eta_i)_{i=1}^p\in(\mathcal M_N^s)^p}\left(\sum_{i=1}^p2\sigma_i:\eta_i-g^c(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_p)\right).
\]
Moreover, \(g^*\) is continuous, convex, strictly positive unless all \(\sigma_i\) vanish, and homogeneous of degree two.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an elastic composite with a void constituent, the effective complementary energy is bounded below by the material-B energy plus a scaled conjugate term. That conjugate is continuous, convex, positive away from the zero stress tuple, and two-homogeneous.
assumptions_latex: The displayed expressions are defined under the underlying G-closure hypotheses
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_i A^{*-1}\sigma_i:\sigma_i\geq\sum_i B^{-1}\sigma_i:\sigma_i+\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}g^*(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_p)\), and \(g^*\) has the stated continuity, convexity, positivity, and homogeneity properties.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Three-Dimensional Zero-Lambda Bound and Optimal Laminates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two spectral regimes when the first Lamé parameter vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the hypotheses of bound (2.150), assume \(N=3\), \(\lambda=0\), and label the eigenvalues so that \(|\sigma_1|\leq|\sigma_2|\leq|\sigma_3|\). If \(|\sigma_3|\leq|\sigma_1|+|\sigma_2|\), then
\[
A^{*-1}\sigma:\sigma\geq B^{-1}\sigma:\sigma+\frac{\theta}{4\mu(1-\theta)}\bigl(|\sigma_1|+|\sigma_2|+|\sigma_3|\bigr)^2.
\]
Optimality is achieved by a rank-3 sequential laminate with
\[
m_1=\frac{|\sigma_3|+|\sigma_2|-|\sigma_1|}{S},\quad
m_2=\frac{|\sigma_1|-|\sigma_2|+|\sigma_3|}{S},\quad
m_3=\frac{|\sigma_1|+|\sigma_2|-|\sigma_3|}{S},
\]
where \(S=|\sigma_1|+|\sigma_2|+|\sigma_3|\).
If \(|\sigma_3|\geq|\sigma_1|+|\sigma_2|\), then
\[
A^{*-1}\sigma:\sigma\geq B^{-1}\sigma:\sigma+\frac{\theta}{2\mu(1-\theta)}\left((|\sigma_1|+|\sigma_2|)^2+|\sigma_3|^2\right),
\]
and optimality is achieved by a rank-2 sequential laminate with
\[
m_1=\frac{|\sigma_2|}{|\sigma_1|+|\sigma_2|},\qquad
m_2=\frac{|\sigma_1|}{|\sigma_1|+|\sigma_2|},\qquad m_3=0,
\]
whenever the displayed parameterizations are defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When lambda is zero, the three-dimensional bound has two regimes according to whether the largest absolute principal stress satisfies the triangle inequality. The regimes are attained by explicit rank-3 and rank-2 sequential laminates.
assumptions_latex: The applicable displayed laminate parameterization is defined
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The applicable one of the two stated lower bounds holds and is attained by the corresponding rank-3 or rank-2 sequential laminate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimality and sequential-laminate realization of a relaxed eigenvalue design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes a maximizer of a relaxed two-phase elastic first-eigenvalue design and gives a sequential-laminate realization, with a rank bound when the eigenvalue is simple.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If $(\theta,A^*)$ maximizes the relaxed formulation and $u$ is a corresponding first eigenvector, then, almost everywhere in $\Omega$, $$A^*e(u):e(u)=g(\theta,e(u))=\max_{B^*\in G_\theta} B^*e(u):e(u),$$ where $g$ is the upper Hashin--Shtrikman bound, and $\theta$ maximizes over $L^\infty(\Omega;[0,1])$ the functional $$\vartheta\mapsto\frac{\int_\Omega g(\vartheta,e(u))\,dx}{\int_\Omega \bar\rho(\vartheta)|u|^2\,dx}+\ell\int_\Omega\vartheta\,dx.$$ Moreover, there exists a sequential laminate $\widetilde A^*$ such that $(\theta,\widetilde A^*)$ is also a maximizer with the same first eigenvector $u$. If the first eigenvalue is simple, $\widetilde A^*$ may be chosen as a rank-$N$ sequential laminate whose lamination directions are the eigenvectors of $e(u)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any maximizing relaxed two-phase design and corresponding first eigenvector, the effective elasticity tensor pointwise attains the upper Hashin–Shtrikman bound over the admissible G-closure, while the phase fraction maximizes the induced scalar functional. An equally optimal sequential-laminate tensor exists with the same eigenvector; for a simple first eigenvalue it can be chosen of rank N with directions given by the strain tensor's eigenvectors.
assumptions_latex: (\theta,A^*)\text{ is a maximizer of the relaxed formulation}
u\text{ is a corresponding first eigenvector}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^*e(u):e(u)=g(\theta,e(u))=\max_{B^*\in G_\theta}B^*e(u):e(u)\ \text{a.e. in }\Omega;\quad \theta\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\vartheta\in L^\infty(\Omega;[0,1])}\left\{\frac{\int_\Omega g(\vartheta,e(u))\,dx}{\int_\Omega\bar\rho(\vartheta)|u|^2\,dx}+\ell\int_\Omega\vartheta\,dx\right\},\quad \exists\widetilde A^*\text{ sequential laminate giving the same optimum and first eigenvector};\ \lambda_1\text{ simple}\Rightarrow\widetilde A^*\text{ can be rank-}N\text{ with directions equal to the eigenvectors of }e(u).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lamination-stable elasticity class and sequential recursion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-phase effective elasticity tensors generated by repeated lamination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For elasticity phases $A$ and $B$ in proportions $\theta$ and $1-\theta$, $L_\theta\subset G_\theta$ is the smallest subset containing all simple laminates of the two phases and stable under lamination. A sequential laminate repeatedly laminates the preceding laminate with the same pure phase $A$. With $A_0^*=B$, directions $e_i$, and stage proportions $1-\theta_i,\theta_i$, it satisfies
\[
(1-\theta_p)(A_p^*-A)^{-1}=(A_{p-1}^*-A)^{-1}+\theta_p f_A(e_p),
\]
and
\[
\Bigl(\prod_{i=1}^p(1-\theta_i)\Bigr)(A_p^*-A)^{-1}=(B-A)^{-1}+\sum_{i=1}^p\theta_i\Bigl(\prod_{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\theta_j)\Bigr)f_A(e_i).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The laminated-material class is the smallest class containing all simple two-phase laminates and closed under further lamination. Sequential laminates repeatedly laminate the current material with the same matrix phase, and their effective Hooke tensors obey the displayed recursion and iterated formula.
assumptions_latex: A,B\text{ are the two elasticity phases}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_\theta\text{ is the lamination-stable hull of the simple laminates, and }A_p^*\text{ satisfies the displayed sequential-lamination formulas.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Dimensional Complementary-Energy Bound and Optimal Rank-2 Laminate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-dimensional specialization of the void-constituent Hashin–Shtrikman bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the hypotheses of the complementary-energy bound, let \(\sigma\in\mathcal M_2^s\) have eigenvalues \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\). Then
\[
A^{*-1}\sigma:\sigma\geq B^{-1}\sigma:\sigma+\frac{(\kappa+\mu)\theta}{4\kappa\mu(1-\theta)}\bigl(|\sigma_1|+|\sigma_2|\bigr)^2.
\]
An optimal rank-2 sequential laminate is obtained by using eigenvectors of \(\sigma\) as lamination directions and choosing
\[
m_1=\frac{|\sigma_2|}{|\sigma_1|+|\sigma_2|},\qquad m_2=\frac{|\sigma_1|}{|\sigma_1|+|\sigma_2|},
\]
when \(|\sigma_1|+|\sigma_2|>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In two dimensions, the complementary-energy lower bound is an explicit function of the absolute principal stresses. It is attained by a stress-eigenvector-aligned sequential laminate whose weights are proportional to the opposite absolute principal stress.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated two-dimensional lower bound holds, and the displayed eigenvector-aligned sequential laminate attains it.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Three-Dimensional Piecewise Complementary-Energy Bound and Optimal Laminates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-dimensional spectral regimes for material B with nonnegative Lamé parameter lambda.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the hypotheses of bound (2.150), assume \(N=3\), \(\lambda\geq0\), and order the eigenvalues as \(\sigma_1\leq\sigma_2\leq\sigma_3\). Then
\[
A^{*-1}\sigma:\sigma\geq B^{-1}\sigma:\sigma+\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}g^*(\sigma).
\]
For \(0\leq\sigma_1\leq\sigma_2\leq\sigma_3\),
\[
g^*(\sigma)=\frac{2\mu+\lambda}{4\mu(2\mu+3\lambda)}(\sigma_1+\sigma_2+\sigma_3)^2
\quad\text{if }\sigma_3\leq\sigma_1+\sigma_2,
\]
and
\[
g^*(\sigma)=\frac{(\sigma_1+\sigma_2)^2+\sigma_3^2}{2\mu}-\frac{\lambda(\sigma_1+\sigma_2+\sigma_3)^2}{2\mu(2\mu+3\lambda)}
\quad\text{if }\sigma_3\geq\sigma_1+\sigma_2.
\]
For \(\sigma_1\leq0\leq\sigma_2\leq\sigma_3\),
\[
g^*(\sigma)=\frac{2\mu+\lambda}{4\mu(2\mu+3\lambda)}\left(\sigma_3+\sigma_2-\frac{\mu+2\lambda}{\mu+\lambda}\sigma_1\right)^2
\]
if \(\sigma_3+\sigma_2\geq-\frac\mu{\mu+\lambda}\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_3-\sigma_2\leq-\frac\mu{\mu+\lambda}\sigma_1\);
\[
g^*(\sigma)=\frac{(\sigma_3+\sigma_2)^2+\sigma_1^2}{2\mu}-\frac{\lambda(\sigma_1+\sigma_2+\sigma_3)^2}{2\mu(2\mu+3\lambda)}
\]
if \(\sigma_3+\sigma_2\leq-\frac\mu{\mu+\lambda}\sigma_1\); and
\[
g^*(\sigma)=\frac{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2+\sigma_3^2}{2\mu}-\frac{\sigma_1\sigma_2}{\mu+\lambda}-\frac{\lambda(\sigma_1+\sigma_2+\sigma_3)^2}{2\mu(2\mu+3\lambda)}
\]
if \(\sigma_3-\sigma_2\geq-\frac\mu{\mu+\lambda}\sigma_1\). Other sign cases follow by replacing \(\sigma\) with \(-\sigma\).

The bound is attained in every regime by a sequential laminate aligned with the eigenvectors of \(\sigma\). In the five regimes above, respectively, the ranks are \(3,2,3,2,2\), and the parameters are
\[
(m_1,m_2,m_3)=\frac{(\sigma_3+\sigma_2-\sigma_1,\,\sigma_1-\sigma_2+\sigma_3,\,\sigma_1+\sigma_2-\sigma_3)}{\sigma_1+\sigma_2+\sigma_3},
\]
\[
(m_1,m_2,m_3)=\left(\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1+\sigma_2},\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_1+\sigma_2},0\right),
\]
\[
m_1=\frac{\sigma_3+\sigma_2+\frac\mu{\mu+\lambda}\sigma_1}{\sigma_3+\sigma_2-\frac{\mu+2\lambda}{\mu+\lambda}\sigma_1},\quad
m_2=\frac{\mu+\lambda}{\mu}\frac{\sigma_3-\sigma_2-\frac\mu{\mu+\lambda}\sigma_1}{\sigma_3+\sigma_2-\frac{\mu+2\lambda}{\mu+\lambda}\sigma_1},
\]
\[
m_3=-\frac{\mu+\lambda}{\mu}\frac{\sigma_3-\sigma_2+\frac\mu{\mu+\lambda}\sigma_1}{\sigma_3+\sigma_2-\frac{\mu+2\lambda}{\mu+\lambda}\sigma_1},
\]
\[
(m_1,m_2,m_3)=\left(0,\frac{\sigma_3}{\sigma_2+\sigma_3},\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_2+\sigma_3}\right),
\]
and
\[
(m_1,m_2,m_3)=\left(\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_2-\sigma_1},\frac{-\sigma_1}{\sigma_2-\sigma_1},0\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For three-dimensional material with nonnegative lambda, the complementary-energy conjugate has five spectral formulas determined by eigenvalue signs and inequalities. Each regime is sharp and is attained by an eigenvector-aligned rank-2 or rank-3 sequential laminate; the remaining sign cases follow by stress reversal.
assumptions_latex: The applicable displayed laminate parameterization is defined
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The complementary-energy bound holds with the stated piecewise formula for \(g^*(\sigma)\), and each regime is attained by the specified eigenvector-aligned sequential laminate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Effective Hooke Tensor of a Rank-p Void-Core Sequential Laminate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constitutive representation for a sequential laminate of material B around a void core.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A^*\) be a rank-\(p\) sequential laminate of material \(B\) around a void core, with proportions \(1-\theta\) and \(\theta\), respectively, lamination directions \((e_i)_{i=1}^p\), and parameters \(0\leq m_i\leq1\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^p m_i=1\). Then
\[
\theta\left[A^{*-1}-B^{-1}\right]^{-1}=(1-\theta)\sum_{i=1}^p m_i f_B^c(e_i),
\]
where, for every \(\xi\in\mathcal M_N^s\),
\[
f_B^c(e_i)\xi:\xi=B\xi:\xi-\frac1\mu|B\xi e_i|^2+\frac{\mu+\lambda}{\mu(2\mu+\lambda)}\bigl((B\xi)e_i\cdot e_i\bigr)^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective Hooke tensor of a rank-p sequential laminate of material B around void is represented by a weighted sum of direction-dependent fourth-order tensors, with nonnegative lamination parameters summing to one.
assumptions_latex: \(A^*\) is a rank-\(p\) sequential laminate of material \(B\) around a void core
The proportions of material \(B\) and void are \(1-\theta\) and \(\theta\), respectively
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta[A^{*-1}-B^{-1}]^{-1}=(1-\theta)\sum_{i=1}^p m_i f_B^c(e_i)\), with \(f_B^c(e_i)\) defined by the stated quadratic form.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit optimal sequential-laminate construction for a two-dimensional stress with positive determinant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\det\sigma>0\). Let \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\) be the eigenvalues of \(\sigma\), with corresponding orthogonal unit eigenvectors \(n_1,n_2\), labeled so that \(|\sigma_1|\geq|\sigma_2|\). There exists a nondegenerate rank-4 laminate attaining the lower Hashin--Shtrikman bound, with directions \[e_1=n_1,\quad e_2=n_2,\quad e_3=\frac{n_1+n_2}{|n_1+n_2|},\quad e_4=\frac{n_1-n_2}{|n_1-n_2|},\] and parameters \[m_1=\frac{|\sigma_2|}{2(|\sigma_1|+|\sigma_2|)},\quad m_2=\frac{2|\sigma_1|-|\sigma_2|}{2(|\sigma_1|+|\sigma_2|)},\quad m_3=m_4=m_1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a two-dimensional stress having positive determinant, the displayed four directions and eigenvalue-dependent parameters define a nondegenerate rank-4 laminate that attains the lower Hashin–Shtrikman bound.
assumptions_latex: \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\) are the eigenvalues of \(\sigma\), with corresponding orthogonal unit eigenvectors \(n_1,n_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a nondegenerate rank-4 laminate with the displayed directions and parameters that attains the lower Hashin--Shtrikman bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal realization by rank-N sequential laminates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded optimal-microstructure result for the relaxed compliance objective and the stated admissible classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the objective \(J^*\), \[\min_{(\theta,A^*)\in\mathcal{CD}}J^*(\theta,A^*)=\min_{(\theta,A^*)\in\mathcal{LD}^{+}}J^*(\theta,A^*).\] If \((\theta,A^*)\) minimizes \(J^*\) over \(\mathcal{CD}\) and \(\sigma\) minimizes its associated compliance, then there exists a sequential laminate \(\widetilde A^*\) such that \((\theta,\widetilde A^*)\) minimizes \(J^*\) over \(\mathcal{LD}^{+}\), \(\sigma\) remains its associated stress tensor, and \[A^{*-1}\sigma=\widetilde A^{*-1}\sigma.\] Moreover, \(\widetilde A^*\) may be chosen as a rank-\(N\) perforated sequential laminate whose orthogonal lamination directions are the eigenvectors of \(\sigma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relaxed composite class and the sequential-laminate class have the same optimal value. Every relaxed optimum, together with an associated compliance-minimizing stress, has a rank-N perforated sequential-laminate realization preserving that stress response and aligned with the stress eigenvectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{\mathcal{CD}}J^*=\min_{\mathcal{LD}^{+}}J^*,\qquad \exists\widetilde A^*:\ (\theta,\widetilde A^*)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathcal{LD}^{+}}J^*,\quad A^{*-1}\sigma=\widetilde A^{*-1}\sigma,\quad \widetilde A^*\text{ may be chosen as the stated rank-}N\text{ laminate.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential laminates with prescribed lamination parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional probability-weight representations for two-phase sequential elastic laminates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $e_1,\ldots,e_p\in S_{N-1}$, $\theta\in[0,1]$, and $m_i\ge 0$ with $\sum_{i=1}^p m_i=1$. There exists a rank-$p$ sequential laminate $A_p^*$ with matrix $A$, core $B$, respective phase proportions $\theta$ and $1-\theta$, and directions $(e_i)$ such that
\[
(1-\theta)(A_p^*-A)^{-1}=(B-A)^{-1}+\theta\sum_{i=1}^p m_i f_A(e_i).
\]
After interchanging the phases, there exists a rank-$p$ sequential laminate $B_p^*$ with core $A$ of proportion $\theta$ and matrix $B$ of proportion $1-\theta$ such that
\[
\theta(B_p^*-B)^{-1}=(A-B)^{-1}+(1-\theta)\sum_{i=1}^p m_i f_B(e_i).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any probability weights on prescribed lamination directions can be realized by a rank-p sequential elastic laminate with the stated effective-tensor representation. Interchanging the matrix and core phases gives the phase-dual representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists A_p^*,B_p^*\text{ satisfying the displayed phase-dual sequential-laminate representations.}

children.title: Finite-Order Laminates
children.top_down_role: Hierarchical laminate constructions with finitely many mixing stages.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite combinatorial representation of a sequential laminate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An atomic probability measure is a finite-order laminate exactly when it is the leaf measure of a finite rooted binary tree whose root is its barycenter and whose internal node \(A\) has children \(B,C\) satisfying \[A=\theta B+(1-\theta)C,\qquad 0<\theta<1,\qquad \operatorname{rank}(B-C)=1.\] Each leaf mass is the product of branch weights along its root-to-leaf path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-order laminates are exactly the leaf measures of finite barycenter-preserving rank-one splitting trees.
assumptions_latex: The probability measure has finite support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite sequential splitting and finite admissible binary-tree representations are equivalent.

notation.meaning: Leaf mass determined by branch-weight products

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Splitting-Tree Representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Jensen property inherited through finitely many rank-one splittings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu=\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i\delta_{F_i}\) be a finite-order laminate with barycenter \(\bar\mu=\sum_i\lambda_iF_i\). For every finite-valued rank-one-convex function \(h:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\), \[h(\bar\mu)\le\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i h(F_i)=\int h(F)\,d\mu(F).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite-order laminate satisfies Jensen's inequality for finite-valued rank-one-convex functions.
assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is rank-one convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(\bar\mu)\le\int h\,d\mu\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Laminate Jensen Inequality
Finite-Order Laminates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive definition of atomic sequential laminates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(F_0\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and set \(\mu_0=\delta_{F_0}\). A finite-order laminate with barycenter \(F_0\) is any atomic probability measure obtained after finitely many steps in which an atom \(\lambda\delta_A\) is replaced by \(\lambda\theta\delta_B+\lambda(1-\theta)\delta_C\), where \(0<\theta<1\), \[A=\theta B+(1-\theta)C\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{rank}(B-C)=1.\] Every such replacement preserves total mass and barycenter; consequently, every resulting measure \(\mu\) satisfies \(\int F\,d\mu(F)=F_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-order laminate is an atomic probability measure obtained through finitely many barycenter-preserving rank-one splittings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every measure produced by finitely many admissible rank-one splittings is a finite-order laminate with barycenter \(F_0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential-laminate enclosure of effective Hooke tensors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes quadratic-form enclosure of each effective tensor by lower and upper phase-oriented sequential laminates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every effective Hooke tensor \(A^*\in G_\theta\), there exist \(A^+\in L_\theta^+\), with core \(A\) and matrix \(B\), and \(A^-\in L_\theta^-\), with matrix \(A\) and core \(B\), such that \[A^-\leq A^*\leq A^+\] in the sense of quadratic forms. The laminates \(A^-\) and \(A^+\) may depend on \(A^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every effective Hooke tensor in the two-phase G-closure is bounded in quadratic-form order by a lower and an upper sequential laminate having opposite phase orientations. The enclosing laminates may depend on the effective tensor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists A^-\in L_\theta^-,\ A^+\in L_\theta^+\text{ such that }A^-\leq A^*\leq A^+\text{ in quadratic-form order}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-stage sequential lamination with fixed matrix and core phases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A composite $A_p^*$ defined by the sequential-lamination formula is a rank-$p$ sequential laminate with matrix phase $A$ and core phase $B$. It is characterized by directions $(e_i)_{i=1}^p$ and stage proportions $(\theta_i)_{i=1}^p$, with every stage laminating the preceding material with the same pure phase $A$. Its overall volume fraction of $A$ is
\[
\theta=1-\prod_{i=1}^p(1-\theta_i).
\]
For fixed $\theta$, varying the admissible stage proportions and directions produces a parametrized family of rank-$p$ sequential laminates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-p sequential laminate is produced by p successive laminations with the same matrix phase. Its directions and stage proportions characterize it, and its overall matrix-phase fraction is one minus the product of the complementary stage proportions.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is the matrix phase and }B\text{ is the core phase}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A_p^*\text{ is a rank-}p\text{ sequential laminate with }\theta=1-\prod_{i=1}^p(1-\theta_i).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Families obtained over all finite ranks, directions, and lamination parameters for each choice of matrix phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed phase proportions $\theta$ and $1-\theta$, $L_\theta^-$ is the set of all finite-rank sequential laminates $A_p^*$ with matrix $A$ and core $B$ defined by
\[
(1-\theta)(A_p^*-A)^{-1}=(B-A)^{-1}+\theta\sum_{i=1}^p m_i f_A(e_i),
\]
as $p$, the directions $e_i$, and the lamination parameters $m_i$ vary over their admissible choices. Likewise, $L_\theta^+$ is the set of all finite-rank sequential laminates $B_p^*$ with core $A$ and matrix $B$ defined by the phase-swapped representation, with rank, directions, and lamination parameters varying over all admissible choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The families L-minus and L-plus contain all finite-rank sequential laminates obtained by varying rank, directions, and lamination parameters, distinguished by whether A or B is the matrix phase.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_\theta^-\text{ and }L_\theta^+\text{ are the two matrix-oriented families of admissible finite-rank sequential laminates.}

children.title: Lamination Closure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Limits and closures of laminate-generated configurations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Escape-of-mass obstruction to barycenter preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^{1\times1}\), define \[\mu_j=\left(1-\frac1j\right)\delta_0+\frac1j\delta_j.\] Each \(\mu_j\) is a first-order laminate with barycenter \(1\), but \(\mu_j\rightharpoonup^*\delta_0\), whose barycenter is \(0\). Thus narrow convergence alone does not preserve barycenters on unbounded matrix space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even first-order laminates can lose their barycenter when mass escapes to infinity.
assumptions_latex: Supports are allowed to escape every compact subset of matrix space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak-star convergence of probabilities alone need not preserve first moments or barycenters.

notation.meaning: Dirac probability measure at the scalar matrix \(t\)

knowledge_statements.title: Barycenter Loss Without Moment Control

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Passage of rank-one-convex Jensen inequalities through compactly supported weak-star closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be compact, let \(\mu_j\in\mathcal L_{\mathrm{fin}}(K)\) have common barycenter \(F\), and suppose \(\mu_j\rightharpoonup^*\mu\). Then \(\mu\) is supported in \(K\), has barycenter \(F\), and satisfies \[h(F)\le\int_K h(A)\,d\mu(A)\] for every continuous rank-one-convex function \(h\) defined on an open convex set containing the splitting trees and \(K\). In particular, the assertion holds for every continuous rank-one-convex \(h:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compactly supported weak-star limits preserve barycenters and finite-laminate Jensen inequalities when the test function is defined on the required rank-one segments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The limit preserves support, barycenter, and the stated rank-one-convex Jensen inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Jensen Stability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noncompact replacement for the common-compact-support hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu_j\) be probability measures with \(\mu_j\rightharpoonup^*\mu\). If their first moments are uniformly integrable, \[\lim_{R\to\infty}\sup_j\int_{|A|>R}|A|\,d\mu_j(A)=0,\] then \[\int A\,d\mu_j(A)\to\int A\,d\mu(A).\] Consequently, a common barycenter is retained by the limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform integrability of first moments preserves barycenters under noncompact narrow convergence.
assumptions_latex: The first moments of \(\mu_j\) are uniformly integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\int A\,d\mu_j(A)\to\int A\,d\mu(A)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Moment-Controlled Barycenter Stability

assumptions_latex: All finite-order laminates under consideration are supported in \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lamination closure consists of weak-star limits of finite-order laminates and preserves probability mass, support in \(K\), and barycenter.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact-support closure avoids loss of mass or moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the compactly supported lamination closure by \[\mathcal L(K)=\overline{\mathcal L_{\mathrm{fin}}(K)}^{\,*}.\] Thus \(\mu\in\mathcal L(K)\) when some sequence \(\mu_j\in\mathcal L_{\mathrm{fin}}(K)\) satisfies \(\int h\,d\mu_j\to\int h\,d\mu\) for every continuous \(h:K\to\mathbb R\). If all \(\mu_j\) have a common barycenter \(F\), then \(\mu\) also has barycenter \(F\). Every continuous rank-one convex function on a neighborhood of \(K\) obeys \(h(F)\le\int_Kh(A)\,d\mu(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compactly supported laminates arise as weak-star limits of finite-order laminates, retaining barycenters and rank-one-convex Jensen inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Lamination Closure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compact-support closure statement is coherent and fits the container, but the exact closure convention and rank-one-convex Jensen assertion have no supporting locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the class generated from simple two-phase laminates by repeated lamination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For phases $A$ and $B$ in proportions $\theta$ and $1-\theta$, respectively, $L_\theta\subset G_\theta$ is the smallest subset of $G_\theta$ that contains all simple laminates defined from these phases and is stable under lamination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The laminated-material class L_theta is the smallest subset of G_theta containing all simple laminates of the two phases and closed under further lamination.
assumptions_latex: \text{The phases }A\text{ and }B\text{ occur in proportions }\theta\text{ and }1-\theta.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_\theta\text{ contains all simple laminates and is stable under lamination, and every subset of }G_\theta\text{ with these properties contains }L_\theta.

children.title: Null Lagrangians
children.top_down_role: Variationally invariant densities and their role in minor structures and boundary dependence.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: General Variational Formulas and null-Lagrangian discussion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piola Identity for the Determinant Minor
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conservation law underlying boundary dependence of the determinant null Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cofactor of a gradient is divergence-free, making the determinant a divergence-form null Lagrangian whose integral is fixed by boundary data.
assumptions_latex: \(u\in C^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^n)\); weaker distributional forms require suitable Sobolev integrability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The determinant minor is a divergence-form null Lagrangian and its integral is boundary-determined in the stated regularity regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Piola Identity for the Determinant Minor

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent variational characterizations of continuous autonomous first-order null Lagrangians.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite continuous autonomous density \(L:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\), the following are equivalent: (i) \(L\) is a first-order null Lagrangian; (ii) both \(L\) and \(-L\) are quasiconvex; and (iii) for every \(F\) and \(\varphi\in W^{1,\infty}_0(Q;\mathbb R^m)\), \[L(F)=\frac1{|Q|}\int_Q L(F+\nabla\varphi)
\,dx.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous autonomous density is a null Lagrangian exactly when every zero-boundary quasiconvexity test holds with equality, equivalently when both signs are quasiconvex.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is a bounded Lipschitz reference domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Null-Lagrangian, quasiaffine, and two-sided-quasiconvex formulations are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiaffine Characterization

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A first-order autonomous null Lagrangian is exactly an affine combination of minors, and its integral is invariant under fixed-trace variations.

notation.meaning: Minor using row set \(I\) and column set \(J\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of continuous autonomous first-order null Lagrangians.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The density \(L\) is a null Lagrangian when, for every \(u\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) and \(\varphi\in W_0^{1,\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), \[\int_\Omega L(
abla u+
abla\varphi)\,dx=\int_\Omega L(
abla u)\,dx.\] Continuous autonomous first-order null Lagrangians have the representation \[L(F)=c_0+\sum_{k=1}^{\min\{m,n\}}\ \sum_{|I|=|J|=k}c_{I,J}M_{I,J}(F).\] Hence their integrals depend only on boundary trace data, subject to the regularity needed for the minors to be integrable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous first-order null Lagrangians are affine combinations of matrix minors, and their integrals remain unchanged under fixed-boundary variations.
knowledge_statements.title: Null Lagrangians

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine-minors classification is a nontrivial theorem and the representation content kind fits the container, but the classification and boundary-trace conclusion require a specific authoritative theorem or section locator.

children.title: Variational Convexity Separation Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Implications and strict separations among convexity, polyconvexity, quasiconvexity, and rank-one convexity.

children.title: Convexity Implication Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Implication structure among major convexity notions for gradient integrands.

assumptions_latex: \(m,n\in\mathbb N\) and \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is finite-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{convex}\Longrightarrow\text{polyconvex}\Longrightarrow\text{quasiconvex}\Longrightarrow\text{rank-one convex}.\]

notation.meaning: Morrey quasiconvexity with compactly supported smooth variations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical hierarchy for autonomous finite-valued gradient integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Convexity means convexity on \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). Polyconvexity means that \(f(F)=g(M(F))\) for some convex function \(g\), where \(M(F)\) is the vector of all minors of \(F\). Quasiconvexity means
\[f(F)\leq \frac{1}{|Q|}\int_Q f(F+\nabla\varphi(x))\,dx\]
for every matrix \(F\), cube \(Q\subset\mathbb R^n\), and \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)\). Rank-one convexity is convexity of \(t\mapsto f(F+tA)\) whenever \(\operatorname{rank}A\leq1\). Under these conventions, the displayed implication chain holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity implies polyconvexity, which implies quasiconvexity, which in turn implies rank-one convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Implication Hierarchy

children.title: Strict Separation Phenomena
children.top_down_role: Regimes where neighboring convexity notions do not coincide.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank-One Convexity Need Not Imply Quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-sensitive outer-link separation; the classical construction occurs on three-by-two matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a finite rank-one convex integrand \(f:\mathbb R^{3\times2}\to\mathbb R\) that is not quasiconvex. Consequently, \(\operatorname{quasiconvex}\Rightarrow\operatorname{rank\text{-}one\ convex}\) is strict in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On three-by-two matrix space, rank-one convexity does not imply quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is rank-one convex but not quasiconvex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-One Convexity Need Not Imply Quasiconvexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-sensitive middle-link separation for quadratic integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a finite quadratic form \(Q:\mathbb R^{3\times3}\to\mathbb R\) that is quasiconvex but not polyconvex. Hence \(\operatorname{polyconvex}\Rightarrow\operatorname{quasiconvex}\) is strict in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasiconvex quadratic form on three-by-three matrices need not be polyconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\text{ is quasiconvex but not polyconvex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvexity Need Not Imply Polyconvexity

assumptions_latex: \(m,n\geq2\), unless a more restrictive dimension is stated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{convex}\subsetneq\text{polyconvex}\subseteq\text{quasiconvex}\subseteq\text{rank-one convex}\), with strictness known for the indicated outer separations in suitable dimensions.

notation.meaning: The determinant of a square matrix.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separations among convexity notions for matrix integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For square matrices of order at least two, \(f(F)=\det F\) is polyconvex, because it is affine in a maximal minor, but it is not convex; hence convexity is strictly stronger than polyconvexity. Moreover, in suitable matrix dimensions there exist finite rank-one convex integrands that are not quasiconvex, so the implication from quasiconvexity to rank-one convexity cannot generally be reversed. These examples show that the hierarchy does not collapse merely from continuity or finite dimensionality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Determinants separate convexity from polyconvexity, while specialized matrix integrands separate quasiconvexity from rank-one convexity in suitable dimensions.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Separation Phenomena

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The determinant separation is standard, but the rank-one-convex/nonquasiconvex separation is dimension-sensitive and requires a specific authoritative source and exact matrix dimensions. The counterexample content kind fits the leaf.

children.title: Dimension-Dependent Collapses
children.top_down_role: Coincidences among convexity notions in special dimensional settings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic Collapse with One Matrix Dimension Two
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-dependent coincidence for quadratic forms when the smaller matrix dimension is two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) be a quadratic form and suppose \(\min\{m,n\}=2\). Then \[q\text{ is rank-one convex}\Longleftrightarrow q\text{ is Morrey quasiconvex}\Longleftrightarrow q\text{ is polyconvex}.\] In particular, for \(2\times2\) matrices a rank-one-convex quadratic form can be written as a convex quadratic form plus a scalar multiple of the determinant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For quadratic forms with one matrix dimension equal to two, rank-one convexity, quasiconvexity, and polyconvexity coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(q\) is a quadratic form on \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\text{ rank-one convex}\Longleftrightarrow q\text{ quasiconvex}\Longleftrightarrow q\text{ polyconvex}.\)

notation.meaning: Value of the quadratic form on a rank-one matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Collapse with One Matrix Dimension Two

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ is convex}\Longleftrightarrow f\text{ is polyconvex}\Longleftrightarrow f\text{ is quasiconvex}\Longleftrightarrow f\text{ is rank-one convex}.\]

notation.meaning: Dimensions of the target and domain, respectively.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar-valued or one-dimensional-domain gradient integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(m=1\) or \(n=1\), every matrix difference in \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has rank at most one. Consequently, rank-one convexity is ordinary convexity. Combining this fact with the general implication hierarchy yields equivalence of convexity, polyconvexity, Morrey quasiconvexity, and rank-one convexity for finite-valued autonomous integrands in these dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When either the domain or target is one-dimensional, the four standard convexity notions for gradient integrands coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Dependent Collapses

children.title: Regularity-Dependent Collapses
children.top_down_role: Coincidences induced by additional structural or regularity restrictions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collapse for finite quadratic forms on matrix space, independent of the matrix dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) be a quadratic form. Then \(Q\) is quasiconvex if and only if \(Q\) is rank-one convex; equivalently, \(Q(a\otimes b)\geq0\) for every \(a\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For quadratic matrix integrands, quasiconvexity and rank-one convexity coincide and are characterized by nonnegativity on rank-one matrices.
assumptions_latex: \(Q:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is a quadratic form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\text{ is quasiconvex}\iff Q\text{ is rank-one convex}\iff Q(a\otimes b)\geq0\ \forall a,b.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Quasiconvexity–Rank-One Convexity Collapse

assumptions_latex: \(Q\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a bounded Lipschitz domain.
\(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is continuous and satisfies \(|f(F)|\leq C(1+|F|^p)\) for some \(1\leq p<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quasiconvexity inequality tested on \(C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)\) is equivalent to the same inequality tested on \(W_0^{1,p}(Q;\mathbb R^m)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collapse of smooth and Sobolev quasiconvexity tests under continuity and growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the stated continuity and \(p\)-growth assumptions, density of smooth zero-boundary maps in \(W_0^{1,p}(Q;\mathbb R^m)\), together with continuity of the associated integral, gives
\[f(F)|Q|\leq\int_Q f(F+\nabla\varphi(x))\,dx\quad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)\]
if and only if the same inequality holds for every \(\varphi\in W_0^{1,p}(Q;\mathbb R^m)\). Thus these two test-regularity formulations of quasiconvexity coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuity and suitable growth make smooth and Sobolev zero-boundary tests of quasiconvexity equivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularity-Dependent Collapses

children.title: Sobolev Integral Representation
children.top_down_role: Local functional representations on Sobolev spaces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued first-order representation under locality, measure structure, strong-Lp lower semicontinuity, and Sobolev growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(1<p<\infty\) and \(F:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\times\mathcal A(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)\). Assume: (i) \(A\mapsto F(u,A)\) is the restriction of a finite Radon measure; (ii) \(F\) is local; (iii) for every open \(A\), \(F(\cdot,A)\) is sequentially lower semicontinuous for strong \(L^p\)-convergence on \(W^{1,p}\); and (iv) \[F(u,A)\le C\int_A(1+|u|^p+|\nabla u|^p)\,dx.\] Then there is a Borel integrand \(f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to[0,\infty)\) such that \[F(u,A)=\int_A f(x,u(x),\nabla u(x))\,dx.\] The density has corresponding \(p\)-growth, and for almost every \(x\), \(\xi\mapsto f(x,s,\xi)\) is quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local, measure-valued Sobolev functional that is lower semicontinuous in strong Lp and satisfies an integral upper bound has a first-order density quasiconvex in the gradient variable.
assumptions_latex: The stated measure, locality, strong-\(L^p\) lower-semicontinuity, and growth hypotheses hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(u,A)=\int_A f(x,u,\nabla u)\,dx\) for a Borel density quasiconvex in its gradient variable almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Sobolev Integral Representation Theorem

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) is bounded and open, and \(1<p<\infty\).
\(F:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\times\mathcal A(\Omega)\to[0,\infty]\) is local, lower semicontinuous, measure-valued in its set argument, and has \(p\)-growth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a Borel integrand \(f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to[0,\infty]\) such that \[F(u,A)=\int_A f(x,u(x),\nabla u(x))\,dx.\]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order local integral representation on Sobolev spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume additionally that the growth bounds have the form
\[c|\nabla u|^p-C\leq F\text{ locally }\leq C\bigl(1+|u|^p+|\nabla u|^p\bigr)\]
in the standard integral-functional sense. Then a Borel density \(f\) exists for which
\[F(u,A)=\int_A f(x,u(x),\nabla u(x))\,dx\]
for every \(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) and \(A\in\mathcal A(\Omega)\). The density is determined up to equality for almost every \(x\) on values sampled by Sobolev jets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local, lower-semicontinuous, measure-valued Sobolev functional with suitable growth admits a first-order integral density.
knowledge_statements.title: Sobolev Integral Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuous Convex Functionals Are Weakly Lower Semicontinuous
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak lower semicontinuity under convexity and norm continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(F:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous and convex. If \(x_k\rightharpoonup x\) in \(X\), then \(F(x)\leq\liminf_{k\to\infty}F(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every real-valued continuous convex functional on a Banach space is lower semicontinuous for weak sequential convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(x)\leq\liminf_{k\to\infty}F(x_k)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of \(W_0^{k,p}(\Omega)\) and its inherited completeness and density properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[W_0^{k,p}(\Omega):=\overline{C_0^\infty(\Omega)}^{\,W^{k,p}(\Omega)},\qquad H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega).\]
With the inherited \(W^{k,p}\)-norm, \(W_0^{k,p}(\Omega)\) is a closed subspace of the Banach space \(W^{k,p}(\Omega)\), and hence is Banach. By definition, \(C_0^\infty(\Omega)\) is dense in \(H_0^1(\Omega)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The space W_0^{k,p}(Omega) is the closure of smooth compactly supported functions in W^{k,p}(Omega), and H_0^k is its p=2 case. It is Banach under the inherited norm, and smooth compactly supported functions are dense in H_0^1 by definition.
assumptions_latex: W^{k,p}(\Omega)\text{ is a Banach Sobolev space with norm }\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_0^{k,p}(\Omega)=\overline{C_0^\infty(\Omega)}^{W^{k,p}},\quad H_0^k(\Omega)=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega),\quad W_0^{k,p}(\Omega)\text{ is Banach},\quad \overline{C_0^\infty(\Omega)}^{H_0^1}=H_0^1(\Omega).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp critical Sobolev inequality and dual variational principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the normalized extremal profile from the preceding definition; the corrupted displayed comparison is recorded through its self-contained normalized variational consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(1<p<n\), \(p^\star=np/(n-p)\), and \(p'=p/(p-1)\). For normalized admissible \(f,g\) with \(\|f\|_{L^{p^\star}}=\|g\|_{L^{p^\star}}=1\), \[ rac{\int_{\mathbb R^n}|g|^{p^\star(1-1/n)}}{\left(\int_{\mathbb R^n}|y|^{p'}|g(y)|^{p^\star}\,dyight)^{1/p'}}\le  rac{p(n-1)}{n(n-p)}\|
abla f\|_{L^p}.\] Consequently, \[\sup_{\|g\|_{L^{p^\star}}=1} rac{\int |g|^{p^\star(1-1/n)}}{\left(\int |y|^{p'}|g(y)|^{p^\star}\,dyight)^{1/p'}}= rac{p(n-1)}{n(n-p)}\inf_{\|f\|_{L^{p^\star}}=1}\|
abla f\|_{L^p}.\] The normalized profile \(h_p\) is extremal in both problems. Equivalently, every nonzero admissible \(f\) satisfies \[ rac{\|
abla f\|_{L^p}}{\|f\|_{L^{p^\star}}}\ge \|
abla h_p\|_{L^p},\] and hence \(W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)\hookrightarrow L^{p^\star}(\mathbb R^n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For 1<p<n, a weighted moment maximization problem is dual to minimizing the Lp norm of the gradient under unit critical norm. The normalized power-law profile is extremal for both problems and yields the sharp critical Sobolev inequality and embedding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\sup_{\|g\|_{p^\star}=1} rac{\int |g|^{p^\star(1-1/n)}}{(\int |y|^{p'}|g(y)|^{p^\star}dy)^{1/p'}}= rac{p(n-1)}{n(n-p)}\inf_{\|f\|_{p^\star}=1}\|
abla f\|_p,\quad  rac{\|
abla f\|_p}{\|f\|_{p^\star}}\ge\|
abla h_p\|_p,\quad W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)\hookrightarrow L^{p^\star}(\mathbb R^n).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local graph characterization with uniform chart width and interior/exterior thickness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A domain \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) has Lipschitz boundary if there exist \(\alpha,\beta>0\), finitely many local coordinate systems, and Lipschitz functions \(a_r\) on \(\{\widehat\xi^r\in\mathbb R^{n-1}:|\widehat\xi^r|\leq\alpha\}\), \(1\leq r\leq R\), such that \(\partial\Omega=\bigcup_{r=1}^R\{(a_r(\widehat\xi^r),\widehat\xi^r):|\widehat\xi^r|<\alpha\}\), while \(a_r(\widehat\xi^r)<\xi_1^r<a_r(\widehat\xi^r)+\beta\) lies in \(\Omega\) and \(a_r(\widehat\xi^r)-\beta<\xi_1^r<a_r(\widehat\xi^r)\) lies in \(\mathbb R^n\setminus\overline\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain has Lipschitz boundary when its boundary is covered by finitely many uniformly sized coordinate neighborhoods in which it is the graph of a Lipschitz function, with a uniform one-sided interior strip and an opposite exterior strip.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial\Omega\text{ is a Lipschitz boundary in the stated finite-chart sense.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sobolev–Lipschitz density, extension, and Banach-space properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compound foundational facts stated together with the definition of the endpoint space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(H^{m,\infty}(\Omega)\) as the functions in \(C^{m-1}(\overline\Omega)\) whose derivatives of order \(m-1\) are Lipschitz on \(\overline\Omega\). For every bounded open \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^N\), \(H^{1,\infty}(\Omega)\) is dense in \(H^{1,s}(\Omega)\) for \(1\le s<\infty\), and \(C^1(\overline\Omega)\subset H^{1,\infty}(\Omega)\subset H^{1,s}(\Omega)\). If \(\partial\Omega\) is Lipschitz and \(\Omega\subset\widetilde\Omega\subset\Omega_0\), each \(u\in H^{1,s}(\Omega)\) has an extension \(\widetilde u\in H^{1,s}(\Omega_0)\), which may be chosen nonnegative when \(u\ge0\) a.e. Poincaré's inequality gives \(\|\zeta\|_{L^2}^2\le\beta\|\nabla\zeta\|_{L^2}^2\) on \(H_0^1(\Omega)\), so \(\|\nabla\zeta\|_{L^2}\) is an equivalent norm there. For \(1<s<\infty\), \(H^{m,s}(\Omega)\) and \(H_0^{m,s}(\Omega)\) are reflexive Banach spaces; for \(s=2\), they are Hilbert spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The endpoint space H^{m,infinity} is defined by Lipschitz continuity of derivatives of order m-1. Lipschitz functions are dense in H^{1,s} on every bounded open domain. Lipschitz-boundary domains admit Sobolev extensions, including positivity-preserving extensions. On H_0^1 the gradient norm is equivalent to the usual Sobolev norm, and the stated Sobolev spaces are reflexive Banach spaces for 1<s<infinity and Hilbert spaces when s=2.
assumptions_latex: For the domain-extension statement, \(\partial\Omega\) is Lipschitz and \(\Omega\subset\widetilde\Omega\subset\Omega_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated density, extension, Poincaré norm-equivalence, reflexivity, and Hilbert-space properties hold under their respective hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Density of Smooth Functions in Sobolev Spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior smooth approximation on arbitrary open sets and up-to-boundary approximation on bounded Lipschitz domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open, \(k\in\mathbb N_0\), and \(1\le p<\infty\). Then \(C^\infty(\Omega)\cap W^{k,p}(\Omega)\) is dense in \(W^{k,p}(\Omega)\); equivalently, \(W^{k,p}(\Omega)\) is the completion in the \(W^{k,p}\)-norm of \(\{u\in C^\infty(\Omega):\|u\|_{W^{k,p}}<\infty\}\). If, moreover, \(\Omega\) is bounded and has \(C^{0,1}\)-boundary, then \(C^\infty(\overline\Omega)\) is dense in \(W^{k,p}(\Omega)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finite p, Sobolev functions on any open set can be approximated in Sobolev norm by smooth functions that remain in the space. On a bounded Lipschitz domain, the approximants may be chosen smooth up to the boundary.
assumptions_latex: \Omega\text{ is bounded with }C^{0,1}\text{-boundary for the up-to-boundary density conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \overline{C^\infty(\Omega)\cap W^{k,p}(\Omega)}^{\,W^{k,p}}=W^{k,p}(\Omega),\quad \overline{C^\infty(\overline\Omega)}^{\,W^{k,p}}=W^{k,p}(\Omega)\text{ in the bounded Lipschitz case.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-order Sobolev spaces over an open Euclidean domain for all exponents from one through infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open, \(k\in\mathbb N_0\), and \(p\in[1,\infty]\). Define \[W^{k,p}(\Omega):=\{u\in L^p(\Omega):D^\alpha u\in L^p(\Omega)\text{ for every }|\alpha|\le k\}.\] For \(1\le p<\infty\), \[\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}:=\left(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},\] while \[\|u\|_{W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: W^{k,p}(Ω) consists of the L^p functions whose weak derivatives through order k also belong to L^p. Its norm aggregates the L^p norms of all such derivatives by an ℓ^p sum for finite p and, under this definition, by their sum for p equal to infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W^{k,p}(\Omega)=\{u\in L^p(\Omega):D^\alpha u\in L^p(\Omega)\ \forall |\alpha|\le k\}\text{ with the stated norm.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular Boundaries, Outer Unit Normals, and Normal Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local graph characterization of a bounded domain's boundary, including the Lipschitz case and its normal field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open and bounded. For \(k\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}\) and \(0\le eta\le1\), \(\Omega\) has \(C^{k, eta}\)-boundary if, for every \(x\in\partial\Omega\), there exist \(r>0\), \(l\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\), and \(\gamma\in C^{k, eta}(\mathbb R^{n-1})\) such that \[\Omega\cap B(x;r)=\{y\in B(x;r):\sigma y_l<\gamma(y_1,\ldots,y_{l-1},y_{l+1},\ldots,y_n)\}.\] A \(C^{0,1}\)-boundary is called Lipschitz. For a Lipschitz boundary, the outward unit normal \(
u:\partial\Omega	o\mathbb R^n\) is defined almost everywhere, with \(\|
u(x)\|_2=1\); where \(
abla u\) is defined, the normal derivative is \( rac{\partial u}{\partial
u}(x):=
u(x)\cdot
abla u(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded open set has C^{k,β} boundary when it is locally the strict subgraph or supergraph of a C^{k,β} function after selecting a coordinate direction. The C^{0,1} case is a Lipschitz boundary, which has an outward unit normal almost everywhere; the normal derivative is the gradient dotted with that normal.

u	ext{ exists a.e. on a Lipschitz boundary};\quad \partial_
u u=
u\cdot

knowledge_statements.statement_title: The Spaces L2, Hm, and H0m
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions, Hilbert structure, and the completion definition of the zero-boundary Sobolev space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(m\geq0\), \(L_2(\Omega)=\{v:\int_\Omega |v|^2\,d\xi<\infty\}\), with \((u,v)_{L_2(\Omega)}=\int_\Omega uv\,d\xi\). Moreover, \(H^m(\Omega)=\{v:D^\alpha v\in L_2(\Omega)\text{ for every }|\alpha|\leq m\}\), with \((u,v)_{m,\Omega}=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq m}\int_\Omega D^\alpha uD^\alpha v\,d\xi\) and \(\|v\|_{m,\Omega}^2=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq m}\|D^\alpha v\|_{L_2(\Omega)}^2\). Both \(L_2(\Omega)\) and \(H^m(\Omega)\) are Hilbert spaces, and \(H_0^m(\Omega)\) is the completion of \(\mathcal D(\Omega)\) in \(\|\cdot\|_{m,\Omega}\), hence a subspace of \(H^m(\Omega)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: L2 consists of square-integrable functions. Hm consists of functions whose weak derivatives through order m are square-integrable, equipped with the sum-of-derivatives inner product and norm. These are Hilbert spaces, and H0m is the closure of the test functions in the Hm norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_2(\Omega)\text{ and }H^m(\Omega)\text{ are Hilbert spaces, and }H_0^m(\Omega)=\overline{\mathcal D(\Omega)}^{\|\cdot\|_{m,\Omega}}\subset H^m(\Omega).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integration by Parts on a Lipschitz Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise integration-by-parts identity for continuously differentiable functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open and bounded with \(C^{0,1}\)-boundary, and let \(\nu_i\) denote the \(i\)-th component of the outward unit normal. Then, for every \(u,v\in C^1(\overline\Omega)\), \[\int_\Omega u_{x_i}(x)v(x)\,dx=-\int_\Omega u(x)v_{x_i}(x)\,dx+\int_{\partial\Omega}u(x)v(x)\nu_i(x)\,dS(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a bounded Lipschitz domain, moving a coordinate derivative from u to v changes its sign and produces the boundary integral of uv times the corresponding component of the outward unit normal.
assumptions_latex: \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is open and bounded with }C^{0,1}\text{-boundary}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \int_\Omega u_{x_i}v\,dx=-\int_\Omega uv_{x_i}\,dx+\int_{\partial\Omega}uv\nu_i\,dS.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized zero-boundary Sobolev class defined by finite gradient energy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a given integrand \(\varphi\), define
\[W_0^{1,\varphi}(\Omega):=\left\{u\in W_0^{1,1}(\Omega):\int_\Omega \varphi(\nabla u(x))\,dx<+\infty\right\}.\]
If \(\varphi(\xi)=|\xi|^\alpha\) with \(1\leq\alpha<\infty\), this set is \(W_0^{1,\alpha}(\Omega)\), disregarding topology. Positive quadratic forms yield anisotropic examples, while an extended-valued integrand that is infinite for \(|\xi|\geq1\) can force membership in \(W_0^{1,\infty}(\Omega)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: W₀^{1,φ}(Ω) consists of zero-boundary W^{1,1} functions whose gradient has finite φ-energy. Power integrands recover the usual Sobolev classes as sets, while quadratic or extended-valued integrands produce anisotropic or uniformly gradient-constrained variants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_0^{1,\varphi}(\Omega)=\{u\in W_0^{1,1}(\Omega):\int_\Omega\varphi(\nabla u)\,dx<\infty\}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional definition for locally integrable functions on an open Euclidean domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open, \(u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)\), and let \(\alpha\) be a multi-index. A function \(w\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)\) is the \(\alpha\)-th weak partial derivative of \(u\), denoted \(D^\alpha u=w\), if \[\int_\Omega w\varphi\,dx=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega uD^\alpha\varphi\,dx\qquad\forall\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an open set Ω and a locally integrable function u, a locally integrable function w is the α-th weak derivative of u when integration against every smooth compactly supported test function transfers the derivative to the test function with sign (−1)^|α|.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D^\alpha u:=w\iff \int_\Omega w\varphi\,dx=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega uD^\alpha\varphi\,dx\quad\forall\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the trace, its continuity interpretation, and the stated higher-order analogue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(v\in H^1(\Omega)\), \(\operatorname{tr}v:=\gamma_0v\) is called the trace of \(v\). Continuity of \(\gamma_0:H^1(\Omega)\to L_2(\partial\Omega)\) implies that \(v_k\to v\) in \(H^1(\Omega)\) entails \(\operatorname{tr}v_k\to\operatorname{tr}v\) in \(L_2(\partial\Omega)\). Analogous operators \(\gamma_j\), \(j>0\), give traces of the normal derivatives \(\partial^jv/\partial n^j\) on their applicable domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The image of a Sobolev function under the boundary operator is its trace. Trace values depend continuously on the H1 function, and analogous higher-order operators represent traces of normal derivatives where defined.
assumptions_latex: \gamma_0:H^1(\Omega)\to L_2(\partial\Omega)\text{ is the continuous trace operator}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{tr}v=\gamma_0v,\qquad v_k\to v\text{ in }H^1(\Omega)\Rightarrow\operatorname{tr}v_k\to\operatorname{tr}v\text{ in }L_2(\partial\Omega).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sobolev space, critical exponent, and extremal profile
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the inhomogeneous Sobolev space and the sharp constant for the critical homogeneous inequality; the extremal profile need not itself belong to the inhomogeneous space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n>1\) be an integer and \(p\ge 1\). Define \(W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n):\nabla f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)\}\). If \(1\le p<n\), set \(p^\star=np/(n-p)\) and let \(S_n(p)\) be the least constant such that \(\|f\|_{L^{p^\star}}\le S_n(p)\|\nabla f\|_{L^p}\) for every admissible \(f\). For \(1<p<n\), with \(p'=p/(p-1)\), define \(h_p(x)=(\sigma_p+|x|^{p'})^{-(n-p)/p}\), where \(\sigma_p\) is chosen so that \(\|h_p\|_{L^{p^\star}}=1\). This profile is extremal for the sharp Sobolev inequality, although it need not lie in \(L^p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The first-order Sobolev space consists of Lp functions whose gradients are also in Lp. Below the dimension, the critical exponent is np/(n−p), and the sharp Sobolev constant is the smallest constant controlling the critical norm by the gradient norm. For 1<p<n, a normalized power-law profile is an extremizer, even when it is not itself in Lp.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in L^p:\nabla f\in L^p\},\quad p^\star=\frac{np}{n-p},\quad S_n(p)=\inf\{S>0:\|f\|_{p^\star}\le S\|\nabla f\|_p\ \forall f\},\quad h_p(x)=(\sigma_p+|x|^{p'})^{-(n-p)/p}\text{ is extremal}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sobolev space by completion and weak derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the integer-order Sobolev space used in the extract, together with its weak-derivative characterization on Lipschitz domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\in\mathbb N_0\) and \(1\le s<\infty\), define \(\|u\|_{H^{m,s}(\Omega)}=\sum_{0\le|\alpha|\le m}\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^s(\Omega)}\), and let \(H^{m,s}(\Omega)\) be the completion of \(C^m(\overline\Omega)\) in this norm; write \(H^m(\Omega)=H^{m,2}(\Omega)\). If \(\partial\Omega\) is Lipschitz, this space consists precisely of the \(u\in L^s(\Omega)\) for which, for every \(|\alpha|\le m\), there is \(g_\alpha\in L^s(\Omega)\) satisfying \(\int_\Omega uD^\alpha\zeta\,dx=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega g_\alpha\zeta\,dx\) for all \(\zeta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The integer-order Sobolev space is the completion of functions smooth up to the boundary under the sum of the L^s norms of all derivatives through order m. On a Lipschitz domain, its elements are exactly the L^s functions possessing all corresponding weak derivatives in L^s.
assumptions_latex: For the weak-derivative characterization, \(\partial\Omega\) is Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H^{m,s}(\Omega)=\overline{C^m(\overline\Omega)}^{\|\cdot\|_{H^{m,s}}}\), and on a Lipschitz domain it equals the class of \(L^s\) functions having weak derivatives through order \(m\) in \(L^s\).
