children.title: Minimizer Recovery Families
children.top_down_role: Prelimit decision families approximating limiting minimizers.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise inner recovery of the limiting argmin set by exact prelimit minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F_n,F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) on a metric space, an exact minimizer-recovery family assigns to each \(x\in\operatorname{argmin}F\) a sequence \(x_n^x\in\operatorname{argmin}F_n\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), with \(x_n^x\to x\). This is equivalent to \(\operatorname{argmin}F\subseteq\liminf_n\operatorname{argmin}F_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every limiting minimizer has a convergent sequence of exact prelimit minimizers; equivalently, the limiting argmin lies in the inner set limit.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(F_n,F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{An exact recovery family exists}\iff\operatorname{argmin}F\subseteq\liminf_n\operatorname{argmin}F_n.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Minimizer-Recovery Family

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate-minimizer interpretation of recovery sequences at limiting minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\inf_XF_n\to\min_XF\). If \(x\in\operatorname{argmin}F\) and \(x_n^x\to x\) with \(F_n(x_n^x)\to F(x)\), then \(\delta_n^x:=F_n(x_n^x)-\inf_XF_n\to0\), so \(x_n^x\) is a vanishing-error minimizing sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When optimal values converge, every energy-recovery sequence at a limiting minimizer has a vanishing optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_n^x:=F_n(x_n^x)-\inf_XF_n\to0.\)

children.title: Inner Minimizer Stability
children.top_down_role: Approximation of each limiting minimizer by prelimit solutions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inner-limit definition using one prescribed vanishing tolerance sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume \(\inf_XF_n\in\mathbb R\) and let
\[M_n^{\delta_n}:=\{x\in X:F_n(x)\le \inf_XF_n+\delta_n\},\qquad \delta_n\downarrow0.\]
The approximate minimizers are inner-stable for \(F\) when
\[\operatorname{argmin}F\subset\operatorname{Li}_{n\to\infty}M_n^{\delta_n}.\]
In a metric space this is equivalent to requiring that every \(x\in\operatorname{argmin}F\) admit points \(x_n\in M_n^{\delta_n}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), with \(x_n\to x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inner minimizer stability means that every limiting minimizer is approximated at every sufficiently large index by prelimit approximate minimizers using one prescribed vanishing tolerance sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{argmin}F\subset\operatorname{Li}_nM_n^{\delta_n}\) if and only if every limiting minimizer admits a full-tail convergent selection from \(M_n^{\delta_n}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Inner Stability of Approximate Minimizers

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is metrizable, \(F_n\) epiconverges to proper \(F\), and \(\inf_XF_n\to\min_XF\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(\delta_n\downarrow0\) such that \(\operatorname{argmin}F\subset\operatorname{Li}_{n\to\infty}M_n^{\delta_n}\) whenever a common tolerance can be chosen for the recovery family.
review_flags: source supports inner-limit terminology; uniform common-tolerance hypothesis needs exact theorem verification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inner stability of approximate-minimizer sets under a uniform recovery tolerance.

source_refs.locator: A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the recovery sequences can be selected with a common error sequence \(\delta_n\downarrow0\): for every \(x\in\operatorname{argmin}F\), there are \(x_n^x\to x\) satisfying \(F_n(x_n^x)\le\inf_XF_n+\delta_n\). Then \(x_n^x\in M_n^{\delta_n}\), so by the sequential definition of the inner limit, \[\operatorname{argmin}F\subset\operatorname{Li}_{n\to\infty}M_n^{\delta_n}.\] Thus every limit minimizer is recoverable by approximate minimizers at every sufficiently large index.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform vanishing-gap recovery places every limit minimizer in the inner limit of the approximate-minimizer sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Inner Minimizer Stability

source_witnesses.locator: A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109

children.title: Isolated-Minimizer Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery behavior for locally isolated limiting minimizers.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isolation within the global limiting argmin set, without requiring global uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(\bar x\in\operatorname{argmin}F\), \(\bar x\) is an isolated minimizer when there is a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that \(U\cap\operatorname{argmin}F=\{\bar x\}\); equivalently, \(\bar x\) is an isolated point of \(\operatorname{argmin}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A limiting minimizer is isolated when some neighborhood contains no other global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\text{ is isolated}\iff\exists U\in\mathcal N(\bar x):U\cap\operatorname{argmin}F=\{\bar x\}.\)

notation.meaning: Neighborhood system of the limiting minimizer

knowledge_statements.title: Isolated Limiting Minimizer

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compact Localized Recovery of an Isolated Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery by exact minimizers restricted to a compact isolating set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be metrizable, let \(F_n\xrightarrow{e}F\), and let \(K\subset X\) be compact. Suppose \(\bar x\) is the unique minimizer of \(F\) on \(K\), there is a recovery sequence \(z_n\in K\) with \(z_n\to\bar x\) and \(F_n(z_n)\to F(\bar x)\), and each \(F_n\) attains its minimum on \(K\). Then every choice \(x_n\in\operatorname{argmin}_K F_n\) satisfies \(x_n\to\bar x\) and \(F_n(x_n)\to F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact isolating set, uniqueness of the limiting minimizer and an internal recovery sequence force all localized exact minimizers and their values to converge.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is metrizable, \(F_n\xrightarrow{e}F\), and \(K\subset X\) is compact.
\(\operatorname{argmin}_K F=\{\bar x\}\), and some \(z_n\in K\) satisfies \(z_n\to\bar x\) and \(F_n(z_n)\to F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_n\in\operatorname{argmin}_K F_n\implies x_n\to\bar x\text{ and }F_n(x_n)\to F(\bar x).\)

notation.meaning: Exact minimizers restricted to the compact isolating set

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Localized Recovery of an Isolated Minimizer

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is metrizable, \(F_n\) epiconverges to lower-semicontinuous \(F\), and \(K\subset X\) is compact.
A point \(\bar x\) is the unique minimizer of \(F\) on \(K\), and \(\bar x\) admits a recovery sequence contained in \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every choice \(x_n\in\operatorname{argmin}_K F_n\) converges to \(\bar x\), and \(F_n(x_n)\to F(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Minimizers restricted to the compact isolating set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: compact localization plus uniqueness yields full minimizer recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery through minimization on a compact neighborhood where the limit minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(x_n\in\operatorname{argmin}_{y\in K}F_n(y)\). Compactness gives cluster points in \(K\). A recovery sequence for \(\bar x\), together with the epiliminf inequality, shows that every cluster point minimizes \(F\) over \(K\). Uniqueness forces every cluster point to equal \(\bar x\); hence the whole sequence satisfies \[x_n\to\bar x,\qquad F_n(x_n)\to F(\bar x).\] Thus compact localization converts isolation of the limit minimizer into recovery by localized exact minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unique minimizer on a compact isolating neighborhood is recovered by minimizers of the approximating functionals restricted to that neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Isolated-Minimizer Recovery

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compact-localization theorem is plausible and fits the isolated-minimizer recovery leaf, but the precise restricted-recovery and value-convergence hypotheses require an inspectable theorem locator. The statement also includes a proof outline.

children.title: Inner-Stability Failures
children.top_down_role: Obstructions preventing prelimit approximation of limiting minimizers.

assumptions_latex: Minimizers are global and set-valued inner convergence is understood through sequential recovery.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}F_n=\{0\}\) does not converge inward to \(\operatorname*{argmin}F=X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact scalar example showing failure of inner minimizer recovery despite uniform convergence.

source_refs.locator: A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\geq1\), define \(F_n:X\to\mathbb R\) by \(F_n(x)=x^2/n\), and define \(F(x)=0\). Then \(F_n\to F\) uniformly, hence also epigraphically. Nevertheless, \(\operatorname*{argmin}_X F_n=\{0\}\) for every \(n\), whereas \(\operatorname*{argmin}_X F=X\). Thus, for every \(\bar x\in X\setminus\{0\}\), no sequence \(x_n\in\operatorname*{argmin}F_n\) can satisfy \(x_n\to\bar x\). Outer minimizer stability may therefore hold while inner recovery of every limiting minimizer fails when the limiting minimum is nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform objective convergence can preserve outer minimizer limits while failing to recover nonzero members of a nonunique limiting minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Stability Failures

children.title: Nonunique-Minimizer Selection
children.top_down_role: Perturbation-dependent selection within nonunique limiting solution sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every cluster point of any sequence \(x_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}(F(x)+\varepsilon_k g(x))\) belongs to \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in M}g(x)\), where \(M=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic selection by a continuous vanishing perturbation on a compact metric space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}F(x)\). For each \(k\), choose \(x_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}(F(x)+\varepsilon_k g(x))\). Every cluster point \(\bar x\) of \((x_k)\) belongs to \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in M}g(x)\). Thus a vanishing perturbation selects only minimizers of its secondary objective within the limiting minimizer set, and different secondary objectives may select different subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vanishing continuous perturbation selects, among the limiting minimizers, only those minimizing its secondary objective; different perturbations may produce different selections.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Realizability of Any Prescribed Limiting Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous tie-breaking perturbation selecting an arbitrary prescribed primary minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be compact metric, let \(F:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, and fix \(x^\star\in M:=\operatorname{argmin}F\). With \(g_{x^\star}(x)=d(x,x^\star)\), one has \(\operatorname{argmin}(F+\varepsilon g_{x^\star})=\{x^\star\}\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\). Consequently every sequence of perturbed minimizers equals, and hence converges to, \(x^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a prescribed primary minimizer is a continuous tie breaker that selects that point uniquely for every positive perturbation size.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is compact metric, \(F\) is continuous, and \(x^\star\in\operatorname{argmin}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{argmin}(F+\varepsilon g_{x^\star})=\{x^\star\}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Realizability of Any Prescribed Limiting Minimizer

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique Secondary Minimizer Gives Full Selection Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upgrade from cluster-point selection to full convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be compact metric, let \(F,g:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, let \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), and set \(M=\operatorname{argmin}F\). If \(\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in M}g(x)=\{x^\star\}\), then every choice \(x_k\in\operatorname{argmin}(F+\varepsilon_k g)\) satisfies \(x_k\to x^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unique secondary minimizer on the primary argmin set forces every vanishing-perturbation minimizer to converge to that selected point.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is compact metric; \(F,g\) are continuous; \(\varepsilon_k>0\) and \(\varepsilon_k\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\in\operatorname{argmin}(F+\varepsilon_k g)\implies x_k\to x^\star.\)

children.title: Epi-Integral Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Obstructions to commuting epigraphical limits with integration.

children.title: Loss of Integral Lower Compactness
children.top_down_role: Failure from uncontrolled negative energy or concentration.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of integral lower-limit interchange through concentration on shrinking sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \((0,1)\), let \(f_n(t)=-n\mathbf 1_{(0,1/n)}(t)\). Then \(f_n(t)\to0\) almost everywhere, but \[\int_0^1f_n(t)\,dt=-1\quad\text{for every }n.\] The negative parts \(f_n^-=n\mathbf 1_{(0,1/n)}\) are not uniformly integrable. Consequently, \[\int_0^1\liminf_n f_n(t)\,dt=0>-1=\liminf_n\int_0^1f_n(t)\,dt.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative energy concentrated on shrinking sets defeats the integral lower-limit inequality despite almost-everywhere convergence to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The negative parts are not uniformly integrable and the integral lower-limit inequality fails.
knowledge_statements.title: Concentration of Negative Parts

assumptions_latex: The integral functional has an uncontrolled negative quadratic part.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The functional \(I(u)=-\int_0^1|u(t)|^2\,dt\) satisfies \(\inf_{u\in L^2(0,1)}I(u)=-\infty\), and none of its lower level sets is relatively compact in the strong or weak \(L^2\) topology.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uncontrolled negative energy destroys bounded lower level sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Negative-energy escape illustrating failure of integral lower compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(I:L^2(0,1)\to\mathbb R\) by \(I(u)=-\int_0^1|u(t)|^2\,dt\). For \(u_k(t)=k\), one has \(I(u_k)=-k^2\to-\infty\) and \(\lVert u_k\rVert_{L^2}=k\to\infty\). Hence \(\inf I=-\infty\), and for every \(c\in\mathbb R\), the lower level set \(\{u\in L^2(0,1):I(u)\leq c\}\) is unbounded and therefore not relatively compact in either the strong or weak \(L^2\) topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An uncontrolled negative quadratic integral diverges downward along unbounded constant functions, and every lower level set fails to be relatively compact in both the strong and weak L2 topologies.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Integral Lower Compactness

children.title: Nonuniform Coercivity
children.top_down_role: Degeneration of compactness across a family of integral problems.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-space characterization using arbitrary functional indices, avoiding the insufficient one-point-per-index formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a metric space and \((F_n)\) a family of extended-real functions. The family is equicoercive if and only if every pair of sequences \((i_k)\subset\mathbb N\) and \((u_k)\subset X\) satisfying \(\sup_kF_{i_k}(u_k)<+\infty\) has a convergent subsequence. Hence failure is certified by bounded-energy points selected from possibly varying sublevels with no convergent subsequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equicoercivity is equivalent to precompactness of every bounded-energy selection from the family; an escaping bounded-energy selection certifies failure.
assumptions_latex: Equicoercivity means relative compactness, equivalently compact containment, of each fixed-height union of sublevels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (F_n)\text{ is equicoercive}\Longleftrightarrow\bigl[\sup_kF_{i_k}(u_k)<\infty\Rightarrow(u_k)\text{ has a convergent subsequence}\bigr].

notation.meaning: Arbitrary bounded-energy selection from the family

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Failure Criterion for Equicoercivity

assumptions_latex: Coercivity is distinguished from equicoercivity of the family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every function \(F_n(x)=x^2/n\) is coercive, but the family \((F_n)_{n\geq1}\) is not equicoercive.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise coercivity does not imply family-wide equicoercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\geq1\), define \(F_n:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \(F_n(x)=x^2/n\). Each \(F_n\) is coercive. Its level-one sublevel set is \(L_n=[-\sqrt n,\sqrt n]\), and \(\bigcup_{n\geq1}L_n=\mathbb R\). Consequently, the family \((F_n)_{n\geq1}\) is not equicoercive. In particular, \(x_n=\sqrt n\) satisfies \(F_n(x_n)=1\) and has no convergent subsequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each objective is coercive, but the fixed-level sublevel sets expand without bound, so the family is not equicoercive.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniform Coercivity

children.title: Measurability Loss Under Limits
children.top_down_role: Failure of normal-integrand structure under inadequate limiting operations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive preservation boundary complementing the deferred uncountable-supremum counterexample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_n:T\times X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be jointly measurable, and suppose every section \(f_n(t,\cdot)\) is lower semicontinuous. Then \[f(t,x)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}f_n(t,x)\] is jointly measurable and lower semicontinuous in \(x\). Thus countable suprema preserve this normal-integrand structure, whereas arbitrary uncountable suprema need not preserve measurability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Countable suprema preserve joint measurability and lower semicontinuity; arbitrary uncountable suprema may not.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}f_n\) is jointly measurable and lower semicontinuous in the decision variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Countable-Supremum Preservation Boundary

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An uncountable pointwise supremum of measurable normal integrands need not be measurable and therefore need not be a normal integrand.

notation.meaning: Singleton-supported integrand indexed by a in V

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uncountable suprema need not preserve measurability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An uncountable supremum showing why measurable limiting operations require structural hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(a\in V\), define \(f_a:[0,1]\times\mathbb R\to\{0,1\}\) by \(f_a(t,x)=\mathbf 1_{\{a\}}(t)\). Each \(f_a\) is jointly Lebesgue measurable, and \(x\mapsto f_a(t,x)\) is continuous for every \(t\), so each \(f_a\) is a normal integrand. The pointwise supremum \(f(t,x)=\sup_{a\in V}f_a(t,x)=\mathbf 1_V(t)\) is not Lebesgue measurable. Thus an arbitrary uncountable supremum can destroy normal-integrand measurability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every indexed integrand is measurable and continuous in the decision variable, but their uncountable pointwise supremum is nonmeasurable.
knowledge_statements.title: Measurability Loss Under Limits

children.title: Nonlocal Variational Limits
children.top_down_role: Limits leaving the original local integral-functional class.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary locality property distinguishing normalized pointwise integral energies from genuinely nonlocal limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(u)=\int_T f(t,u(t))\,d\mu(t)\), where \(f(t,0)=0\) almost everywhere. If \(u\) and \(v\) have essentially disjoint supports, then \(F(u+v)=F(u)+F(v)\). Therefore, violation of disjoint-support additivity excludes such a local representation. For example, \(G(u)=|\int_Tu\,d\mu|^2\) violates the identity whenever two disjointly supported fields have nonzero integrals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized pointwise integral energies are additive on disjoint supports; failure of this property certifies genuinely nonlocal dependence.
assumptions_latex: The integral is well defined and \(f(t,0)=0\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{supp}u\cap\operatorname{supp}v=\varnothing\ \text{a.e.}\Longrightarrow F(u+v)=F(u)+F(v).
knowledge_statements.title: Locality Test for Integral Representability

assumptions_latex: The state space is \(C([0,1])\) with the uniform norm.
Integration is with respect to Lebesgue measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The integral functionals \(F_n\) converge continuously to \(F(u)=|u(0)|^2\), a functional represented by the singular measure \(\delta_0\) rather than an ordinary Lebesgue density of the same local form.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: concentrating measures generate singular variational limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concentration produces a singular point-evaluation limit outside the original Lebesgue-density class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F_n:C([0,1])\to[0,+\infty)\) by \(F_n(u)=n\int_0^{1/n}|u(t)|^2\,dt\). If \(u_n\to u\) uniformly, then \(F_n(u_n)\to|u(0)|^2\). Hence \(F_n\) converges continuously, and therefore epigraphically, to \(F:C([0,1])\to[0,+\infty)\) defined by \(F(u)=|u(0)|^2\). The limit has the singular-measure representation \(F(u)=\int_{[0,1]}|u(t)|^2\,d\delta_0(t)\) and lies outside the original class of integrals with ordinary Lebesgue densities of the displayed form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Concentrating Lebesgue weights converge to a point-evaluation energy represented by a Dirac measure, outside the original ordinary-density integral class.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonlocal Variational Limits

knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a fixed differential system and slope conditions imposed at two points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal S\) be the solution set of a fixed differential system. The conditions \(y_i'(x_1)=\psi_i^{(1)}(y_1(x_1),\ldots,y_n(x_1))\) and \(y_i'(x_2)=\psi_i^{(2)}(y_1(x_2),\ldots,y_n(x_2))\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), are mutually consistent if and only if
\[
\forall y\in\mathcal S:\quad \bigl[\forall i,\ y_i'(x_1)=\psi_i^{(1)}(y(x_1))\bigr]\Longleftrightarrow\bigl[\forall i,\ y_i'(x_2)=\psi_i^{(2)}(y(x_2))\bigr].
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two sets of slope boundary conditions at x1 and x2 are mutually consistent when every solution of the fixed differential system satisfying the first set also satisfies the second set, and conversely.
assumptions_latex: x_1,x_2\text{ are points at which the respective boundary conditions are prescribed}
y\in\mathcal S\text{ solves the fixed differential system}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{y\in\mathcal S:y'(x_1)=\psi^{(1)}(y(x_1))\}=\{y\in\mathcal S:y'(x_2)=\psi^{(2)}(y(x_2))\}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local minima and maxima of a functional on admissible continuously differentiable real-valued curves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\subseteq \mathcal C^1([a,b];\mathbb R)\) be the admissible class and let \(J\) be a functional on \(\mathcal X\). A local minimum \(y_*\) is called strong if there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(J(y_*)\le J(y)\) for every \(y\in\mathcal X\) satisfying \(\lVert y-y_*\rVert_0<\varepsilon\); it is called weak when the corresponding neighborhood is defined by \(\lVert y-y_*\rVert_1<\varepsilon\). For local maxima, reverse the inequality. Thus extrema relative to the 0-norm are strong, while extrema relative to the 1-norm are weak.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a functional on admissible continuously differentiable curves, a local minimum or maximum measured in the 0-norm is a strong extremum, while one measured in the 1-norm is a weak extremum. The same definitions cover minima and maxima, with the comparison inequality reversed for maxima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{0-norm local extremum}=\text{strong extremum},\qquad \text{1-norm local extremum}=\text{weak extremum}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local and Strict Local Extrema on an Admissible Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a real-valued functional on a subset of a normed space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb R\), where \(\Omega\subset X\) and \(X\) is a normed space. A point \(x_0\in\Omega\) is a local minimum if there exists an open ball \(N\ni x_0\) such that \(f(x_0)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in\Omega\cap N\). It is a strict local minimum if \(f(x_0)<f(x)\) for every \(x\in(\Omega\cap N)\setminus\{x_0\}\). Local and strict local maxima are defined by reversing the inequalities. An extremum is a minimum or maximum; \(\Omega\) is the admissible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a real-valued functional on a subset of a normed space, a local minimum dominates all feasible points in some open ball, and a strict local minimum strictly dominates every other feasible point in that ball. Local maxima use reversed inequalities. An extremum means a minimum or maximum, and the domain of the extremum problem is the admissible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists N\ni x_0\text{ open ball such that }f(x_0)\le f(x)\ \forall x\in\Omega\cap N;\text{ strictness replaces }\le\text{ by }<\text{ for }x\ne x_0.

children.title: Local-Optimality Gap Phenomena
children.top_down_role: Settings where weak and strong local extrema differ.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit separation of weak and strong local minimality by oscillatory gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A=W^{1,\infty}_0(0,1)\) and \(J(u)=\int_0^1(|u'|^2-|u'|^3)\,dt\). Then \(0\) is a weak local minimizer in the \(W^{1,\infty}\) regime. Let \(\tau(s)=2\operatorname{dist}(s,\mathbb Z)\) and \(u_k(t)=k^{-1}\tau(kt)\) for integers \(k\ge1\). These competitors belong to \(\mathcal A\), satisfy \(\|u_k\|_{L^\infty}=k^{-1}\to0\), have \(|u_k'|=2\) almost everywhere, and satisfy \(J(u_k)=-4<J(0)=0\). Thus \(0\) is not a strong local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly vanishing triangular waves retain large gradients and lower the energy, so weak local minimality does not imply strong local minimality.
assumptions_latex: Weak and strong neighborhoods use the classical \(W^{1,\infty}\) and \(L^\infty\) conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\text{ is a weak local minimizer of }J\text{ but not a strong local minimizer.}
knowledge_statements.title: Small-Amplitude Oscillations Destroy Strong Minimality

assumptions_latex: Weak and strong neighborhoods use the \(W^{1,\infty}\) and \(L^\infty\) norms, respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The zero function is a weak local minimizer of \(J\) but is not a strong local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oscillatory gradients separate weak from strong local minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(J:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R\) by \(J(u)=\int_0^1(|u'(t)|^2-|u'(t)|^4)\,dt\). The zero function is a weak local minimizer with respect to the \(W^{1,\infty}\) norm. It is not a strong local minimizer with respect to the \(L^\infty\) norm: for every \(\rho>0\), there exists \(u\in\mathcal A\) such that \(\lVert u\rVert_{L^\infty}<\rho\) and \(J(u)<J(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero function is locally minimizing against derivative-small perturbations but is defeated by arbitrarily small-amplitude perturbations with large oscillatory gradients.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-Optimality Gap Phenomena

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of Sobolev variations by constraints on traces over a specified boundary portion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\to Y\) be the trace operator, let \(R_\Gamma:Y\to Y_\Gamma\) restrict traces to a specified boundary portion, and let \(B\subset Y_\Gamma\). The associated boundary-trace regime is \(\mathcal V_B=\{v\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m):R_\Gamma Tv\in B\}\). Fixed trace uses \(B=\{0\}\); free trace uses \(B=Y_\Gamma\); linear or affine regimes use a subspace or affine subset; and unilateral regimes use a one-sided cone or tangent cone. For a nonhomogeneous state constraint, \(B\) describes admissible variation traces at the reference state, not the state traces themselves.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boundary-trace regime is defined in an explicit restricted trace space by requiring variation traces to lie in a prescribed set, subspace, affine set, or cone.

A fixed Dirichlet regime uses \(B=\{0\}\) on the prescribed boundary portion; a free regime imposes no trace restriction there; and a unilateral regime takes \(B\) to be a one-sided cone. First-order stationarity is tested only against directions in the selected class \(\mathcal V_B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boundary-trace regime specifies admissible variations by requiring their Sobolev traces to lie in a prescribed set, subspace, or cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Trace Regimes

children.title: Inner Variations
children.top_down_role: Perturbations induced through changes of independent variables.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inner Variation of a First-Order Integral
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse-composition convention and its configurational-stress representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J(u)=\int_\Omega F(x,u(x),Du(x))\,dx\), let \(\xi\in C_c^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^n)\), set \(\Phi_t=\operatorname{id}+t\xi\), and define the inner variation \(u_t=u\circ\Phi_t^{-1}\). Under hypotheses permitting differentiation after pullback, \[\left.\frac{d}{dt}J(u_t)\right|_{t=0}=\int_\Omega\left[F_x\cdot\xi+F\operatorname{div}\xi-F_p:(Du\,D\xi)\right]dx.\] If \(F\) is autonomous, this is \(\int_\Omega(FI-Du^{\mathsf T}F_p):D\xi\,dx\). A local minimizer against the two-sided family satisfies this expression equal to zero for every such \(\xi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverse spatial composition gives an inner variation whose first derivative has the configurational-stress form; an inner-stationary minimizer annihilates it.
assumptions_latex: \(\xi\in C_c^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^n)\), and \(\Phi_t=\operatorname{id}+t\xi\) is a diffeomorphism for sufficiently small \(|t|\).
\(F,u\), and their growth satisfy conditions sufficient for the displayed pullback derivative to exist and be integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_{\mathrm{in}}J(u)[\xi]=\int_\Omega[F_x\cdot\xi+F\operatorname{div}\xi-F_p:(DuD\xi)]\,dx\), with the autonomous stress specialization stated above.

notation.meaning: derivative of the integrand with respect to its gradient argument
configurational stress for an autonomous integrand

knowledge_statements.title: Inner Variation of a First-Order Integral

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) is open, \(u:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m\), and \(\xi\in C_c^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^n)\).
\(\Phi_t(x)=x+t\xi(x)\) is a diffeomorphism for sufficiently small \(|t|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_t=u\circ\Phi_t^{-1}\), and \(\delta_{\mathrm{in}}J(u)[\xi]=\left.\frac{d}{dt}J(u_t)\right|_{t=0}\) whenever the derivative exists.

notation.meaning: flow generated by the spatial field

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inner variations obtained by reparametrizing the independent variable while retaining the underlying domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inner variation generated by \(\xi\) is the family \(u_t=u\circ\Phi_t^{-1}\), where \(\Phi_t(x)=x+t\xi(x)\). Because \(\xi\) is compactly supported in \(\Omega\), one has \(\Phi_t(\Omega)=\Omega\) for sufficiently small \(|t|\); hence the domain is unchanged and only its parametrization relative to \(u\) varies. For a functional \(J\), the corresponding inner first variation is \(\delta_{\mathrm{in}}J(u)[\xi]=\left.\frac{d}{dt}J(u_t)\right|_{t=0}\), provided this derivative exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inner variation composes a field with the inverse of a small spatial diffeomorphism that leaves the domain fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Inner Variations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is plausible, but conventions for inner variations differ between inverse and direct composition. An exact source is needed to establish the convention and hypotheses used here.

children.title: Domain Variations
children.top_down_role: Perturbations produced by deformation of the underlying domain.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) is open and \(\Phi_t\) is a differentiable family of bi-Lipschitz maps with \(\Phi_0=\operatorname{id}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_{\mathrm{dom}}J(\Omega,u)[\xi]=\left.\frac{d}{dt}J(\Omega_t,u_t)\right|_{t=0}\), where \(\xi=\left.\partial_t\Phi_t\right|_{t=0}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Material transport of both the integration domain and the field defined upon it.

source_refs.locator: Chapter VI. Free Boundary Problems Governed by Elliptic Equations and Systems p. 184
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A domain variation generated by a deformation family \(\Phi_t\) replaces \(\Omega\) by \(\Omega_t=\Phi_t(\Omega)\) and transports the field as \(u_t=u\circ\Phi_t^{-1}\). If \(\xi=\left.\partial_t\Phi_t\right|_{t=0}\), the domain first variation of a domain-dependent functional is \(\delta_{\mathrm{dom}}J(\Omega,u)[\xi]=\left.\frac{d}{dt}J(\Omega_t,u_t)\right|_{t=0}\), whenever the derivative exists. Unlike a compactly supported inner variation, a nonzero normal boundary velocity can change the set \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain variation deforms the domain through maps and transports the field with the same deformation.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain Variations

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter VI. Free Boundary Problems Governed by Elliptic Equations and Systems p. 184
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First variation of an integral transported by a smooth domain deformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega_t=\Phi_t(\Omega)\), let \(\xi=\partial_t\Phi_t|_{t=0}\), and define the material derivative \(\dot f=\partial_t(f_t\circ\Phi_t)|_{t=0}\). Under hypotheses permitting differentiation after pullback, \[\left.\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega_t}f_t(y)\,dy\right|_{t=0}=\int_\Omega\bigl(\dot f+f_0\operatorname{div}\xi\bigr)\,dx.\] If \(f_t=f_0\circ\Phi_t^{-1}\), then \(\dot f=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transported domain integral differentiates into a material derivative and a Jacobian-divergence term.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi_t\) is a differentiable family of bi-Lipschitz deformations with \(\Phi_0=\operatorname{id}\).
The pulled-back integrands are differentiable at zero and admit integrable domination sufficient to interchange differentiation and integration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left.\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega_t}f_t\right|_{0}=\int_\Omega(\dot f+f_0\operatorname{div}\xi)\,dx\).
knowledge_statements.title: Transport Formula for Domain Integrals

children.title: Shape-Perturbation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Domain-deformation families distinguished by geometric admissibility.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order quotient of deformation velocities by tangential reparametrizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\) and the deformation space have sufficient regularity for boundary traces, and let the shape functional \(\mathcal J\) possess a continuous Eulerian shape derivative. Then velocities with the same normal trace induce the same derivative. Consequently there is a continuous linear functional \(g\) on the normal-trace space such that \(d\mathcal J(\Omega)[\xi]=g(\xi\cdot n)\). If this functional has an integral density in the chosen trace duality, then \(g(\eta)=\int_{\partial\Omega}G\eta\,dS\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the Hadamard structure hypotheses, a first-order shape derivative depends only on normal boundary velocity; an integral shape gradient requires additional representation assumptions.
assumptions_latex: The boundary and velocity space are regular enough to define continuous normal traces.
\(\mathcal J\) is a shape functional with a continuous Eulerian derivative in the specified velocity topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\mathcal J(\Omega)[\xi]=g(\xi\cdot n)\) for a continuous linear functional \(g\) on the normal-trace space.

notation.meaning: Eulerian shape derivative in velocity direction \(\xi\)

knowledge_statements.title: Hadamard Normal-Trace Structure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationarity for a realized cone of feasible shape velocities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(d\mathcal J(\Omega)[\xi]=g(\xi\cdot n)\), and let \(K\) be the cone of normal traces realized by feasible forward deformation curves. At a local minimum, \(g(\eta)\geq0\) for every \(\eta\in K\), equivalently \(-g\in K^\circ:=\{\ell:\ell(\eta)\leq0\ \forall\eta\in K\}\). If \(K\) is a linear space, then \(g\) annihilates \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The shape derivative is nonnegative on the feasible normal-trace cone and vanishes on every two-sided admissible trace space.
assumptions_latex: Every element of \(K\) is realized by an admissible forward deformation curve.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(\eta)\geq0\ \forall\eta\in K\iff-g\in K^\circ;\qquad K=-K\Rightarrow g|_K=0.

notation.meaning: shape derivative as a functional of normal traces
polar cone in the trace-space duality

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Trace Cone Optimality Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order classification of shape perturbations by admissible normal boundary traces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be an admissible velocity space with continuous normal-trace map \(\gamma_n\xi=\xi\cdot n\in Y\). A first-order shape-perturbation regime is specified by a set or cone \(K\subset Y\) and admits velocities \(\xi\in X\) satisfying \(\gamma_n\xi\in K\). Standard regimes are: zero first-order shape change, \(K=\{0\}\); localization to \(\Gamma\subset\partial\Omega\), \(\eta=0\) on \(\partial\Omega\setminus\Gamma\); outward unilateral motion, \(K=Y_+\); volume-tangent motion, \(K=\{\eta\in Y:\int_{\partial\Omega}\eta\,dS=0\}\); and free motion, \(K=Y\). These are tangent regimes and do not by themselves impose the corresponding constraint for nonzero deformation times.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shape-perturbation regimes are first-order classes of normal boundary velocities: zero, localized, unilateral, volume-tangent, or unrestricted.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\) and the velocity space admit a continuous normal-trace map into a specified trace space \(Y\).
For the volume-tangent regime, traces are surface-integrable and Gauss–Green is applicable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal X_K=\{\xi\in X:\gamma_n\xi\in K\}\), with the standard choices of \(K\) listed above.

notation.meaning: admissible set or cone of normal boundary velocities
cone of nonnegative outward normal traces

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Trace Shape-Perturbation Regimes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinction between exact volume-preserving deformations and the volume-tangent regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi_t\) be a sufficiently regular deformation flow, \(\Omega_t=\Phi_t(\Omega)\), and \(\xi_t=\partial_t\Phi_t\circ\Phi_t^{-1}\). Then \(\frac{d}{dt}|\Omega_t|=\int_{\Omega_t}\operatorname{div}\xi_t\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega_t}\xi_t\cdot n_t\,dS\). Exact volume preservation requires the flux to vanish at every relevant time; \(\int_{\partial\Omega}\xi_0\cdot n\,dS=0\) is only the first-order condition at \(t=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero initial boundary flux is the tangent condition for volume preservation, while exact preservation requires zero flux throughout the deformation.
assumptions_latex: The flow and velocity have sufficient regularity for the transport and Gauss–Green formulas.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\Omega_t|\equiv|\Omega|\Rightarrow\int_{\partial\Omega_t}\xi_t\cdot n_t\,dS=0\text{ for all }t,\quad \int_{\partial\Omega}\xi_0\cdot n\,dS=0\text{ is only first-order.}
knowledge_statements.title: Exact and First-Order Volume Preservation

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) has Lipschitz boundary with outward unit normal \(n\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is determined by the allowed boundary values of \(\xi\cdot n\): zero, localized, one-sided, volume-preserving, or unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Taxonomy of shape deformations according to restrictions on boundary velocity and induced domain changes.

source_refs.locator: Chapter VI. Free Boundary Problems Governed by Elliptic Equations and Systems p. 184
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A shape-perturbation regime is specified by an admissible class of deformation velocities \(\xi\). Fixed-boundary perturbations require \(\xi\cdot n=0\) on \(\partial\Omega\); localized perturbations require \(\xi\cdot n=0\) outside a designated boundary portion; outward-only perturbations require \(\xi\cdot n\geq0\); first-order volume preservation requires \(\int_{\partial\Omega}\xi\cdot n\,dS=0\); and free-shape perturbations leave \(\xi\cdot n\) unrestricted. Tangential velocity changes parametrization but not the shape to first order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shape-perturbation regimes classify deformations by restrictions on their normal boundary velocity, including fixed, localized, unilateral, volume-preserving, and free cases.
knowledge_statements.title: Shape-Perturbation Regimes

children.title: Domain-Regularity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits imposed by insufficient boundary or deformation regularity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bounded open domain for which the usual finite-perimeter boundary measure is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega=\bigcup_{k\geq1}(2^{-2k},2^{-2k+1})\subset\mathbb R\). This bounded open set has infinitely many disjoint interval components, and its characteristic function has total variation \(P(\Omega)=\infty\). Hence \(\Omega\) is not a finite-perimeter set and has no finite perimeter measure supporting the standard finite-measure Gauss–Green boundary formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded open set with infinitely many interval components can have infinite perimeter, preventing the standard finite-perimeter boundary representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(\Omega)=\infty\), so the standard finite-perimeter Gauss–Green framework does not apply.

notation.meaning: De Giorgi perimeter of the set

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Perimeter Domain Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes regularity needed for bulk change of variables from that needed for normal-trace shape formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bi-Lipschitz deformation \(\Phi_t\) permits the bulk change of variables \(\int_{\Phi_t(\Omega)}f(y)\,dy=\int_\Omega f(\Phi_t(x))|\det D\Phi_t(x)|\,dx\) for measurable \(\Omega\) whenever the integrals are defined. By contrast, a representation \(\int_{\partial\Omega}g(\xi\cdot n)\,dS\) requires an appropriate boundary measure, normal trace, and Gauss–Green formula. Measurability alone supplies none of these, so a bulk domain derivative need not possess a classical boundary representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bulk pullbacks can remain meaningful on measurable domains, whereas normal-velocity boundary formulas require additional geometric regularity.
assumptions_latex: All displayed bulk integrals are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Existence of a bulk deformation formula does not, without additional boundary structure, imply a classical normal-trace representation.

notation.meaning: normal boundary velocity when a suitable normal trace exists

knowledge_statements.title: Bulk–Boundary Regularity Separation

assumptions_latex: Domain variations are generated by spatial vector fields and interpreted through traces or boundary integrals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Below Lipschitz or finite-perimeter regularity, classical normal-trace formulas cannot be used without additional weak geometric structure.

notation.meaning: reduced boundary of a finite-perimeter set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity threshold separating classical boundary velocities from measure-theoretic formulations of domain variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a Lipschitz domain, Sobolev traces and an outward normal exist almost everywhere, so boundary conditions on \(\xi\cdot n\) and standard change-of-variables formulas are meaningful. For a finite-perimeter set, the corresponding boundary object is the reduced boundary \(\partial^*\Omega\) with measure-theoretic normal \(\nu_\Omega\), and formulas must be interpreted using geometric measure theory. For a general measurable domain, neither a classical normal nor a suitable boundary trace need exist; consequently, boundary-velocity classifications and classical Hadamard-type boundary representations may be undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classical domain-variation formulas require regular boundaries; rougher sets need reduced boundaries and weak normals, while arbitrary measurable domains may support neither.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Regularity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary is framework-dependent, particularly between Lipschitz, finite-perimeter, and arbitrary measurable sets. No source supports the asserted thresholds or Hadamard-representation limitation.

children.title: Feasibility-Preserving Variation Classes
children.top_down_role: Perturbations preserving unilateral or nonlinear admissibility.

children.title: One-Sided Variations
children.top_down_role: Perturbations restricted to a single admissible direction.

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a feasible subset of a normed space \(X\), and \(u\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(u\) is a local minimizer and \(u+t v\in K\) for all sufficiently small \(t\geq0\), then \(J'(u;v)\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order necessary condition along directions feasible only for nonnegative perturbation parameters.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Extremal Principle in Variational Analysis p. 171
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A direction \(v\in X\) is an affine one-sided variation at \(u\in K\) if there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(u+t v\in K\) for every \(t\in[0,\varepsilon)\). If \(u\) locally minimizes \(J\) over \(K\) and \(J'(u;v)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}[J(u+t v)-J(u)]/t\) exists, then \(J'(u;v)\geq0\). Equality need not hold because the opposite direction \(-v\) may be infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a constrained minimum, the directional derivative is nonnegative along every direction feasible for small nonnegative step sizes.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Variations

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Extremal Principle in Variational Analysis p. 171

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical one-sided variations generated by comparison points in a convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K\) is convex and \(u,y\in K\), then \(u+t(y-u)=(1-t)u+ty\in K\) for every \(t\in[0,1]\). Consequently, if \(u\) locally minimizes a directionally differentiable functional \(J\) over \(K\), then \(J'(u;y-u)\geq0\) for every \(y\in K\). If \(J\) is Fréchet differentiable, this is \(\langle J'(u),y-u\rangle\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every chord from a point of a convex feasible set to another feasible point is a one-sided variation and yields the standard variational inequality at a minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is convex in a normed space and \(u\in K\).
\(u\) locally minimizes \(J\) over \(K\), and the indicated directional derivatives exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J'(u;y-u)\geq0\) for every \(y\in K\).

notation.meaning: feasible chord direction from the reference point

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Feasible-Chord Variations

children.title: Constraint-Preserving Variations
children.top_down_role: Perturbations remaining within nonlinear admissible sets.

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a feasible subset of a normed space \(X\), and \(u\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A constraint-preserving variation is an admissible curve \(\gamma:[0,\varepsilon)\to K\) with \(\gamma(0)=u\); its direction is \(v=\gamma'(0+)\) when defined.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible curves that satisfy the original constraint at every sufficiently small perturbation parameter.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Sensitivity Analysis for Constraint Systems p. 406
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A constraint-preserving variation of \(u\in K\) is a curve \(\gamma:[0,\varepsilon)\to X\) satisfying \(\gamma(0)=u\) and \(\gamma(t)\in K\) for every \(t\in[0,\varepsilon)\). If the right derivative exists, its variation direction is \(v=\gamma'(0+)\). For an equality constraint \(G(u)=0\) with differentiable \(G\), every such direction satisfies the linearized condition \(DG(u)v=0\), although that condition alone need not produce an exactly feasible curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint-preserving variation is a curve that remains feasible for every small parameter; its initial derivative is the associated direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Preserving Variations

source_witnesses.locator: 4.3 Sensitivity Analysis for Constraint Systems p. 406
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasible curves for regular smooth equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G:X\to Y\) be continuously Fréchet differentiable between Banach spaces, let \(G(u)=0\), and suppose \(DG(u)\) is surjective with complemented kernel. Then every \(v\in\ker DG(u)\) is realized by a \(C^1\) curve \(\gamma:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to G^{-1}(0)\) satisfying \(\gamma(0)=u\) and \(\gamma'(0)=v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a regular equality constraint, every linearized feasible direction is realized by an exactly feasible differentiable curve.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Banach spaces and \(G:X\to Y\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable.
\(G(u)=0\), and \(DG(u)\) is surjective with complemented kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker DG(u)\) is exactly the set of velocities at \(u\) of local \(C^1\) curves in \(G^{-1}(0)\).

notation.meaning: Fréchet derivative of the constraint mapping

knowledge_statements.title: Lifting Linearized Equality Variations

children.title: Tangent Variation Regimes
children.top_down_role: First-order feasible perturbations organized by tangent geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Tangent Variation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes affine-feasible, contingent, and two-sided tangent directions at a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The contingent tangent regime at \(u\in K\) uses \(T_K(u)=\{v\in X:\exists\,t_k\downarrow0,\ u_k\in K,\ u_k\to u,\ (u_k-u)/t_k\to v\}\). The affine-feasible regime uses \(F_K(u)=\{v\in X:\exists\,\varepsilon>0,\ u+t v\in K\text{ for every }t\in[0,\varepsilon)\}\), and \(F_K(u)\subseteq T_K(u)\). A two-sided contingent regime uses \(T_K(u)\cap[-T_K(u)]\), whose directions and negatives are both contingent at \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tangent variation regimes distinguish sequential tangent directions, directions generating feasible small affine steps, and contingent directions whose negatives are also contingent.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(K\subseteq X\), and \(u\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_K(u)\subseteq T_K(u)\), while the two-sided contingent directions form \(T_K(u)\cap[-T_K(u)]\).

notation.meaning: set of directions generating feasible sufficiently small affine steps

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure relation between radial, affine-feasible, and contingent directions for convex feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be convex in a normed space and \(u\in K\). Define \(R_K(u)=\{\lambda(y-u):\lambda\geq0,\ y\in K\}\). Then \(R_K(u)=F_K(u)\) and \(T_K(u)=\overline{R_K(u)}\). Thus affine-feasible directions can be strictly fewer than contingent directions when the radial cone is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex feasible set, affine-feasible directions form the radial cone, and the contingent cone is its closure.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is convex in a normed space and \(u\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_K(u)=F_K(u)\subseteq T_K(u)=\overline{R_K(u)}\).

notation.meaning: radial cone at the feasible point
directions generating all sufficiently small feasible affine steps

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Tangent-Cone Representation

children.title: Variation Feasibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Obstructions to constructing admissible one-sided or constrained perturbations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degenerate Linearization Exceeds the Tangent Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth equality whose first-order linearization admits directions that no feasible sequence realizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y^2=x^3\}\), \(u=(0,0)\), and \(G(x,y)=y^2-x^3\). Since \(DG(u)=0\), the linearized equation \(DG(u)v=0\) admits every \(v\in\mathbb R^2\). However \(K\subseteq\{x\geq0\}\), so \((-1,0)\notin T_K(u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a cusp, the zero derivative of the defining equation makes every direction linearly feasible, although negative-horizontal directions are not tangent.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Linearization Exceeds the Tangent Cone

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Curved-Boundary Tangency Does Not Give Affine Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth convex boundary where a tangent direction is realized by a curve but not by its straight ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\|x\|\leq1\}\), \(u=(1,0)\), and \(v=(0,1)\). The feasible curve \(\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)\) has \(\gamma(0)=u\) and \(\gamma'(0)=v\), so \(v\in T_K(u)\). Nevertheless \(\|u+t v\|=\sqrt{1+t^2}>1\) for every \(t>0\), hence \(v\notin F_K(u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tangent direction to the unit disk is realized by a boundary curve although every positive straight step in that direction leaves the disk.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is the closed unit disk, \(u=(1,0)\), and \(v=(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in T_K(u)\setminus F_K(u)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Curved-Boundary Tangency Does Not Give Affine Feasibility
Variation Feasibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A contingent tangent direction need not generate an exactly feasible affine perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y\geq x^2\}\), \(u=(0,0)\), and \(v=(1,0)\). Then \(v\in T_K(u)\), but \(u+t v\notin K\) for every \(t>0\). Thus contingent tangency does not imply feasibility of the corresponding straight-line variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the epigraph of a parabola, the horizontal direction is contingent at the origin, although every positive straight-line step in that direction is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in T_K(u)\), while \(u+t v\notin K\) for every \(t>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\ge 2\), let \(\Lambda\) be of class \(C^m\), and let \(x_*\in\operatorname{Lip}[a,b]\) satisfy the integral Euler equation. If \(\Lambda_{vv}(t,x_*(t),v)\) is positive definite for every \(t\in[a,b]\) and every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(x_*\in C^m[a,b]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the integrand is of class C^m and its velocity Hessian is positive definite along a Lipschitz solution of the integral Euler equation for every time and velocity, then the solution is of class C^m.
assumptions_latex: x_*\text{ satisfies the integral Euler equation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_*\in C^m[a,b]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Superlinear lower growth of a variational integrand in velocity along a specified arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integrand \(\Lambda\) has Nagumo growth along \(x_*\) if there exists \(\theta:\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R\) such that \[\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{\theta(r)}{r}=+\infty\] and \[\Lambda(t,x_*(t),v)\ge \theta(|v|)\qquad\forall t\in[a,b],\ \forall v\in\mathbb R^n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrand has Nagumo growth along an arc when it is bounded below there by a function of the velocity norm that grows faster than linearly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Lambda(t,x_*(t),v)\ge\theta(|v|)\) for every \(t\in[a,b]\) and \(v\in\mathbb R^n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Regularity under Convex Nagumo Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz regularity of weak local minimizers under smooth derivative growth, velocity convexity, and Nagumo growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_*\) be a weak local minimizer. Assume that \(\Lambda,\Lambda_x,\Lambda_v\) are continuous in \((t,x,v)\), and that for every bounded \(S\subset\mathbb R^n\) there exist \(c_S\) and \(d_S\in L^1([a,b])\) satisfying \[|\Lambda_x(t,x,v)|+|\Lambda_v(t,x,v)|\le c_S\bigl(|v|+|\Lambda(t,x,v)|\bigr)+d_S(t)\] on \([a,b]\times S\times\mathbb R^n\). If \(v\mapsto\Lambda(t,x,v)\) is convex and there exists \(\theta:\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R\) with \(\theta(r)/r\to+\infty\) such that \(\Lambda(t,x_*(t),v)\ge\theta(|v|)\) for all \(t\in[a,b]\) and \(v\in\mathbb R^n\), then \(x_*\) is Lipschitz on \([a,b]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weak local minimizer is Lipschitz when the integrand satisfies the Tonelli–Morrey derivative-growth hypotheses, is convex in velocity, and has Nagumo growth along that minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(\forall S\subset\mathbb R^n\) bounded, \(\exists c_S\) and \(d_S\in L^1([a,b])\) satisfying the Tonelli–Morrey derivative-growth inequality on \([a,b]\times S\times\mathbb R^n\).
\(\exists\theta:\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R\) with \(\theta(r)/r\to+\infty\) and \(\Lambda(t,x_*(t),v)\ge\theta(|v|)\) for all \(t\in[a,b]\), \(v\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_*\in W^{1,\infty}([a,b];\mathbb R^n)\), equivalently \(x_*\) is Lipschitz on \([a,b]\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J(w)=\int_a^b L(x,w(x),w'(x))\,dx\). If \(L\in C^2\) and \(u\in C^2([a,b];\mathbb R^m)\) is a local minimizer among \(C^1\) competitors satisfying \(w(a)=u(a)\) and \(w(b)=u(b)\), then each component satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation \(\frac{d}{dx}L_p(x,u(x),u'(x))=L_z(x,u(x),u'(x))\) on \((a,b)\). Equivalently, \(L_z-\frac{d}{dx}L_p=0\) pointwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sufficiently smooth fixed-endpoint minimizer satisfies the pointwise Euler–Lagrange differential equation throughout the open interval.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Form-preserving transformations of Hamiltonian canonical equations with the independent variable fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \((y_i,p_i)\) satisfy \(\frac{dy_i}{dx}=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i}\) and \(\frac{dp_i}{dx}=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial y_i}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\). A transformation \(Y_i=Y_i(x,y_1,\ldots,y_n,p_1,\ldots,p_n)\), \(P_i=P_i(x,y_1,\ldots,y_n,p_1,\ldots,p_n)\) is canonical if there is a function \(H^*(x,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n,P_1,\ldots,P_n)\) for which the transformed equations are \(\frac{dY_i}{dx}=\frac{\partial H^*}{\partial P_i}\) and \(\frac{dP_i}{dx}=-\frac{\partial H^*}{\partial Y_i}\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transformation of the phase variables, with x unchanged, is canonical when it carries Hamiltonian canonical equations into canonical equations for some transformed Hamiltonian H*.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists H^*:\quad \frac{dY_i}{dx}=\frac{\partial H^*}{\partial P_i},\quad \frac{dP_i}{dx}=-\frac{\partial H^*}{\partial Y_i}\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for a first-order variational functional when its momentum relations determine the component derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For J[y_1,\ldots,y_n]=\int_a^b F(x,y,y')\,dx, set p_i=\frac{\partial F}{\partial y_i'}(x,y,y') for i=1,\ldots,n. If p=F_{y'}(x,y,y') can be solved as y'=v(x,y,p), define H(x,y,p)=-F(x,y,v(x,y,p))+\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(x,y,p)p_i. The quantities x,y_1,\ldots,y_n,p_1,\ldots,p_n,H are the associated canonical variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate momenta are the partial derivatives of the integrand with respect to the component derivatives. If these relations can be inverted for those derivatives, the Hamiltonian is the momentum–velocity pairing minus the integrand, expressed in position–momentum variables; the source calls these quantities the associated canonical variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H(x,y,p)=-F(x,y,v(x,y,p))+\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(x,y,p)p_i,\qquad (x,y_1,\ldots,y_n,p_1,\ldots,p_n,H)\ \text{are the associated canonical variables}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A Hamiltonian one-form criterion sufficient for a transformation to be canonical.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x,y,p)\mapsto(x,Y,P)\) be a differentiable change of variables. If there exists a differentiable function \(\Phi(x,y_1,\ldots,y_n,p_1,\ldots,p_n)\) such that \[\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\,dy_i-H\,dx=\sum_{i=1}^n P_i\,dY_i-H^*\,dx+d\Phi,\] then the transformation is canonical. The function \(\Phi\) is a generating function of the transformation and is determined by this differential identity up to an additive constant on each connected component of its domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the old and new Hamiltonian one-forms differ by the total differential of a function, the transformation is canonical. That function is a generating function and is unique up to an additive constant on each connected component.
assumptions_latex: (x,y,p)\mapsto(x,Y,P)\text{ is a differentiable change of variables}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The transformation is canonical, and }\Phi\text{ is a generating function determined up to an additive constant on each connected component.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of a canonical transformation by a generating function expressed in the variables \(x,y,P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\Phi\) is a generating function satisfying \[\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\,dy_i-H\,dx=\sum_{i=1}^n P_i\,dY_i-H^*\,dx+d\Phi.\] If \[\Psi(x,y,P)=\Phi+\sum_{i=1}^nP_iY_i\] can be regarded as a differentiable function of \((x,y,P)\), then the corresponding canonical transformation is represented by \[p_i=\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial y_i},\qquad Y_i=\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial P_i},\qquad H^*=H+\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial x},\quad i=1,\ldots,n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a generating function Φ, form Ψ = Φ + ΣP_iY_i and express it in the mixed variables x, y, and P. The canonical transformation is then recovered from p_i = ∂Ψ/∂y_i and Y_i = ∂Ψ/∂P_i, with H* = H + ∂Ψ/∂x.
assumptions_latex: \Psi\text{ can be regarded as a differentiable function of }(x,y,P)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_i=\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial y_i},\quad Y_i=\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial P_i},\quad H^*=H+\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial x}\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Euler Stationarity Is Not Sufficient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a zero weak first variation to certify Sobolev minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(W_0^{1,2}(0,1)\), let \[J(u)=-\int_0^1|u'(x)|^2\,dx.\] Then \(u=0\) satisfies \(DJ(0)[\varphi]=0\) for every \(\varphi\in W_0^{1,2}(0,1)\), yet \(J(\varepsilon\varphi)<J(0)\) for every nonzero \(\varphi\) and every \(\varepsilon\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero weak Euler residual does not imply Sobolev local minimality without additional convexity or second-order assumptions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: DJ(0)=0\centernot\Rightarrow0\text{ is a local minimizer}
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Euler Stationarity Is Not Sufficient

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between weak Euler equality and a one-sided variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The equality \(DJ(u)[\varphi]=0\) follows when both \(u+\varepsilon\varphi\) and \(u-\varepsilon\varphi\) are admissible for small \(\varepsilon>0\). If feasibility permits only the forward perturbation, local minimality yields only \[DJ(u)[\varphi]\ge0,\] not the weak Euler–Lagrange equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak Euler equality requires two-sided admissible perturbations; one-sided feasibility yields only a variational inequality.
assumptions_latex: J\text{ is directionally differentiable at }u\text{ along the stated directions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pm\varphi\text{ feasible}\Rightarrow DJ(u)[\varphi]=0;\qquad\varphi\text{ only forward feasible}\Rightarrow DJ(u)[\varphi]\ge0
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Sided Variation Requirement

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tonelli–Morrey Theorem for the Integral Euler Equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral-form Euler–Lagrange stationarity for absolutely continuous weak local minimizers under derivative-growth control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Lambda\) admit gradients \(\Lambda_x,\Lambda_v\), with \(\Lambda,\Lambda_x,\Lambda_v\) continuous in \((t,x,v)\). Suppose that for every bounded \(S\subset\mathbb R^n\), there exist a constant \(c_S\) and \(d_S\in L^1([a,b])\) such that \[|\Lambda_x(t,x,v)|+|\Lambda_v(t,x,v)|\le c_S\bigl(|v|+|\Lambda(t,x,v)|\bigr)+d_S(t)\] for every \((t,x,v)\in[a,b]\times S\times\mathbb R^n\). Then every weak local minimizer \(x_*\) satisfies the Euler equation in integral form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the integrand and its state and velocity gradients are continuous and satisfy the stated derivative-growth bound on every bounded state set, every weak local minimizer satisfies the Euler equation in integral form.
assumptions_latex: For every bounded \(S\subset\mathbb R^n\), there exist \(c_S\) and \(d_S\in L^1([a,b])\) satisfying the stated inequality on \([a,b]\times S\times\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_*\) satisfies the Euler equation in integral form.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral Euler equation for a Lipschitz weak local minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary first-order condition in integral form for the fixed-endpoint Lipschitz variational problem under the preceding integrand hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $a<b$, $A,B\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and suppose that $\Lambda_x$ and $\Lambda_v$ exist and that $\Lambda$, $\Lambda_x$, and $\Lambda_v$ are continuous. If $x_*\in\operatorname{Lip}([a,b];\mathbb{R}^n)$, with $x_*(a)=A$ and $x_*(b)=B$, is a weak local minimizer of $J(x)=\int_a^b\Lambda(t,x(t),x'(t))\,dt$, then there exists $c\in\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\Lambda_v(t,x_*(t),x_*'(t))=c+\int_a^t\Lambda_x(s,x_*(s),x_*'(s))\,ds$ for almost every $t\in[a,b]$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-endpoint Lipschitz weak local minimizer satisfies the integral Euler equation: almost everywhere, the velocity gradient equals a constant vector plus the accumulated state gradient.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong-Form Regularity Boundary for Multiple Integrals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates the multidimensional variational identity from its pointwise divergence form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Stationarity under compactly supported variations gives \[\int_\Omega\bigl(L_u\cdot\varphi+L_P:D\varphi\bigr)\,dx=0,\] equivalently \(L_u-\operatorname{Div}L_P=0\) in distributions. A pointwise classical system additionally requires classical differentiability of \(x\mapsto L_P(x,u(x),Du(x))\); assumptions \(L\in C^1\) and \(u\in C^2\) alone do not generally ensure the required derivatives of the flux.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The multidimensional Euler system is naturally distributional; its pointwise form requires additional flux regularity.
assumptions_latex: u\text{ is stationary under compactly supported smooth variations}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_u-\operatorname{Div}L_P=0\text{ in }\mathcal D'(\Omega),\quad\text{but not necessarily pointwise}

assumptions_latex: \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is bounded with Lipschitz boundary}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical strong system for first-gradient vector-valued multiple integrals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J(u)=\int_\Omega L(x,u(x),Du(x))\,dx\). If \(u\) is stationary with respect to every \(\varphi\in C_c^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), then each component \(\alpha=1,\ldots,m\) satisfies \[\partial_{u^\alpha}L(x,u,Du)-\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_{x_i}\!\left(\partial_{p_{\alpha i}}L(x,u,Du)\right)=0\quad\text{in }\Omega.\] Equivalently, \(L_u-\operatorname{Div}L_p=0\), where the divergence is taken row-wise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationarity of a smooth vector-valued multiple integral forces the derivative in the state variable to equal the row-wise divergence of the derivative in the gradient variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Integral Euler–Lagrange Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record has no inspectable citation. Moreover, L in C^1 does not by itself ensure that the displayed derivatives of L_p exist classically; a strong pointwise system requires additional regularity or a weak/distributional formulation.

children.title: Higher-Order Euler–Lagrange Systems

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical Regularity Boundary for Euler–Poisson Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes a justified pointwise higher-order equation from its distributional form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pointwise expression \[\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^jD_t^jL_{y^{(j)}}=0\] is justified only when each composite coefficient \(L_{y^{(j)}}(t,y,\ldots,y^{(k)})\) possesses the required \(j\) total derivatives. If this composite regularity is unavailable, stationarity yields the corresponding identity only in the distributional sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A higher-order Euler formula is pointwise only when all repeated composite total derivatives exist; otherwise it is distributional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{insufficient composite regularity}\Rightarrow\text{only a distributional Euler identity is justified}
knowledge_statements.title: Classical Regularity Boundary for Euler–Poisson Equations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized-Momentum Form of the Higher-Order Equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ostrogradsky-type momentum representation of a smooth order-k variational equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L(t,y,y',\ldots,y^{(k)})\), define \[p_j:=\sum_{r=j+1}^{k}(-D_t)^{r-j-1}L_{y^{(r)}},\qquad j=0,\ldots,k-1.\] Whenever all displayed total derivatives exist, the order-\(k\) Euler–Lagrange equation is equivalent to \[D_tp_0=L_y.\] The momenta also satisfy \(p_{k-1}=L_{y^{(k)}}\) and \(p_{j-1}=L_{y^{(j)}}-D_tp_j\) for \(j=1,\ldots,k-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The alternating higher-order Euler expression can be organized recursively through generalized momenta.
assumptions_latex: All displayed composite total derivatives exist classically.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical one-dimensional order-\(k\) Euler–Poisson equation with fixed endpoint jets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(J(y)=\int_a^bL(t,y(t),y'(t),\ldots,y^{(k)}(t))\,dt\), suppose the endpoint jets through order \(k-1\) are fixed. If \(y\) is stationary under all smooth variations having corresponding zero endpoint jets, then \[\sum_{j=0}^k(-1)^j\frac{d^j}{dt^j}L_{y^{(j)}}(t,y(t),y'(t),\ldots,y^{(k)}(t))=0\quad\text{on }(a,b).\] For vector-valued \(y\), the same equation holds componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary functional depending on derivatives through order k satisfies the alternating sum of successive total derivatives of its partial derivatives.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed endpoint times with freely varying endpoint states and differentiable endpoint costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(J(y)=\Phi_a(y(a))+\int_a^bL(t,y,y')\,dt+\Phi_b(y(b))\), free endpoint states require \(-L_v(a)+\nabla\Phi_a(y(a))=0\) and \(L_v(b)+\nabla\Phi_b(y(b))=0\). With zero endpoint costs these reduce to vanishing conjugate momentum at each free endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Endpoint costs shift the zero-momentum natural condition, with opposite orientation signs at the two ends.
assumptions_latex: The endpoint times are fixed and the indicated endpoint states are freely variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_v(a)=\nabla\Phi_a(y(a)),\qquad L_v(b)=-\nabla\Phi_b(y(b)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed Endpoint Suppresses the Natural Momentum Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact applicability boundary between prescribed and free endpoint values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an endpoint where \(y\) is prescribed, admissible variations satisfy \(\eta=0\), so stationarity imposes no natural equation on \(L_v\) there. Imposing \(L_v=0\) in addition is generally an extra boundary condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prescribed endpoint removes the corresponding boundary variation and therefore suppresses its natural momentum condition.
assumptions_latex: The endpoint state is fixed in the admissible class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \eta(t_e)=0\Rightarrow\text{stationarity yields no condition }L_v(t_e)=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Endpoint Suppresses the Natural Momentum Condition

assumptions_latex: y(a)\text{ and }y(b)\text{ vary freely while }a,b\text{ remain fixed}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed independent-variable endpoints with freely varying endpoint values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(J(y)=\int_a^bL(t,y(t),y'(t))\,dt\), integration of the first variation produces the boundary term \([L_v(t,y,y')\cdot\eta(t)]_a^b\). If both endpoint values are unconstrained, \(\eta(a)\) and \(\eta(b)\) are arbitrary. Stationarity therefore requires \[L_v(a,y(a),y'(a))=0,\qquad L_v(b,y(b),y'(b))=0.\] If only one endpoint value is free, only the corresponding equality is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each fixed-time endpoint whose state value is free, the momentum derivative of the integrand must vanish.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak solution of the Neumann state system by transposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transposition definition for a hyperbolic state system using terminal-value test solutions with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(y\) with \((y,y_t)\in C([0,T];L^2(\Omega))\times C([0,T];H^1(\Omega)^*)\) is a weak solution of the Neumann state system if, for every \(\varphi\in L^1(0,T;L^2(\Omega))\), letting \(z\) solve \[z_{tt}-\Delta z=\varphi\ \text{in }Q,\qquad \partial_\nu z=0\ \text{on }\Sigma,\qquad z(T)=z_t(T)=0\ \text{in }\Omega,\] one has \[\int_Q-\vartheta(\cdot,y)z\,dx\,dt=\int_Q y\varphi\,dx\,dt-\langle y_t(0),z(0)\rangle_{H^1(\Omega)^*,H^1(\Omega)}+\int_\Omega y(0)z_t(0)\,dx+\int_\Sigma zu\,dS\,dt.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state is a weak solution when it satisfies the specified transposition identity against every terminal-value test solution of the wave equation with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y\text{ is a weak solution}\iff \text{the stated transposition identity holds for every admissible }\varphi\text{ and corresponding }z.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Dirichlet-natural boundary partition of \(\partial\Omega\) is a pair of relatively measurable sets \(\Gamma_D\) and \(\Gamma_N\) satisfying \[\mathcal H^{n-1}(\Gamma_D\cap\Gamma_N)=0,\qquad \mathcal H^{n-1}\!\left(\partial\Omega\setminus(\Gamma_D\cup\Gamma_N)\right)=0.\] For \(1\le p<\infty\), its associated space of admissible variations is \[V_0=\{\eta\in W^{1,p}(\Omega):\operatorname{Tr}\eta=0\ \mathcal H^{n-1}\text{-almost everywhere on }\Gamma_D\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Dirichlet-natural boundary partition covers the boundary, up to a surface-null set, by essentially disjoint trace-constrained and natural portions; admissible Sobolev variations have zero trace on the Dirichlet portion.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be bounded, connected, and Lipschitz and let \(V_0=\{v\in W^{1,p}(\Omega):\operatorname{Tr}v=0\text{ a.e. on }\Gamma_D\}\). If \(\mathcal H^{n-1}(\Gamma_D)>0\), then \[\|v\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\qquad(v\in V_0).\] If \(\mathcal H^{n-1}(\Gamma_D)=0\), constants belong to \(V_0\), so this estimate fails unless constants are removed by a quotient or normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-measure Dirichlet portion removes the constant kernel and yields a boundary Poincaré inequality; a null Dirichlet portion does not.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasiconformal Extension and Sobolev Regularity of the Conformal Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A consequence under all hypotheses of the preceding boundary-regularity theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(g\in H^{1,\infty}(\omega)\), \(\alpha\in C^{0,\lambda}(U)\) with \(0<\lambda<1\), \(g_{\bar z}=\alpha\) in \(\omega\), \(g=0\) on the represented arc \(\gamma\subset\partial\omega\), \(|\alpha|\ge\alpha_0>0\) on the neighborhood \(U\supset\overline\omega\), and that \(\varphi:G\to\omega\) is conformal. Then \(\varphi\) has a quasiconformal extension to a neighborhood of the real axis and \(\varphi\in H^{1,s}(G\cap B_R)\) for every \(1\le s<\infty\) and every \(0<R<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the preceding inhomogeneous Cauchy–Riemann and boundary-arc hypotheses, the conformal parametrization extends quasiconformally across the real axis and belongs locally to every finite first-order Sobolev integrability class.
