knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Regularity from an Inhomogeneous Cauchy–Riemann Equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity of a conformal parametrization along a represented boundary arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\in H^{1,\infty}(\omega)\) and \(\alpha\in C^{0,\lambda}(U)\), where \(U\) is a neighborhood of \(\overline\omega\) and \(0<\lambda<1\). Assume \(g_{\bar z}=\alpha\) in \(\omega\), \(g=0\) on \(\gamma\subset\partial\omega\), and \(|\alpha(z)|\ge \alpha_0>0\) for every \(z\in U\). If \(\varphi:G\to\omega\) is conformal and \(\gamma\) has the boundary representation (3.2), then \(\varphi\in C^{1,\tau}(\overline G\cap B_R)\) for every \(\tau<\lambda\) and every \(R<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an inhomogeneous Cauchy–Riemann solution vanishes on a represented boundary arc and its forcing is Hölder continuous and bounded away from zero, then the conformal parametrization of that arc is continuously differentiable with every Hölder exponent below the forcing exponent, locally away from the endpoint radius.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\tau<\lambda\;\forall R<1,\quad \varphi\in C^{1,\tau}(\overline G\cap B_R)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jordan-Curve Regularity of a Strictly Concave Obstacle Free Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Free-boundary geometry for a planar Dirichlet obstacle problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2\) be strictly convex with smooth boundary, and let \(\psi\in C^{2,\lambda}(\overline\Omega)\) satisfy \(\max_\Omega\psi>0\), \(\psi<0\) on \(\partial\Omega\), and \(-\psi_{x_i x_j}(z)\xi_i\xi_j>0\) for every \(z\in\Omega\) and every \(0\ne\xi\in\mathbb R^2\). Define \(K=\{v\in H_0^1(\Omega):v\ge\psi\text{ in }\Omega\}\), and let \(u\in K\) satisfy \(\int_\Omega u_{x_i}(v-u)_{x_i}\,dx\ge0\) for every \(v\in K\). If \(I=\{z\in\Omega:u(z)=\psi(z)\}\), then \(\Gamma=\partial I\) is a Jordan curve admitting a \(C^{1,\tau}\) parametrization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a planar obstacle problem on a smooth strictly convex domain with a strictly concave obstacle that is positive somewhere and negative on the boundary, the boundary of the coincidence set is a Jordan curve with a continuously differentiable Hölder parametrization.
assumptions_latex: \Omega\subset\mathbb R^2\text{ is strictly convex with smooth }\partial\Omega
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Gamma=\partial I\text{ is a Jordan curve admitting a }C^{1,\tau}\text{ parametrization}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mixed Fixed and Free Endpoint Jets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise natural conditions for partially prescribed endpoint jets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(y^{(r)}(t_e)\) is fixed, then \(\eta^{(r)}(t_e)=0\) and no equation \(P_r(t_e)=0\) follows. If that jet component is free independently, then \(P_r(t_e)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each prescribed endpoint derivative suppresses its conjugate natural condition, while each free derivative activates it.
assumptions_latex: A subset of \((y,y',\ldots,y^{(k-1)})\) is prescribed at the endpoint.
The remaining components admit independent variations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \eta^{(r)}(t_e)=0\text{ for fixed jets};\qquad P_r(t_e)=0\text{ for free jets}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional kth-order functional with independently variable endpoint jets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(J(y)=\int_a^bL(t,y,y',\ldots,y^{(k)})\,dt\), define \(P_r=\sum_{j=r+1}^{k}(-D_t)^{j-r-1}L_{y^{(j)}}\), \(r=0,\ldots,k-1\). At a fixed-time endpoint, independent freedom of \(y^{(r)}\) requires \(P_r=0\) there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every freely varying endpoint jet component forces its conjugate generalized boundary momentum to vanish.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) and \(y\) have enough regularity for the displayed total derivatives.
The indicated endpoint jet components vary independently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y^{(r)}\text{ free at }t_e\Rightarrow P_r(t_e)=0.

knowledge_statements.title: General Higher-Order Endpoint Natural Conditions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary-condition count for functionals of order at least two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(k\ge2\), the condition \(L_{y^{(k)}}=0\) does not exhaust endpoint stationarity when lower endpoint jets are also free. Every independently free \(y^{(r)}\), \(0\le r<k\), has its distinct condition \(P_r=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher-order problems require the complete hierarchy of natural endpoint conditions, not only the highest momentum condition.
assumptions_latex: At least two endpoint jet components are independently free.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_{y^{(k)}}=0\text{ alone does not imply endpoint stationarity}.
knowledge_statements.title: Highest-Derivative Condition Alone Is Insufficient

assumptions_latex: y\text{ and }y'\text{ are free at the endpoint under consideration}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_{y''}=0,\qquad L_{y'}-\frac{d}{dt}L_{y''}=0\quad\text{at each free endpoint}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order one-dimensional prototype with free endpoint value and slope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(J(y)=\int_a^bL(t,y,y',y'')\,dt\), the boundary part of the first variation is \[\left[\left(L_{y'}-\frac{d}{dt}L_{y''}\right)\eta+L_{y''}\eta'\right]_a^b.\] If \(y\) and \(y'\) are independently free at an endpoint, then \(\eta\) and \(\eta'\) are arbitrary there, giving \[L_{y''}=0,\qquad L_{y'}-\frac{d}{dt}L_{y''}=0.\] A fixed endpoint jet suppresses its corresponding natural condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a second-derivative functional, free endpoint slope and value respectively force the highest momentum and the corrected lower momentum to vanish.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transversality for mixed endpoint equality and inequality constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier and adjoint necessary conditions for a differential-inclusion Mayer problem with locally Lipschitz endpoint data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\bar x(\cdot)$ be an intermediate local minimizer of $(P_M)$ with $$\Omega=\{x\in X\mid \varphi_i(x)\leq0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ \varphi_i(x)=0\ (i=m+1,\ldots,m+r)\},$$ where $\varphi_0:=\varphi$ and all $\varphi_i$, $i=0,\ldots,m+r$, are locally Lipschitz around $\bar x(b)$. Suppose all assumptions of Theorem 6.27 hold except SNEC of $\varphi_\Omega$. Then there exist nonnegative multipliers $(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_{m+r})\neq0$ and an absolutely continuous adjoint arc $p$ satisfying the Euler--Lagrange and maximum conditions, $$\lambda_i\varphi_i(\bar x(b))=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),$$ and $$-p(b)\in\sum_{i=0}^{m}\lambda_i\partial\varphi_i(\bar x(b))+\sum_{i=m+1}^{m+r}\lambda_i\left[\partial\varphi_i(\bar x(b))\cup\partial(-\varphi_i)(\bar x(b))\right].$$ If all $\varphi_i$ are strictly differentiable at $\bar x(b)$, there exist nonzero multipliers with $\lambda_i\geq0$ for $i=0,\ldots,m$ such that $$-p(b)=\sum_{i=0}^{m+r}\lambda_i\nabla\varphi_i(\bar x(b)),$$ together with the same Euler--Lagrange, maximum, and complementary-slackness conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For locally Lipschitz mixed endpoint constraints, the differential-inclusion hypotheses yield nontrivial nonnegative multipliers and an adjoint arc satisfying Euler–Lagrange and maximum conditions, inequality complementary slackness, and a nonsmooth endpoint transversality inclusion. If all endpoint functions are strictly differentiable, transversality becomes a gradient multiplier equation; only the cost and inequality multipliers are required to be nonnegative in this specialization.
assumptions_latex: \bar x(\cdot)\text{ is an intermediate local minimizer of }(P_M).
\varphi_0:=\varphi\text{ and every }\varphi_i\text{ is locally Lipschitz around }\bar x(b).
\text{All assumptions of Theorem 6.27 hold except the SNEC property of }\varphi_\Omega.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_{m+r})\neq0\text{ and }p\in AC([a,b];X^*)\text{ satisfying the Euler--Lagrange, maximum, complementary-slackness, and stated transversality conditions.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the additional boundary necessary conditions associated with endpoint values that are not fully prescribed, with a fixed-initial-value and free-terminal-value model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
When one or more endpoint values of the competing curves are not prescribed, the resulting additional endpoint conclusions in the necessary conditions are called transversality conditions. A model problem is
\[
\min_{x\in C^2([a,b]),\,x(a)=A}\left\{\ell(x(b))+\int_a^b\Lambda(t,x(t),x'(t))\,dt\right\},
\]
where \(x(b)\) is unprescribed and \(\ell\in C^1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transversality conditions are the additional endpoint conclusions in necessary conditions that arise when an admissible curve's endpoint values are not fully prescribed. The displayed model fixes the initial value while leaving the terminal value free and includes a differentiable terminal cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The additional endpoint conclusions are called transversality conditions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Endpoint Transversality under Lipschitz Functional Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded multiplier and endpoint-adjoint conditions for mixed locally Lipschitz equality and inequality endpoint constraints in the evolution-system Bolza problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega:=\{(x_a,x_b)\in X^2\mid \varphi_i(x_a,x_b)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ \varphi_i(x_a,x_b)=0,\ i=m+1,\ldots,m+r\}\), where \(\varphi_0:=\varphi\), and suppose \(\varphi_i\) is locally Lipschitz around \((\bar x(a),\bar x(b))\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m+r\). Under all assumptions of Corollary 6.23 except those concerning the SNC/PSNC properties of \(\Omega\), there exist multipliers \((\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_{m+r})\ne0\), with \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m+r\), and an absolutely continuous arc \(p:[a,b]\to X^*\) satisfying the inherited extended Euler\text{--}Lagrange inclusions, the complementary-slackness conditions \(\lambda_i\varphi_i(\bar x(a),\bar x(b))=0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and
\[
(p(a),-p(b))\in\sum_{i=0}^{m}\lambda_i\partial\varphi_i(\bar x(a),\bar x(b))+\sum_{i=m+1}^{m+r}\lambda_i\left[\partial\varphi_i(\bar x(a),\bar x(b))\cup\partial(-\varphi_i)(\bar x(a),\bar x(b))\right].
\]
If every \(\varphi_i\) is strictly differentiable at the endpoint pair, then there exist nonzero multipliers satisfying complementary slackness and \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\), while the equality-constraint multipliers are unrestricted in sign, such that
\[
(p(a),-p(b))=\sum_{i=0}^{m+r}\lambda_i\nabla\varphi_i(\bar x(a),\bar x(b)).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For mixed locally Lipschitz endpoint inequalities and equalities, the inherited hypotheses of Corollary 6.23, apart from endpoint-set SNC or PSNC, yield a nonzero multiplier system and an absolutely continuous adjoint satisfying the inherited Euler–Lagrange conditions, inequality complementary slackness, and a nonsmooth endpoint transversality inclusion. Under strict differentiability, transversality becomes the usual gradient multiplier equation; cost and inequality multipliers are nonnegative, while equality multipliers have unrestricted sign.
assumptions_latex: \varphi_0:=\varphi,\qquad \varphi_i\text{ is locally Lipschitz around }(\bar x(a),\bar x(b))\text{ for }i=0,\ldots,m+r.
\text{All assumptions of Corollary 6.23 hold except those concerning the SNC/PSNC properties of }\Omega.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,\lambda\ne0,\ \exists\,p\in AC([a,b];X^*)\text{ satisfying the inherited extended Euler\text{--}Lagrange inclusions, complementary slackness, and the stated transversality inclusion; if every }\varphi_i\text{ is strictly differentiable, the stated gradient equality holds with }\lambda_i\ge0\text{ for }i=0,\ldots,m.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transversality Conditions for Endpoints on Two Prescribed Curves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order endpoint conditions when the initial and terminal points vary independently along prescribed planar curves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the initial endpoint lie on $y=\varphi(x)$ and the terminal endpoint lie on $y=\psi(x)$. If $\delta x_0$ and $\delta x_1$ are independent, then the boundary conditions are
\[
\left.\left[F+(\varphi'-y')F_{y'}\right]\right|_{x=x_0}=0,
\qquad
\left.\left[F+(\psi'-y')F_{y'}\right]\right|_{x=x_1}=0.
\]
These are the transversality conditions. A curve satisfying them is called a transversal of $y=\varphi(x)$ and $y=\psi(x)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the two endpoints vary independently along the prescribed curves y = φ(x) and y = ψ(x), the corresponding boundary expressions must vanish at the initial and terminal endpoints. These are the transversality conditions, and a curve satisfying them is a transversal of the prescribed curves.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left.\left[F+(\varphi'-y')F_{y'}\right]\right|_{x=x_0}=0,\qquad \left.\left[F+(\psi'-y')F_{y'}\right]\right|_{x=x_1}=0

\]

children.top_down_role: Endpoint stationarity relative to smooth or nonsmooth terminal sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed terminal time and a smooth terminal manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[J(y)=\Phi(y(T))+\int_a^T L(t,y,y')\,dt\] with \(y(T)\in M\), where \(M\) is a \(C^1\) embedded manifold, endpoint stationarity is \[\bigl(p(T)+\nabla\Phi(y(T))\bigr)\cdot w=0\quad(w\in T_M(y(T))),\] equivalently \[p(T)+\nabla\Phi(y(T))\in N_M(y(T))=T_M(y(T))^\perp.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Terminal momentum plus terminal-cost gradient annihilates the manifold tangent space, equivalently lying in its normal space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate maximum principle under smooth endpoint constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary conditions for optimal discrete approximations of an evolution-system control problem with smooth endpoint constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(N\in\mathbb N\), let \((\bar u_N,\bar x_N)\) be optimal for \((P_N)\) under its standing assumptions. Suppose \(\varphi_i\), \(i=0,\ldots,m+r\), are continuously differentiable near the limiting point or points of \(\{\bar x_N(b)\}\), the controls \(\{\bar u_N\}\) are proper, and consistency condition (6.80) holds for the perturbations \(\xi_{iN}\) of every equality constraint. Then there exist multipliers \(\lambda_{iN}\) such that \(\lambda_{iN}(\varphi_i(\bar x_N(b))-\gamma_{iN})=O(h_N)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), \(\lambda_{iN}\ge0\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\), and \(\sum_{i=0}^{m+r}\lambda_{iN}^2=1\). The approximate maximum condition (6.85) holds with \(\varepsilon_N(t,h_N)\to0\) uniformly for \(t\in T_N\), where \(p_N\) solves the adjoint system (6.78) and satisfies \(p_N(b)=-\sum_{i=0}^{m+r}\lambda_{iN}\nabla\varphi_i(\bar x_N(b))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimal discrete controls satisfying properness and equality-perturbation consistency admit normalized endpoint multipliers. The inequality multipliers are nonnegative and satisfy approximate complementarity, while the associated adjoint trajectory satisfies the endpoint transversality equation and an approximate maximum condition whose error converges uniformly to zero.

\varphi_i\in C^1\text{ near every limiting point of }\{\bar x_N(b)\},\quad i=0,\ldots,m+r.
\text{Consistency condition (6.80) holds for the perturbations }\xi_{iN}\text{ of all equality constraints.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\{\lambda_{iN}\}_{i=0}^{m+r}:\quad \lambda_{iN}(\varphi_i(\bar x_N(b))-\gamma_{iN})=O(h_N)\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\quad \lambda_{iN}\ge0\ (i=0,\ldots,m),\quad \sum_{i=0}^{m+r}\lambda_{iN}^2=1,\quad \varepsilon_N(t,h_N)\to0\text{ uniformly on }T_N,\quad p_N(b)=-\sum_{i=0}^{m+r}\lambda_{iN}\nabla\varphi_i(\bar x_N(b)).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(G_1,\ldots,G_m)\), where each \(G_i\) may be an integral functional. Under the stated hypotheses, there is a unique multiplier vector only when \(DG(\bar u)^*\) is injective; existence does not require uniqueness. At least one \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfies
\[DJ(\bar u)h+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iDG_i(\bar u)h=0\qquad\text{for every }h\in X.\]
Equivalently, \(\bar u\) is stationary for the Lagrangian \(u\mapsto J(u)+\lambda\cdot(G(u)-c)\). Surjectivity excludes an abnormal objective multiplier, so the coefficient of \(J\) has been normalized to one.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary first-order condition for a fixed-endpoint variational extremum subject to one integral equality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J[y]=\int_a^b F(x,y,y')\,dx\) and \(K[y]=\int_a^b G(x,y,y')\,dx\). Suppose \(y(a)=A\), \(y(b)=B\), \(K[y]=l\), and \(y\) is an extremizer of \(J\) among admissible curves. If \(y\) is not an extremal of \(K\), then there exists a constant \(\lambda\) such that \(y\) is an extremal of \(\int_a^b(F+\lambda G)\,dx\), and hence \[F_y-\frac{d}{dx}F_{y'}+\lambda\left(G_y-\frac{d}{dx}G_{y'}\right)=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed-endpoint variational problem with one integral equality constraint, if the optimizing curve is not itself an extremal of the constraint functional, then a constant multiplier exists and the curve satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation for the objective integrand plus that multiplier times the constraint integrand.
assumptions_latex: y\text{ is an extremizer of }J\text{ over the admissible curves}
y\text{ is not an extremal of }K
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\lambda\in\mathbb{R}:\quad F_y-\frac{d}{dx}F_{y'}+\lambda\left(G_y-\frac{d}{dx}G_{y'}\right)=0

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flux-multiplier form for a convex almost-everywhere gradient restriction when the inverse-image normal rule is exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), \(A u=Du\), and
\[K=\{u\in X:Du(x)\in C(x)\text{ a.e.}\}.\]
If the convex inverse-image normal formula \(N_K(\bar u)=A^*N_Q(A\bar u)\) holds for \(Q=\{P\in L^p:P(x)\in C(x)\text{ a.e.}\}\), then every differentiable local minimizer \(\bar u\) admits \(\sigma\in L^q\) satisfying
\[\sigma(x)\in N_{C(x)}(D\bar u(x))\text{ a.e.},\qquad DI(\bar u)+A^*\sigma=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the inverse-image normal rule is exact, a convex pointwise gradient constraint contributes a pointwise normal flux whose adjoint balances the objective derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(1<p<\infty\), and \(C(x)\subset\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) is measurable, nonempty, closed, and convex almost everywhere.
\(\bar u\) locally minimizes a Fréchet differentiable functional over the displayed feasible set.
The inverse-image normal-cone equality \(N_K(\bar u)=A^*N_Q(A\bar u)\) holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\sigma(x)\in N_{C(x)}(D\bar u(x))\ \text{a.e.},\qquad DI(\bar u)+A^*\sigma=0.\]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal cone to a decomposable convex pointwise state constraint in an Lp space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[K=\{u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m):u(x)\in C(x)\text{ for a.e. }x\},\qquad 1<p<\infty,\]
where \(C\) is measurable with nonempty closed convex values. For \(\bar u\in K\),
\[N_K(\bar u)=\{\xi\in L^q(\Omega;\mathbb R^m):\xi(x)\in N_{C(x)}(\bar u(x))\text{ a.e.}\},\qquad q=\frac p{p-1}.\]
Consequently, a differentiable local minimizer satisfies \(-DI(\bar u)=\xi\) for a field with this pointwise-normal property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex pointwise state constraints in Lp, global normals are exactly integrable fields that are pointwise normal almost everywhere.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) is a finite measure space and \(1<p<\infty\).
\(C:\Omega\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) is measurable with nonempty closed convex values.
The feasible set \(K\) is nonempty and \(\bar u\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[N_K(\bar u)=\{\xi\in L^q:\xi(x)\in N_{C(x)}(\bar u(x))\text{ a.e.}\}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every feasible comparison field \(v\in K\), convexity of \(K\) makes \(\bar u+s(v-\bar u)\) feasible for \(0\le s\le1\). First-order necessity is therefore
\[\int_\Omega\!\left[F_z(x,\bar u,D\bar u)\cdot(v-\bar u)+F_P(x,\bar u,D\bar u):(Dv-D\bar u)\right]dx\ge0.\]
Equivalently, \(-DI(\bar u)\in N_K(\bar u)\), with \(N_K(\bar u)=\{\ell\in(W^{1,p})^*: \ell(v-\bar u)\le0\text{ for all }v\in K\}\). This condition covers almost-everywhere restrictions on the state, gradient, or both.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a minimizer under convex almost-everywhere state or gradient restrictions, the first variation is nonnegative in every feasible comparison direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplier certificate for the box-control variational inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent stationarity and complementary-slackness certificate for lower and upper pointwise control bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The variational inequality is equivalent to the existence of functions $\mu_a,\mu_b\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfying $\mu_a,\mu_b\ge 0$ almost everywhere, $\beta p+\lambda\bar u-\mu_a+\mu_b=0$, and $\mu_a(x)(u_a(x)-\bar u(x))=\mu_b(x)(\bar u(x)-u_b(x))=0$ for almost every $x\in\Omega$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The box-control variational inequality holds exactly when nonnegative lower- and upper-bound multipliers satisfy stationarity and complementary slackness almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{VI}(\bar u)\iff\exists\mu_a,\mu_b\in L^2(\Omega):\ \mu_a,\mu_b\ge0\ \text{a.e.},\ \beta p+\lambda\bar u-\mu_a+\mu_b=0,\ \mu_a(u_a-\bar u)=\mu_b(\bar u-u_b)=0\ \text{a.e.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise characterization of the box-control variational inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For the box-constrained linear-quadratic elliptic control problem and its adjoint variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The variational inequality is satisfied if and only if, for almost every $x\in\Omega$, writing $g(x)=\beta(x)p(x)+\lambda\bar u(x)$, one has $\bar u(x)=u_a(x)$ when $g(x)>0$, $\bar u(x)\in[u_a(x),u_b(x)]$ when $g(x)=0$, and $\bar u(x)=u_b(x)$ when $g(x)<0$. Equivalently, $g(x)(v-\bar u(x))\ge 0$ for every $v\in[u_a(x),u_b(x)]$ and almost every $x\in\Omega$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The box-control variational inequality holds exactly when the control selects the lower bound for a positive reduced gradient, the upper bound for a negative reduced gradient, and any admissible value when it vanishes; equivalently, the corresponding scalar variational inequality holds pointwise almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{VI}(\bar u)\iff \bigl[g(x)(v-\bar u(x))\ge0\ \forall v\in[u_a(x),u_b(x)]\text{ for a.e. }x\bigr]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise minimum principles for optimal box controls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality characterization for the stated linear-quadratic elliptic control problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A control $\bar u\in U_{ad}$ is optimal if and only if, together with its adjoint state $p$, it satisfies for almost every $x\in\Omega$ either equivalent minimum condition: $\min_{v\in[u_a(x),u_b(x)]}(\beta(x)p(x)+\lambda\bar u(x))v=(\beta(x)p(x)+\lambda\bar u(x))\bar u(x)$, or $\min_{v\in[u_a(x),u_b(x)]}\{\beta(x)p(x)v+\frac{\lambda}{2}v^2\}=\beta(x)p(x)\bar u(x)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\bar u(x)^2$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An admissible control is optimal exactly when, with its adjoint state, it minimizes almost everywhere either the linearized pointwise expression or the corresponding pointwise quadratic control Hamiltonian over the control interval.
assumptions_latex: p\text{ is the adjoint state associated with }\bar u
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar u\text{ is optimal}\iff\text{ either stated pointwise minimum condition holds for a.e. }x\in\Omega

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the convex normal cone by \(N_K(y)=\{y^*\in Y^*: \langle y^*,w-y\rangle\le0\text{ for every }w\in K\}\). Under the qualification, there exists \(y^*\in N_K(A\bar u)\) such that
\[D\Phi(\bar u)h+\langle y^*,Ah\rangle=0\qquad\text{for every }h\in X.\]
Thus stationarity is the adjoint balance \(D\Phi(\bar u)+A^*y^*=0\), coupled with dual feasibility and complementarity encoded by the normal cone. When \(A\) is a differential operator, interpreting \(A^*y^*\) weakly yields the corresponding adjoint differential equation and boundary conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A qualified differential-operator constraint supplies a normal-cone multiplier whose adjoint balances the objective's first derivative.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of the Adjoint Multiplier Rule Without Qualification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional operator-constraint model showing failure of the accepted adjoint balance without its normal-chain qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2\) be \(Ax=(x,0)\), let \(K=\{(a,b):b\ge a^2\}\), and minimize \(\Phi(x)=x\) subject to \(Ax\in K\). The feasible set is \(\{0\}\), so \(\bar x=0\) is a local minimizer. Yet \[N_K(0,0)=\{(0,\beta):\beta\le0\},\qquad A^*(0,\beta)=0,\] and no \(y^*\in N_K(0,0)\) satisfies \(D\Phi(0)+A^*y^*=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without the preimage qualification, a constrained minimizer may have no normal multiplier whose adjoint balances the objective derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x=0\) is a constrained local minimizer, but \(1+A^*y^*\ne0\) for every \(y^*\in N_K(A\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of the Adjoint Multiplier Rule Without Qualification

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Derivative representation and quadratic expansion of the value function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous derivative candidate and uniform compact-set remainder estimate for the parameterized value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\varphi':\mathbb R_+^n\to\mathbb R^n\) by \(\varphi'(\bar x):=j(\psi^y(\bar x))\). Then \(\varphi'\) is continuous, and for every compact \(\widehat X\subset\mathbb R_+^n\) there exists \(C>0\) such that \(|\varphi(x)-\varphi(\bar x)-\varphi'(\bar x)\cdot(x-\bar x)|\le C|x-\bar x|_2^2\) for all \(x,\bar x\in\widehat X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The value-function derivative is represented by j evaluated at the optimal state. This derivative mapping is continuous, and on each compact parameter set the first-order expansion has a uniformly quadratic remainder.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi'\text{ is continuous and }|\varphi(x)-\varphi(\bar x)-\varphi'(\bar x)\cdot(x-\bar x)|\le C|x-\bar x|_2^2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz regularity of the optimal state and control mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter sensitivity estimates and compact-set Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist continuous \(C_y,C_u:\mathbb R_+^n\to\mathbb R\) such that, for all \(x_1,x_2\in\mathbb R_+^n\), \(\|\psi^y(x_1)-\psi^y(x_2)\|_{\mathcal Y}\le C_y(x_1)|x_1-x_2|_2\) and \(\|\psi^u(x_1)-\psi^u(x_2)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_u(x_1)|x_1-x_2|_2\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform second-order estimates along the optimal-state mapping

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Every pointwise condition holds almost everywhere on \(\Omega\); the displayed measurable sets are defined up to null sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar u)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathcal Y\times L^2(\Omega)\) be feasible for \((\mathrm{IOC})\), and set \(I^{a+}(\bar u)=\{\omega\in\Omega\mid\bar u(\omega)>u_a(\omega)\}\) and \(I^{b-}(\bar u)=\{\omega\in\Omega\mid\bar u(\omega)<u_b(\omega)\}\). The point is W-stationary if there exist \(\bar z\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\bar\mu\in\mathcal Y\), \(\bar p,\bar\rho\in\mathcal W^*\), and \(\bar\lambda,\bar w,\bar\xi\in L^2(\Omega)\) satisfying \(0=F_x'(\bar x,\bar y,\bar u)+\bar z+j'(\bar y)\bar\mu\), \(0=F_y'(\bar x,\bar y,\bar u)+A^*\bar\rho+j''(\bar y)(\bar\mu)^*\bar x\), \(0=F_u'(\bar x,\bar y,\bar u)+\sigma\bar w-B^*\bar\rho+\bar\xi\), \(0=A\bar\mu-B\bar w\), \(\bar z\in N_{X_{\mathrm{ad}}}(\bar x)\), \(0=j'(\bar y)^*\bar x+A^*\bar p\), \(0=\sigma\bar u-B^*\bar p+\bar\lambda\), \(\bar\lambda\geq0\) on \(I^{a+}(\bar u)\), \(\bar\lambda\leq0\) on \(I^{b-}(\bar u)\), \(\bar\xi=0\) on \(I^{a+}(\bar u)\cap I^{b-}(\bar u)\), and \(\bar w=0\) on \(\{\omega\mid\bar\lambda(\omega)\neq0\}\). It is C-stationary when these multipliers additionally satisfy \(\bar\xi\bar w\geq0\) on \(\Omega\). It is S-stationary when this condition is strengthened to \(\bar\xi\leq0\) and \(\bar w\leq0\) on \(\{\omega\mid\bar\lambda(\omega)=0,\ \bar u(\omega)=u_a(\omega)\}\), and \(\bar\xi\geq0\) and \(\bar w\geq0\) on \(\{\omega\mid\bar\lambda(\omega)=0,\ \bar u(\omega)=u_b(\omega)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible IOC point is weakly stationary when it admits multipliers satisfying the stated adjoint, normal-cone, sign, and complementarity system. Nonnegative ξw defines Clarke stationarity, while the stronger bound-active sign conditions define strong stationarity.
assumptions_latex: (\bar x,\bar y,\bar u)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathcal Y\times L^2(\Omega)\text{ is feasible for }(\mathrm{IOC}).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The multiplier system defines W-stationarity; adding }\bar\xi\bar w\geq0\text{ a.e. defines C-stationarity, and the stated bound-active sign conditions define S-stationarity.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normality of an Arc and of the Differential-Inclusion Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source-local multiplier sets associated with the differential-inclusion problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An arc $x$ is normal if, for every $r>0$, each multiplier $[p,\gamma,\mu,\zeta,0]\in M_r^{\circ}(x)$ satisfies $p\equiv0$ and $\mu\equiv0$. The problem $P_D$ is normal if, for every $r>0$, every multiplier in $M_r^{\circ}(Y)$ has $p\equiv0$ and $\mu\equiv0$. Normality of $P_D$ implies weak normality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc is normal when every zero-objective multiplier in its multiplier set, for every positive radius, has identically zero p and mu components. The problem is normal when the analogous condition holds over its feasible family. Every normal problem is weakly normal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}x\text{ normal}&\iff \forall r>0,\ [p,\gamma,\mu,\zeta,0]\in M_r^{\circ}(x)\Rightarrow p\equiv0,\ \mu\equiv0,\\ P_D\text{ normal}&\iff \forall r>0,\ [p,\gamma,\mu,\zeta,0]\in M_r^{\circ}(Y)\Rightarrow p\equiv0,\ \mu\equiv0,\\ P_D\text{ normal}&\Rightarrow P_D\text{ weakly normal}.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A constrained extremal \(\bar u\) is normal when its first-order multiplier system has a nontrivial solution \((\lambda_0,\lambda)\) with \(\lambda_0>0\), where \(\lambda_0\) multiplies the objective variation and \(\lambda\) multiplies the active subsidiary constraints. Because a homogeneous multiplier system is invariant under common positive rescaling, normality permits the normalization \(\lambda_0=1\). The resulting stationarity condition retains the objective derivative and has the form
\[DJ(\bar u)+D\mathcal G(\bar u)^*\widehat\lambda=0,\qquad \widehat\lambda=\lambda/\lambda_0,\]
with the appropriate feasibility, sign, and complementarity conditions for \(\widehat\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extremal is normal when some nontrivial multiplier system gives the objective a positive coefficient, which can then be normalized to one.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal Extremals

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A constrained extremal \(\bar u\) is abnormal when a valid nontrivial first-order multiplier tuple satisfies \(\lambda_0=0\), so necessarily \(\lambda\ne0\). Its stationarity relation consequently reduces to
\[D\mathcal G(\bar u)^*\lambda=0,\]
with any required multiplier signs and complementarity relations, and contains no objective derivative. If every nontrivial multiplier tuple has \(\lambda_0=0\), the extremal is strictly abnormal; if both normal and abnormal tuples exist, the extremal remains normal under the existential convention for normality. Abnormality typically signals degeneracy of the active constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An abnormal multiplier system has zero objective coefficient and a nonzero constraint multiplier, so stationarity may contain no information about the objective.

children.title: Multiplier-Normalization Failure
children.top_down_role: The structural boundary where ordinary multiplier normalization ceases to apply.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rescaling criterion for a positively homogeneous first-order multiplier system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\subset[0,\infty)\times Y^*\) be positively homogeneous. A nonzero tuple \((\lambda_0,\lambda)\in M\) can be positively rescaled to an admissible tuple having objective coefficient one if and only if \(\lambda_0>0\). Thus normalization fails for every admissible nonzero tuple exactly when
\[M\cap\bigl((0,\infty)\times Y^*\bigr)=\varnothing.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous multiplier tuple can be normalized to objective coefficient one exactly when that coefficient is positive; universal failure means every nonzero admissible tuple has coefficient zero.
assumptions_latex: \(M\subset[0,\infty)\times Y^*\) is a positively homogeneous admissible multiplier set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(\lambda_0,\lambda)\sim(1,\lambda/\lambda_0)\iff\lambda_0>0.\]
knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Boundary for Objective-Multiplier Normalization

assumptions_latex: Consider minimizing \(J(x)=x\) over \(x\in\mathbb R\) subject to \(G(x)=x^2=0\).
The feasible point is \(\bar x=0\), with \(J'(0)=1\) and \(G'(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\lambda_0J'(0)+\mu G'(0)=0\Longrightarrow\lambda_0=0,\qquad \mu\ne0.\]
review_flags: an exact external source for this illustrative counterexample is not supplied
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete degeneracy showing why the objective multiplier cannot always be normalized.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The feasible set of \(G(x)=x^2=0\) is the singleton \(\{0\}\), so \(\bar x=0\) is a local minimizer of \(J(x)=x\). A Fritz John multiplier pair \((\lambda_0,\mu)\ne(0,0)\), with \(\lambda_0\ge0\), must satisfy
\[0=\lambda_0J'(0)+\mu G'(0)=\lambda_0.\]
Hence every admissible nontrivial pair has \(\lambda_0=0\) and \(\mu\ne0\). No common rescaling can produce \(\lambda_0=1\). The failure is caused by the vanished constraint derivative \(G'(0)=0\), which violates the usual equality-constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimizing x subject to x squared equaling zero, every nontrivial Fritz John multiplier is abnormal, so objective-multiplier normalization fails.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier-Normalization Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional calculation is correct and the counterexample content kind fits the normalization-failure leaf. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical smooth one-dimensional Du Bois–Reymond identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the functional \(I(u)=\int_a^bL(t,u(t),u'(t))\,dt\), let \(u\) satisfy the Euler–Lagrange equation under the stated smoothness assumptions. Then the Du Bois–Reymond quantity obeys
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left[L(t,u(t),u'(t))-u'(t)\cdot L_v(t,u(t),u'(t))\right]=L_t(t,u(t),u'(t))\qquad(t\in(a,b)).\]
Thus explicit dependence of \(L\) on \(t\) is exactly the source term for this energy-type quantity. In particular, when \(L_t=0\), the bracketed expression is constant along the extremal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a smooth Euler–Lagrange extremal, the derivative of the energy-type expression equals the integrand's explicit time derivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Du Bois–Reymond Family

assumptions_latex: \(L:[a,b]\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) is an integrand.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Autonomy with respect to the independent variable in a first-order integral functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The integrand \(L\) is autonomous when it has no explicit dependence on the independent variable: there exists a function \(\ell\) such that
\[L(t,z,v)=\ell(z,v)\qquad\text{for all }(t,z,v)\in[a,b]\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^m.\]
Equivalently, if \(L\) is differentiable in \(t\), autonomy is the identity \(L_t(t,z,v)=0\) throughout its domain. Dependence through the trajectory values \(z=u(t)\) and \(v=u'(t)\) does not violate autonomy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrand is autonomous when it depends on the state and velocity but not explicitly on the independent variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Autonomous Integrands

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of autonomy is precise, internally consistent, and correctly classified as a definition, but no cited source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constrained Erdmann Condition and Nagumo Regularity Consequence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An almost-everywhere Erdmann first integral for a constrained autonomous variational problem, followed by a Lipschitz conclusion under the additional Nagumo-growth hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\Lambda$ be continuous and autonomous and let $v\mapsto\Lambda(x,v)$ be convex and differentiable. Suppose $x_*$ is a strong local minimizer of $J(x)$ over $x\in AC([a,b])$ subject to $x(t)\in S$, $x'(t)\in C$, $x(a)=A$, and $x(b)=B$, where $S\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is a cone. Then there exists a constant $h$ such that $\langle x_*'(t),\Lambda_v(x_*(t),x_*'(t))\rangle-\Lambda(x_*(t),x_*'(t))=h$ almost everywhere. If, additionally, $\Lambda$ has Nagumo growth along $x_*$, then $x_*$ is Lipschitz continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong local minimizer satisfying the stated state, cone-valued velocity, and endpoint constraints has an almost-everywhere constant Erdmann expression. If the Lagrangian also has Nagumo growth along the minimizer, the minimizer is Lipschitz.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth vector-valued Beltrami identity for autonomous first-order integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(u\) be a smooth Euler–Lagrange extremal of \(I(u)=\int_a^bL(u(t),u'(t))\,dt\). Since autonomy gives \(L_t=0\), the Du Bois–Reymond identity implies
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left[L(u(t),u'(t))-u'(t)\cdot L_v(u(t),u'(t))\right]=0.\]
Consequently, on each connected interval of definition there exists \(C\in\mathbb R\) such that \(L-u'\cdot L_v=C\). The sign-reversed quantity \(u'\cdot L_v-L\) is an equivalent conserved Hamiltonian convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an autonomous smooth integrand, the Beltrami energy expression is constant along every smooth Euler–Lagrange extremal.
knowledge_statements.title: Beltrami First Integrals

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Beltrami First Integral for an Autonomous Variational Integrand
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conservation law for an autonomous first-order variational problem admitting the canonical Euler representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=F(y_1,\ldots,y_n,y_1',\ldots,y_n')\) have no explicit dependence on \(x\), let \(p_i=\partial F/\partial y_i'\), and suppose the extremal is represented by the canonical Euler equations. Then \[H=-F+\sum_{i=1}^n y_i'p_i\] satisfies \(dH/dx=0\) along the extremal and hence is a first integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an autonomous variational integrand, the momentum–velocity pairing minus the integrand is constant along every extremal represented by the canonical Euler equations.
assumptions_latex: F=F(y_1,\ldots,y_n,y_1',\ldots,y_n')\text{ is sufficiently differentiable and has no explicit }x\text{-dependence}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{d}{dx}\left(-F+\sum_{i=1}^n y_i'p_i\right)=0\quad\text{along the extremal}

children.title: Loss-of-Autonomy Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where explicit base-variable dependence obstructs the autonomous reduction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit base-variable dependence replaces Beltrami conservation by the Du Bois–Reymond source balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L=L(t,z,v)\) be continuously differentiable in \(t\) and sufficiently smooth in \((z,v)\), and let \(u\in C^2\) satisfy
\[\frac{d}{dt}L_v(t,u,u')=L_z(t,u,u').\]
Then along \(u\),
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left[L(t,u,u')-u'\cdot L_v(t,u,u')\right]=L_t(t,u,u').\]
Thus the Beltrami expression is constant on an interval exactly when its source \(L_t(t,u(t),u'(t))\) vanishes there; global autonomy is sufficient but not necessary for this trajectorywise vanishing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonautonomous integrand, the derivative of the Beltrami quantity equals the explicit-time derivative of the integrand, so conservation survives only when that source vanishes along the extremal.
assumptions_latex: \(L(t,z,v)\) has the differentiability needed for the displayed derivatives and chain rule.
\(u\in C^2\) satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation on an interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\frac{d}{dt}(L-u'\cdot L_v)=L_t.\]

notation.meaning: explicit derivative of the integrand with respect to the base variable

assumptions_latex: Let \(u\in C^2([a,b])\) satisfy the Euler–Lagrange equation for \(\int_a^bL(t,u,u')\,dt\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\frac{d}{dt}\left(L-u'L_v\right)=1,\quad\text{so }L-u'L_v\text{ is not constant}.\]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit time dependence destroys Beltrami conservation through the Du Bois–Reymond source term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(L(t,z,v)=\frac12v^2+t\), the Euler–Lagrange equation is \(u''=0\), so every extremal has \(u'(t)=c\) for some constant \(c\). Along such an extremal,
\[L(t,u,u')-u'L_v(t,u,u')=t-\frac12c^2,\]
and hence
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(L-u'L_v\right)=1=L_t.\]
Therefore the Beltrami expression is not conserved. This example isolates the boundary of the autonomous result: once \(L_t\ne0\), the correct statement is a balance law with source \(L_t\), not a first integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding explicit time dependence can make the Beltrami quantity vary; for one-half velocity squared plus time, it grows at unit rate.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss-of-Autonomy Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The calculation correctly identifies explicit time dependence as the boundary of Beltrami conservation, and failure_boundary is the appropriate content kind. No external source with an inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Noether Conservation Families
children.top_down_role: Conservation structures associated with continuous variational symmetries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual identity underlying the one-dimensional first Noether theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set p=L_v, E(L)=L_z-D_tL_v, Q=\xi-u'\tau, and X=\tau\partial_t+\xi\cdot\partial_z. Then
\[\operatorname{pr}^{(1)}X(L)+L D_t\tau=Q\cdot E(L)+D_t\!\left[p\cdot\xi+(L-p\cdot u')\tau\right].\]
If the left side is D_tB, then
\[D_t\!\left[p\cdot\xi+(L-p\cdot u')\tau-B\right]=-Q\cdot E(L),\]
so the bracket is conserved on Euler–Lagrange extremals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infinitesimal density change splits into an Euler–Lagrange residual and the total derivative of the Noether current.
assumptions_latex: L, \tau, and \xi are sufficiently smooth for the displayed total derivatives.
X generates a one-parameter point transformation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{pr}^{(1)}X(L)+L D_t\tau=Q\cdot E(L)+D_t[p\cdot\xi+(L-p\cdot u')\tau].
review_flags: Signs are fixed by the explicit convention E(L)=L_z-D_tL_v.
knowledge_statements.title: Off-Shell Noether Identity

assumptions_latex: \(L\in C^2([a,b]\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^m)\), and \(u\in C^2\) satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation.
A one-parameter point transformation has infinitesimal generators \(\tau(t,z)\) and \(\xi(t,z)\).
The transformed density is invariant to first order up to a total derivative \(\frac{d}{dt}B(t,u(t))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[L_v\cdot\xi+\left(L-u'\cdot L_v\right)\tau-B=C.\]

notation.meaning: infinitesimal change of the independent variable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional first Noether theorem with a gauge term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the infinitesimal transformation \(t\mapsto t+\varepsilon\tau(t,z)\), \(z\mapsto z+\varepsilon\xi(t,z)\) changes the density \(L(t,u,u')\,dt\), to first order in \(\varepsilon\), only by \(\frac{d}{dt}B(t,u(t))\,dt\). Then every smooth Euler–Lagrange extremal satisfies
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left[L_v(t,u,u')\cdot\xi(t,u)+\left(L(t,u,u')-u'\cdot L_v(t,u,u')\right)\tau(t,u)-B(t,u)\right]=0.\]
Thus each continuous variational symmetry yields a conserved quantity; time translations and state translations recover energy and momentum families, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every smooth one-parameter variational symmetry, allowing a boundary term, produces a conserved Noether quantity along Euler–Lagrange extremals.
knowledge_statements.title: Noether Conservation Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement has the standard form of the first Noether theorem with a gauge term and fits the conservation-family container, but no source is supplied to verify the precise infinitesimal-invariance and sign conventions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Invariance of a variational functional under a transformation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact invariance of a first-order integral functional under the induced transformation of a curve, its variables, and its endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J[\gamma]=\int_{x_0}^{x_1}F\!\left(x,y,\frac{dy}{dx}\right)\,dx\). The functional is invariant under a transformation taking \(\gamma\) and its endpoints to \(\gamma^*\) and \((x_0^*,x_1^*)\) if \[J[\gamma^*]=J[\gamma],\] equivalently, \[\int_{x_0^*}^{x_1^*}F\!\left(x^*,y^*,\frac{dy^*}{dx^*}\right)\,dx^*=\int_{x_0}^{x_1}F\!\left(x,y,\frac{dy}{dx}\right)\,dx.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variational functional is invariant under the specified transformation when its value on the transformed curve and endpoints equals its value on the original curve and endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J[\gamma^*]=J[\gamma]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Noether theorem for one-parameter variational symmetries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-integral consequence of invariance of a first-order integral functional under a one-parameter transformation family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[J[y]=\int_{x_0}^{x_1}F(x,y,y')\,dx.\] Suppose \(J\) is invariant under a one-parameter family of transformations for arbitrary endpoints \(x_0,x_1\). If \[\varphi=\left.\frac{\partial\Phi(x,y,y';\varepsilon)}{\partial\varepsilon}\right|_{\varepsilon=0},\qquad \psi_i=\left.\frac{\partial\Psi_i(x,y,y';\varepsilon)}{\partial\varepsilon}\right|_{\varepsilon=0},\] then along every extremal of \(J\), \[\sum_{i=1}^n F_{y_i}\psi_i+\left(F-\sum_{i=1}^n y_i'F_{y_i}\right)\varphi=\mathrm{const}.\] Thus every such one-parameter invariance family yields a first integral of the Euler equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a first-order variational functional is invariant, for arbitrary endpoints, under a one-parameter transformation family, then the expression determined by the infinitesimal generators of that family is constant along every extremal; hence the symmetry gives a first integral of the Euler equations.
assumptions_latex: J\text{ is invariant under the one-parameter family for arbitrary }x_0,x_1
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i=1}^n F_{y_i}\psi_i+\left(F-\sum_{i=1}^n y_i'F_{y_i}\right)\varphi=\mathrm{const}\quad\text{along each extremal}

children.title: Inner-Variation Conservation Laws
children.top_down_role: Conservation and monotonicity structures generated by domain variations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radial consequence of inner stationarity for the unnormalized p-Dirichlet density |Du|^p.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let u\in W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m), 1<p<\infty, be stationary under compactly supported domain variations for E(u)=\int_\Omega|Du|^p\,dx. If B_R(x_0)\Subset\Omega, then for almost every r\in(0,R),
\[\frac{d}{dr}\left(r^{p-n}\int_{B_r(x_0)}|Du|^p\,dx\right)=p r^{p-n}\int_{\partial B_r(x_0)}|Du|^{p-2}|\partial_r u|^2\,d\mathcal H^{n-1}\ge0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scale-normalized p-energy of a stationary map is nondecreasing on concentric balls.
assumptions_latex: u is stationary for \int|Du|^p under compactly supported inner variations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r\mapsto r^{p-n}\int_{B_r(x_0)}|Du|^p\,dx\text{ is nondecreasing}.

notation.meaning: radial derivative on spheres centered at x_0

review_flags: The factor p corresponds to the density |Du|^p rather than |Du|^p/p.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Formula for Stationary p-Energy

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) is open, \(F\in C^1(\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^{m\times n})\) is autonomous, and \(u\in W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\).
The integral \(I(u)=\int_\Omega F(u,Du)\,dx\) is stationary under compactly supported domain diffeomorphisms.
All displayed products are locally integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{div}\left(F(u,Du)I_n-Du^TF_P(u,Du)\right)=0\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Omega;\mathbb R^n).\]

notation.meaning: integrand derivative with respect to the gradient matrix

tensor orientation convention requires source confirmation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional stress-energy conservation generated by compactly supported inner variations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\eta\in C_c^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^n)\), stationarity under the inner variation generated by \(x\mapsto x+\varepsilon\eta(x)\) gives
\[\int_\Omega\left[F(u,Du)\operatorname{div}\eta-F_P(u,Du):(Du\,D\eta)\right]dx=0.\]
Equivalently, with \(T=F(u,Du)I_n-Du^TF_P(u,Du)\),
\[\int_\Omega T:D\eta\,dx=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}T=0\text{ in }\mathcal D'(\Omega;\mathbb R^n).\]
This is the conservation law associated with domain-translation invariance. For explicitly position-dependent \(F(x,u,Du)\), the corresponding balance acquires the source \(\operatorname{div}T=F_x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationarity under compactly supported domain deformations makes the autonomous energy-momentum tensor divergence-free in the distributional sense.
knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Variation Conservation Laws

children.title: Weierstrass–Erdmann Corner Conditions
children.top_down_role: Junction-condition families for piecewise-smooth extremals.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variation Freedoms Behind the Two Corner Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates the independent corner displacements responsible for momentum and energy matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the corner first-variation condition, freedom of the common junction-state displacement yields \([L_v]_{\tau}=0\), while independent freedom of the corner-time displacement yields \([L-\dot y\cdot L_v]_{\tau}=0\). If either displacement is prohibited, its corresponding equality is not implied by corner stationarity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Momentum and energy matching require different independent corner freedoms; restricting one freedom removes the corresponding necessary condition.
assumptions_latex: The one-sided first variation exists for a continuous piecewise-smooth corner.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta y(\tau)\text{ free}\Rightarrow[L_v]_{\tau}=0,\qquad\delta\tau\text{ free}\Rightarrow[L-\dot y\cdot L_v]_{\tau}=0
knowledge_statements.title: Variation Freedoms Behind the Two Corner Conditions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise-smooth extremals with prescribed corner time and freely variable common corner state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J[y]=\int_a^bL(t,y,\dot y)\,dt\), where \(L\in C^1\), and let \(y\) be a continuous piecewise-\(C^1\) stationary arc with a prescribed interior corner \(\tau\). If admissible continuous variations can change \(y(\tau)\) arbitrarily while keeping \(\tau\) fixed, then \[L_v(\tau,y(\tau),\dot y(\tau^-))=L_v(\tau,y(\tau),\dot y(\tau^+)).\] Fixed-time variations alone do not require continuity of \(L-\dot y\cdot L_v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a prescribed corner with freely variable junction state, conjugate momentum is continuous, but the energy-type corner condition is not forced.
assumptions_latex: y\text{ is continuous and piecewise }C^1\text{ at the prescribed corner }\tau

notation.meaning: jump of a one-sided quantity across the corner

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Corner Momentum Matching

assumptions_latex: \(L\in C^1\) near the two arcs and their one-sided velocities.
The extremal is \(C^1\) on each side of a freely movable interior corner \(\tau\).

notation.meaning: Jump from the left trace to the right trace at the corner.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical first-order conditions at a freely movable interior corner.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J[y]=\int_a^b L(t,y(t),\dot y(t))\,dt\), and let \(y\) be a piecewise-\(C^1\) local extremal with a free interior corner at \(\tau\in(a,b)\). If variations may independently displace the corner in time and state while preserving continuity of \(y\), then the one-sided traces satisfy
\[
L_v(\tau,y(\tau),\dot y(\tau^-))=L_v(\tau,y(\tau),\dot y(\tau^+))
\]
and
\[
L-\dot y\cdot L_v\quad\text{has equal one-sided traces at }\tau.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a free interior corner, both the conjugate momentum and the quantity L minus velocity times momentum are continuous.
knowledge_statements.title: Weierstrass–Erdmann Corner Conditions

Common first-order displacement of the junction state.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-time variations of arcs joined through a smooth state interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An interface variation is a piecewise-smooth variation \(y_\varepsilon\) of two arcs meeting at the fixed time \(\tau\), such that their common junction state remains in \(M\). If \(\eta^\pm(\tau)\) are the one-sided variation traces, linearized matching and interface feasibility require
\[
\eta^-(\tau)=\eta^+(\tau)=\zeta,
\qquad \zeta\in T_M(y(\tau)).
\]
Thus admissible interface variations share a single tangential displacement at the junction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a fixed interface time, both arc variations have the same junction trace, and that trace is tangent to the interface.
knowledge_statements.title: Interface Variations

children.title: Movable-Junction Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric regimes governing displacement of junction locations.

assumptions_latex: The reference trajectory is continuous and piecewise differentiable at \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\sigma,\eta^-,\eta^+)\in\mathcal J\) exactly when \(\eta^-+v^-\sigma=\eta^++v^+\sigma\).

notation.meaning: One-sided velocities at the reference junction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linearized geometry induced by continuity at a moving junction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a continuous junction of two arcs with one-sided velocities \(v^-\) and \(v^+\), the linearized movable-junction geometry is
\[
\mathcal J:=\left\{(\sigma,\eta^-,\eta^+):
\eta^-+v^-\sigma=\eta^++v^+\sigma\right\}.
\]
Here \(\sigma\) is the temporal displacement and \(\eta^\pm\) are the material trace displacements. The corresponding spatial displacement of the physical junction is the common vector \(\eta^-+v^-\sigma=\eta^++v^+\sigma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The junction’s temporal and one-sided state displacements form a linear space determined by continuity of the displaced meeting point.
knowledge_statements.title: Movable-Junction Geometry

children.title: Weak Extremals Without Classical Equations
children.top_down_role: Minimizers lacking the regularity needed for classical stationarity systems.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Minimizer with No Classical Euler Equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly convex variational problem whose Sobolev minimizer satisfies the Euler equation weakly but is not twice continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(t)=1\) on \((0,1/2)\) and \(g(t)=-1\) on \((1/2,1)\), and minimize \[J(u)=\int_0^1\left(\frac12|u'(t)|^2-g(t)u(t)\right)dt\] over \(H_0^1(0,1)\). The unique minimizer \(\bar u\) satisfies \[\int_0^1\bar u'(t)v'(t)\,dt=\int_0^1g(t)v(t)\,dt\qquad(v\in H_0^1(0,1)),\] equivalently \(-\bar u''=g\) distributionally and almost everywhere. Its second derivative jumps at \(t=1/2\), so \(\bar u\notin C^2([0,1])\) and the equation is not classical throughout \((0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discontinuous forcing produces a Sobolev minimizer satisfying the Euler equation weakly but not as a classical equation at every interior point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-\bar u''=g\) distributionally and almost everywhere, while \(\bar u\notin C^2([0,1])\).

notation.meaning: Sobolev functions with zero endpoint trace

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Minimizer with No Classical Euler Equation

assumptions_latex: \(u\) is only a Sobolev local minimizer of an integral functional.
The available hypotheses do not imply the regularity required by the classical Euler–Lagrange equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Classical pointwise stationarity cannot be inferred; only an appropriate weak or generalized condition is justified.

notation.meaning: Sobolev space of integrable functions with integrable weak derivative.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity boundary between weak stationarity and classical differential equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(u\in W^{1,1}(a,b;\mathbb R^n)\) locally minimize \(J(u)=\int_a^b L(t,u,Du)\,dt\). Without sufficient differentiability of \(L\), integrability of its partial derivatives, and regularity of \(u\), one cannot conclude that
\[
\frac{d}{dt}L_v(t,u(t),\dot u(t))=L_y(t,u(t),\dot u(t))
\]
holds pointwise. Stationarity may instead exist only as a distributional identity, variational inequality, or generalized-subdifferential inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Sobolev minimizer need not satisfy a pointwise Euler–Lagrange equation when the integrand or minimizer lacks the required regularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Extremals Without Classical Equations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the node, but phrases such as "sufficient differentiability," "integrability," and "appropriate weak or generalized condition" do not identify a precise regularity regime. children.title: Failure of Differentiation Under Integration
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of ordinary first-variation calculations for inadequately controlled integrands.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vitali criterion for interchanging a parameter derivative and integration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a finite measure space, set \(q_h=[f(h,\cdot)-f(0,\cdot)]/h\). If \(q_h\to q\) in measure and \(\{q_h:0<|h|<h_0\}\) is uniformly integrable, then \(q_h\to q\) in \(L^1\) and \[\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\int_T f(h,t)\,d\mu-\int_T f(0,t)\,d\mu}{h}=\int_Tq(t)\,d\mu(t).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergence in measure of the difference quotients permits differentiation under the integral when those quotients are uniformly integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_h\to q\) in \(L^1\), and the derivative of the integral equals \(\int_Tq\,d\mu\).
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Integrability Criterion for Difference Quotients

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary one-sided counterexample driven by non-uniformly-integrable difference quotients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon\ge0\) and \(t\in(0,1)\), let \(f(0,t)=0\) and \(f(\varepsilon,t)=\mathbf 1_{(0,\varepsilon)}(t)\). For every fixed \(t>0\), \(\partial_\varepsilon f(0^+,t)=0\), but \[I(\varepsilon)=\int_0^1f(\varepsilon,t)\,dt=\varepsilon\quad(0\le\varepsilon\le1),\qquad I'(0^+)=1.\] The quotients \(\varepsilon^{-1}\mathbf 1_{(0,\varepsilon)}\) concentrate at zero and are not uniformly integrable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shrinking moving interval has zero pointwise right derivative but an integral with right derivative one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I'(0^+)=1\ne0=\int_0^1\partial_\varepsilon f(0^+,t)\,dt\).
knowledge_statements.title: Moving-Interval Concentration Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard integrable-domination regime preventing concentration of parameter derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:(-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)\times T\to\mathbb R\) be measurable in \(t\), differentiable in \(\varepsilon\) for almost every \(t\), and suppose \(f(0,\cdot)\in L^1(\mu)\). If some \(g\in L^1(\mu)\) satisfies \(|\partial_\varepsilon f(\varepsilon,t)|\le g(t)\) for almost every \(t\) and all \(|\varepsilon|<\varepsilon_0\), then \[\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\int_Tf(\varepsilon,t)\,d\mu(t)\right|_{\varepsilon=0}=\int_T\partial_\varepsilon f(0,t)\,d\mu(t).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrable bound on the parameter derivative justifies differentiation under the integral sign.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I'(0)=\int_T\partial_\varepsilon f(0,t)\,d\mu(t)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Dominated Differentiation Boundary

assumptions_latex: The parameter satisfies \(\varepsilon>0\) and the integration domain is \((0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\int_0^1 f(\varepsilon,t)\,dt\right|_{0^+}=1\neq0=\int_0^1\partial_\varepsilon f(0^+,t)\,dt\).

notation.meaning: Parameterized integrand exhibiting concentration near zero.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete concentration counterexample to unqualified differentiation under the integral sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f(0,t)=0\) and, for \(\varepsilon>0\), \(f(\varepsilon,t)=\varepsilon^2/(t+\varepsilon)^2\) on \((0,1)\). For every fixed \(t>0\),
\[
\partial_\varepsilon f(0^+,t)=0.
\]
Nevertheless,
\[
I(\varepsilon):=\int_0^1 f(\varepsilon,t)\,dt=\frac{\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon},
\qquad I'(0^+)=1.
\]
Hence differentiation and integration do not commute because the difference quotients lack a common integrable dominating function near \(t=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise parameter derivatives vanish, but concentration near the integration boundary makes the derivative of the integral equal one.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Differentiation Under Integration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically consistent: the pointwise right derivative vanishes while the right derivative of the integral equals one. The counterexample kind exactly fits the failure leaf, but the record has no citation with an inspectable locator; standard-field rationale alone does not satisfy the citation review requirement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent and limiting-normal description of a closed nonsmooth feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Bouligand tangent cone and limiting normal cone of \(C\) at \(\bar x\) are
\[
T_C(\bar x):=\left\{d:\exists t_k\downarrow0,\ x_k\in C,\ x_k\to\bar x,\frac{x_k-\bar x}{t_k}\to d\right\},
\]
\[
N_C(\bar x):=\left\{v:\exists x_k\to_C\bar x,\ v_k\to v,\ v_k\in\widehat N_C(x_k)\right\}.
\]
Unlike smooth constraint geometry, these cones may be nonconvex and need not be linear subspaces or mutual polars.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsmooth feasibility is modeled by contingent directions and limiting normals, which may be nonconvex and need not form complementary subspaces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary boundary where nearby branch normals produce additional limiting normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R)\). At the crossing point, \[\widehat N_C(0,0)=\{(0,0)\},\qquad N_C(0,0)=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R).\] Hence normal regularity fails and the limiting normal cone is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the crossing of the coordinate axes, the regular normal is zero while the limiting normal retains both branch-normal axes.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is the union of the two coordinate axes in \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat N_C(0)=\{0\}\subsetneq N_C(0)=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Crossing-Branches Normal Irregularity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical regularity regime for nonsmooth convex boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\), \[\widehat N_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)=\{v:\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle\le0\ \text{for every }x\in C\}.\] Thus a convex corner may be nonsmooth while remaining normally regular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convex sets have coincident regular, limiting, and convex-analytic normal cones, including at corners.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat N_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)=N_C^{\mathrm{conv}}(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Boundaries Are Normally Regular

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is closed and \(\bar x\in\partial C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Clarke regularity at \(\bar x\) is the equality \(\widehat N_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Topological boundary of the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone regularity criterion at a nonsmooth feasible boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A closed set \(C\) is Clarke regular at \(\bar x\in C\) when its regular and limiting normal cones coincide:
\[
\widehat N_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x).
\]
Equivalently, every limiting normal at \(\bar x\) already satisfies the first-order regular-normal inequality there. Failure of this equality identifies boundary points where nearby normal directions create additional limiting normals and smooth-style first-order geometry is unreliable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsmooth boundary is Clarke regular when its regular and limiting normal cones coincide at the point.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Boundary Geometry

children.title: Coderivative Stationarity Regimes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar failure of coderivative stationarity when metric subregularity is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(x)=\{x^2\}\) and minimize \(f(x)=x\) subject to \(0\in G(x)\). The feasible set is \(S=\{0\}\), so \(\bar x=0\) is a constrained local minimizer. However \[D^*G(0,0)(y^*)=\{0\}\quad\text{for every }y^*\in\mathbb R,\] and hence \(0\notin\partial f(0)+D^*G(0,0)(y^*)=\{1\}\). Metric subregularity fails because \(|x|\le\kappa x^2\) cannot hold near zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The degenerate squaring constraint has a singleton feasible set but no coderivative multiplier balancing a nonzero objective gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\) is a constrained minimizer, but coderivative stationarity fails for every multiplier.
knowledge_statements.title: Squaring-Constraint Coderivative Failure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coderivative Multiplier Rule Under Metric Subregularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional stationarity for a generalized-equation constraint with an explicit error-bound qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) have locally closed graph at \((\bar x,0)\), put \(S=G^{-1}(0)\), and suppose \(G\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,0)\): \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,G(x))\quad\text{near }\bar x.\] If a locally Lipschitz function \(f\) has a local minimum over \(S\) at \(\bar x\), then there exist \(x^*\in\partial f(\bar x)\) and \(y^*\in\mathbb R^m\) such that \[-x^*\in D^*G(\bar x,0)(y^*).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity converts generalized-normal stationarity into a coderivative multiplier condition.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is locally Lipschitz near the constrained local minimizer \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)+D^*G(\bar x,0)(y^*)\) for some \(y^*\in\mathbb R^m\).

For the generalized-equation constraint \(0\in G(x)\), suppose an applicable inverse-image normal-cone qualification gives

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonnegative Second Variation Alone Is Not Sufficient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate fixed-endpoint example separating second-order necessity from minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(W_0^{1,4}(0,1)\), define \[J[y]=-\int_0^1|y'(t)|^4\,dt.\] At \(\bar y=0\), \(DJ(0)=0\) and \(D^2J(0)[h,h]=0\ge0\) for every fixed-endpoint variation \(h\). Nevertheless, \(J[\varepsilon h]<J[0]\) for every nonzero \(h\) and every \(\varepsilon\ne0\). Thus stationarity and nonnegative second variation do not imply fixed-endpoint local minimality without stricter curvature or higher-order control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary fixed-endpoint arc can have identically zero second variation and still fail to be a local minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D^2J(0)[h,h]\ge0\text{ for all }h,\quad\text{but }0\text{ is not a local minimizer}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coercive Second Variation Implies Fixed-Endpoint Quadratic Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract sufficient condition on the affine Sobolev space with fixed endpoint trace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=H_0^1(a,b;\mathbb R^n)\), and suppose \(J\) is twice Fréchet differentiable near a stationary arc \(\bar y\) in \(\bar y+X\). If some \(c>0\) satisfies \[D^2J(\bar y)[h,h]\ge c\lVert h\rVert_{H^1}^2\qquad(h\in X),\] then for every \(\gamma\in(0,c/2)\) there is \(\rho>0\) such that \[J(\bar y+h)\ge J(\bar y)+\gamma\lVert h\rVert_{H^1}^2\] whenever \(h\in X\) and \(\lVert h\rVert_{H^1}<\rho\). Hence \(\bar y\) is an isolated strict fixed-endpoint local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform coercivity of the fixed-endpoint second variation yields local quadratic growth and isolated strict minimality.
assumptions_latex: J is twice Fréchet differentiable near \(\bar y\) on the fixed-trace affine Sobolev space.
D^2J(\bar y)\text{ is coercive on }H_0^1(a,b;\mathbb R^n).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J(\bar y+h)\ge J(\bar y)+\gamma\lVert h\rVert_{H^1}^2\text{ locally for every }0<\gamma<c/2.

knowledge_statements.title: Coercive Second Variation Implies Fixed-Endpoint Quadratic Growth

assumptions_latex: \(L:[a,b]\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is twice continuously differentiable in its state and velocity arguments near the reference arc.
\(y\in C^2([a,b];\mathbb R^n)\) is a weak local minimizer of \(J[y]=\int_a^b L(t,y(t),\dot y(t))\,dt\) among arcs with the fixed endpoint values \(y(a)\) and \(y(b)\).

notation.meaning: Second variation of the integral functional.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical quadratic second variation and its necessary nonnegativity condition for fixed endpoint data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J[y]=\int_a^b L(t,y(t),\dot y(t))\,dt\). For a fixed-endpoint variation \(\eta\in C^1([a,b];\mathbb R^n)\) with \(\eta(a)=\eta(b)=0\), the second variation is
\[
\delta^2J[y](\eta)=\int_a^b\left(\eta^{\mathsf T}L_{yy}\eta+2\eta^{\mathsf T}L_{yv}\dot\eta+\dot\eta^{\mathsf T}L_{vv}\dot\eta\right)\,dt,
\]
where all derivatives of \(L\) are evaluated at \((t,y(t),\dot y(t))\). If \(y\) is a weak local minimizer, then \(\delta^2J[y](\eta)\ge 0\) for every such fixed-endpoint variation \(\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed-endpoint weak local minimizer, the quadratic integral formed from the state and velocity Hessian blocks of the Lagrangian is nonnegative for every fixed-endpoint variation.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Endpoint Second Variations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract multiplier-based second-order necessity on the critical variation cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\bar y\) be a constrained local minimizer and let \(\lambda\) satisfy the corresponding first-order multiplier system. For every critical variation \(h\in K(\bar y,\lambda)\), second-order necessity requires
\[
D^2_{yy}\mathcal L(\bar y,\lambda)[h,h]\ge0.
\]
The cone \(K(\bar y,\lambda)\) consists of directions satisfying the linearized equality constraints, the appropriate tangent conditions for active inequalities, and zero first-order Lagrangian-compatible objective decrease. Thus positivity is required on the critical cone, not on the entire ambient variation space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a constrained minimum, the Lagrangian’s second derivative must be nonnegative on variations that are both linearly feasible and first-order critical.
knowledge_statements.title: Constrained Second Variations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines directionwise mapping-relative outer regularity, pointwise outer regularity, and second-order regularity, including necessary nonemptiness and tangent-set consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset Y\), \(y\in K\), \(d\in T_K(y)\), and let \(M:X\to Y\) be linear. The set \(K\) is outer second-order regular at \(y\) in direction \(d\) with respect to \(M\) if every sequence \(y_n=y+t_nd+\tfrac12t_n^2r_n\in K\), with \(t_n\downarrow0\), \(r_n=Mw_n+a_n\), \(a_n\) convergent, and \(t_nw_n\to0\), satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(r_n,T_K^2(y,d))\to0\). It is outer second-order regular at \(y\) if this holds in every \(d\in T_K(y)\) for arbitrary \(X,M\), equivalently for every such sequence satisfying \(t_nr_n\to0\). It is second-order regular at \(y\) if it is outer second-order regular there and \(T_K^2(y,d)=T_K^{i,2}(y,d)\) for every \(d\). These definitions also apply to nonconvex \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer second-order regularity requires every admissible feasible second-order remainder to approach the outer second-order tangent set. Pointwise outer regularity requires this in every tangent direction, and full second-order regularity additionally requires equality of the outer and inner second-order tangent sets. The definition is meaningful for convex and nonconvex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(r_n,T_K^2(y,d))\to0;\qquad K\text{ is second-order regular at }y\iff K\text{ is outer second-order regular and }T_K^2(y,d)=T_K^{i,2}(y,d)\ \forall d

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Growth Characterization under Outer Second-Order Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives sufficiency, and under Robinson qualification and tangent-set convexity necessity, for second-order growth; also records a regularity failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(X\) is finite dimensional, \(x_0\) is feasible for \((P)\), and the associated generalized-multiplier set is nonempty. Suppose that for every \(h\in C(x_0)\), \(K\) is outer second-order regular at \(G(x_0)\) in direction \(DG(x_0)h\) with respect to \(M=DG(x_0)\). Then condition (3.162) implies second-order growth at \(x_0\). If, additionally, Robinson's constraint qualification holds at \(x_0\) and \(\mathcal T(h)=T_K^2(G(x_0),DG(x_0)h)\) is convex for every \(h\in C(x_0)\), then second-order growth at \(x_0\) is equivalent to \[\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda(x_0)}\{D_{xx}^2L(x_0,\lambda)(h,h)-\sigma(\lambda,\mathcal T(h))\}>0\quad\forall h\in C(x_0)\setminus\{0\}.\] Moreover, outer second-order regularity in \((y,d)\) requires \(T_K^2(y,d)\ne\varnothing\), and full second-order regularity requires \(T_K^{i,2}(y,d)\ne\varnothing\); equality of empty inner and outer tangent sets does not establish regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-dimensional constrained problem, outer second-order regularity makes the stated generalized-multiplier curvature condition sufficient for second-order growth. With Robinson's qualification and convex outer second-order tangent sets, strict positivity of the supremal Lagrangian curvature minus the tangent-set support term in every nonzero critical direction is necessary and sufficient. Empty second-order tangent sets rule out the corresponding regularity, even when the inner and outer sets coincide because both are empty.
assumptions_latex: \forall h\in C(x_0),\ K\text{ is outer second-order regular at }G(x_0)\text{ in direction }DG(x_0)h\text{ relative to }DG(x_0)
\text{For necessity and sufficiency: Robinson's constraint qualification holds and }\mathcal T(h)\text{ is convex for every }h\in C(x_0)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (3.162)\Longrightarrow\text{second-order growth};\quad \text{under the additional assumptions, second-order growth}\iff \forall h\ne0,\ \sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda(x_0)}[D_{xx}^2L(x_0,\lambda)(h,h)-\sigma(\lambda,\mathcal T(h))]>0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank-One Positivity Does Not Imply Pointwise Matrix Positivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary specific to genuinely vectorial multidimensional second variations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When \(m,n\ge2\), a quadratic form \(A\) may satisfy \(A[a\otimes\xi,a\otimes\xi]\ge0\) for every rank-one matrix while taking negative values on some higher-rank matrices. For variable coefficients, pointwise rank-one nonnegativity also does not by itself provide a uniform coercive bound for the complete second-variation integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Legendre–Hadamard positivity tests rank-one gradients and is not full pointwise positivity or a uniform coercivity certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a quadratic form on \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\ge0\text{ on rank-one matrices}\not\Rightarrow A\ge0\text{ on all matrices, nor uniform variable-coefficient coercivity.}

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) is bounded and \(F\in C^2(\overline\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^{m\times n})\).
\(u\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) is stationary and \(v\in C_c^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\).
