knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical smooth second variation for vector-valued fields on a multidimensional domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every admissible variation \(v\), the second variation is
\[
Q_u[v]=\int_\Omega\!\left[v^{\mathsf T}F_{zz}v+2v^{\mathsf T}F_{zP}:\nabla v+\nabla v:F_{PP}:\nabla v\right]_{(x,u(x),\nabla u(x))}\,dx.
\]
Here the mixed contractions are taken over the field and spatial indices. Equivalently, \(Q_u[v]=\left.\frac{d^2}{d\varepsilon^2}I(u+\varepsilon v)\right|_{\varepsilon=0}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second variation of a smooth multiple integral is the integral quadratic form obtained from the Hessian of its integrand in the field and gradient variables.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Acoustic-Tensor Form of the Legendre–Hadamard Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent pointwise representation of rank-one nonnegativity and its uniform strengthening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_{\alpha i\beta j}=\partial^2F/\partial P_{\alpha i}\partial P_{\beta j}\) at a fixed \((x,z,P)\), and define \(Q(b)_{\alpha\beta}=A_{\alpha i\beta j}b_i b_j\). Then \[D^2_{PP}F[a\otimes b,a\otimes b]=a^{\mathsf T}Q(b)a.\] Hence the Legendre–Hadamard condition is equivalent to \(Q(b)\succeq0\) for every \(b\). Its strengthened form requires a constant \(c>0\) such that \(a^{\mathsf T}Q(b)a\ge c\lVert a\rVert^2\lVert b\rVert^2\) for all \(a,b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank-one nonnegativity is equivalent to positive semidefiniteness of every acoustic tensor; a uniform rank-one lower bound is its strengthened form.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is twice differentiable in the matrix variable \(P\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict Legendre positivity does not imply nonnegative second variation or local minimality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed-endpoint example separating pointwise gradient positivity from minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
I[y]=\int_0^1\bigl((y')^2-\lambda y^2\bigr)\,dt,
\]
the zero arc is stationary and \(F_{pp}=2>0\), so the strengthened Legendre condition holds. Nevertheless, with \(v(t)=\sin(\pi t)\),
\[
\delta^2I(0)[v,v]=2\int_0^1\bigl((v')^2-\lambda v^2\bigr)\,dt=\pi^2-\lambda<0.
\]
Hence pointwise positivity in the derivative variable alone is insufficient for minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A functional can have a uniformly positive derivative Hessian yet possess a negative second-variation direction because of its field-variable term.
knowledge_statements.title: Legendre-Condition Scope Limits

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hamiltonian representation for an invertible strengthened-Legendre block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(p=P\eta'+R\eta\). If \(P\) is invertible, the Jacobi equation is equivalent to \[ \frac d{dt}\begin{pmatrix}\eta\\p\end{pmatrix}= \begin{pmatrix} -P^{-1}R & P^{-1}\\ Q-R^{\mathsf T}P^{-1}R & R^{\mathsf T}P^{-1} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\eta\\p\end{pmatrix}. \] The coefficient matrix is Hamiltonian. Hence its fundamental matrix \(\Phi(t,s)\) is symplectic, and \[ \eta_1^{\mathsf T}p_2-p_1^{\mathsf T}\eta_2 \] is constant for every pair of Jacobi solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible leading block converts the Jacobi equation into a Hamiltonian system with symplectic flow and conserved Wronskian.
assumptions_latex: \(P=P^{\mathsf T}\) is pointwise invertible and \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Jacobi flow is symplectic and preserves the Jacobi boundary concomitant.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix Jacobi equation for vector-valued one-dimensional variational problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The quadratic second-variation integrand is
\[
\eta'^{\mathsf T}P\eta'+2\eta'^{\mathsf T}R\eta+\eta^{\mathsf T}Q\eta.
\]
Its Euler equation, called the Jacobi equation, is
\[
-\frac d{dt}\bigl(P\eta'+R\eta\bigr)+R^{\mathsf T}\eta'+Q\eta=0.
\]
Varying the initial data produces the Jacobi equation family; equivalently, its members are linearizations of smooth one-parameter families of Euler–Lagrange extremals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearizing the Euler–Lagrange equation yields a matrix second-order Jacobi equation whose solutions are Jacobi fields.
knowledge_statements.title: Jacobi Equation Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed Euler equation is consistent with the stated quadratic integrand, and representation is suitable for the Jacobi-equation-family leaf. A source is required for the stronger claim that its solutions are equivalently linearizations of smooth one-parameter families of extremals, especially without an explicit regularity or nondegeneracy assumption on the leading block.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry, monotonicity, endpoint interpolation, and determinant properties of fundamental Jacobi matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J_0^1\) and \(J_1^0\) be Jacobi matrices satisfying
\[
J_0^1(0)=I_n,\quad \dot J_0^1(0)=0,\quad J_1^0(0)=0,\quad \dot J_1^0(0)=I_n,
\]
so that every Jacobi matrix can be written as
\[
J(t)=J_0^1(t)J(0)+J_1^0(t)\dot J(0).
\]
Assume \(J_1^0(t)\) is invertible for every \(t\in(0,1]\). Then:
(a) \(S(t):=J_1^0(t)^{-1}J_0^1(t)\) is symmetric and positive on \((0,1]\), and is decreasing in \(t\).
(b) There is a unique pair of Jacobi matrices \((J^{1,0},J^{0,1})\) such that
\[
J^{1,0}(0)=I_n,\quad J^{1,0}(1)=0,\quad J^{0,1}(0)=0,\quad J^{0,1}(1)=I_n,
\]
and \(\dot J^{1,0}(0)\) and \(\dot J^{0,1}(1)\) are symmetric.
(c) Define \(K(t)=tJ_1^0(t)^{-1}\) for \(t>0\) and \(K(0)=I_n\). If \(J(0)\) is invertible, \(J(0)^*S(1)J(0)^{-1}=S(1)\), and \(\dot J(0)J(0)^{-1}\) is symmetric, then for every \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[
K(t)\bigl(J^{1,0}(t)J(0)\bigr)J(0)^{-1}
\quad\text{and}\quad
K(t)\bigl(J^{0,1}(t)J(1)\bigr)J(0)^{-1}
\]
are symmetric. Moreover, \(\det K(t)>0\) for every \(t\in[0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invertibility of the fundamental matrix J₁⁰ gives a symmetric positive decreasing matrix ratio, unique Jacobi matrices interpolating the two endpoint data, symmetry of the stated cosymmetrized endpoint expressions under the additional initial-data assumptions, and positivity of det K before the terminal time.
assumptions_latex: For part (c), \(J(0)\) is invertible, \(J(0)^*S(1)J(0)^{-1}=S(1)\), and \(\dot J(0)J(0)^{-1}\) is symmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S(t)=J_1^0(t)^{-1}J_0^1(t)\text{ is symmetric, positive, and decreasing};\quad (J^{1,0},J^{0,1})\text{ exists uniquely with the stated endpoint data and symmetric endpoint derivatives};\quad \text{the stated }K\text{-weighted matrices are symmetric and }\det K(t)>0\text{ on }[0,1).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent positivity criteria for Jacobi matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence among an initial endpoint condition, positivity of associated matrix expressions, and determinant positivity for a normalized Jacobi matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S(t)\), \(K(t)\), and \(J^{0,1}(t)\) be as in the Jacobi cosymmetrization construction. Let \(J\) be a Jacobi matrix with \(J(0)=I_n\) and symmetric \(\dot J(0)\). Then the following are equivalent:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{(i)}\quad \dot J(0)+S(1)>0;\\
&\text{(ii)}\quad K(t)J^{0,1}(t)J(1)>0 &&\text{for all }t\in(0,1);\\
&\text{(iii)}\quad K(t)J(t)>0 &&\text{for all }t\in[0,1];\\
&\text{(iv)}\quad \det J(t)>0 &&\text{for all }t\in[0,1].
\end{aligned}
\]
The equivalence also holds after replacing the strict inequalities in (i) and (ii) by nonstrict inequalities and replacing \([0,1]\) by \([0,1)\) in (iii) and (iv); the inequalities in (iii) and (iv) remain strict in that variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a normalized Jacobi matrix with symmetric initial derivative, the initial endpoint positivity condition, positivity of the two associated matrix expressions, and positivity of the determinant throughout the closed interval are equivalent. In the boundary variant, only conditions (i) and (ii) become nonstrict, while conditions (iii) and (iv) retain strict positivity on the half-open interval.
assumptions_latex: \(S(t)\), \(K(t)\), and \(J^{0,1}(t)\) are defined by the preceding Jacobi cosymmetrization construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dot J(0)+S(1)>0\iff K(t)J^{0,1}(t)J(1)>0\ \forall t\in(0,1)\iff K(t)J(t)>0\ \forall t\in[0,1]\iff \det J(t)>0\ \forall t\in[0,1],\text{ together with the stated variant using nonstrict inequalities only in (i)-(ii) and }[0,1)\text{ in (iii)-(iv).}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines conjugacy by higher-than-first-order contact with neighboring extremals issuing from the same initial point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y\) be an extremal through \(M=(a,y(a))\), and let \(y^*\) range over neighboring extremals through the same point \(M\). The point \(\widetilde M=(\widetilde a,y(\widetilde a))\) is conjugate to \(M\) if and only if, at \(\widetilde M\),
\[
y^*(\widetilde a)-y(\widetilde a)=o\!\left(\lVert y^*-y\rVert_1\right)
\quad\text{as }\lVert y^*-y\rVert_1\to0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point on an extremal is conjugate to the common initial point when the difference between the extremal and neighboring extremals through that initial point is of higher than first order there relative to their stated norm distance.
assumptions_latex: y^*\text{ ranges over neighboring extremals through the same initial point }M.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widetilde M\text{ is conjugate to }M\iff y^*(\widetilde a)-y(\widetilde a)=o\!\left(\lVert y^*-y\rVert_1\right).

children.title: Focal Points
children.top_down_role: Second-order obstructions associated with variable or constrained endpoint geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convention-independent representation after the linearized endpoint conditions have been fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal J_M\) be the finite-dimensional space of Jacobi fields satisfying the prescribed linearized admissibility and transversality conditions at the endpoint manifold \(M\). Define \(E_c:\mathcal J_M\to\mathbb R^m\) by \(E_c\eta=\eta(c)\). Then \[ c\text{ is focal to }M\iff\ker E_c\ne\{0\},\qquad \operatorname{mult}_M(c)=\dim\ker E_c. \]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Focality is loss of injectivity of terminal evaluation on Jacobi fields satisfying the manifold endpoint conditions.
assumptions_latex: A fixed linearized endpoint convention determines the Jacobi-field space \(\mathcal J_M\).
Jacobi evolution is regular up to \(c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Focal multiplicity equals \(\dim\ker E_c\).

assumptions_latex: The initial endpoint lies on a smooth constraint manifold \(M\).

notation.meaning: Jacobi field satisfying initial linearized endpoint conditions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-initial-endpoint focality relative to a smooth endpoint manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(c\in(a,b]\) is focal to \(M\) along the reference extremal if there exists a nonzero Jacobi field \(\eta\) such that
\[
\eta(a)\in T_{\bar y(a)}M,
\qquad
\eta(c)=0,
\]
and \(\eta\) satisfies the linearized natural transversality condition at \(a\). The focal multiplicity is the dimension of the space of such fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A focal point occurs when a nonzero Jacobi field allowed by the initial endpoint constraint vanishes later along the extremal.
knowledge_statements.title: Focal Points

assumptions_latex: \(Y(t)\) is a fundamental matrix of Jacobi fields with \(Y(a)=0\).
The initial momentum normalization of \(Y\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c\) is conjugate to \(a\) if and only if \(\det Y(c)=0\).

notation.meaning: Fundamental matrix of initially vanishing Jacobi fields

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental-matrix geometry for fixed endpoint conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed endpoints, the Jacobi fields satisfying \(\eta(a)=0\) are represented by
\[
\eta(t)=Y(t)c,
\qquad c\in\mathbb R^m.
\]
A point \(t=c_0\) is conjugate to \(a\) precisely when the evaluation map loses injectivity, equivalently
\[
\ker Y(c_0)\ne\{0\}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\det Y(c_0)=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed endpoints, conjugate points are exactly the locations where the fundamental matrix of initially vanishing Jacobi fields becomes singular.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Endpoint Point Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fundamental-matrix representation fits the Fixed-Endpoint Point Geometry leaf, and singularity of the evaluation matrix is the expected conjugacy criterion under a valid normalization. A source is needed to specify the regular Jacobi system, matrix dimension, and initial momentum normalization that make the representation complete.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jacobi–Legendre Sufficient Condition for a Weak Minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient weak-minimality criterion for an admissible extremal in an n-function variational problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the variational functional with integrand F along an admissible curve \gamma:x\mapsto y(x)=(y_1(x),\ldots,y_n(x)) on [a,b]. Suppose (i) \gamma satisfies F_{y_i}-\frac{d}{dx}F_{y_i'}=0 for every i=1,\ldots,n; (ii) P(x)=\frac12F_{y'y'}[x,y(x),y'(x)] is positive definite along \gamma; and (iii) [a,b] contains no point conjugate to a. Then \gamma furnishes a weak minimum of the functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An admissible curve is a weak minimizer if it satisfies all Euler equations, the Hessian of the integrand with respect to the derivatives is positive definite along the curve, and the interval contains no point conjugate to its initial point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma\text{ is a weak minimizer of the variational functional.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Determinantal Definition of Conjugacy for Multiple Unknown Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The historical infinitesimal formulation of conjugacy for neighboring extremals issuing from a common fixed initial point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the neighboring extremals be y_j=y_{ij}(x), i,j=1,\ldots,n, and suppose that they issue from the same n-dimensional point with close but linearly independent directions. Set D(x)=\det\bigl(y_{ij}(x)\bigr)_{i,j=1}^n. The point \widetilde a is conjugate to a if D(\widetilde a) is an infinitesimal of higher order than the values D(x) for a<x<\widetilde a.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For n neighboring extremals starting from the same point with close, linearly independent directions, form the determinant of their component values. The parameter point a-tilde is conjugate to a when the determinant at a-tilde is an infinitesimal of higher order than its values between a and a-tilde.
assumptions_latex: \text{The neighboring extremals issue from the same point with close, linearly independent directions.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D(\widetilde a)\text{ has higher infinitesimal order than }D(x)\text{ for }a<x<\widetilde a\;\Longrightarrow\;\widetilde a\text{ is conjugate to }a.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symplectic Criterion for Self-Adjoint Endpoint Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural criterion for linearized endpoint subspaces in Jacobi Cauchy-data space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For Jacobi Cauchy data \(z=(\eta,p)\), where \(p=P\eta'+R\eta\), define \[ \omega(z_1,z_2)=\eta_1^{\mathsf T}p_2-p_1^{\mathsf T}\eta_2. \] Jacobi evolution preserves \(\omega\). A linear endpoint-data subspace \(L\subset\mathbb R^{2m}\) annihilates the integration-by-parts boundary form exactly when \(\omega|_{L\times L}=0\). A maximal such \(m\)-dimensional subspace is Lagrangian and supplies self-adjoint separated endpoint data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Self-adjoint linear endpoint conditions correspond to Lagrangian subspaces of Jacobi Cauchy-data space.
assumptions_latex: The Jacobi equation is regular and uses momentum \(p=P\eta'+R\eta\).
Endpoint conditions have been linearized into Cauchy-data subspaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Maximal endpoint subspaces annihilating the Jacobi boundary form are Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.title: Symplectic Criterion for Self-Adjoint Endpoint Data

assumptions_latex: Admissible endpoint variations define linear boundary subspaces \(L_a\) and \(L_c\) in Jacobi Cauchy-data space.
Jacobi evolution from \(a\) to \(c\) is the linear map \(\Phi_{c,a}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Endpoint degeneracy occurs exactly when \(\Phi_{c,a}(L_a)\cap L_c\ne\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary-subspace formulation covering variable endpoint constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nontrivial Jacobi field satisfies the linearized variable-endpoint conditions at \(a\) and \(c\) exactly when its initial Cauchy datum lies in \(L_a\) and its evolved datum lies in \(L_c\). Consequently, endpoint degeneracy is characterized by
\[
\Phi_{c,a}(L_a)\cap L_c\ne\{0\}.
\]
For a fixed terminal endpoint this reduces to vanishing of the field component; for a free endpoint it includes the linearized natural boundary condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable-endpoint focality is an intersection of the evolved admissible initial boundary data with the admissible terminal boundary data.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Endpoint Point Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary-data intersection representation fits the variable-endpoint geometry leaf. The spaces containing the Cauchy data, the transport identification, and the precise endpoint boundary subspaces are not defined sufficiently to validate the intersection formula or its fixed/free endpoint reductions without a source.

children.title: Accessory Variational Problems
children.top_down_role: Quadratic auxiliary problems organizing Jacobi theory.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar completion-of-squares certificate for the accessory index form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[ I[h]=\int_a^b(Ph'^2+2Rhh'+Qh^2)dt, \] let \(u\) be a nowhere-zero solution of \[ -(Pu'+Ru)'+Ru'+Qu=0. \] Then \[ Ph'^2+2Rhh'+Qh^2=Pu^2\left(\frac hu\right)'^2+\frac d{dt}\left(\frac{Pu'+Ru}{u}h^2\right). \] If \(h(a)=h(b)=0\) and \(P>0\), then \[ I[h]=\int_a^bPu^2\left(\frac hu\right)'^2dt\ge0. \]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonvanishing scalar Jacobi solution converts the index form into a square plus an endpoint term.
assumptions_latex: The problem is scalar, \(P>0\), and all quantities have the stated differentiability.
\(u\) solves the Jacobi equation and has no zero on \([a,b]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For fixed-zero endpoint variations, \(I[h]\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Jacobi–Picone Completion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric bilinear representation of the accessory quadratic functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=P^{\mathsf T}\), \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), and define \[ I(\eta,\zeta)=\int_a^b\left(\eta'^{\mathsf T}P\zeta'+\eta'^{\mathsf T}R\zeta+\eta^{\mathsf T}R^{\mathsf T}\zeta'+\eta^{\mathsf T}Q\zeta\right)dt. \] Then \(I\) is symmetric, \(\mathcal A[\eta]=\tfrac12I(\eta,\eta)\), and, when the endpoint conditions annihilate the boundary concomitant, \[ I(\eta,\zeta)=\int_a^b\eta^{\mathsf T}\left[-\frac d{dt}(P\zeta'+R\zeta)+R^{\mathsf T}\zeta'+Q\zeta\right]dt. \]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The accessory functional is the diagonal of a symmetric index form representing the Jacobi operator.
assumptions_latex: \(P,Q\) are symmetric and the coefficients permit integration by parts.
The homogeneous endpoint conditions annihilate the boundary concomitant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A[\eta]=\tfrac12I(\eta,\eta)\), and \(I\) represents the Jacobi operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Polarized Index Form

assumptions_latex: \(P(t)=P(t)^{\mathsf T}\), \(Q(t)=Q(t)^{\mathsf T}\), and the coefficients are continuous.
Variations satisfy the prescribed homogeneous linear endpoint conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Euler equation of the accessory functional is the Jacobi equation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic functional whose Euler equation organizes Jacobi theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The accessory variational problem is the quadratic problem
\[
\mathcal A[\eta]=\frac12\int_a^b\left(\eta'^{\mathsf T}P\eta'+2\eta'^{\mathsf T}R\eta+\eta^{\mathsf T}Q\eta\right)dt
\]
subject to the linearized endpoint conditions. Its Euler equation is
\[
-\frac d{dt}(P\eta'+R\eta)+R^{\mathsf T}\eta'+Q\eta=0,
\]
so its stationary fields are precisely the admissible Jacobi fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The accessory problem minimizes or studies the quadratic second-variation functional; its stationary fields solve the Jacobi equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Accessory Variational Problems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind is appropriate for the accessory variational problem, and the formal Euler equation matches the displayed quadratic functional. A source is required for the admissible function space, endpoint conditions, coefficient regularity, and the assertion that stationary fields are precisely the admissible Jacobi fields.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source's definition, which requires symmetry and tridiagonal sparsity but does not require nonzero adjacent-diagonal entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$. The matrix $A$ is called a Jacobi matrix if and only if $A=A^{\mathsf T}$ and $a_{ij}=0$ whenever $|i-j|>1$. A quadratic form $q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Ax$ represented by such a matrix is called a Jacobi form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real square matrix is a Jacobi matrix when it is symmetric and every entry outside the main diagonal and the two adjacent diagonals is zero. A quadratic form represented by such a matrix is a Jacobi form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is a Jacobi matrix}\iff\left(A=A^{\mathsf T}\ \text{and}\ a_{ij}=0\ \text{whenever }|i-j|>1\right);\quad q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Ax\text{ is then a Jacobi form.}

assumptions_latex: \(\bar y\) is a weak local minimizer with fixed endpoints.
The second variation is regular and \(P(t)=F_{pp}(t,\bar y,\bar y')\) is positive definite on \([a,b]\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical fixed-endpoint Jacobi necessary condition under regular Legendre positivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(\bar y\) is a weak local minimizer and the regular Legendre condition holds, then there is no nonzero Jacobi field \(\eta\) satisfying
\[
\eta(a)=0,
\qquad
\eta(c)=0
\]
for any \(c\in(a,b)\). Thus the open interval contains no point conjugate to \(a\). Conjugacy at \(b\) is a borderline degeneracy and is not excluded by this necessary statement alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular fixed-endpoint weak minimum cannot contain an interior point conjugate to the initial endpoint; terminal conjugacy remains a borderline case.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal Q[h]=\int_a^b\bigl[(Ph',h')+(Qh,h)\bigr]dx\), where \(P=P^\top\succ0\). If \(\mathcal Q[h]\ge 0\) for every admissible vector function \(h\) satisfying \(h(a)=h(b)=0\), then \((a,b)\) contains no point conjugate to \(a\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar, regular, fixed-endpoint Jacobi sufficiency with the strengthened Legendre condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J[y]=\int_a^b L(t,y(t),y'(t))\,dt\), and let \(\bar y\) satisfy the Euler–Lagrange equation. Put \(P=L_{vv}[\bar y]\) and \(Q=L_{yy}[\bar y]-\frac{d}{dt}L_{yv}[\bar y]\). A point \(c\in(a,b]\) is conjugate to \(a\) when \(-(Pu')'+Qu=0\) has a nonzero solution with \(u(a)=u(c)=0\). If \(P>0\) and no such \(c\) exists, then \[\delta^2J[\bar y](h)=\int_a^b\bigl(P(h')^2+Qh^2\bigr)\,dt>0\] for every nonzero \(h\in H_0^1(a,b)\); consequently \(\bar y\) is a strict weak local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strengthened Legendre condition and absence of conjugate points through the terminal endpoint make the second variation positive and yield strict weak local minimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Jacobi Sufficient Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the Jacobi sufficient-regime leaf, and the scalar fixed-endpoint formulation is mathematically plausible. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-valued fixed-endpoint Jacobi criterion for a quadratic functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal Q[h]=\int_a^b\bigl[(Ph',h')+(Qh,h)\bigr]dx\), where \(P=P^\top\succ0\). If \(\mathcal Q[h]>0\) for every nonzero admissible vector function \(h\) satisfying \(h(a)=h(b)=0\), then \([a,b]\) contains no point conjugate to \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the fixed-endpoint quadratic functional is strictly positive on every nonzero admissible variation and P is symmetric positive definite, then the closed interval contains no point conjugate to its left endpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [a,b]\text{ contains no point conjugate to }a.

children.title: Endpoint-Sensitive Jacobi Regimes
children.top_down_role: Jacobi classifications whose force depends on terminal geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-coefficient model showing how terminal geometry changes the first Jacobi degeneracy threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[ I_\lambda[h]=\int_0^L(h'^2-\lambda h^2)dt, \qquad h(0)=0, \] the fixed-terminal condition \(h(L)=0\) has first degeneracy at \[ \lambda_D=\left(\frac{\pi}{L}\right)^2,\qquad h_D(t)=\sin\frac{\pi t}{L}. \] If the terminal value is free, the natural linearized condition is \(h'(L)=0\), and first degeneracy occurs at \[ \lambda_N=\left(\frac{\pi}{2L}\right)^2,\qquad h_N(t)=\sin\frac{\pi t}{2L}. \] Thus changing only the terminal boundary geometry changes both the admissible Jacobi field and the degeneracy threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same Jacobi differential equation has different first degeneracy thresholds for fixed and natural terminal conditions.
assumptions_latex: Variations satisfy \(h(0)=0\), together with either \(h(L)=0\) or \(h'(L)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_D=(\pi/L)^2\), whereas \(\lambda_N=(\pi/(2L))^2\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes interior conjugacy from conjugacy exactly at the fixed terminal endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the fixed-endpoint problem \(J[y]=\int_a^bL(t,y,y')\,dt\), the Jacobi necessary and sufficient regimes treat \(b\) differently. Under \(L_{vv}[\bar y]>0\), weak local minimality implies that no \(c\in(a,b)\) is conjugate to \(a\). Positive-definite Jacobi sufficiency requires that no \(c\in(a,b]\) be conjugate to \(a\). Thus a first conjugate point at \(c=b\) is compatible with the necessary condition but violates the usual strict sufficient condition because a nonzero endpoint-vanishing Jacobi field can lie in the nullspace of \(\delta^2J[\bar y]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Necessary Jacobi conditions exclude interior conjugate points, while strict sufficiency also excludes conjugacy at the terminal endpoint.

children.title: Borderline Conjugate-Point Cases
children.top_down_role: Threshold configurations separating decisive Jacobi tests from inconclusive cases.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Opposite Higher-Order Outcomes at the Jacobi Threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar fixed-endpoint pair showing that terminal conjugacy alone is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \([0,\pi]\), with \(y(0)=y(\pi)=0\), define \[ J_{\pm}[y]=\int_0^\pi\left[\frac12(y'^2-y^2)\pm y^4\right]dt. \] At \(\bar y=0\), both have \[ \delta^2J_{\pm}(0)[h]=\int_0^\pi(h'^2-h^2)dt\ge0, \] with nullspace \(\operatorname{span}\{\sin t\}\); thus \(\pi\) is the first conjugate point to \(0\). Nevertheless, \(J_+[y]\ge0=J_+[0]\), with equality only at \(y=0\), whereas \[ J_-[\varepsilon\sin t]= -\varepsilon^4\int_0^\pi\sin^4t\,dt<0. \] Hence \(0\) is a strict minimizer for \(J_+\) but not a minimizer for \(J_-\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identical degenerate second variations and endpoint conjugacy can have opposite minimality outcomes because of higher-order terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Terminal conjugacy with a nonnegative degenerate second variation does not determine minimality.

notation.meaning: Functionals differing in the sign of their quartic term

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The terminal endpoint is the first conjugate point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose no point of \((a,b)\) is conjugate to \(a\), but \(b\) is conjugate to \(a\). Then there exists a nonzero Jacobi field \(u\) satisfying \(u(a)=u(b)=0\). Under the strengthened Legendre condition, the index form obeys \[\delta^2J[\bar y](h)\ge 0\quad\text{for all }h\in H_0^1(a,b),\qquad \delta^2J[\bar y](u)=0.\] Hence the second variation is degenerate. Strict minimality cannot be concluded from the Jacobi criterion, while failure of minimality also does not follow without examining higher-order terms or additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the first conjugate point is the terminal endpoint, the second variation has a null Jacobi direction and is inconclusive.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Local Minimizer and Strong Neighborhood
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines strong local minimality for the variational problem (P), records its implication for weak local minimality, and defines a strong neighborhood along the reference arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An admissible function \(x_*\) is a strong local minimizer of \((P)\) if there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that every admissible \(x\) with \(\lVert x-x_*\rVert\leq\varepsilon\) satisfies \(J(x)\geq J(x_*)\). Every strong local minimizer is a weak local minimizer. A property holds in a strong neighborhood of \(x_*\) if, for some \(\varepsilon>0\), it holds at every \((t,x)\) with \(t\in[a,b]\) and \(|x-x_*(t)|\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An admissible function x* is a strong local minimizer when all admissible functions within some positive norm distance have objective value at least J(x*). Such a minimizer is also weakly locally minimizing. A property holds in a strong neighborhood of x* when it holds uniformly for points whose state is within a fixed positive distance of x*(t).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\varepsilon>0\;\forall x\text{ admissible},\quad \lVert x-x_*\rVert\leq\varepsilon\implies J(x)\geq J(x_*)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weierstrass necessary condition for a strong minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong minimality requires nonnegative Weierstrass excess along the extremal for every finite derivative deviation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\gamma\) be an extremal of
\[
J[y]=\int_a^b F(x,y,y')\,dx,\qquad y(a)=A,\quad y(b)=B.
\]
If \(J\) has a strong minimum at \(\gamma\), then along \(\gamma\),
\[
E(x,y(x),y'(x),w)\ge0
\]
for every finite vector \(w\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a fixed-endpoint extremal gives a strong minimum, its Weierstrass excess is nonnegative along the extremal for every finite trial derivative vector.
assumptions_latex: J\text{ has a strong minimum at }\gamma
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E(x,y(x),y'(x),w)\ge0\quad\text{along }\gamma\text{ for every finite }w\in\mathbb R^n.

children.top_down_role: Finite-gradient deviation geometry for strong local extrema.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise convexity characterization supplied by the Weierstrass excess.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \((t,x)\), and let \(v\mapsto L(t,x,v)\) be differentiable on an open convex set \(V\). Then \[E(t,x,v,w)\ge0\quad\text{for all }v,w\in V\] if and only if \(v\mapsto L(t,x,v)\) is convex on \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global nonnegativity of the excess is exactly the differentiable supporting-hyperplane characterization of velocity convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\forall v,w\in V)\ E(t,x,v,w)\ge0\iff L(t,x,\cdot)\text{ is convex on }V.
knowledge_statements.title: Excess Nonnegativity and Velocity Convexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral Hessian Representation of the Excess
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order representation of finite velocity-deviation geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(L(t,x,\cdot)\in C^2\) on a convex neighborhood of \([v,w]\), then \[E(t,x,v,w)=\int_0^1(1-s)\,\langle L_{vv}(t,x,v+s(w-v))(w-v),w-v\rangle\,ds.\] Hence \(L_{vv}\succeq0\) along the segment implies \(E\ge0\), and \(L_{vv}\succeq\alpha I\) implies \(E\ge\frac{\alpha}{2}|w-v|^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a twice-smooth Lagrangian, the excess is velocity curvature accumulated along the finite comparison segment.
assumptions_latex: \(L(t,x,\cdot)\in C^2\) on a convex neighborhood of \([v,w]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E(t,x,v,w)=\int_0^1(1-s)\langle L_{vv}(t,x,v+s(w-v))(w-v),w-v\rangle\,ds.

notation.meaning: Uniform velocity-convexity modulus along the segment.

assumptions_latex: \((t,x,v)\) and \((t,x,w)\) lie in the domain of \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Weierstrass excess is \(E(t,x,v,w)=L(t,x,w)-L(t,x,v)-\langle L_v(t,x,v),w-v\rangle\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite velocity deviations for first-order integral functionals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integral Lagrangian \(L(t,x,v)\) differentiable in its velocity argument, the Weierstrass excess associated with a reference velocity \(v\) and comparison velocity \(w\) is \[E(t,x,v,w):=L(t,x,w)-L(t,x,v)-\langle L_v(t,x,v),w-v\rangle.\] It is the remainder after subtracting the affine tangent approximation of \(w\mapsto L(t,x,w)\) at \(v\). The Weierstrass condition along an extremal \(\bar y\) is \(E(t,\bar y(t),\bar y'(t),w)\ge0\) for every admissible comparison velocity \(w\) and every relevant \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The excess function measures how much the Lagrangian at a comparison velocity exceeds its affine velocity linearization at the reference velocity.
knowledge_statements.title: Weierstrass Excess-Function Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the excess-function container, and the displayed formula is the standard finite-velocity Weierstrass excess. No source or specific locator is supplied for either the definition or the stated scope of the Weierstrass condition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the finite-derivative-deviation excess for a first-order integral functional and states its second-order Taylor-remainder representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(J[y]=\int_a^b F(x,y,y')\,dx\), with \(y(a)=A\), \(y(b)=B\), the Weierstrass excess function is
\[
E(x,y,z,w)=F(x,y,w)-F(x,y,z)-\sum_{i=1}^n(w_i-z_i)F_{p_i}(x,y,z),
\]
where \(p\) denotes the last \(n\) arguments of \(F\). If \(F(x,y,\cdot)\) is twice continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of the segment from \(z\) to \(w\), then for some \(\theta\in(0,1)\),
\[
E(x,y,z,w)=\frac12\sum_{i,k=1}^n(w_i-z_i)(w_k-z_k)F_{p_i p_k}(x,y,z+\theta(w-z)).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Weierstrass excess is the integrand at a trial derivative w minus its first-order Taylor approximation about z. With the required second differentiability, it is the quadratic Taylor remainder at an intermediate point between z and w.
assumptions_latex: F(x,y,\cdot)\text{ is twice continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of }[z,w]\text{ for the remainder formula}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E(x,y,z,w)=F(x,y,w)-F(x,y,z)-\langle F_p(x,y,z),w-z\rangle,\quad E(x,y,z,w)=\tfrac12(w-z)^\top F_{pp}(x,y,z+\theta(w-z))(w-z)\text{ for some }\theta\in(0,1).

assumptions_latex: \(\bar y\in W^{1,\infty}([a,b];\mathbb R^n)\), \(t_0\in(a,b)\), and \(\phi\in W_0^{1,\infty}(0,1;\mathbb R^n)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_\varepsilon\to\bar y\) uniformly while its derivative undergoes an order-one perturbation on an interval of length \(\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[y_\varepsilon(t)=\begin{cases}\bar y(t)+\varepsilon\phi\!\left((t-t_0)/\varepsilon\right),&t\in[t_0,t_0+\varepsilon],\\ \bar y(t),&t\notin[t_0,t_0+\varepsilon].\end{cases}\] Because \(\phi\) has zero trace, \(y_\varepsilon\) is continuous and agrees with \(\bar y\) outside the needle interval. Moreover, \(\|y_\varepsilon-\bar y\|_\infty=O(\varepsilon)\), whereas \(y_\varepsilon'(t)-\bar y'(t)=\phi'((t-t_0)/\varepsilon)\) almost everywhere inside that interval. Thus the arc perturbation is uniformly small although its velocity deviation need not be small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A needle variation changes velocity by order one on a shrinking interval while the perturbed arc remains uniformly close to the reference arc.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative concentration rates for the accepted Lipschitz needle profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the needle family in the seed record and every \(1\le p<\infty\), \[\|y_\varepsilon-\bar y\|_{L^p}=\varepsilon^{1+1/p}\|\phi\|_{L^p(0,1)},\qquad \|y_\varepsilon'-\bar y'\|_{L^p}=\varepsilon^{1/p}\|\phi'\|_{L^p(0,1)}.\] Moreover, \(\|y_\varepsilon-\bar y\|_{L^\infty}=\varepsilon\|\phi\|_\infty\) and \(\|y_\varepsilon'-\bar y'\|_{L^\infty}=\|\phi'\|_\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Needle arcs converge in every finite-order first Sobolev norm and uniformly in value, while their derivative perturbations generally do not vanish in the supremum norm.
assumptions_latex: \(y_\varepsilon\) is the accepted needle family generated by \(\phi\in W^{1,\infty}_0(0,1;\mathbb R^n)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y_\varepsilon\to\bar y\text{ in }W^{1,p}\text{ for finite }p,\quad\text{but generally not in }W^{1,\infty}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient condition for local optimality relative to a tube around an arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x$ and $p$ be arcs on $[a,b]$. Suppose that, for almost every $t$ and every $v\in\mathbb R^n$, $L(t,x(t),\dot x(t)+v)-L(t,x(t),\dot x(t))\ge \langle p(t),v\rangle$. Suppose also that there exist $\varepsilon>0$ and a Lipschitz symmetric matrix-valued function $Q:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ such that, for almost every $t$ and every $y\in\varepsilon B$, $$H(t,x(t)+y,p(t)-Q(t)y)-H(t,x(t),p(t))\le-\langle\dot p(t)+Q(t)\dot x(t),y\rangle+\tfrac12\langle y,\dot Q(t)y\rangle,$$ and, for every $u,v\in\varepsilon B$, $$l(x(a)+u,x(b)+v)-l(x(a),x(b))\ge-\langle p(b),v\rangle+\langle p(a),u\rangle-\tfrac12\langle u,Q(a)u\rangle+\tfrac12\langle v,Q(b)v\rangle.$$ Then $x$ solves $P_B$ locally relative to $T(x;\varepsilon)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an arc admits a supporting costate for velocity perturbations, a Lipschitz symmetric quadratic field giving the stated Hamiltonian upper bound for all sufficiently small state perturbations, and the corresponding endpoint-cost lower bound, then the arc is a local solution of the variational problem within the prescribed tube.
assumptions_latex: L(t,x(t),\dot x(t)+v)-L(t,x(t),\dot x(t))\ge\langle p(t),v\rangle\quad\forall v\in\mathbb R^n\text{, a.e. }t.
\exists\varepsilon>0\ \exists Q\in\operatorname{Lip}([a,b];\mathbb S^n)\text{ satisfying the stated Hamiltonian inequality for a.e. }t\text{ and all }y\in\varepsilon B.
\text{The stated endpoint-cost inequality holds for all }u,v\in\varepsilon B.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ solves }P_B\text{ locally relative to }T(x;\varepsilon).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integer Combinations of Needle Endpoint Increments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a fixed nonnegative-integer combination of single-needle endpoint increments by one multineedle endpoint increment to first order in the mesh size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \{u_N(\cdot)\}_{N\in\mathbb N} be a proper sequence of reference controls. Let p\in\mathbb N and m_j\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\}, j=1,\ldots,p, be independent of N, and let (\theta_j(N),v_j(N)), j=1,\ldots,p, be parameters of single-needle variations. Then there exist r\in\mathbb N independent of N and parameters \{(\widetilde\theta_j(N),\widetilde v_j(N))\}_{j=1}^r of an r-needle variation such that \Delta_N(p,m_j)=\Delta^r_{\{\widetilde\theta_j,\widetilde v_j\}}x_N(b)+o(h_N) as N\to\infty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper sequence of reference controls, a fixed nonnegative-integer combination of finitely many single-needle endpoint increments can be represented, up to an error of order smaller than the mesh size, by one multineedle endpoint increment whose number of needles is independent of N.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete r-Needle Control Variation and Trajectory Increment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines single and multineedle perturbations on a finite time grid and their induced state and endpoint increments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let u_N(t)\in U for every t\in T_N, and let 1\le r\le N-1. Choose v_j(N)\in U and pairwise distinct integers 0\le\theta_j(N)\le N-1, and set \tau_{\theta_j(N)}=a+\theta_j(N)h_N. Define \widetilde u_N(\tau_{\theta_j(N)})=v_j(N) for j=1,\ldots,r and \widetilde u_N(t)=u_N(t) at all other t\in T_N. If \widetilde x_N is the trajectory corresponding to \widetilde u_N in the finite-difference system x_N(t+h_N)=x_N(t)+h_Nf(x_N(t),u_N(t),t),\ x_N(a)=x_0, then \Delta^r_{\{\theta_j,v_j\}}x_N(\cdot):=\widetilde x_N(\cdot)-x_N(\cdot). For r=1 it is denoted \Delta_{\theta,v}x_N(\cdot), and its value at t=b is the corresponding endpoint increment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An r-needle variation replaces the discrete control at r distinct grid points and leaves it unchanged elsewhere. The perturbed trajectory minus the reference trajectory is the r-needle trajectory increment; its terminal value is the endpoint increment. The cases r=1 and r>1 are respectively single and multineedle variations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widetilde u_N(\tau_{\theta_j(N)})=v_j(N),\quad \widetilde u_N(t)=u_N(t)\text{ otherwise},\qquad \Delta^r_{\{\theta_j,v_j\}}x_N(\cdot)=\widetilde x_N(\cdot)-x_N(\cdot).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order uniform trajectory sensitivity to the duration of a fixed-value needle perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Delta\bar x(\cdot)\) be the trajectory increment corresponding to the needle variation of \(\bar u(\cdot)\) with parameters \((\tau,\varepsilon,v)\). Then there exists \(K>0\), independent of \((\tau,\varepsilon)\) but possibly dependent on \(v\), such that \[\|\Delta\bar x(t)\|\le K\varepsilon\qquad\text{for every }t\in[a,b].\]

The bound is independent of the needle location and duration parameters, although its constant may depend on the inserted value.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists K>0\ \text{independent of }(\tau,\varepsilon)\ \text{and possibly dependent on }v:\ \forall t\in[a,b],\ \|\Delta\bar x(t)\|\le K\varepsilon.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed Corner Times Yield Only Momentum Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissibility boundary for the second corner equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the corner value may vary but the corner time \(t_c\) is fixed, stationarity yields \([L_v]_{t_c}=0\). It does not by itself yield \([L-y'\cdot L_v]_{t_c}=0\); the latter condition requires an admissible variation of the junction time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed corner tests momentum matching, while the energy jump condition requires movable-corner variations.
assumptions_latex: The corner value can vary compatibly with continuity and the endpoint constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [L_v]_{t_c}=0\text{ is forced, but }[L-y'\cdot L_v]_{t_c}=0\text{ need not be.}
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Corner Times Yield Only Momentum Matching

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary junction conditions exposed by admissible movable-corner broken variations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\) be a piecewise \(C^1\) local minimizer of \(J[y]=\int_a^bL(t,y,y')\,dt\), smooth on both sides of a free interior corner \(t_c\). If the corner value and corner time admit the usual independent compatible variations and \(L\in C^1\), then \[[L_v]_{t_c}=0,\qquad[L-y'\cdot L_v]_{t_c}=0.\] Thus momentum and the negative Hamiltonian are continuous across the free corner.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a freely movable corner of a minimizing broken extremal, momentum and the energy expression are continuous.
assumptions_latex: The reference arc is piecewise \(C^1\) and satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation on each smooth piece.
The corner value and time admit the required compatible independent variations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [L_v]_{t_c}=0,\qquad[L-y'\cdot L_v]_{t_c}=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Weierstrass–Erdmann Corner Conditions

assumptions_latex: Each restriction \(y|_{[t_{i-1},t_i]}\) is continuously differentiable and adjacent restrictions have matching values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\) is a continuous, piecewise-\(C^1\) admissible arc whose one-sided velocities may jump at finitely many corner times.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous piecewise-smooth arcs with finitely many velocity discontinuities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A broken variation is a family of arcs \(y_\varepsilon:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n\) for which each \(y_\varepsilon\) is continuous and piecewise \(C^1\) on a finite partition \(a=t_0<\cdots<t_m=b\), satisfies the prescribed endpoint and path constraints, and may have unequal one-sided derivatives at the interior corner times. Thus \[y_\varepsilon(t_i^-)=y_\varepsilon(t_i^+),\qquad y_\varepsilon'(t_i^-)\ne y_\varepsilon'(t_i^+)\] is permitted. A localized broken variation additionally agrees with the reference arc outside a union of partition intervals whose total length tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Broken variations are continuous admissible arcs formed from finitely many smooth pieces, allowing velocity jumps at their corners.
knowledge_statements.title: Broken Variations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind is suitable for the Broken Variations leaf, and the statement consistently describes continuous piecewise-C1 admissible arcs with finitely many velocity jumps. A source with a specific definition or section locator is absent.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a broken extremal and gives a variational problem whose minimum requires admitting a corner.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A piecewise-smooth extremal having one or more corners, that is, points where its first derivative is discontinuous, is called a broken extremal. For
\[
J[y]=\int_{-1}^{1}y(x)^2\bigl(1-y'(x)\bigr)^2\,dx,
\qquad y(-1)=0,\quad y(1)=1,
\]
the infimum over smooth admissible curves equals \(0\) but is not attained by any such curve. After extending the admissible class to piecewise-smooth curves, the minimum \(0\) is attained by
\[
y_*(x)=\begin{cases}0,&-1\le x\le0,\\x,&0<x\le1,\end{cases}
\]
which is a broken extremal with a corner at \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-smooth extremal with a discontinuous first derivative at a corner is called a broken extremal. For the stated functional and endpoint conditions, the infimum over smooth curves is zero but is unattained, while the displayed piecewise-smooth curve attains zero and has a corner at the origin.
assumptions_latex: y\in C^1([-1,1]),\quad y(-1)=0,\quad y(1)=1\quad\text{for the smooth admissible class}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{\substack{y\in C^1([-1,1])\\y(-1)=0,\ y(1)=1}}J[y]=0\ \text{and the infimum is unattained, whereas }J[y_*]=0\text{ in the piecewise-smooth class; }y_*\text{ is a broken extremal.}

children.title: Localized Strong-Perturbation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Strong-topology regimes organized by concentration of admissible changes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shrinking Support Alone Does Not Ensure Strong Closeness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Amplitude-concentration boundary for localized perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The condition \(|S_k|\to0\) alone does not imply \(\|y_k- ar y\|_\infty\to0\). The controlling quantity is the accumulated velocity perturbation \(\int_{S_k}|y_k'-\bar y'|\,dt\). Velocity amplitudes of order \(|S_k|^{-1}\) can keep this quantity, and hence the possible state displacement, of order one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shrinking support can carry a sufficiently large velocity concentration to prevent uniform convergence.
assumptions_latex: The arcs are absolutely continuous, share the initial endpoint, and their derivative difference is supported in \(S_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |S_k|\to0\text{ without }\int_{S_k}|y_k'-\bar y'|\,dt\to0\text{ does not guarantee uniform closeness.}
knowledge_statements.title: Shrinking Support Alone Does Not Ensure Strong Closeness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topology distinction realized by localized derivative concentration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequence may satisfy \(\|y_k-\bar y\|_\infty\to0\) while \(\|y_k'-\bar y'\|_\infty\not\to0\). It therefore enters every classical strong neighborhood based on uniform state distance but need not enter weak neighborhoods that also control the derivative. Localized derivative concentrations consequently test strong minimality beyond derivative-small variations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Localized concentration separates uniform state closeness from simultaneous state-and-velocity closeness.
assumptions_latex: The classical convention is used: strong neighborhoods control the state uniformly, while weak neighborhoods also control its derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|y_k-\bar y\|_\infty\to0\not\Rightarrow\|y_k'-\bar y'\|_\infty\to0.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong–Weak Topology Separation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative mechanism allowing order-one velocity changes in strong neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y_k,\bar y\) be absolutely continuous with the same initial value, and let \(w_k=y_k'-\bar y'\) be supported in an interval \(S_k\). Then \[y_k(t)-\bar y(t)=\int_a^t w_k(s)\,ds,\qquad \|y_k-\bar y\|_\infty\le\int_{S_k}|w_k|\,dt\le |S_k|\|w_k\|_\infty.\] If the final endpoint is also fixed, \(\int_{S_k}w_k=0\) is required. Thus bounded order-one velocity deviations on shrinking intervals give uniformly vanishing state deviations without derivative-norm convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shrinking support converts bounded velocity changes into uniformly small state displacements; endpoint preservation additionally requires cancellation.
assumptions_latex: The arcs are absolutely continuous and share their initial endpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|y_k-\bar y\|_\infty\le\int_{S_k}|w_k|\le |S_k|\|w_k\|_\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Support–Amplitude Scaling

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong perturbations control \(\|y_k-\bar y\|_\infty\) but need not control \(\|y_k'-\bar y'\|_\infty\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong topology localized in time but not in velocity magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A localized strong-perturbation regime consists of admissible arcs \(y_k\) and measurable sets \(S_k\subset[a,b]\) such that \[\|y_k-\bar y\|_\infty\to0,\qquad y_k(t)=\bar y(t)\ \text{for }t\notin S_k,\qquad |S_k|\to0.\] No convergence of \(y_k'\) to \(\bar y'\) is required; the derivatives may differ by order one on \(S_k\). This regime therefore probes strong local minimality, which is defined through closeness of arcs in the uniform norm, rather than weak local minimality based on simultaneous arc-and-velocity closeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Localized strong perturbations are uniformly small and supported on shrinking sets, but their derivative deviations may remain large.
knowledge_statements.title: Localized Strong-Perturbation Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind matches the localized strong-perturbation leaf and distinguishes uniform arc closeness from derivative closeness. The added shrinking-support requirement is a particular localized regime rather than the general definition of strong topology, so an authoritative locator is needed to establish this exact formulation and terminology.

children.title: Localized-Variation Admissibility
children.top_down_role: Structural limits determining which localized perturbations remain feasible.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active State Constraints Can Exclude Needle Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary obstruction to localized admissibility at an active unilateral state constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let admissible arcs satisfy \(y(t)\ge 0\) on \([a,b]\), let \(\bar y\equiv0\), and choose \(\phi\in W^{1,\infty}_0(0,1)\) with \(\phi(s_*)<0\) for some \(s_*\in(0,1)\). Define \(y_\varepsilon(t)=\varepsilon\phi((t-t_0)/\varepsilon)\) on \([t_0,t_0+\varepsilon]\) and extend it by zero outside. Then \(y_\varepsilon(t_0+\varepsilon s_*)<0\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shrinking the support and amplitude does not make a profile admissible when it points outside an active state constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar y\equiv0\) lies on the active boundary of the constraint \(y\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y_\varepsilon(t_0+\varepsilon s_*)=\varepsilon\phi(s_*)<0,\quad\text{so }y_\varepsilon\text{ is inadmissible for every }\varepsilon>0.
knowledge_statements.title: Active State Constraints Can Exclude Needle Profiles

assumptions_latex: Admissibility is specified by \((y(t),y'(t))\in A(t)\) almost everywhere and \((y(a),y(b))\in B\).
\(y_\varepsilon\in W^{1,\infty}([a,b];\mathbb R^n)\) is a proposed localized variation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The localized variation is admissible exactly when it satisfies the path, differential, and endpoint constraints for every sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic state-velocity and endpoint feasibility for localized Lipschitz variations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A localized family \(y_\varepsilon\) is admissible when there exists \(\varepsilon_0>0\) such that, for every \(0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0\), \[y_\varepsilon\in W^{1,\infty}([a,b];\mathbb R^n),\qquad (y_\varepsilon(t),y_\varepsilon'(t))\in A(t)\ \text{for almost every }t,\qquad (y_\varepsilon(a),y_\varepsilon(b))\in B.\] It must also remain inside the domain of the Lagrangian almost everywhere. For fixed endpoints this reduces to \(y_\varepsilon(a)=\bar y(a)\) and \(y_\varepsilon(b)=\bar y(b)\), in addition to the pointwise feasibility requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A localized variation is usable only if every sufficiently small member respects the Lagrangian domain, path constraints, derivative constraints, and endpoint conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Localized-Variation Admissibility

children.title: Weierstrass-Condition Scope Limits
children.top_down_role: Boundaries between necessary excess geometry and sufficient strong minimality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Minimality Does Not Imply the Global Weierstrass Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topology boundary showing why arbitrary finite velocity comparisons are specific to strong minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \([0,1]\) with fixed endpoints, let \(J[y]=\int_0^1((y')^2-(y')^4)\,dt\) and \(\bar y\equiv0\). If \(\|y'\|_\infty<1\), then \(J[y]\ge0=J[\bar y]\), so \(\bar y\) is a weak local minimizer in the derivative-controlling \(W^{1,\infty}\) topology. However, \(L_v(0)=0\) and \(E(0,2)=L(2)-L(0)=-12<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weak neighborhood restricts velocity deviations, so a weak minimum can coexist with negative excess at distant comparison velocities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar y\text{ is a weak local minimizer but fails the global finite-velocity Weierstrass inequality.}
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Minimality Does Not Imply the Global Weierstrass Condition

assumptions_latex: The admissible class has fixed endpoints on \([0,2\pi]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Weierstrass condition holds everywhere, but \(\bar y\) is not a local minimizer; excess nonnegativity alone is not sufficient.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete separation of Weierstrass necessity from sufficient minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(J[y]=\int_0^{2\pi}((y')^2-y^2)\,dt\) with \(y(0)=y(2\pi)=0\), the zero arc \(\bar y\equiv0\) is an extremal. Its excess function is \[E(t,y,v,w)=w^2-v^2-2v(w-v)=(w-v)^2\ge0,\] so the Weierstrass condition holds globally. Nevertheless, for \(y_\varepsilon(t)=\varepsilon\sin(t/2)\), \[J[y_\varepsilon]=-\frac{3\pi}{4}\varepsilon^2<0=J[\bar y].\] Thus nonnegative excess controls finite velocity deviations but, without a positive second variation or another sufficiency mechanism, does not ensure even weak local minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A globally nonnegative excess function can coexist with a negative second-variation direction, so the Weierstrass condition alone is not sufficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Weierstrass-Condition Scope Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind is appropriate for the scope-limits container. children.title: Positive Second Variation
children.top_down_role: Second-order sufficient-condition families for weak local minimality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary between second-order necessity and quantitative sufficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a twice differentiable weak local minimizer, \(\delta^2J[\bar y](h,h)\ge0\) for every admissible variation. Semidefiniteness alone does not imply strict minimality or quadratic growth. A stationary point satisfies the standard sufficient condition when \[\delta^2J[\bar y](h,h)\ge\alpha\|h\|^2\quad(\alpha>0)\] and the second-order remainder is uniform in the chosen weak neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative second variation is necessary, while strict weak minimality with quadratic growth requires a uniform coercive gap and controlled remainder.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is twice differentiable along admissible variations.
\(\bar y\) is stationary for the sufficiency implication.
The Taylor remainder is uniform in the stated weak topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta^2J\ge0\text{ is necessary; coercivity plus a uniform second-order expansion is sufficient for quadratic growth.}
knowledge_statements.title: Semidefiniteness Versus Coercive Sufficiency

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Positivity Need Not Be Coercive
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional spectral-gap failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\ell^2\), define \[Q(h)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{|h_k|^2}{k}.\] Then \(Q(h)>0\) for every \(h\ne0\), but no \(\alpha>0\) satisfies \(Q(h)\ge\alpha\|h\|_{\ell^2}^2\), because \(Q(e_k)=1/k\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive quadratic form can have eigenvalues tending to zero and therefore lack a uniform quadratic-growth constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q(h)>0\ \forall h\ne0\not\Rightarrow\exists\alpha>0:\ Q(h)\ge\alpha\|h\|^2.

notation.meaning: The kth standard unit vector of \(\ell^2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Positivity Need Not Be Coercive

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical scalar fixed-endpoint test for positivity of the second variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a regular scalar one-dimensional fixed-endpoint extremal, assume the strengthened Legendre condition \(L_{vv}>0\) along the extremal and that no point of \((a,b]\) is conjugate to \(a\) for the Jacobi equation. Then the second variation is positive definite. Under uniform strengthened Legendre and regularity bounds it is coercive on \(H_0^1(a,b)\), so the standard uniform-remainder hypothesis yields strict weak local minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strengthened Legendre positivity and absence of conjugate points provide the classical fixed-endpoint test for positive, and under uniform bounds coercive, second variation.
assumptions_latex: The problem is scalar, one-dimensional, regular, and has fixed endpoints.
There is no conjugate point to \(a\) in \((a,b]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta^2J[\bar y](h,h)>0\quad\forall h\in H_0^1(a,b)\setminus\{0\},\text{ with coercivity under uniform hypotheses.}
review_flags: Cross-indexed to fixed-endpoint second-variation geometry; retained here only as a sufficiency test.
knowledge_statements.title: Jacobi–Legendre Positivity Criterion

assumptions_latex: \(L\in C^2\) near a fixed-endpoint extremal \(\bar y\).
There exists \(\alpha>0\) such that \(\delta^2J[\bar y](h)\ge\alpha\|h\|_{H^1}^2\) for every \(h\in H_0^1(a,b)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There are \(c,r>0\) such that \(J[\bar y+h]\ge J[\bar y]+c\|h\|_{H^1}^2\) whenever \(h\in W_0^{1,\infty}\) and \(\|h\|_{W^{1,\infty}}<r\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coercive second variation yielding strict weak local minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J[y]=\int_a^bL(t,y,y')\,dt\), with \(L\in C^2\) on a neighborhood of the graph of a fixed-endpoint extremal \(\bar y\). If the second variation is coercive, meaning that some \(\alpha>0\) satisfies \[\delta^2J[\bar y](h)\ge\alpha\|h\|_{H^1(a,b)}^2\quad\text{for all }h\in H_0^1(a,b),\] then there exist \(c,r>0\) such that \[J[\bar y+h]\ge J[\bar y]+c\|h\|_{H^1(a,b)}^2\] for every \(h\in W_0^{1,\infty}(a,b)\) with \(\|h\|_{W^{1,\infty}}<r\). Hence \(\bar y\) is a strict weak local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coercively positive second variation at an extremal gives quadratic growth and strict weak local minimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Second Variation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the positive-second-variation leaf. Coercivity leading to quadratic growth in the stated weak neighborhood is a nontrivial sufficiency theorem whose regularity and norm hypotheses require verification against an authoritative source with a precise locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First and second variations of a functional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source's convention in which the quadratic term itself, without an additional numerical factor, is the second variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J:\mathcal R\to\mathbb R\) and fix \(y\in\mathcal R\). The functional is differentiable at \(y\) if \(J[y+h]-J[y]=\varphi[h]+\varepsilon(h)\|h\|\), where \(\varphi\) is linear and \(\varepsilon(h)\to0\) as \(\|h\|\to0\); then \(\delta J[y;h]=\varphi[h]\). It is twice differentiable at \(y\) if \(J[y+h]-J[y]=\varphi_1[h]+\varphi_2[h]+\varepsilon(h)\|h\|^2\), where \(\varphi_1\) is linear, \(\varphi_2\) is quadratic, and \(\varepsilon(h)\to0\); then \(\delta^2J[y;h]=\varphi_2[h]\), and this quadratic functional is uniquely determined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a fixed point, the first variation is the linear principal part of the functional's increment with an error that is little-o of the perturbation norm. The second variation is the quadratic term in a second-order expansion with an error that is little-o of the squared norm, and this quadratic term is unique.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal R\) is a normed linear space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta J[y;h]=\varphi_1[h],\qquad \delta^2J[y;h]=\varphi_2[h],\qquad \varphi_2\text{ is uniquely determined}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly positive second variation ensures weak local minimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order sufficient condition in the norm topology used for weak extrema.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\) be twice differentiable at \(\widehat y\) in the source's norm-based sense. If \(\delta J[\widehat y;h]=0\) for every admissible variation \(h\), and the second variation is strongly positive, meaning that some \(k>0\) satisfies \(\delta^2J[\widehat y;h]\ge k\lVert h\rVert^2\) for every admissible \(h\), then \(\widehat y\) is a strict weak local minimum of \(J\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary point is a strict weak local minimum when its second variation uniformly dominates a positive multiple of the squared perturbation norm.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is twice differentiable at \(\widehat y\) with respect to the norm defining weak variations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second variation of a vector integral functional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the quadratic term in the increment expansion and gives its fixed-endpoint integral representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\Delta J[h]=\varphi_1[h]+\varphi_2[h]+\varepsilon\|h\|^2\), where \(\varphi_1\) is linear, \(\varphi_2\) is quadratic, and \(\varepsilon\to0\) as \(\|h\|\to0\), then \(\delta^2J[h]:=\varphi_2[h]\). For \(J[y]=\int_a^b F(x,y,y')\,dx\) and \(h(a)=h(b)=0\), \[\delta^2J[h]=\frac12\int_a^b\sum_{i,k=1}^n\left(F_{y_i y_k}h_i h_k+2F_{y_i y_k'}h_i h_k'+F_{y_i' y_k'}h_i'h_k'\right)dx.\] After integration by parts this has the index form \[\delta^2J[h]=\int_a^b\bigl(\langle P h',h'\rangle+\langle Qh,h\rangle\bigr)dx,\quad P=\tfrac12F_{y'y'},\quad Q=\tfrac12\left(F_{yy}-\frac d{dx}F_{yy'}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second variation is the quadratic term in the small-increment expansion of a functional. For a vector-valued integral functional with fixed endpoint variations, it is an integral quadratic form in h and h′, which can be reduced by integration by parts to an index form with coefficient matrices P and Q.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta^2J[h]=\varphi_2[h]=\int_a^b\left(\langle Ph',h'\rangle+\langle Qh,h\rangle\right)dx

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes positive definiteness and the finite-dimensional matrix representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scalar functional \(B:\mathcal R\times\mathcal R\to\mathbb R\) is bilinear if, for all \(x,y,z\in\mathcal R\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), it is linear in each argument separately. Its diagonal restriction \(A[x]=B[x,x]\) is a quadratic functional and is positive definite when \(A[x]>0\) for every \(x\ne0\). If \(\dim\mathcal R=n\), then relative to any basis, \(B[x,y]=\sum_{i,k=1}^n b_{ik}\xi_i\eta_k\), and hence \(A[x]=\sum_{i,k=1}^n b_{ik}\xi_i\xi_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar functional of two vectors is bilinear when it is linear in each argument separately. Evaluating it on the same vector twice gives a quadratic functional, which is positive definite if it is positive on every nonzero vector. In finite dimensions, every such bilinear functional has a matrix-coordinate representation, whose diagonal restriction is the corresponding quadratic form.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal R\) is a real normed linear space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\text{ bilinear}\implies A[x]=B[x,x]\text{ is quadratic};\quad A\text{ positive definite}\iff \forall x\ne0,\ A[x]>0,\quad B[x,y]=\sum_{i,k=1}^n b_{ik}\xi_i\eta_k\text{ in finite dimensions}.

children.title: Convexity-Based Sufficiency

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convex sufficiency without joint or functional convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(T>\pi\), consider fixed-zero-endpoint arcs and \[J[y]=\int_0^T\bigl((y')^2-y^2\bigr)\,dt.\] The integrand is strictly convex in the velocity and \(\bar y\equiv0\) satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation. For \(y(t)=c\sin(\pi t/T)\), \[J[y]=\frac{c^2T}{2}\left(\frac{\pi^2}{T^2}-1\right)<0=J[0].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity only in the derivative variable does not make an Euler extremal a minimizer when the state dependence has negative curvature.
assumptions_latex: The admissible class contains the displayed smooth fixed-endpoint arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Convexity of }L\text{ in }v\text{ alone does not imply sufficiency of the Euler equation.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsmooth convex form of first-order sufficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space, \(\mathcal A\subset X\) be convex, and \(J:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. If \(\bar u\in\mathcal A\) and some \(g\in\partial J(\bar u)\) satisfies \[\langle g,u-\bar u\rangle\ge0\quad\forall u\in\mathcal A,\] then \(J(u)\ge J(\bar u)\) for every \(u\in\mathcal A\). With the convex-analytic normal-cone convention, this condition is equivalent to \(0\in\partial J(\bar u)+N_{\mathcal A}(\bar u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex functional on a convex admissible set, the convex first-order condition is sufficient for global minimality.
assumptions_latex: The displayed subgradient and normal-cone objects are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\partial J(\bar u)+N_{\mathcal A}(\bar u)\Longrightarrow\bar u\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in\mathcal A}J(u).

notation.meaning: Convex normal cone to the admissible set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Convexity Gives Global Quadratic Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative convex sufficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(J\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex on a convex admissible set \(\mathcal A\) and \(\bar u\) satisfies \(0\in\partial J(\bar u)+N_{\mathcal A}(\bar u)\), then \[J(u)\ge J(\bar u)+\frac\mu2\|u-\bar u\|^2\quad\forall u\in\mathcal A.\] Consequently \(\bar u\) is the unique global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity upgrades convex first-order sufficiency to global quadratic growth and uniqueness.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar u\) satisfies the convex first-order condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J(u)-J(\bar u)\ge\frac\mu2\|u-\bar u\|^2\quad\forall u\in\mathcal A.

assumptions_latex: The admissible set \(\mathcal A\subset W^{1,1}([a,b];\mathbb R^n)\) is convex and has fixed endpoints.

\(\bar y\in\mathcal A\) satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J[y]\ge J[\bar y]\) for every \(y\in\mathcal A\); strict convexity gives uniqueness up to null directions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global sufficiency for a jointly convex differentiable Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J[y]=\int_a^bL(t,y(t),y'(t))\,dt\) on a convex fixed-endpoint admissible set \(\mathcal A\). Suppose \((x,v)\mapsto L(t,x,v)\) is differentiable and convex for almost every \(t\), and let \(\bar y\in\mathcal A\) satisfy \[\frac{d}{dt}L_v(t,\bar y,\bar y')=L_x(t,\bar y,\bar y')\] in the weak sense. Then the supporting-hyperplane inequality for \(L\), followed by integration by parts, gives \(J[y]-J[\bar y]\ge0\) for every \(y\in\mathcal A\). Thus \(\bar y\) is a global minimizer; if the integral functional is strictly convex on \(\mathcal A\), this minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex admissible set and jointly convex Lagrangian, every Euler–Lagrange extremal is a global minimizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weierstrass field sufficient condition for a strong minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A field covering a neighborhood of an extremal, together with nonnegative Weierstrass excess throughout that neighborhood, certifies strong minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\gamma\) be an extremal of
\[
J[y]=\int_a^b F(x,y,y')\,dx,\qquad y(a)=A,\quad y(b)=B,
\]
and let \(y'=\psi(x,y)\) be a field for the functional covering an open region \(U\) containing \(\gamma\). If
\[
E(x,y,\psi(x,y),w)\ge 0
\]
for every \((x,y)\in U\) and every finite vector \(w\in\mathbb R^n\), then \(J\) has a strong minimum at \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an extremal lies in an open region covered by a field for the functional and the Weierstrass excess is nonnegative there for every finite trial derivative, then the extremal gives a strong minimum of the fixed-endpoint functional.
assumptions_latex: y'=\psi(x,y)\text{ is a field for }J\text{ covering an open region }U\supset\gamma
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J\text{ has a strong minimum at }\gamma.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hamilton–Jacobi compatibility criterion for a direction field
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when a first-order direction system has trajectories satisfying a prescribed second-order system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
y_i'=\psi_i(x,y_1,\ldots,y_n),\qquad a\le x\le b,
\]
and the second-order system
\[
y_i''=f_i(x,y_1,�ldots,y_n,y_1',\ldots,y_n'),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
\]
The first-order system is a field for the second-order system if and only if, pointwise on its domain and for every \(i=1,\ldots,n\),
\[
\frac{\partial\psi_i}{\partial x}+\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{\partial\psi_i}{\partial y_k}\psi_k
=f_i(x,y_1,\ldots,y_n,\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_n).
\]
Consequently, every sufficiently differentiable solution \(\psi\) of this compatibility system defines a field for the second-order system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-order direction system is a field for the prescribed second-order system exactly when the derivative of every direction component along the field equals the corresponding second-order right-hand side evaluated at the field. Every sufficiently differentiable solution of this compatibility system therefore yields a field.
assumptions_latex: \psi_i\text{ has the displayed partial derivatives on the domain}
y_i''=f_i(x,y,y')\text{ is the prescribed second-order system}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y'=\psi(x,y)\text{ is a field for }y''=f(x,y,y')\iff \partial_x\psi_i+\sum_{k=1}^n(\partial_{y_k}\psi_i)\psi_k=f_i(x,y,\psi)\quad(1\le i\le n)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Field of directions for a differential system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a field by pairwise consistency of a continuously differentiable first-order slope system and records its trajectory interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\psi_i\in C^1(R)\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), and prescribe for every \(x\in[a,b]\)
\[
y_i'=\psi_i(x,y_1,\ldots,y_n),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
\]
If these slope conditions are mutually consistent for every pair \(x_1,x_2\in[a,b]\), then they constitute a field of directions for the given differential system. Equivalently, every solution of \(y'=\psi(x,y)\) also satisfies the given system. Wherever the applicable existence-and-uniqueness hypotheses hold, exactly one field trajectory passes through each point of \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuously differentiable first-order slope system is a field for a given differential system when its conditions are mutually consistent at every pair of points in the interval. Its integral curves then solve the given system; under the applicable existence-and-uniqueness hypotheses, exactly one trajectory passes through each point of the region.

\text{the stated trajectory uniqueness is restricted to where the applicable existence-and-uniqueness hypotheses hold}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y'=\psi(x,y)\text{ is a field for the given system, and under existence and uniqueness }\forall(x_0,y_0)\in R\ \exists!\text{ a field trajectory through }(x_0,y_0)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-coordinate criterion for a differentiable extremal family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an \(n\)-parameter family of extremals \(y(t,\alpha)\), the columns of \(D_\alpha y(t,\alpha)\) solve the Jacobi system. The family supplies regular local field coordinates exactly where \[\det D_\alpha y(t,\alpha)\ne0.\] At determinant zero the parameter-to-state map is not locally invertible, so locally unique extremal coordinates can fail; conjugate or focal points provide the classical occurrences of this obstruction.

The family has as many parameters as the state dimension.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Self-Adjoint Boundary Conditions for a Variational Functional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines self-adjoint boundary data through a scalar potential for the momenta.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(J[y]=\int_a^b F(x,y,y')\,dx\), let \(p_i=F_{y_i'}\). Boundary conditions \(y'=\psi(y)\) prescribed at \(x=a\) are self-adjoint if there exists a scalar function \(g(x,y)\) such that \(p_i(a,y,\psi(y))=\frac{\partial g}{\partial y_i}(a,y)\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundary conditions y′=ψ(y) at x=a are self-adjoint when the associated momentum vector, evaluated on those conditions, is the y-gradient of a scalar function g at x=a.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists g\;\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:\quad p_i(a,y,\psi(y))=g_{y_i}(a,y).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a field of extremals by pointwise self-adjointness and pairwise consistency with the Euler–Lagrange system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J[y]=\int_a^b F(x,y,y')\,dx\), with momenta \(p_i=F_{y_i'}\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family y′=ψ(x,y) is a field of the functional when it is self-adjoint at every point of the interval and its conditions at every pair of points are mutually consistent along extremals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\forall x\in[a,b],\;y'=\psi(x,y)\text{ is self-adjoint at }x\bigr]\land\bigl[\forall x_1,x_2\in[a,b],\;\text{the corresponding conditions are mutually consistent}\bigr].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differential Characterization of a Field of Extremals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives necessary and sufficient self-adjointness and consistency equations for a variational field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_i(x,y,y')=F_{y_i'}(x,y,y')\) and \(H(x,y,y')=-F(x,y,y')+\sum_{j=1}^n p_j(x,y,y')y_j'\). A family \(y'=\psi(x,y)\) is a field of \(J[y]=\int_a^bF(x,y,y')\,dx\) if and only if, at every point of the field over \(x\in[a,b]\), \[\partial_{y_k}p_i(x,y,\psi(x,y))=\partial_{y_i}p_k(x,y,\psi(x,y))\quad(i,k=1,\ldots,n),\] and \[\partial_xp_i(x,y,\psi(x,y))=-\partial_{y_i}H(x,y,\psi(x,y))\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The family y′=ψ(x,y) is a field exactly when the evaluated momentum Jacobian is symmetric and each momentum satisfies the stated Hamiltonian consistency equation throughout the field.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y'=\psi(x,y)\text{ is a field}\iff\begin{cases}\partial_{y_k}p_i=\partial_{y_i}p_k,&i,k=1,\ldots,n,\\ \partial_xp_i=-\partial_{y_i}H,&i=1,\ldots,n,\end{cases}\quad\text{after evaluation at }y'=\psi(x,y).
